articles.title: 30 rescued after tourist boat sinks off Manicani Island, Guiuan
articles.summary: TACLOBAN CITY — Thirty passengers were rescued after a tourist boat carrying them from mainland Guiuan to Manicani Island in Eastern Samar submerged off Barangay Buenavista on Sunday, Aug. 30, the…

blocks.text: TACLOBAN CITY — Thirty passengers were rescued after a tourist boat carrying them from mainland Guiuan to Manicani Island in Eastern Samar submerged off Barangay Buenavista on Sunday, Aug. 30, the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) reported.

The passengers were rescued by local fisherfolk with assistance from tugboats MTUG Don Antonio Two and MTUG Joshmar III after the passenger motorbanca, identified as MBCA Vemstac 3, began taking in seawater at 10:50 a.m.

The PCG said the boat departed mainland Guiuan at 10:30 a.m. carrying 30 passengers bound for Barangay Buenavista. When it reached waters about 0.76 nautical mile from the shoreline, seawater reportedly entered through the rear portion of the vessel, causing it to gradually take in water before sinking.

Responding personnel from Coast Guard Station (CGS) South Eastern Samar, Coast Guard Sub-Station Guiuan, the Maritime Environmental Protection Unit-Eastern Samar and the Guiuan Municipal Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office arrived at the reported distress area at about 12:50 p.m.
By then, all 30 passengers had been safely brought ashore and had returned to their respective homes. No deaths or injuries were reported.

The PCG and Municipal Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office personnel later conducted surface monitoring in the area for possible oil or other pollutants from the submerged boat. No visible oil was observed on the water, although the vessel was reportedly carrying about 20 liters of diesel fuel.
The PCG also reported that the boat had departed mainland Guiuan without the required clearance from the agency.

An initial inquiry with boat captain and owner Tito Abucejo showed that the vessel was originally registered as RBCA Jalexa Zanicus. The owner had initiated the process of changing its name to MBCA Vemstac, but the change had not yet been approved by the proper authorities.
The 14.5-meter fiberglass-hulled boat was built in 2024, has a gross tonnage of 3.86 and is powered by a Mitsubishi engine.

The PCG advised Abucejo to fully cooperate with the ongoing investigation into the incident, including efforts to determine its cause, identify possible safety deficiencies and recommend measures to prevent similar maritime accidents.
Authorities are still verifying and consolidating the complete names and other details of the 30 passengers, who had already returned to their respective residences following the rescue. /mcm

articles.title: Student dies from ‘heat stroke’ during Agusan intramurals
articles.summary: SAN FRANCISCO, Agusan del Sur — A Grade 10 student died during school intramural activities in Cabadbaran City, Agusan del Norte, allegedly due to heat stroke. In an interview, Vilma Bag-ao said her…

blocks.text: SAN FRANCISCO, Agusan del Sur — A Grade 10 student died during school intramural activities in Cabadbaran City, Agusan del Norte, allegedly due to heat stroke.
In an interview, Vilma Bag-ao said her son, Yusho Steve Bag-ao, a student at Mindanao Institute, was rushed to Cabadbaran District Hospital and declared dead around 4 p.m. on Aug. 26.
Bag-ao said doctors told the family that Yusho had suffered a heat stroke.

She later said his cause of death was ventricular tachyarrhythmia, or an abnormally rapid heart rhythm originating in the heart’s lower chambers, citing a medical abstract from Cabadbaran District Hospital.
Yusho had a congenital heart condition discovered when he was an infant, Bag-ao said. Doctors had previously recommended surgery but told the family it was not urgent.

His death occurred two weeks after extreme heat prompted Cabadbaran City Mayor Judy Chin Amante to suspend face-to-face classes in public schools on Aug. 12. Heat indices across parts of Caraga at the time ranged from 42 to 46 degrees Celsius.

Mindanao Institute also suspended classes because of the heat and advised students to stay hydrated and avoid unsafe heat exposure. The school later scheduled its Intramurals Meet and Buwan ng Wika activities for Aug. 24 to 28.
Bag-ao questioned the timing of the parental consent for her son’s participation in the intramurals.
She said Yusho’s father signed the consent form only after the students had already participated in a parade.
Bag-ao noted that the family has yet to receive a clear account of what happened after Yusho became ill, including whether CPR was performed before he was taken to the hospital.
The mother said she wants a clear explanation of what happened during her son’s final hours and whether adequate precautions were taken during the school activity. /mcm

articles.title: Minor rescued in Ilocos Sur hostage crisis incident
articles.summary: ALILEM, Ilocos Sur — A tense overnight hostage crisis involving a minor ended without bloodshed after police rescued the child and persuaded an armed suspect to surrender following hours of…

blocks.text: ALILEM, Ilocos Sur — A tense overnight hostage crisis involving a minor ended without bloodshed after police rescued the child and persuaded an armed suspect to surrender following hours of negotiations in Barangay Daddaay here.
The minor was safely rescued on Saturday, August 29, but the standoff continued through the night as police negotiators tried to convince the suspect to peacefully lay down his weapons.
Rather than storm the area, responding police officers, assisted by barangay officials and members of the community, maintained negotiations in a bid to prevent further violence.

The suspect finally began surrendering his weapons on Sunday morning, August 30, first handing over a bolo. About an hour later, he surrendered a 10.5-inch kitchen knife, followed by another bladed weapon before eventually giving himself up without anyone being injured.
Ilocos Sur Police Provincial Office director PCol Agosto M. Asuncion said police prioritized saving lives and peacefully ending the confrontation.

“Our duty as protectors encompasses every individual, including those in acute crisis,” Asuncion said. “True operational excellence is defined by restraint, sound judgment, and an unyielding respect for human life.”
Authorities withheld the identities of the suspect and the minor.
Police have yet to disclose what triggered the hostage-taking, how long the child was held, whether the suspect and the victim were related, and what criminal charges the suspect may face.
The incident remains under investigation.

articles.title: Woman dies and 4 hurt as tricycle collided with truck in Quezon
articles.summary: GUMACA, Quezon- A 65-year-old woman who was suffering from a stroke died, and four others were injured on board a tricycle that lost control and collided with a truck loaded with relief goods while…

blocks.text: GUMACA, Quezon- A 65-year-old woman who was suffering from a stroke died, and four others were injured on board a tricycle that lost control and collided with a truck loaded with relief goods while traveling on Maharlika Highway in Barangay Villa Bota, here, Sunday morning.

Police identified the fatality as Maribela Dastas, and the injured were Ronalyn Gimenez, 38; Gennylyn Dimaano, 41; Jayron Gimenez, 18; and Ken Mergenio, 30, the tricycle driver, who is in critical condition, all residents of Brgy. Inaclagan, this town.

The investigation said that at about 10:12 a.m., the truck, which was loaded with 1,700 boxes of DSWD relief goods and driven by Reynaldo Malupa, 49, was traveling in the northbound lane toward Bicol.
Upon reaching a curved portion of the highway, the tricycle driven by Ken Mergenio, 30, was travelling in the opposite lane.
The tricycle driver allegedly lost control of the steering wheel, causing it to encroach into the lane of the truck and collide.
The victims were taken by Kalasag-MDRRMO-Gumaca and the Bureau of Fire Protection to Gumaca District Hospital, where Dastas was declared dead while undergoing treatment.

Further investigation revealed that the driver of the tricycle was allegedly travelling in haste because Dastas, who was on board, was reportedly suffering from a stroke and needed to be immediately taken to the hospital for emergency medical treatment.

Police investigated the incident while the complaint of reckless imprudence resulting in homicide, multiple physical injuries, and property damage was being processed, and the truck was in the temporary custody of the Gumaca police station.

articles.title: Documents leaked by Trump official to bolster a conspiracy show ‘absolutely nothing’
articles.summary:
Inside the US state department, critics are still attacking a shuttered office established to counter foreign propaganda. Now, some of its work is also being resumed

A botched leak of…

blocks.text: A botched leak of purportedly explosive government files to a prominent conservative online personality was supposed to offer proof of what the Trump administration and its allies have long alleged: that a little-known office inside the US state department, created to fight foreign propaganda, had secretly become a tool for domestic censorship.

Two former high-ranking officials at the Global Engagement Center (GEC), a target of Republican ire that lost its funding in 2024 and was disbanded after Donald Trump’s return to office in 2025, say the documents show nothing of the kind.

Instead, they argue, the files are a symptom of a protracted and bitter political fight over an office that spent nearly a decade tracking and countering foreign influence operations, particularly from Russia, China and Iran.

And the state department is now resuming some of this work in other parts of its operation, including plans – laid out in a proposal reviewed by the Guardian – to pay social media influencers across south-east Asia as part of an $11m campaign to counter Chinese propaganda.

Sarah Rogers, the state epartment’s undersecretary for public diplomacy, provided the so-called “GEC files” to Jennica Pounds, a rightwing online data analyst known as DataRepublican – only for Pounds to claim earlier this month she was leaked the documents as part of a bid to “entrap” her.

Rogers, who denied this claim, then published the files herself, claiming officials inside the center “betrayed their stated mission”. The files included a 2022 GEC report on “gendered disinformation”, a flashpoint in the culture wars.

“These guys have consistently misrepresented what the GEC did, and this was a great example of that,” said Daniel Kimmage, who served as the center’s principal deputy coordinator and acting coordinator from its founding in 2017 until its complete dissolution in 2025. His own congressional testimony was included in the leaked files.

Kimmage and Carrie Goux, a Joe Biden appointee and the center’s former acting deputy coordinator, say nothing in the material shows the GEC, whose mandate was explicitly foreign-facing, ever turned its tools on Americans.
“If the smoking gun was a gendered disinformation report, that feels like they came up short,” Goux said. “There seems to be absolutely nothing here.”
Weaponization
The dispute is the latest chapter in a years-long campaign by conservatives to portray the GEC as part of a broader effort by the US government and technology companies to suppress rightwing speech.

Republican congressmen including Michael McCaul, former chair of the House foreign affairs committee, argued in a July 2024 letter that the GEC was “at best indifferent to, and at worst complicit in” stretching the definition of disinformation to “censor” conservative speech in the US.
Trump’s return to the presidency drew this view into the heart of the federal government. The center was abolished in 2025, and what remained of its work scattered across the state department.

Much of that Republican-led campaign centered on how the GEC had funded the Global Disinformation Index (GDI), a UK-based non-profit that rates media outlets by how likely they are to spread disinformation, to help monitor propaganda in Asia. But in 2022 the GDI separately published its own study of the US media market that rated several conservative outlets, including Newsmax, One America News and the New York Post, as high-risk – a finding its critics have cited ever since as evidence that a foreign-facing office had funded a group meddling in domestic politics.
The question raised by the files leaked this month is narrower, however: whether they show the GEC itself ran a domestic censorship operation. Kimmage and Goux insist they do not.

Kimmage said his own congressional testimony, which Rogers included in the leak, had been selectively read. “If you look at the transcript, [the question was], ‘Does GEC take positions on US outlets?’ And I said, ‘No, it didn’t,’” he said.

Rogers “tried to twist that into something that it wasn’t”, according to Kimmage. “For people who talk a lot about weaponization of government, this seems a lot closer to the weaponization of government and psy-opping of the American people than anything that the emails from the Global Engagement Center show.”
‘False’ allegations

Pounds, the rightwing analyst, is not a neutral bystander. Days after the documents were released, she disclosed that she had been quietly working since July as a special government employee for the defense department.

On Friday, Pounds released a database to track US citizens in the Democratic Socialists of America. The Pentagon did not respond when asked whether the database is included in her scope of government work.

Both former senior officials, Kimmage and Goux, draw a sharp line between the accusations made by critics of the GEC and what the center actually did. “We were not ever looking at Americans,” Goux said. “We were looking at the foreign actors and what their [tactics, techniques and procedures] … are doing overseas.”
The GEC “did what its congressional mandate charged it to do, which is to fight foreign [misinformation and] disinformation”, added Kimmage. “This allegation that it’s censoring Americans is false.”

During its almost decade-long existence, the center published eight detailed public reports on Russian and Chinese information operations and ran four major exposures of Russian disinformation campaigns – in Latin America, Africa and Moldova, and on the Kremlin-linked network RT.

Its largest such operation traced a Kremlin-backed effort called the “African Initiative”, which the center said had recruited local journalists, bloggers and public figures to spread conspiracy theories about US-funded health programs across the continent.

In January 2024, the GEC helped broker an international pact on countering foreign state disinformation that eventually drew more than two dozen government signatories, among them Moldova, Spain, Estonia, Poland and Finland – a framework its backers hoped other countries would use to build their own version of the office.

A 2022 inspector general review found the GEC “generally effective” at supporting counter-disinformation programs overall, while flagging weaknesses in its internal controls, contractor oversight and strategic planning. That record was enough to sustain bipartisan support: senators Rob Portman, a Republican, and Chris Murphy, a Democrat, repeatedly pushed to fund and strengthen the center, and its authorization survived multiple renewal fights before House Republicans, increasingly focused on the domestic-speech question, declined to extend it again in 2024.

That mandate cost roughly $61m per year. The GEC employed about 120 people before Congress declined to reauthorize it, letting the office lapse at the end of 2024. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, later folded what remained of its work into a new counter foreign information manipulation and interference office, framing the closure as an end to wasteful, censorious government overreach.
Trust exercise

Now, less than a year after the GEC shut down, a proposal reviewed by the Guardian shows the state department preparing to pay up to 30 online influencers across 11 countries in south-east Asia $2,500 apiece as part of an $11m, multi-year campaign to counter Chinese propaganda.

The project, which would be operated by the US Mission to USEAN, has three parts: a $5m messaging campaign, a $3m program training influencers and journalists to counter Chinese propaganda, and a $3m trip bringing about 180 participants to studios in Washington and Houston “for intensive collaboration, studio production and first-hand engagement with US institutions and creators”.

The proposal’s planning materials describe the ideal recruit as starting from a “welcoming” position of what one document calls the “rejecting-affirming continuum”: someone not yet sold on the US, but not hostile either. As participants move through the accelerator, the materials say, exposure to evidence of US commitment in the region and training in spotting propaganda from China (which has reportedly invested billions of dollars in disinformation efforts globally) is meant to carry them toward the “affirming” end of that scale, publicly backing closer ties with Washington on trade, tech standards and the South China Sea.
The document cited the rightwing analyst and new Pentagon special government employee, Jennica Pounds, the DataRepublican, as an ideal model to seek out in other recruits abroad.

Contacted for comment, the state department declined to directly address questions about the documents released by Rogers, the influencer proposal, the department’s current foreign influence programs and whether other regions are being targeted as well.

A state department official said: “Undersecretary Rogers has been clear that the department will continue to confront censorship, anti-American propaganda and coercive influence directly while demonstrating the enduring advantages of freedom, accountability and open communication.”

Meanwhile, the office of policy, planning and resources for public diplomacy (R/PPR) was separately shopping for commercial help with a similar mission this spring. A government filing from May 2026 shows the R/PPR requesting information from vendors on software that can mine open-source data, map “adversarial propaganda influence networks” and detect deepfakes.
That apparent contradiction is not lost on the GEC’s former staff.
“Are they trying to re-create it? Probably,” Goux said. “But now they’re spending a lot more tax dollars doing that, trying to get contractors to do some of the stuff that we were doing.”

Goux put the broader cost in plainer terms still. “The US has lost their seat at the table to do that, and that’s unfortunate,” she said. “I hope we can gain it back, but we’re losing trust too, and that’s significant.”

articles.title: Negros Oriental illegal gambling crackdown: 6 arrested, 7 cops relieved
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine National Police (PNP) said Sunday that six alleged illegal numbers game collectors were arrested in simultaneous operations across Negros Oriental, leading to the…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine National Police (PNP) said Sunday that six alleged illegal numbers game collectors were arrested in simultaneous operations across Negros Oriental, leading to the relief of seven police officers for failing to curb illegal gambling in their areas.
The arrests were made on Aug. 28 by the Regional Special Operations Group of the Police Regional Office Negros Island Region (PRO NIR) in Ayungon, Tayasan, Sibulan, Pamplona, Bayawan and Guihulngan.
The suspects were allegedly caught soliciting and collecting bets for illegal numbers games, in violation of Republic Act No. 9287, or the Anti-Illegal Numbers Games Law.
Authorities recovered betting slips, improvised receipts, claim stubs, notebooks containing number combinations, marked money and cash believed to be proceeds from the illegal activity.
Under RA No. 9287, anyone found acting as a bettor in an illegal numbers game may face imprisonment ranging from 30 to 90 days.

In a statement on Sunday, the PNP said it will “sustain its intensified campaign against illegal gambling and hold police commanders accountable for failing to address unlawful activities within their jurisdictions.”

“Police leadership demands accountability, and we will not hesitate to impose decisive action when commanders fail to address illegal activities within their areas of responsibility,” said PNP chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr.
The PNP relieved the police chiefs of the six affected areas and the provincial director of the Negros Oriental Police Provincial Office.
Following the provincial police director’s removal, the Deputy Regional Director for Operations of PRO NIR was designated as officer-in-charge.
“Our operations must be backed by firm command responsibility and sustained enforcement,” said Nartatez.
“It is not enough that arrests are being made; every police chief must ensure that there is no room for illegal gambling in their areas of responsibility,” Nartatez added. /mcm

The historic polls are seen as a pivotal moment in the decades-long peace process in a region that was mired in conflict and socioeconomic and political challenges. The upcoming elections are also a test for the Bangsamoro transition and the institutions and systems established in the last seven years.

How will those in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) vote?

Because this is a parliamentary election, they will vote for a regional political party and one district representative. Voters don’t get to choose the BARMM chief minister. Rather, the elected parliament will pick the chief minister.

articles.title: [Inside the Newsroom] Trust and public funds: why and how we obsess over the national budget
articles.summary: There are reasons why 'trust' should never be something you assume when it comes to the people’s money, even if (and maybe, particularly if) they are labelled confidential or intelligence funds

blocks.text: There are reasons why 'trust' should never be something you assume when it comes to the people’s money, even if (and maybe, particularly if) they are labelled confidential or intelligence funds

items: The author reflects on the reliance on 'trust' in handling confidential and intelligence funds, emphasizing the need for skepticism and accountability in government spending.
Historical abuses of confidential funds highlight the importance of checks and balances, as demonstrated by past scandals involving military funds.
Rappler is committed to scrutinizing the budget process and providing transparency through training and accessible data, urging public support to combat corruption.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Ten years ago, when funds allocated to confidential and intelligence expenditures skyrocketed under the Duterte administration, I asked then Budget Secretary Benjamin Diokno for his thoughts on what safeguards should be put in place to prevent potential abuse of these funds.
Diokno’s response then: “We just have to trust him (President Rodrigo Duterte) na mabuting tao siya (that he is a good person),” he said.
I was astounded. Trust? Journalists are trained to be skeptical and suspicious, particularly when it comes to matters that involve power and money.
The word “trust” is also anathema to the checks and balances that is embedded in our system of government.
It therefore felt surreal that — 10 years later — there is that word again: trust.

People reporting to Duterte’s daughter, Vice President Sara Duterte, are saying the same thing before an impeachment court: they trusted Colonel Raymund Lachica, the VP’s chief security officer. They trusted the Vice President.

Hello! I am Gemma Mendoza, head for strategic programs at Rappler. As a journalist, I am particularly obsessed with the budget process. I have been scrutinizing budget, procurement, and audit documents for over two decades now.
There are reasons why “trust” should never be something you assume when it comes to the people’s money, even if (and maybe, particularly if) they are labelled confidential or intelligence funds.
Former heads of the Commission on Audit (COA) have already said that confidential and intelligence funds are difficult to audit.

Prior to that specific interview with Diokno, I co-wrote the book The Enemy Within with Aries Rufo and Glenda Gloria. That book dived deep into how the military top brass abused confidential and intelligence funds allocated to the armed forces and, among other things, diverted these funds to their pabaon retirement system.
A former military general took his own life following congressional investigations into this scandal.
While there are legitimate reasons why certain funds cannot go through the usual processes, the Constitution is explicit about subjecting all kinds of funds to audit.
It says: “No law shall be passed exempting any entity of the Government or its subsidiary in any guise whatever, or any investment of public funds, from the jurisdiction of the Commission on Audit.”
This was precisely why in 2015 the budget department and COA worked with the local government and defense departments to come up with Joint Circular No. 2015-01.

Within each government office, each vote and signature in the budget request, procurement, and liquidation process is supposed to represent checks to misuse. Each signatory is supposed to be responsible. They are not supposed to “trust” each other.

The fact that the confidential funds of Sara Duterte are now at the center of an impeachment trial is a demonstration of how various steps in this process of checks and balances failed the Filipino people. Rappler has reported on this every step of the way.

This is why we require every journalist at Rappler to be familiar with the national budget and the budget process. We remind our reporters that the scrutiny of how public funds are allocated and spent needs to happen at each phase of the process: planning and formulation, approval, implementation, and audit.

Beyond the numbers themselves, everything requires sharp eyes: the logic of the budget, the expected outcomes, the process of fund release up to the point the project funded by said item is marked as completed.

This is not an easy endeavor. Many parts of this process remain opaque, despite various transparency initiatives. And so journalists need to learn not just how the formal and informal processes work, where to get paper trail, and how to read between the lines of each document.
In the past couple of weeks, our team went through another budget refresher sessions for this purpose.

Spotting issues requires the ability to analyze budget data over a period of time. Formats in which data is made available is not always consistent, and so we have been training our journalists in data processing and analysis.

We have gone a step further. On RappLearn, we now have a training module on understanding the budget process, which serves as a supplement to onground training for staff, fellows, and stakeholders. Budget toplines as well as granular budget data are now available and visualized on our website.
If you want to know how much each department received for its staff since 2020, you should be able to see that on our #BudgetWatch page.

Our pages for each department now have the department’s detailed budget. For example, if you want to know if the public high school in your city received funding for internet services, then you may check our topic page for the Department of Education.
All of these require resources. And this is where we need support.
If you have not yet signed up for Rappler Plus, please do so, and please ask your friends to do the same. If you want to give further assistance, please consider donating or volunteering.
Work with us to ensure that every peso spent from the public treasury counts, connects to improvements in the lives of Filipinos, and is not lost to corruption or misuse. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Iceland voters reject EU accession talks
articles.summary: A nationwide referendum failed to win enough support to restart negotiations on European Union membership, despite geopolitical tensions in the North Atlantic.

image.caption: Iceland is already closely linked to the EU as a member of the European Economic Area and the free-movement Schengen zoneImage: Leonhard Foeger/REUTERS

blocks.text: Icelandic voters have rejected a plan to restart accession talks with the European Union, final referendum results showed on Sunday.
The 'No' camp secured victory with 52.8% of the votes, while the 'Yes' camp garnered 47.2% support, the official count published by public broadcaster RUV showed.
The capital, Reykjavik, was the only area in the island nation of 400,000 people to support the referendum.
Some 270,000 Icelanders were eligible to vote. There was no information yet about voter turnout.
Iceland debates joining EU amid Trump's Greenland interest
Neck-and-neck vote after long debate
Iceland has spent the better part of two decades wrestling with the question of becoming the bloc's 28th member.
The Nordic country originally applied to join the EU in 2009 following the global financial crisis, which hit the country particularly hard.
Accession talks were suspended in 2013 after a euroskeptic government took office.

Iceland's current left-leaning government, elected in 2024, originally vowed to hold a vote next year but brought it forward because of rising geopolitical tension over Russia's war in Ukraine and Greenland.
Fishing industry pulled weight
However, the decision puts to bed concerns among many voters that joining the bloc would undermine Iceland's sovereignty, with fishing rights a major concern.
The fisheries sector has been fiercely opposed to joining the bloc, with 90% of industry players against the idea.
The result is a disappointment to Brussels, which had appeared willing to compromise on thorny issues, including fishing and farming, to facilitate Iceland's accession.

articles.title: Definitely no or maybe yes: what tipped the Icelandic referendum | Miranda Bryant
articles.summary:
The no campaign was well-funded and accused of scaremongering, but the wording of the question may also have made a difference

It was always going to be a close contest. But on the night,…

blocks.text: It was always going to be a close contest. But on the night, the figures showed just how divided Iceland was on the issue of whether or not to restart negotiations with the European Union.

After a nail-biting overnight count, the well-funded no campaign rejoiced on Sunday morning as the broadcaster RUV declared it the winner with about 52.8% of the vote. Given the size of Iceland’s population- barely 400,000 – the margins were tiny.

Opponents had criticised the no campaign as fearmongering, its tactics compared by some to those deployed by Brexit activists in the UK’s 2016 referendum. Its depiction of fishing and farming, two issues inextricably tied to Icelandic national identity, as threatened by EU membership were central to its success. Results showed a big split between voters in the capital region and the rest of the largely rural country, where among some there is a sense that national identity is at risk of being forgotten.

But it was perhaps also the question on the ballot paper that, despite the allure of a closer relationship with Europe at a time of global volatility and an erratic US president threatening Iceland’s larger neighbour, Greenland, helped them win the day.
The question Icelanders were asked was “Should Iceland resume accession negotiations with the European Union?” A second referendum would be held once a deal had been reached.

This meant that a vote yes would have actually been a “yes, maybe”, whereas a no vote was always a clearer, more decisive move. One of the “yes, maybe” campaign’s slogans was “Já til að sjá” (“yes to see”), which felt vague in comparison to the bullish claims of the no campaign.

At a bouncing yes campaign party at Reykjavík Art Museum in the Icelandic capital’s downtown area, at a point in the election night where yes seemed to have edged ahead, the yes supporter Þòrir Snoor said: “The no side has done a lot of fearmongering and done it very very well.”

While he had a lot of peers who, like him, thought the euro could be the solution to the country’s high inflation and high interest rates, the 25-year-old added: “A lot of my friends have said they are scared of the European Union.”

Wearing a blue EU cap, Snædis Inga Rúnarsdóttir, 30, agreed that the no campaign had been louder – and better funded. She said she would have to make peace with a potential win by no, but hit out at a swirl of misinformation around the referendum.
after newsletter promotion

Iceland’s foreign minister, Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir, had previously said she feared her country faced a “Brexit moment” amid warnings over the potential influence of misinformation, foreign interference and AI in the referendum. Just before midnight when votes were still being counted, she told the Guardian that whatever the result “at least Icelandic people have shown it was the right thing to have a vote”.
Before being ushered deeper on to the dancefloor, she added: “And what I like the most is now foreign policy is, everything is, on the agenda.”

articles.title: Police slammed over arrest of 11 anti-mining protesters in Nueva Vizcaya; municipal top cop speaks up
articles.summary: Police forces faced sharp criticism following a violent dispersal operation of anti-mining protesters in Kasibu, Nueva Vizcaya that led to the arrest of 11 individuals over the weekend. According to…

blocks.text: Police forces faced sharp criticism following a violent dispersal operation of anti-mining protesters in Kasibu, Nueva Vizcaya that led to the arrest of 11 individuals over the weekend.

According to the provincial government of Nueva Vizcaya, a “tense mining standoff” occurred in Barangay Paquet around 4 p.m. last Friday, Aug. 28, as anti-mining protesters blocked the entry of personnel from the North Luzon Mineral Resources Corporation (NLMRC) in the exploration area located within the village.

Lawyer Fidel Santos, counsel for the anti-mining advocates, said the protesters had formed a barricade to prevent the company personnel from entering the site. Police personnel from the Kasibu Municipal Police Station had arrived in the area to disperse the protesters and remove the barricade, but the commotion turned into a tense confrontation.

Snapshots from viral videos of the confrontation on social media were shared by the provincial government, showing cops pulling several individuals while the protesters were hugging each other to prevent their comrades from being torn away from their community.

Santos said he asked the police to wait for him before the dispersal so he could talk to the protesters and try to mediate the dispute. By the time he arrived, however, police had already begun the operation.
The clash eventually led to the arrest of 11 protesters, two of them reportedly injured during the confrontation.
Police’s side

However, Kasibu police chief Police Capt. Lloyd Guillermo said Nueva Vizcaya Gov. Jose V. Gambito called him as officers responded to a report that protesters were blocking vehicles trying to pass through a municipal road leading to the mining exploration and drilling site.
“The governor called to ask about the situation and instructed us to see how the tension could be eased and to make sure that nobody would get hurt,” Guillermo said.

The Nueva Vizcaya Police Provincial Office (PPO) said the call was made through 911 by a barangay chairman. The official reported that three vehicles carrying fuel and supplies were being blocked at an anti-mining barricade along a public road in Barangay Pacquet.
The provincial police office said the call required an immediate response because of the number of people at the barricade and the possibility that the confrontation could escalate.
Guillermo rejected the allegation that police were accompanying the mining company.
“We deny that this was an escort operation. The PNP cannot simply conduct an escort without the proper request and procedures,” Guillermo said.
“What we did was purely a police response because they have the right to pass through. There is no law preventing them from using a road that has been lm declared a municipal road,” he added.

According to the Nueva Vizcaya PPO, police first tried to settle the situation through dialogue after arriving at the area. Officers asked the protesters to voluntarily clear the road, which the police said had been certified as a public road by the municipal mayor.

The police said the barricade had grown into a human blockade involving about 400 people. Additional personnel, including Civil Disturbance Management contingents, were deployed after the local police force was reinforced.

Police said repeated requests to clear the road were ignored and, as such, the intervention resulted in the arrest of the protesters who were allegedly positioned at the front of the barricade, where the obstruction was strongest. Those arrested included residents from Barangays Pacquet, Dine, and Catarawan, who were brought to Kasibu Municipal Police Station for documentation and appropriate legal proceedings.
The NVPPO said the protesters were arrested for alleged violations of grave coercion and resistance and disobedience to persons in authority and their agents under the Revised Penal Code.
Five police officers also sustained minor injuries during the operation, according to the provincial police office.
Guillermo said the confrontation could have been avoided if the protesters had allowed the vehicles to pass.

“We only responded to a call for assistance. We do not control when these incidents happen. The PNP remains neutral and does not take sides. Whoever needs police assistance, we will respond,” he said.
Aftermath
After the arrests, police, the anti-mining group, and NLMRC personnel held a dialogue with the participation of Kasibu Vice Mayor Alberto “Chito” Bumolo and members of the Sangguniang Bayan.

The talks resulted in a temporary arrangement as the parties agreed to “prevent the company’s personnel, equipment, and supplies from entering the exploration site while negotiations continue,” according to the provincial government.
The Sangguniang Bayan is expected to meet this week with representatives of the anti-mining group and the mining company to work toward a resolution of the dispute.

articles.title: Zambian opposition leader charged with treason
articles.summary: Mundubile had previously gone into hiding at a United Nations building in Zambia's capital.

blocks.text: Zambian opposition leader Brian Mundubile has been charged with treason, his lawyer has said amid heightened political tensions in the country.
Mundubile was arrested on Thursday, after a deadly raid by the authorities led the opposition politician to go into hiding.
He had disputed the results of the country's recent presidential election, which saw incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema securing a second term.
The authorities then accused Mundubile's NRPUP party of planning an armed insurgency, which it denied.

On Saturday night, Mundubile's lawyer Milner Katolo announced that his client had been charged with treason. The opposition leader looks forward to answering the accusation in court, Katolo told the Zambian Eye, external.
The lawyer said 17 others, including Mundubile's running mate Makebi Zulu, had also been charged with treason.
Mundubile gained 38% of the vote in the 13 August election, while Hichilema secured 60%, official results show.
The day after the poll, security forces raided a property in the capital, Lusaka, linked to Mundubile, killing a former cabinet minister and arresting a number of other politicians.
Following the raid, Mundubile and Zulu took refuge at a United Nations building in the city. The pair were detained after the president put pressure on the UN to hand them over.
The opposition was unable to mount a legal challenge to the election outcome as the courts were sealed off by the authorities on Monday, the final day that a case could be filed.
Hichilema is due to be sworn in for a second term on 1 September.

Regional and international observers described the election day as largely peaceful, but Zambia's Human Rights Commission has called for accountability over people whose whereabouts remain unknown following arrests and security operations around the elections.

articles.title: Greece, Turkey clash over protected Aegean marine areas
articles.summary: Turkey has announced the creation of two protected zones in a disputed area of the Aegean Sea, sparking an angry reaction from Greece. Does this mark a new chapter in a long-running dispute between…

image.caption: Turkey recently designated two marine parks in the Aegean Sea and eastern Mediterranean, one off the Greek island of Lemnos (seen here in May 2025)Image: Diogenis Dimitrakopoulos/DW

blocks.text: A stint of unfamiliar calm between Greece and Turkey lasted less than three years.

After a devastating earthquake struck Turkey in February 2023 and Greece provided substantial aid, the two countries came closer together. They then signed the Athens Declaration on Friendly Relations and Good-Neighbourliness in December 2023, a further step to improved relations.

During this unusual time of calm, neither government moved to resolve long-lasting Greek-Turkish disputes, which mostly involve marking maritime boundaries. As a result, even a measure ostensibly aimed at protecting the environment has reignited regional tensions.

The latest dispute was triggered by Turkey's designation of two marine parks in the Aegean Sea and eastern Mediterranean earlier this month. The park in the northeastern Aegean includes a protected area in the waters between the Greek islands of Lemnos and Samothrace. The southern park lies east of Rhodes and surrounds the Greek island of Kastellorizo.
For decades, Greece and Turkey have been at odds over the delineation of their maritime borders in the Aegean and the related economic rights, such as claims to natural resources like oil.

Greece's Foreign Ministry was quick to react to the announcement, calling the establishment of the parks "illegal." In a statement, it said the designation of Turkish marine parks in areas outside Turkey's territorial waters has no legal validity.

Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said at a Cabinet meeting earlier this week that he wanted to maintain good relations with neighboring countries. However, he stressed that "areas under Greek sovereignty are determined by international law" and that Greece is "always ready to defend them."
Competing to protect the Mediterranean?

For its part, Greece also announced two marine parks in 2025 — in the Ionian Islands and the southern Cyclades, both within Greek territorial waters. At the time, Turkey reacted in a clearly worded statement: "Unilateral actions should be avoided in closed or semi-closed seas such as the Aegean and the Mediterranean."

But Turkey has now declared its own marine parks — and without consulting Greece. Environmental protection appears to have been, at most, a secondary concern for the two countries in announcing their respective conservation parks. Instead, the move appears to be a new tactic for asserting dominance in the disputed maritime area — the latest chapter in a decades-long regional spat.
Kastellorizo caught up in Greece-Turkey dispute (09.2020)

Greece believes Turkey sees the marine parks as a way to challenge the sovereignty of Greek islands. It fears the designation of the two parks is part of Turkey's revisionist "Mavi Vatan" doctrine, Turkish for "Blue Homeland."

Under the doctrine, Turkey lays claim to the exclusive economic zones of Greece and Cyprus — maritime areas in which a coastal state has special rights, including over fishing and the exploitation of natural resources. It also challenges the sovereignty of numerous Greek islands and islets.

Until now, the doctrine has largely remained theoretical and strategic in nature. It is now being advanced through legislative initiatives in Turkey's parliament, and Turkey intends to use the parks to formalize its claims to greater control over parts of the Aegean and eastern Mediterranean.
Greece invests in defense

Greece itself is content with the status quo in the Aegean but feels threatened by Turkey, which is significantly better armed. As a result, Greece has invested heavily in fighter jets, frigates, submarines and air defense systems.

After spending significantly less on arms imports for several years, Greece ranked 19th worldwide among the largest importers of major arms from 2021 to 2025, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.

Even as Athens builds new or closer alliances, Turkey is factored into decisions. In 2021, for example, the Greek government sent Patriot air defense missiles to Saudi Arabia, despite objections from the Greek opposition, to protect Saudi oil refineries from Houthi attacks — at a time when Riyadh and Ankara were at odds politically.
During a state visit with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Prime Minister Mitsotakis explicitly referred to Turkey's "destabilizing and counterproductive" role.

blocks.caption: Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis (right, seen here with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in Athens in July 2022), has worked to build closer ties with Saudi ArabiaImage: dDimtiris Papamitsos/Greek Prime Minister's Office/AP/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Relations between Ankara and Riyadh have since improved. In early August, Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed the Mecca Defense Pact, a major joint defense agreement.
An 'Iron Dome' for Greece

With Turkey in mind, Greece has also pursued strategic cooperation with Israel. Despite heavy criticism in Greece over the dire humanitarian situation in Gaza, Mitsotakis continues to maintain close ties with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

The Greek Defense Ministry is planning an air defense shield over the Aegean modeled on Israel's Iron Dome. The project, dubbed the "Achilles Shield," is designed to protect against all conceivable threats — including those from neighboring countries — and is expected to be fully operational by 2029.

For now, Mitsotakis continues to strike a conciliatory tone toward Turkey. But Greece is due to elect a new parliament by spring 2027 at the latest, and Mitsotakis may face growing pressure to take a tougher nationalist stance As the election approaches.

articles.title: India's citizen-led school audits test limits of activism
articles.summary: The student-led "Cockroach" movement is taking its campaign for accountability to government schools, but the activists' methods are encountering growing resistance from authorities.

image.caption: The CJP has said many government schools are in need of improvement Image: Madhan Kumar/DW

blocks.text: The Indian activist movement dubbing itself the "Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)" shot to national prominence in May by leading weeks-long protests over a scandal involving highly competitive entrance exams.
The student-led campaign put the government under intense political pressure and ended with the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan in July.
Now, the CJP is taking aim at India's government schools, organizing volunteer visits to classrooms, documenting conditions and demanding accountability for problems.

Launched on August 15, Independence Day in India, the campaign asks parents, students and volunteers to inspect schools and record basic facilities including toilets, drinking water, electricity, classroom furniture and school buildings. The CJP has said the findings will be used to pressure authorities to make improvements.
The initial target is to audit 100 rural government schools over two months. It has also proposed giving recognition to village leaders who improve their schools.

Unlike the first campaign, which was based on street protests, the school audits require a more sustained form of local activism. Volunteers are expected to work consistently at the local level, document conditions and follow up with officials, parents and communities.

blocks.caption: Students celebrated in New Delhi after the resignation of India's education minister in JulyImage: Raj K Raj/Hindustan Times/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: The organization is dealing with different layers of the Indian administration. Responsibility for government schools is divided between state governments, local administrations and elected village bodies. The CJP is therefore set to tackle different rules and political interests across the country.
India has over a million government schools, according to Education Ministry data. They make up nearly 70% of all schools in the country but serve less than half of its 247 million schoolchildren.
CJP: 'We are not afraid'
That scale has given CJP a vast field for its campaign. But it has also brought a new set of challenges.
The authorities are raising questions regarding rules and locations for the CJP scrutiny, as well as safeguards when children are present.
The response is already varying from state to state. Some authorities have ordered their own inspections, while others have restricted access or taken police action against CJP volunteers.
Authorities in Maharashtra and Rajasthan states have objected to school visits carried out without permission.
In one case, a complaint by school authorities resulted in police action against CJP members after they entered the premises to conduct an audit.

In Rajasthan, restrictions have been imposed on outsiders entering government schools, as well as on filming, interviews and other forms of documentation. CJP volunteers in Rajasthan have also said they were attacked while inspecting a school.
"We are not afraid. We are seeking accountability from the government," said CJP spokesperson Ashutosh Ranka.
Officials say schools are not open spaces

In the state of Uttar Pradesh, Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath has ordered officials to conduct on-the-spot checks of school facilities and directed police to register cases over what he called misleading videos about schools and colleges.
India's 'Cockroach' protesters claim online censorship
The CJP has said such measures undermine public scrutiny. Authorities have said schools are not open spaces for unauthorized inspections, particularly when children are present.
Vinita Gursahani Singh, managing trustee of We, The People campaign, which works on citizen empowerment, said the limits are set by law.

"Under the Right to Information Act, any citizen can inspect schools but you need to submit an application. And that makes sense as there has to be consideration for students and teaching," Singh told DW.
"All public scrutiny is legitimate. It is our job to scrutinize. But the scrutiny has to follow process. It has to be even-handed. What applies to one citizen must apply to all," she said.
Can activists serve as inspectors?
The CJP maintains government schools are publicly funded institutions and citizens have a legitimate right to ask how they are functioning.
Its volunteers use standardized audit forms to record conditions and send their findings to the CJP, which has said it will use the material to press local administrations to respond.

But critics question whether citizen activists can assume the role of inspectors. There are concerns about whether volunteers have the expertise to assess safety or infrastructure problems and how allegations posted on social media are verified.
Mohandas Pai, an education advocate, supports CJP's focus on government schools but disagrees with its methods.
"I like young people taking interest in school education. It's a broken system, and we need reforms," Pai told DW.
But he objected to large groups entering schools and questioning headmasters and children.
"You can't just barge into a school just because you think you are entitled to do it," Pai said, stressing that "children have to have a safe, secure environment."
India's elementary school helping students escape poverty
Pai said the CJP should instead send small teams with permission, collect systematic data, publish regular reports and use the evidence to pressure governments.
CJP spokesperson Saurav Das rejected the argument that the campaign should rely on conventional channels, saying such approaches have failed to bring meaningful change.
Responding to Pai on X, he challenged him to join the next school visit and show the volunteers how it should be done.
Questions of student privacy
The audit campaign has also raised questions about privacy, consent and disruption of teaching when volunteers enter schools, film inside classrooms or question students.
However, Kavita Srivastava, president of the People's Union for Civil Liberties (PUCL) Rajasthan, opposes restrictions on outsiders entering schools and taking photos and videos in her state.

"Activists were visiting government schools to document their condition and demand accountability. Protecting children's privacy should not be used to prevent legitimate public scrutiny of government schools," Srivastava told DW.
A new role for the CJP
Activist Amrita Johri said the CJP's first campaign tapped into a longstanding accountability gap in India's examination system, which cost millions of young people time and money.
"The demand for accountability had popular resonance because there was no real response from the government," Johri told DW.
She backed the school audit campaign, saying public scrutiny should be welcomed.

"Public audits are an integral part of citizens' right to information and should be welcomed as an opportunity to fix accountability," she said. Johri added that the CJP needs to train volunteers, document problems and follow up with authorities to make the campaign effective.

articles.title: Women in UK arts feel they do not have equal opportunities for roles, says report
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Research says sector is fixated with young talent, with most women experiencing unconscious bias or sexism

Women working in the arts believe they do not have equal opportunities…

blocks.text: Women working in the arts believe they do not have equal opportunities for roles, especially as they get older, according to a report saying that the industry is fixated with “young and emerging” talent.

Nearly all (95%) women working in the arts thought gender inequality persisted, while three-quarters (75%) reported experiencing unconscious bias or sexism, according to a survey of 76 arts professionals. More than two-thirds (69%) felt that age negatively affected their career success – a figure that rose to 100% among those working in artistic rather than managerial roles.

The research said that gender discrimination and ageism were being exacerbated by the use of AI in hiring, which can penalise women for taking career breaks for caring responsibilities, or reinforce historical biases.

Many performers highlighted the additional pressure on women to look young relative to men. “Often younger actresses are cast to play opposite men who are older for parts that are supposed to be the same age,” said one actor.

One participant said that casting opportunities “drop off at 39”, while another female actor said: “There are twice as many roles for my male colleagues as there are for me. There are even fewer roles for actresses over 50.”

One respondent highlighted the obsession with words like “young and emerging” to describe talent. “There seems to be absolutely no celebration of experienced, seasoned, insightful, adult, et cetera. It’s always fresh. As if anything that isn’t fresh is mouldy,” she said.
Another said that writers’ schemes tended to favour young people, while many emerging artist initiatives were aimed at young, graduating artists rather than developing later-life-stage artists.

One person working in arts marketing said there was a prevalent idea that only young people truly understood the online world, while a writer felt that the stories of older women were seldom commissioned.

blocks.caption: Maureen Beattie cited the ‘waste of the great talent and life knowledge and technical skill older women bring to the table’. Photograph: Sarah Lee/The Guardian

blocks.text: The theatre and TV actor Maureen Beattie, who starred in Casualty and was a member of the Royal Shakespeare Company, said: “So, we have proof at last that age discrimination is one of the major issues women face in the entertainment industry. Are we surprised? I’m certainly not. I’m one of the lucky ones who have slipped through this particular net and at the ripe old age of 72 have just come back from playing Lear in Pitlochry.

“We need far more of these great big meaty roles for women so that the current waste of the great talent and life knowledge and technical skill older women bring to the table doesn’t go on disappearing into the night.”

Dr Jennifer Tuckett, the chief executive of the support group Women in the Arts, who authored the report, said: “The findings regarding age discrimination against older women in the arts, and the potential for AI to increase issues for older women in the arts, are particularly worrying.
after newsletter promotion

“Researchers are just starting to look at this area of AI and it is urgent we investigate this issue more – research has shown older women stand to be disadvantaged during any recruitment processes which use AI.”

The findings are from a survey undertaken as part of a five-year research project by Women in the Arts, run in partnership with the Writers’ Guild of Great Britain, Equity, WOW, Sphinx Theatre, ERA 50:50 and the Women in Theatre Lab. It is funded by Arts Council England and intended to feed into a taskforce addressing the needs of women in the cultural sector.

An Arts Council England spokesperson said the group would “consider the challenges women face around issues such as glass ceilings, harassment and caring responsibilities”, with a view to identifying good practice and interventions that support women at work.

The report called for more targeted work to address gender discrimination, including more funding to address the problem, representation targets – potentially mirroring those in Australia, where these are required in funding applications – and leadership programmes, as well as algorithmic audits to minimise bias.
The research will also be handed to ministers on 12 October as part of a campaign to establish an all-party parliamentary group on women in the arts.

The project is part of the local government unit’s (LGU’s) efforts to improve incident reporting and facilitate a quicker response from concerned authorities.
Through the SOS BML Community App, residents can report fires, crimes, accidents, violence, disasters, and other emergencies occurring within the city.

The application also allows residents to report concerns that may not necessarily require a traditional emergency response, including emergencies involving senior citizens and persons with disabilities (PWDs), garbage problems, road obstructions, fallen utility posts, and dangling electrical and telephone wires.

blocks.caption: Carmona LGU launches a mobile app called Safety Order and Service: Bayan Muna Lagi Community App at the City of Carmona Operations Center on Aug. 28, 2026 (Photos from Mayor Dahlia A. Loyola/Facebook)

Carmona LGU launches a mobile app called Safety Order and Service: Bayan Muna Lagi Community App at the City of Carmona Operations Center on Aug. 28, 2026 (Photos from Mayor Dahlia A. Loyola/Facebook)

blocks.text: Residents may likewise use the app to report disturbances caused by unruly or intoxicated neighbors, videoke-related complaints, and other community concerns.
Carmona City Mayor Dahlia A. Loyola said the initiative gives residents an opportunity to take an active role in maintaining a safe, inclusive, and resilient community.
Aside from its reporting functions, the app also provides announcements and updates from the city government, including information on weather and traffic conditions.
It also features a lost-and-found section, providing residents with another channel to report or locate missing belongings.

articles.title: Barbers calls for longer hours for Duterte impeachment trial
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Senate Impeachment Court should consider extending the hours or adding days to Vice President Sara Duterte’s trial to hasten the proceedings, the prosecution panel’s…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Senate Impeachment Court should consider extending the hours or adding days to Vice President Sara Duterte’s trial to hasten the proceedings, the prosecution panel’s adviser Robert Ace Barbers said over the weekend.
Barbers said the public may be growing weary of the trial, now on its 19th day, and showing signs of impatience.
“We’re getting impatient too,” he said in Filipino at a Saturday media briefing. “If we could increase the trial hours and trial days, that would be much better.”

He also said holding Duterte’s trial in the afternoon may be more conducive to the proceedings, recommending that senators hold their plenary session in the morning to act on their legislative agenda.
The trial is expected to last 92 days
“The public is getting impatient, especially when discussions turn technical or legal,” Barbers said. “Even those who understand sometimes find it hard to keep up with the length and duration.” /mcm

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Quezon City Veterinary Department (QCVD) rescued seven dogs from a flooded area in Barangay Fairview amid heavy rains brought by the southwest monsoon on Saturday evening, Aug. 29.
The QCVD said it received reports of seven dogs needing rescue at 12 Mahogany Street, Sapamanai, in Barangay Fairview.
“The seven dogs were safely rescued and brought to the care of the Quezon City Veterinary Department for proper assessment and monitoring,” the QCVD said in a Facebook post.
Many areas in Quezon City have been flooded due to heavy habagat rains since Saturday.
In a separate Facebook post, the Quezon City government shared photos of pet animals seeking temporary shelter at a Pet Evacuation Center.
“The Quezon City Veterinary Department and barangay officials are still looking after the pets of residents who evacuated from Barangay Silangan and Bagong Pag-asa,” the city government said. /mcm

blocks.text: BAGUIO CITY — Several roads in Benguet remained closed on Sunday, Aug. 30, due to landslides and strong water currents triggered by heavy rainfall, according to authorities.
The Halsema-Madaymen-Ampusungan Provincial Road was declared impassable after a landslide deposited debris at the entrance to the Pakpakitan-Taliboy-oc-Lamut Road.
The Tabbak section of the Gov. Bado Dangwa National Road was also closed to traffic due to an ongoing rockslide.

Meanwhile, motorists using the Tokok-Ambalideng-Poblacion section of the Gov. Bado Dangwa National Road were advised to proceed with extreme caution as strong water currents continued to affect the area.

articles.title: Body of last missing victim in Mapanuepe Lake tragedy recovered
articles.summary: SAN MARCELINO, Zambales — The last missing victim in the Aug. 27 drowning incident at Mapanuepe Lake in Barangay Buhawen, San Marcelino, Zambales was successfully retrieved Sunday morning,…

blocks.text: LAST VICTIM RETRIEVED — Authorities recover the remains of the last missing victim, a pregnant woman, from Mapanuepe Lake in San Marcelino, Zambales, on Aug. 30. (Photo Zambales PPO via Liezle Inigo)

SAN MARCELINO, Zambales — The last missing victim in the Aug. 27 drowning incident at Mapanuepe Lake in Barangay Buhawen, San Marcelino, Zambales was successfully retrieved Sunday morning, authorities said. She was reportedly pregnant.

The retrieval was completed at about 11:20 a.m. on Aug. 30 through the coordinated efforts of the Incident Management Team (IMT), according to P Col. Benjamin Ariola, provincial director of the Zambales Police Provincial Office.

The recovered victim was identified by her relative, Anna Liwanag, as Arlene Liwanag, who was reported to be pregnant. Her remains were subsequently brought to Fama Funeral Services for proper disposition.

The operation involved personnel from the San Marcelino Municipal Police Station, Philippine Coast Guard, Bureau of Fire Protection (BFP), 2nd PMFC, San Marcelino Municipal Disaster Reduction and Risk Management Office (MDRRMO), and the Philippine Army’s 69th Infantry Battalion.
Authorities said the retrieval marked the completion of the search, rescue, and retrieval operation for the remaining missing victim in the lake.
The incident earlier resulted in the recovery of two other bodies, with authorities continuing efforts to assist the victims’ families.

articles.title: 32 dead, 8.1 million affected by recent storms, habagat
articles.summary: More than 8.1 million people have been affected by Tropical Cyclones Luis, Maymay and Neneng and the enhanced habagat.

blocks.text: Manila City Department of Social Welfare Director Jay R. Dela Fuente leads the distribution of relief goods and food to 150 families staying at the Baseco Evacuation Center after being evacuated during the southwest monsoon on Aug. 30, 2026.
The STAR / Edd Gumban

MANILA, Philippines — More than 8.1 million people have been affected by Tropical Cyclones Luis, Maymay and Neneng and the enhanced southwest monsoon, or habagat, across 10 regions, the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council said Sunday.

In its Aug. 30 situation report, the NDRRMC said around 2.3 million families, or 8.1 million individuals, were affected across the Ilocos Region, Cagayan Valley, Central Luzon, Bicol Region, Western Visayas, Zamboanga Peninsula, Calabarzon, Mimaropa, the Cordillera Administrative Region and Metro Manila.
Some 43,500 people from 13,500 families were staying in 523 evacuation centers.
The NDRRMC also reported 32 deaths, three missing persons and 19 injuries.
The following are reported deaths, according to the NDRRMC:

items: Benguet (15): Baguio City reported 10 landslide-related deaths, Atok recorded 3, and La Trinidad reported 2.
Batangas (4): Drowning deaths occurred in Batangas City and Mabini, alongside a landslide fatality in Santa Teresita and an electrocution in Lipa.
Rizal (4): Two died from a rockslide in Rodriguez, one from a fallen tree in Antipolo, and one from drowning in Binangonan.
Occidental Mindoro (2): Two fatalities were reported in Rizal due to electrocution and drowning.
Quezon (1): Drowning deaths were reported in Candelaria and Sariaya.
La Union, Oriental Mindoro, and Negros Occidental: One drowning/storm fatality each in Luna, Puerto Galera, and Cadiz, respectively.

blocks.text: P8.48-billion in damage. Infrastructure damage has reached P6.16 billion, while agricultural losses were estimated at P2.32 billion.
The NDRRMC also reported around 3,200 damaged houses, including 355 that were destroyed and about 2,800 that were partially damaged.
A total of 117 local government units have declared a state of calamity, including province-wide declarations in Benguet, Bataan, Bulacan, Pampanga, Zambales and Cavite.
Government agencies and local governments have so far distributed P1.69 billion in humanitarian assistance to affected communities.

articles.title: Jenny Barzaga wins Cavite 4th District special election
articles.summary: CAVITE – Dasmariñas City Mayor Jennifer “Jenny” Austria-Barzaga won the special election for representative of Cavite’s 4th District, securing the congressional seat vacated by her son, former Rep.…

blocks.text: CAVITE – Dasmariñas City Mayor Jennifer “Jenny” Austria-Barzaga won the special election for representative of Cavite’s 4th District, securing the congressional seat vacated by her son, former Rep. Francisco “Kiko” Barzaga Jr.
Comelec proclaims Jenny Austria-Barzaga as the winner of the special election on Aug. 29, 2026 (Screengrab from Comelec)
The Commission on Elections (Comelec) proclaimed Jenny as the winner of the special election on Saturday, Aug. 29, after garnering 201,893 votes.
Former Dasmariñas Vice Mayor Raul Rex Mangubat placed second with 30,373 votes, followed by former councilor Jacinto Frani Jr. with 24,350.
The two other candidates, Marvin Dupal-ag and Leysander Ordenes, received 1,184 and 561 votes, respectively.

The Comelec recorded a 57.75 percent voter turnout, with 258,361 registered voters casting their ballots despite heavy rains brought by the southwest monsoon. Voting hours were extended to 5 p.m. to give more residents a chance to vote amid the rains.

blocks.caption: Jenny Austria-Barzaga casts her vote during the special election for representative of Cavite’s 4th District (Photo from Jenny Barzaga/Facebook)

blocks.text: Jenny Austria-Barzaga casts her vote during the special election for representative of Cavite’s 4th District (Photo from Jenny Barzaga/Facebook)

The special election was conducted to fill the vacancy left by Kiko Barzaga, who was expelled from the House of Representatives over disorderly behavior, conduct unbecoming of a member, and violations of the House’s Code of Conduct.
As Jenny assumes the congressional seat vacated by Kiko, her other son, Vice Mayor Elpidio “Third” Barzaga III, will succeed her as mayor.

articles.title: Iceland appears to have rejected EU accession talks in referendum, reports say
articles.summary:
The no camp looks to have prevailed, holding 52.5% of votes with only a few left to be counted, says public broadcaster

Iceland appears to have ⁠rejected ⁠the government’s proposal ​to hold…

blocks.text: Iceland appears to have ⁠rejected ⁠the government’s proposal ​to hold ⁠accession talks with ⁠the ​EU, ‌the public ‌broadcaster RUV has ‌reported, with only a small ‌number of votes ​left to count.

The no camp had 52.5% of votes and the yes camp 47.5%, with only a few ballots left to be counted in one of Iceland’s six voting districts, which was already leaning towards no, online ballot counting on RUV showed on Sunday.
“The nation rejects accession negotiations with the EU,” RUV wrote.

Barring a major last-minute turnaround, the result deals a blow to Brussels, which had been keen to welcome a wealthy new member and appeared willing to compromise with Iceland on thorny issues to facilitate its accession.

The ‌government in Reykjavik had framed its membership plan as a “now or never” moment, and the prime ‌minister, Kristrún Frostadóttir, told voters in August that a no would put all EU speculation aside.

Yes campaigners said joining the bloc could ease high interest rates and offer more security in a world unsettled by war in Ukraine and the US president, Donald Trump’s rhetoric about annexing another Arctic island, Greenland.
But campaigners for no ‌said EU membership would threaten the island’s sovereignty and fishing waters.
The referendum campaign has fuelled debate about Iceland’s place in the world, ​Kristrun told reporters after casting her ballot in the capital on Saturday.
“This is a great day. We’ve been waiting for this for years to be able to have a vote,” she said, adding that her government would continue ⁠its work regardless of the outcome.
Iceland first applied to join the ​EU in 2009 ​when a financial crisis hit the ​country’s small, exposed economy. A Eurosceptic government ended talks in 2013.
Geopolitical ​turmoil including war ‌in the ​Middle East and US ​import tariffs has brought urgency to an issue Icelanders have debated on and off for decades.

items: Reuters and Agence France-Presse contributed to this story.

articles.title: JV Ejercito: 'Secret funds' should go only to law enforcement, security agencies
articles.summary: Senate Finance Committee chairperson Senator JV Ejercito said Sunday that under the proposed 2027 national budget, confidential and intelligence funds should only be allocated to agencies tasked with…

blocks.text: Published August 30, 2026 4:17pm

Senate Finance Committee chairperson Senator JV Ejercito said Sunday that under the proposed 2027 national budget, confidential and intelligence funds should only be allocated to agencies tasked with law enforcement, intelligence, and national security.
“Confidential and intelligence funds should be limited to agencies whose mandate is law enforcement, intelligence, and national security,” Ejercito told Super Radyo dzBB.
““Confidential funds do not mean they are unaccountable. Just because they are classified as confidential does not mean they should no longer be subject to accountability,” he added.

Under Joint Circular No. 2015-01, confidential funds (CF) refer to lump-sum amounts allocated to national government agencies (NGAs) for “surveillance activities in civilian government agencies intended to support the agency’s mandate or operations.”

Meanwhile, intelligence funds (IF) refer to lump-sum amounts provided to NGAs for “intelligence information gathering activities of uniformed and military personnel, and Intelligence Practitioners that have a direct impact on national security.”
Lawmakers are now scrutinizing confidential and intelligence funds more closely amid the ongoing impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.
Duterte is currently facing an impeachment trial on allegations of culpable violation of the Constitution, betrayal of public trust, graft and corruption, and other high crimes.
Article 1 of the impeachment complaint accuses Duterte of committing impeachable offenses through the “systematic misappropriation and irregular liquidation” of confidential funds.
These include P500 million released to the Office of the Vice President and P112.5 million released to the Department of Education during her tenure as education secretary.
As the trial enters its seventh week, Ejercito said the public should wait for the impeachment court’s decision on whether the trial will return to an afternoon schedule.

The House prosecution team earlier said it favored starting Duterte’s impeachment trial at 3 p.m. onwards, while the Vice President’s defense team said it would comply with any schedule changes implemented by the impeachment court.
However, Senate impeachment court spokesperson Reginald Tongol said the public should focus more on the evidence presented in the impeachment trial rather than changes to its schedule.
“What the public should be talking more about is the evidence being presented and the legal theories of both sides,” Tongol said.— MCG, GMA News
