articles.title: Ejercito: Senate finance panel to observe sub judice rule in tackling 2027 national budget
articles.summary: The Senate Finance Committee will not allow the upcoming hearings on the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for 2027 as a venue to discuss the merits of Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment…

blocks.text: The Senate Finance Committee will not allow the upcoming hearings on the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for 2027 as a venue to discuss the merits of Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial.

Sen. Joseph Victor “JV” Ejercito, chairman of the Senate finance panel, said the committee will observe the sub judice rule adopted by the Senate Impeachment Court, or Rule 18 of the Rules of Impeachment, which governs public statements concerning the merits of a pending impeachment case.

Based on the ruling of Sen. Francis “Chiz” Escudero, Presiding Officer of the Impeachment Court, those covered by the sub judice ruling includes Duterte, her lawyers in the defense team, members of the House prosecution panel, and senator-judges.

“The impeachment trial is ongoing so we need to respect the sub judice rule, especially with the recent ruling of the Presiding Officer of the Impeachment Court,” Ejercito said in an interview over Radio DZBB.

“We need to respect the sub judice rule. We will not use the budget hearings to discuss the factual issues and evidences that are part of the impeachment case. I’m sorry, but our Presiding Officer made a ruling recently and we have to respect that,” he reiterated.

Ejercito made this clarification when asked about the necessity of waiting for the Commission on Audit (COA) to release its final ruling on the allegation that Duterte has misused her confidential funds.

The COA has yet to issue a final decision on its findings on Duterte’s alleged misuse of the confidential funds of the Office of the Vice President (OVP) and the Department of Education (DepEd) which she previously headed.
But Ejercito said what he finds necessary for lawmakers to discuss in the upcoming budget deliberations is how to safeguard the use of confidential and intelligence funds (CIFs) moving forward.

“What’s important now, is not just to revisit the issues that happened in the past. But we also have to ask now, how do we safeguard the funds? How can we make sure that every confidential fund is properly authorized, properly used and properly accounted for?” he pointed out.
Under his watch, the Senate finance committee chief said he will make sure that only agencies whose mandate is law enforcement, intelligence and national security will be entitled to CIFs.

“In order to eliminate the controversy, as chairman of finance, this is what my policy will be: It (CIFs) will be limited to agencies with mandate or law enforcement, intelligence, and national security,” Ejercito said.

“While we respect the need for confidentiality where national security and legitimate operations are concerned, it is part of the duty of government to protect the public from any security risk,” he said.
Ejercito said he strongly believes public funds require accountability, and “it is part of our mandate in government to act as responsible stewards of tax revenue.”
“A confidential fund does not imply a lack of accountability. Just because a fund is classified as confidential does not mean it is exempt from accountability,” he pointed out.
“We must, therefore, strike a balance between the two—security and accountability, or the responsible use of these funds. We need to find that balance,” he stressed.

articles.title: Pet owners at risk of being ripped off by private equity firms as vet ownership rules change
articles.summary:
Critics say changes by CMA will allow multinationals to obscure their ownership of vet practices

Pet owners have been warned that they could be unknowingly ripped off by private equity firms…

blocks.text: Pet owners have been warned that they could be unknowingly ripped off by private equity firms who have bought local vet clinics, after the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) removed requirements for multinational companies to disclose which practices they own.

The CMA recently ran an investigation into the monopolisation of vet practices, and found that the lack of competition and transparency of ownership had led to high prices and a lack of information for customers. Pet owners were often unaware their local vet practice could be owned by an international private equity company.
It revealed pet owners pay 16.6% more on average at large vet groups than at independent practices. It said the £6.3bn market was not fit for purpose and needed to be modernised.

blocks.caption: More than 60% of veterinary practices are owned in whole or in part by six groups. Photograph: Monty Rakusen/Getty Images

blocks.text: As a result, the CMA and ministers announced new rules in a white paper earlier this summer proposing capping prescriptions for pet medicine at £21 and more transparency over ownership.

But the Progressive Veterinary Association (PVA), made up of a group of vets, has threatened the government body with a judicial review, after the CMA changed the wording in its plans in a way the PVA says allows multinational companies to obscure their ownership of vet practices.

More than 60% of veterinary practices are owned in whole or in part by six groups: CVS, Pets at Home, Medivet, IVC and VetPartners, which are owned by private equity investors; and Linnaeus, whose parent company is Mars Petcare, a subsidiary of the US confectionery group Mars.

Rather than the name of one of the large multinational companies or private equity investors being listed as the owner of the vet practice, the new rules will allow corporates to use a brand name, or the name of the original independent practice.

The initial wording of the orders from the CMA said that vets had to disclose their ownership and name the “corporate vet group”. This language has been softened to “network or group”, meaning the name of the vet practice or subsidiary of the company could be named, instead of the large conglomerate.

blocks.caption: Vets argue that pet owners have the right to know if their local veterinary practice is owned by a large conglomerate. Photograph: Catherine Falls Commercial/Getty Images

blocks.text: Dr Iain McGill, a director of the PVA, told the Guardian: “This is bad news for pet-owners and their animals. Ultimately, large corporations would be allowed to hide the fact that they are the ultimate controller of local vet practices and operate behind sometimes misleading brand names.

“Where they have a choice, pet owners often prefer independent practices, which the CMA found, on average, to be cheaper than corporate practices. It would be good to hear from prime minister Andy Burnham that he is on the side of small British-owned businesses rather than often foreign private equity and corporate investors.”

The CMA told vets who complained that the disclosure of the ultimate parent company names might not be of any meaningful benefit to pet owners. They added that these names can be unrecognisable corporate names and that pet owners are more familiar with the high street vet or pet company names.
But the vets argued that pet owners have the right to know if their local vet was owned by a large conglomerate.

The PVA said in its submission to the government regulator: “The suggestion that accurate corporate ownership information may provide no meaningful benefit to pet owners perhaps rather underestimates the intelligence of the average pet owner. Knowing full ownership information is necessary so that pet owners can make an informed choice. Lack of informed market choices is likely to lead to less competition and pet owner detriment.”

A CMA spokesperson said: “It is critical that pet owners know whether their local practice is part of a national group or locally owned, and we are confident the changes we are making will achieve this. In future, all practices will have to make ownership links clear by using brand names that people recognise on signs and online. We will no longer have the unacceptable situation of people thinking they are using a local practice when in fact it is part of a bigger group.

“We consulted extensively on this. Our proposals were supported by large and small vet practices and consumer groups, and we made our decision on this in our final report in March. We’re now considering comments on exactly how the changes should be put in place, to make sure they are clear and workable for pet owners and vets.”

articles.title: S. Korea: COVID-19 surges; masks, test kits return to shopping lists
articles.summary: SEOUL — As COVID-19 infections begin to climb in South Korea, pandemic-era shopping habits are making a comeback, with people once again reaching for masks and self-test kits. All three major…

blocks.text: SEOUL — As COVID-19 infections begin to climb in South Korea, pandemic-era shopping habits are making a comeback, with people once again reaching for masks and self-test kits.
All three major convenience store chains — 7-Eleven, GS25 and CU — have seen a sharp rise in sales of related products over the past month, according to news reports Friday.

Sales of COVID-19 self-test kits at 7-Eleven, for example, recorded a 62 percent on-month rise from Aug. 1-26, while those of masks, cold medicine and fever and pain relievers rose 17 percent, 15 percent and 14 percent, respectively, data showed.

blocks.caption: Masks sit on sale at a GS25 convenience store in Seoul. (Yonhap)

blocks.text: GS25 also reported a 30.3 percent increase in test kits and a 10.3 percent gain in cold medicine over the same period. Demand was particularly strong for masks for children and infants, with sales more than quadrupling from the previous month, up 341 percent, officials said.
CU saw a similar trend from Aug. 1-23, with sales of test kits and cold medicine up 45.7 percent and 12.2 percent, respectively, from the same period a month earlier.

“Since mid-August, we’ve been asking parents to send their children to day care with masks after a series of cold-like illnesses accompanied by high fevers among 1- and 2-year-olds,” Hwang Ji-mi, a teacher at a day care center in Dongjak-gu, Seoul, told The Korea Herald.
Industry sources say the recent uptick in COVID-19 infections is bringing back the shopping habits that became commonplace during the pandemic.
The country’s COVID-19 detection rate reached 9.1 percent for Aug. 9-15, roughly 2.8 times the 3.2 percent recorded three weeks earlier, according to the Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency.
The number of patients hospitalized with COVID-19 at general hospitals also rose 2.4-fold over the same period.
Cases are also on the rise in China, with about 522,000 new COVID-19 cases reported in July, including 487 severe cases and one death, according to local media reports.

“With schools back in session, we expect demand for test kits, masks and cold medicine to remain strong for a while. The change of seasons is also likely to give sales a further boost,” a GS25 official said. /dl

articles.title: 3-year-old boy swept away by floods in Olongapo found dead
articles.summary: OLONGAPO CITY — A three-year-old boy who was swept away by rushing floodwaters in Barangay Old Cabalan in this city was found dead along the boardwalk area inside the Subic Bay Freeport on Sunday…

blocks.text: OLONGAPO CITY — A three-year-old boy who was swept away by rushing floodwaters in Barangay Old Cabalan in this city was found dead along the boardwalk area inside the Subic Bay Freeport on Sunday afternoon, Aug. 30.

Jeffrey Lapid, head of the Olongapo City Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (CDRRMO), said the boy was found at 2:15 p.m. after some children spotted his body at the boardwalk and immediately reported it to authorities.
The boy went missing on Aug. 29 after floodwaters entered his family’s home in Villa Meranda, Old Cabalan Forestry.
Lapid said the child was with his parents when a wall above their house suddenly collapsed, sending a strong rush of water toward the home.
The impact caused the parents to lose their grip on the boy, who was swept away by the floodwaters.
The discovery of the boy’s body ended the search that had continued since Saturday. /mcm

articles.title: N. Korea names new defense minister amid modernization drive
articles.summary: North Korea has replaced its defense minister in a reshuffle of senior military leadership, state media reported Sunday, as the country accelerates its military modernization push and tightens…

blocks.text: North Korea has replaced its defense minister in a reshuffle of senior military leadership, state media reported Sunday, as the country accelerates its military modernization push and tightens discipline within the ranks.

Kim Song-gi, director of the General Political Bureau of the North’s Korean People’s Army, was appointed as the country’s new defense minister, replacing No Kwang-chol, according to the North’s Korean Central News Agency.
No was removed as defense minister and from the party’s central leadership and appointed first vice-director of the Munitions Industry Department of the ruling Workers’ Party of Korea.
The reshuffle was decided at the second meeting of the ninth WPK Central Military Commission held the previous day, which was guided by leader Kim Jong-un, the report said.

In the latest reshuffle, veteran military official Pak Jong-chon was appointed vice-chairman of the WPK Central Military Commission after being re-elected as a member of the party’s Central Committee and Politburo.

Pak returned to the forefront of the North’s military leadership after stepping down from the Politburo and party secretary posts and being dropped from the Central Military Commission’s vice chairmanship in February. His removal at the time sparked speculation that he was stepping back from the front lines due to his age.
The vice chairmanship is a key post overseeing the North’s military policies. Leader Kim Jong-un chairs the commission.
The meeting “discussed a series of structural reorganization plans for the improvement and development of the future overall defense affairs,” the KCNA said.

The newly appointed commanders would “firmly arm themselves with the party’s idea of building a strong army” and implement the party’s military policies with “boundless devotion and extraordinarily high activity,” the report said.

In a separate dispatch, KCNA reported that Kim met with scientists, researchers and officials from major defense research institutions and awarded them state commendations for their contributions to developing new combat weapon systems and improving their performance.

Calling them “the greatest patriots and heroes,” Kim highly appreciated “the recent exclusive innovative military sci-tech achievements … as a great revolution that opened up a sure prospect for radically improving the modernity of our army’s combat weapon systems.”
The leader expressed expectation that the science researchers “would bolster up the arms of the self-defensive power in a more overwhelming and stronger manner,” the report said. (Yonhap) /dl

articles.title: Family in Batangas persists to keep a generations-old pottery tradition alive
articles.summary: In San Juan, Batangas, a family continues to fight to preserve an inherited pottery tradition

blocks.text: BATANGAS, Philippines – A century-old pottery tradition in San Juan, Batangas, faces the risk of fading into memory.
In Barangay Palahanan, however, one family remains steadfast, determined to keep this heritage alive despite the challenges of changing times.
While they continue to shape earthenware by hand in makeshift workshops on sunny days, their production is frequently disrupted by the monsoon season.
Lacking kilns, the potters rely entirely on sunlight to dry their clay, making prolonged rainfall a significant threat to their livelihood.
This struggle is further compounded by the rise of mass-produced ceramics, which offer cheaper and faster alternatives to their traditional craft.
The culture already existed even before Cresencia Panaligan-Ilao, 96, the oldest potter in Barangay Palahanan, was born.
“I started making pottery back when I was 12 years old. Before that, my mother taught me to do this,” Ilao said.
Palayukan, the pottery culture in San Juan, Batangas, took root as a communal livelihood during the Japanese Occupation but bloomed as commercial work in the late 1950s.
Before making the earthenware, potters harvest luad (clay) from nearby riverbanks, grinding it down by foot or with electric grinders before kneading it with water into a smooth, workable dough.

Artisans use the traditional paikot method where they spin the clay on a labbi-an, a potter’s wheel made of rock, using delicate hand pressure without relying on electricity. They shape the vessel with the aid of a traditional wooden beater called pamalo. After forming the base of the pots, the potters form the mouth of the earthenware.

blocks.caption: AN ARTISAN’S WORKSHOP. The humble workspace of a potter in Barangay Palahanan, San Juan, Batangas, tells the story of a living tradition.

blocks.text: The newly shaped wet pots are air-dried under the sun to remove the initial moisture and harden the structure since the artisans do not own a pugon (kiln). The craft was passed down from mother to daughter, and sometimes the skills were inherited by a daughter-in-law if there was no one else to receive them.
The passing of tradition was not the biggest problem, Ilao emphasized. “It was the fact that the money we earn in doing this is not enough.”

In a study by the University of the Philippines Los Baños, pottery sales in San Juan declined significantly when the pandemic struck in 2020. Since then, the financial challenges have become more severe as customer demand continues to decrease.
Despite these dwindling returns, it is Cresencia’s daughter-in-law, Lutgarda Cueto-Ilao, 76, who continues to shoulder the family’s pottery tradition.

blocks.caption: A DAUGHTER’S PROMISE. Lutgarda Cueto-Ilao handcrafted a clay pot using traditional pottery techniques as a vow to keep the legacy that her late mother gifted.

blocks.text: Since Cresencia stopped making pots as a livelihood two years ago due to old age, Lutgarda is now the only elder who creates handmade pots in Barangay Palahanan.
“I wake up at 8 am to start making pots,” Lutgarda said.
Due to the extensive process, it takes four to five hours to create a fully finished handmade earthenware.
“Our craftsmanship is our pride,” she added, “but we sell our raw pots for a very cheap price to retailers.”
“Carrying this tradition also means carrying the burden that comes along with it,” Lutgarda said. “Because this craft is something special to us, but also because this is the only way we survive.”
“The small ones are sold for P30, the medium ones are sold for P50, and the larger ones are sold for P80 to P100,” she added.

With an initial capital of P1,500, a significant amount goes toward paying three workers who collect the clay, each earning P300. Another P300 was spent on 50 sacks at P6 each, while the remaining P300 goes to renting a jeep to transport the clay. By the time the clay reaches the workshop, the entire capital has already been spent.
“We tried asking for a raise when we sell the pots, but the retailers won’t buy our products because they said it is too expensive,” Lutgarda said.
In the market, however, retailers who bake the raw pots in kilns sell the finished earthenware for a much higher price.
For the next generation, keeping the tradition alive may require more than simply continuing the old ways.
Monique Ilao-Alvarez, 26, Cresencia’s great-granddaughter, has begun using social media to promote the family’s pottery.
“I started using social media as a marketing tool to promote our traditional craft,” Alvarez said.

For generations, the family’s products were promoted largely through word of mouth and local retailers. Alvarez believes that approach is no longer enough as customers increasingly discover and purchase products through digital platforms.
By promoting their earthenware online, the family hopes to reach customers outside their local community and introduce younger consumers to San Juan’s pottery tradition.
“The market keeps changing, so we have to adapt to stay competitive,” Alvarez added

That adaptation also includes making products based on changing demand. Aside from their traditional pottery items, Alvarez said her mother now produces takip ng paso, or pot lids, as demand for them grows.

The changes do not mean abandoning the family’s traditional methods. Instead, the family is looking for ways to make the craft more viable while retaining the knowledge handed down through generations.
The question is whether those efforts will be enough.
For the Ilao family, pottery is more than a product. It is a skill learned from parents, a livelihood sustained through decades, and a link to the community’s history.
But heritage alone cannot pay for clay, transportation, labor, or food.
As the family searches for new customers and new ways to earn from the craft, Alvarez remains determined to keep the tradition alive.
People can support the San Juan pottery industry by purchasing authentic earthenware directly from local potters and promoting their products through social media.
“We can’t let this craft die,” Alvarez said.– Rappler.com
Quotes have been translated into English for brevity.
Christian F. Patulot is a poet-journalist, essayist, researcher, and a Mover based in Batangas. He writes about culture, language, and the everyday experiences of Filipinos.

articles.title: Stressed out about politics? It could be impacting your health
articles.summary: Political stress is a distinct type of stress that refers to how political events, decisions and actors, can cause anxiety, even depression, and other health impacts. Academics like a team of…

image.caption: Political stress is a field of study that gained traction around the 2016 U.S. presidential election. Political science professor Amanda Friesen founded the Body Politics Lab at Western University to measure how people feel, emotionally and physically, about politics. (Meagan Fitzpatrick/CBC)

blocks.text: Health·New

Political stress is a distinct type of stress that refers to how political events, decisions and actors, can cause anxiety, even depression, and other health impacts. Academics like a team of researchers at the Body Politics Lab at Western University are digging into how people feel, emotionally and physically, about politics.
Major events can cause anxiety, loss of sleep, loss of appetite and even depression, researcher says
Canada-U.S. trade war news bad for your health, research finds
In downtown Toronto, it doesn't take long to find people with politics on their minds.

"I think everyone is pretty stressed about politics right now. It's hard not to be," said Tonya Facey when stopped by CBC News. "Politics is a part of everyday life and there's a lot going on, politically."
Jamie Haynes, visiting from St. John's, said he too worries about politics.
"Especially with the war on the go with Donald Trump and Canada — it's quite concerning," he said.

The trade war with the U.S., an Alberta referendum and Quebec election this fall, global conflicts: these are the kinds of political events that can trigger stress, researchers say. Political decisions that impact people's daily lives, and political disagreements that cause conflict with others are also sources of worry.

items: 'A train wreck ... I can't stop watching': Canadians grapple with anxiety around Trump's tariff chaos

blocks.text: Political stress is now an entire field of study that gained traction in the U.S. around the 2016 presidential election. Here in Canada, political scientists, psychologists and mental health experts are also investigating the toll this form of stress can take on someone's health.

"There has been a lot of documented evidence, particularly over the past 10 years, in looking at things like loss of sleep, loss of appetite, negative emotions, periodic depression — these sorts of things that people can tie to things like a major election or maybe a particular conflict that's happening in the world,” said Amanda Friesen, a Canada Research Chair in Political Psychology.

The professor of political science at Western University in London, Ont., launched the Body Politics Lab in 2022, where her team carries out studies investigating how people's bodies and minds react to politics.

One study gave 81 undergraduate students a ring-like device that measured their temperature, pulse and sweat level as they scrolled their TikTok accounts. Western University PhD student Samantha Jones said a key takeaway from the results was not so much the physical reactions to viewing political content, but the emotional ones.
"They were more likely to report feeling negatively afterwards, compared to other types of content," said Jones.
They were also more likely to engage with it — by sharing it and viewing the comments — and that informs the algorithm.
"So despite this content making them feel negatively," said Jones, "they are inadvertently saying they want more."
Finding a healthy balance
Friesen said these kinds of studies are aimed at understanding what stresses people out when it comes to politics, and what that stress can mean for their health — and the health of democracy.
"One of our projects right now is balancing democratic and personal health," she said.

If something is shown to harm someone's well-being, they're usually advised to avoid it. But politics trickles into people's everyday lives, and with social media and the 24/7 news cycle, it's hard to avoid. Plus, people need to stay engaged in politics in order to have a thriving democracy, said Friesen.
Noah Vanderhoeven, one of the Body Politics researchers, said he thinks a balance between staying informed and maintaining healthy habits can be struck.
Some people even respond to the stress in ways that are good for democracy, he said.
"These kinds of anxieties about politics in the world can also be addressed through political action and being involved and engaged as a citizen," said Vanderhoeven.
He's leading a study this fall tied to the Alberta referendum, which he said could be a stressful event for some.

Staying informed about politics in a healthy way can be a challenge for some Canadians, according to Dr. Allison Crawford, a psychiatrist at the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health who leads Canada's national 9-8-8 suicide crisis hotline.
She said people are reaching out because of political stress.

"When political worry causes uncertainty in general, especially related to finances or people's sense of security or the safety of the world, we do often see that in our texters and callers," said Crawford.
People report losing sleep, feeling unsettled, overwhelmed and helpless, she said.
Recognizing symptoms is a good first step, said Crawford, then people should reach out to someone they trust for support.
"We do want people involved in our democracy and we want people to not disengage but there are things that we can control and things that we can't control," she said.
Time spent consuming news and social media is something that can be controlled, Crawford advised, and could be limited as a way to de-stress.
Trade war stress 'spike'

Recent news headlines in Canada are dominated by the trade war with the U.S. and Friesen said she believes Canadians’ political stress levels have "spiked" since U.S. President Donald Trump took office a second time and took aim at Canada.

"Suddenly there was this sort of external 'enemy' that pulled Canadians together but increased this stress," said Friesen. "I think there's this kind of element of uncertainty. Is this all posturing? What does this mean? And anytime there's uncertainty, that is going to cause anxiety.”
That’s exactly what Amélie Valois said she’s feeling.

"Politics do stress me out especially what's going on with the U.S. right now, and how it's going to impact our grocery bills, and business, and everything going forward," she told CBC News as she walked towards the Rogers Centre to take in a Blue Jays game. "It's stressful."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Meagan Fitzpatrick is a multiplatform reporter with CBC News in Toronto. She joined the CBC in 2011 and previously worked in the Parliament Hill and Washington bureaus. She has also reported for the CBC from Hong Kong. Meagan started her career as a print reporter in Ottawa.

articles.title: As Germany's far right gains ground, coded symbols are hiding in plain sight
articles.summary: As Germany’s far right gains political ground, researchers say some of its supporters are becoming more comfortable signalling their views in public — sometimes without displaying an explicitly…

image.caption: A man wears a Lonsdale T-shirt at a rally for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in Quedlinburg, Germany, on Aug. 23. The British boxing brand has long been popular with the country's far-right groups, despite publicly distancing itself from the movement and fundraising for anti-hate

blocks.text: World

As Germany’s far right gains political ground, researchers say some of its supporters are becoming more comfortable signalling their views in public — sometimes without displaying an explicitly political symbol at all.
Supporters have co-opted everyday brands to signal their beliefs while skirting the law

As Germany's far right gains political ground in some parts of the country, researchers say some supporters are getting more comfortable showing their views in public — albeit sometimes without displaying an explicitly political symbol.
At recent rallies for the Alternative for Germany, or AfD, that coded language was visible on things as ordinary as a pair of sneakers or a T-shirt.

Researchers say logos for brands including New Balance and Lonsdale are increasingly used as dog whistles for nationalist and Nazi symbolism — something that is especially significant in Germany, where the display of Nazi symbols is restricted by law.

"What we noticed in the last couple of years is that frequently at these events, you see a lot of people who have different signs which relate to the extreme right," said Gideon Botsch, head of the Emil Julius Gumbel Research Unit on Antisemitism and Right-Wing Extremism at Potsdam University.
"Some are clear and open right-wing and neo-Nazi symbols ... others are opaque or playing the game a little bit."
Some have co-opted New Balance, taking the large "N" on the side of its sneakers to mean "nationalist" and "NB" for Nationale Bewegung, or "national movement," Botsch said.

Likewise, Lonsdale has seen renewed use of its sportswear by the far right in part because, he says, when worn a certain way the logo spells out NSDA — the abbreviation for Germany's National Socialist Party.
"Those who know will know; those who don't know will think this is harmless," Botsch said.

The ambiguity is significant because Germany's law against Nazi symbols "expressly covers flags, badges, uniform items, slogans and forms of greeting,” said Sophie Scheuble, digital policy and counter-extremism manager at the Institute for Strategic Dialogue.
So "most of what is worn at far-right events is therefore lawful, and this distinction is well understood within right-wing extremist scenes.”
Those restrictions have led to an increase in the use of symbols recognizable only to those who know what they mean, without crossing legal lines.

When the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt's domestic intelligence service updated its handbook on far-right symbols in May, Scheuble said, its director noted that most extremists avoid prosecutable symbols and instead rely on codes and catchwords.
What has changed, researchers say, is the political environment where those styles are appearing.
Changing political climate

The Alternative for Germany, or AfD, has grown from a fringe party in 2013 into the likely winner of an upcoming state election in Saxony-Anhalt. The party has been legally designated a far-right extremist group in the state.
If it wins, it would mark the first time a far-right party has had an absolute state majority in Germany since the Second World War.
Fabian Wichmann, an expert at the EU Knowledge Hub on Preventing Radicalization, said there is a growing "grey zone" between Germany's hardcore neo-Nazi movement and the broader populist right.
Members of neo-Nazi groups attend AfD rallies and meetings and have encouraged their supporters to vote for the party, he says, seeing its success as a step toward their own political goals.

"The AfD has a widespread and diverse group of followers," Wichmann said. At its election events and marches, "you will see people who look very normal in their clothing," wearing things like New Balance and Lonsdale.

He said not everyone wearing those brands is a neo-Nazi, but there are "also a lot of neo-Nazis who wear this kind of stuff because they have some typical symbols, some typical narratives they share."
But the bigger change researchers say they're seeing isn't in the clothing itself. It's in the willingness to display those signals openly.
Wichmann says that shift matches the growing strength of Germany's far right and the AfD.
"They feel like ... the culture, the temperature of a society is changing. And now it's possible to wear something like this without getting into conflict,” he said.
"There's a feeling of, 'OK, we are on the winner's side right now,' and that's the reason why they are so openly wearing it."
Lonsdale's decades-long battle
New Balance has no affiliation with Germany's far-right movement. The company did not respond to requests for comment, but in the past has said it "does not tolerate bigotry or hate in any form."

Likewise, Lonsdale has spent decades fighting its appropriation by the far right with anti-racism initiatives since it became popular among German skinhead and neo-Nazi subcultures in the 1980s and '90s.
But the British boxing and sportswear company says the phenomenon is returning.

"We have noticed that since around summer 2024, the Lonsdale brand has once again been increasingly worn by far-right extremists,” spokesperson Ralf Elfering said. "This earlier misuse of the Lonsdale brand — and the fact that we are seeing it again today — is very frustrating.”
Elfering said the company stops supplying retailers when it discovers Lonsdale is being sold in a clearly extremist context.

items: Germany tested by new divisions 65 years after Berlin Wall erected
65 years after the Berlin Wall was built, Germany’s east-west scars help feed a rising far-right party

blocks.text: Other brands, however, carry considerably less ambiguity, according to experts.
Botsch points to Thor Steinar, a brand known for Nordic and runic imagery that has long been associated with Germany's far-right scene.
"Thor Steinar … maybe is a clearer sign than New Balance or Lonsdale that somebody is part of the scene," he said.

The company's original rune logo prompted police seizures after German authorities argued it resembled banned SS symbolism. Higher courts ruled in 2008 that displaying the logo was not punishable, according to Scheuble, and the company had by then introduced a replacement logo.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Lisa Mayor is a current Arthur F. Burns Fellow, working with Deutsche Welle in Berlin. Originally from Thunder Bay, she previously spent years as an investigative reporter for The Fifth Estate and The National. Her current role is as a network producer for CBC's Parliamentary Bureau. Her work has been recognized with a Michener Award, several Canadian Screen Awards and RTDNAs. You can reach her at lisa.mayor@cbc.ca.

articles.title: FIBA Women's World Cup begins without Canada. Is it a setback for national team, or a reset for LA28?
articles.summary: It was a cruel twist of fate. Just three days before the WNBA and its players landed on a new collective bargaining agreement — one that would officialize Canada’s first WNBA team’s inaugural season…

image.caption: Syla Swords, right, shown in this July 2024 file photo, won tournament MVP at the Olympic pre-qualifying tournament in Mexico on Sunday after averaging 14.8 points, 3.6 rebounds, 2.2 assists and one steal per game. (Mark J. Terrill/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Basketball

It was a cruel twist of fate. Just three days before the WNBA and its players landed on a new collective bargaining agreement — one that would officialize Canada’s first WNBA team’s inaugural season — the country’s national team was dealt a blow. It was eliminated from World Cup contention. And by Toronto Tempo head coach Sandy Brondello’s Australian team, no less.
On Monday, WNBA will break for 2-and-a-half weeks to allow its players to compete at World Cup without Canada
It was a cruel twist of fate.

Just three days before the WNBA and its players landed on a new collective bargaining agreement — one that would officialize Canada’s first WNBA team’s inaugural season — the country’s national team was dealt a blow.
It was eliminated from World Cup contention. And by Toronto Tempo head coach Sandy Brondello’s Australian team, no less.

“I felt like, they’re going to kick me out now. And in the end I had to remember what hat I’m wearing and what name I have across the front of my chest,” Brondello said, citing a bit of awkwardness at her conflicting roles.

“It was a hard-fought game. I feel sorry for Canada. I think they’re a really strong team and they’ve got some great young players coming through, so they’re gonna be strong for years and sometimes you need a little reset to get back up. We did the same thing after Tokyo.”

“Canada’s going to be fine. I know they’ve got the Swords [sisters] and got some great players from the college system and they get their hands on them and add to that, I think they’re going to be in a good spot.”

On Monday, the WNBA will break for two-and-a-half weeks to allow its players to compete at the World Cup, which begins in Berlin Sept. 4. Canada, thanks to that 82-76 loss to an already-qualified Australian squad in March, won’t be there, even despite a fourth-place finish at the 2022 edition of the event.
Canada wins pre-qualifying tournament
Some better news arrived Sunday, when Canada crushed Mexico 83-53 to complete a 5-0 pre-qualifying tournament in Guadalajara and book its spot in a 2028 Olympic qualifier set for that February.

Syla Swords, the 20-year-old mentioned by Brondello as one of Canada’s bright young stars alongside sister Savvy, won tournament MVP after averaging 14.8 points, 3.6 rebounds, 2.2 assists and one steal per game.

It sets Canada up with a relatively low-stakes next 17 months and a prime opportunity to build chemistry, lay groundwork and allow next-generation players like Swords to continue maturing and evolving as basketball players.

The team that ran through Mexico was made up of six veterans (think Kayla Alexander, Sami Hill) and six younger players, including NCAAers Syla Swords (Michigan), Agot Makeer (South Carolina), Delaney Gibb (BYU) and others. Head coach Nell Fortner called it a perfect mix — and was especially impressed by the latter contingent.
“They're built a little differently. I don't know if that makes any sense, but their commitment is so strong to the sport of basketball and to their country,” Fortner said.
Swords, especially, continued to show that she could be Canada’s next basketball star.

“She played fearless. I tell you what, she showed us all and anybody watching what an extraordinary shooter she is, from her quick release to her accuracy to her consistency. And she's just already a pro, she carries herself like a pro and it was really fun to coach her,” Fortner said.

Still, there’s no denying that giving Swords and her peers the World Cup stage to grow on would have been ideal. Canada, now ranked seventh by FIBA and with its WNBA players on board, lost three of five games in the March tournament in a pool with just one team ranked higher.

“Do I wish we were at the World Cup? Heck yeah,” Fortner said. “But we did the next best thing. And that was important for us to do that. We committed to it. Everybody dug into it, from players to coaching staff. And we accomplished it. And that's very encouraging moving forward.”

The group of six young NCAAers also featured Avery Howell (Washington), Cearah Parchment (Illinois) and Jasmine Bascoe (Villanova). Meanwhile, Michigan’s Mila Holloway was in camp with the team but missed the tournament due to injury, per Fortner. Duke star Toby Fournier was not with the team during the summer, per Fortner, who added that “we surely would have loved to have had her.”
Canadian talent at NCAA level
It is hard, if not impossible, to recall a time when there has been this much Canadian talent at the NCAA level — in line with the explosion of the sport during this decade.
Fortner, the 67-year-old from Jackson, Miss., watched a similar thing happen in her home country as head coach and general manager of the expansion Indiana Fever in 1999.

“All of a sudden, you're looking at players, little girls growing up, knowing that they want to be a professional basketball player. Oh my gosh, that's phenomenal. And the number of young women playing basketball, it'll explode very soon in Canada, and that's exciting,” Fortner said.
In an interview with select media just before the Tempo tipped off their regular season, WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert also mused on how impactful the Tempo could be for the national program.

“Especially on the grassroots. For young girls to be able to come into Toronto no matter where they're from in Canada — obviously we're doing a couple games in Montreal and Vancouver — and see professional basketball players, I think it'll inspire a bunch of girls, as I said, to pick up a basketball who probably wouldn't have otherwise picked up a basketball, especially if they see someone who looks like them, plays like them, is like them,” Engelbert said.
For now, Canada has those 17 months to prepare for its one shot to compete at the Los Angeles Olympics.

Fortner said she hopes to gather the team, including its WNBAers, for a training camp next February. Canada’s biggest tournament ahead of the Olympic qualifier will be the FIBA AmeriCup next July in El Salvador.
“They're not learning something new every time they come to a training camp. We're just building, continuing to grow what we do offensively and defensively,” Fortner said.

After Brondello’s Team Australia “reset” in the wake of an eighth-place finish at Tokyo 2020, it went on to beat Canada for bronze at the 2022 World Cup before claiming another third-place finish at the 2024 Olympics.
Success may not be quite so swift for the Canadians, but the building blocks appear in place to turn the World Cup step backward into two forward.

articles.title: Tenants in Vancouver's Downtown Eastside are working to make their buildings safer during heat waves
articles.summary: A group of tenants in Vancouver’s Downtown Eastside is demonstrating how communities can come together to keep each other safe during extreme heat events.

image.caption: Joe Lauzon, left, and Stephen Nelson, are tenants at Main Rooms in Vancouver's Downtown Eastside, one of around 100 buildings divided into small single rooms, hence the name "single room occupancy" or SROs. (Submitted by Wendy Pedersen)

blocks.text: When British Columbia saw record-breaking temperatures during the 2021 heat dome, Stephen Nelson witnessed firsthand just how quickly those temperatures can turn deadly.
Nelson was living at the Keefer Rooms in Vancouver's Downtown Eastside (DTES) when his friend and neighbour, Mario, began "suffering from the heat," Nelson told What on Earth.

Mario had difficulty taking care of himself, Nelson said, so he and his girlfriend tried to help as temperatures soared. They opened the windows and turned on a fan in Mario's room to try to bring the temperature down. Meanwhile, they looked after him in Nelson's room and made sure he had plenty of water.

"He started feeling better so I put him back in his room and I went to sleep. I woke up and I just had this bad feeling that nobody checked on him, and sure enough, I went next door and he was dead where I put him down to watch TV."
A coroner's report provided to CBC by the B.C. Coroners Service confirmed Mario died during the heat wave after extreme heat compounded existing medical conditions.
BCCS also said it "does not have any files on anyone else dying at the Keefer Rooms during that timeframe."
The Keefer Rooms is one of roughly 100 single-room occupancy buildings, or SROs, in Vancouver, where tenants typically live in small rooms and share bathrooms.
The extreme heat crisis killed 619 people. A report from a panel convened by the B.C. Coroners Service (BCCS) found that 10 per cent of those deaths occurred in social housing, including SROs.

items: 5 years ago, B.C. was trapped under a heat dome. Here’s how it all played out

blocks.text: But the crisis also spurred SRO tenants and their neighbours to action, bringing them together to document temperatures and find ways to stay safe when temperatures spike.
Checking on the neighbours
Wendy Pedersen founded the Downtown Eastside SRO Collaborative Society, which works to improve conditions for tenants.
Pedersen said teams of tenants now work in about 30 SRO buildings, including "H2O teams" — heat and hydration organizers who check on neighbours and deliver bottled water during heat waves.
The organization has also helped tenants open cooling rooms in two SRO buildings and secured funding from Vancouver city council to open six more, Pedersen said.
One opened last month in a building called the Main Rooms.
Roger Haskins is one of the tenants who helped the SRO Collaborative monitor temperatures in the building last summer.
"Pretty much every day was over the 26 C that the City of Vancouver prescribes as too hot," Haskins said. "And there was a couple hours here and there that was like over 40."

Even if tenants can access free air conditioners through a provincial government and B.C. Hydro program for people with lower incomes, the electrical infrastructure in their building can't necessarily support them, Haskins said.
"Every unit has at least two or three other units all on one 15 amp circuit," he said. "So this cooling room is gonna definitely help a lot of people."

Gabby Doebeli, a researcher with the University of British Columbia's Centre for Climate Justice who worked with tenants such as Haskins to study temperatures in the SROs, said the heat doesn't abate much at night.
"We found that indoor temperatures are routinely around 10 degrees hotter than outdoors, which makes it really challenging for people to sleep," Doebeli said.

"And what we're seeing is that there's certain types of housing that are not fit for living in the context of a warming city. Climate issues are housing issues and housing issues are climate issues. So we can't think of them as separate."
Heat physiologist Daniel Gagnon, a researcher at the Montreal Heart Institute, said exposure is a key factor in how people fare during heat waves.

"So obviously buildings that are maybe not ideally built for hot temperatures, where there is no … infrastructure for mechanical cooling like air conditioning, people who live within those types of places are gonna be much more exposed to the environmental conditions," says Gagnon.
But while Vancouver's SRO buildings are far from perfect, they represent an important form of housing that needs to be preserved and protected, Pedersen said.
Together they contain more than 7,000 rooms and are often both the last affordable option for people at risk of becoming homeless and the first step out of homelessness for others.
B.C. deadly heat dome review calls for alert system, building upgrades
Coming for the cooling, staying for the tea
At another SRO building, the Arlington, tenants say they've built community while improving their safety during extreme heat.
The first SRO cooling rooms were set up there about two and a half years ago, with funding from the provincial ministry, the City of Vancouver and a charity called SPARC B.C.
A heat pump cools the room in summer and warms it in winter, while shared appliances give tenants a place to prepare food.
Ty Renney, a member of the tenant leadership team who has lived in the building for 13 years, says the room has made a big difference.
"A lot of times people come in for the cooling room, or come in for the kitchen and end up chit chatting."
Richard Schwab, a 21-year resident, said another tenant brings donated food from a food rescue organization and cooks for the group.
"It's a nice way to spend Sunday night," he said. "Some people don't have families, and this is their extended family."

Pedersen said the SRO Collaborative faces funding gaps for expenses such as renting cooling rooms from landlords, installing heat pumps, buying bottled water for hot weather and paying small honorariums to tenants who take on leadership roles or work as heat and hydration co-ordinators.
"So we're trying to get funding from the province and the feds to keep going," she said.
In the past, the federal government has provided grants to landlords, Pedersen said.
She says additional federal funds could pay for electrical upgrades so tenants can have more cooling options, including in their rooms.
Environment and Climate Change Canada pointed to federal retrofit and climate-resilience programs when asked about funding for SRO upgrades.

B.C.'s Ministry of Housing and Municipal Affairs said in a statement emailed to CBC, "We deeply appreciate the work of community groups like Downtown Eastside Single Room Occupancy Collaborative Society to support people in the DTES."

It also said SRO units "are not a long-term housing solution" and "do not offer the standard of housing we want to see" in B.C. However, the statement acknowledged they can't be eliminated in the short term "without causing more people to shelter outdoors."

The ministry pointed to an $11-million grant to the SRO Collaborative in 2023 and new housing projects in the neighbourhood, including the Ho'-kee-melh Kloshe Lum, which opened in May with 248 homes and shelter spaces.
Doebeli says people often think of Vancouver's Downtown Eastside as a place that needs fixing.
"But what we're seeing is that it's not, that it's a place that has solutions. It's a place where people are taking care of each other," she said.

"All the groups in this neighbourhood have done so much for me when I was homeless. It's kind of nice to, like, give back, you know?" said Stephen Nelson, who now works as a tenant leader at Main Rooms.
"A lot of people get a bad impression, but, like the best people are down here. There's so much goodness down here that people don't see."

articles.title: JV Ejercito pushes nat'l dev't masterplan to help curb corruption
articles.summary: Senate Finance Committee Chair Senator JV Ejercito is pushing for the passage of the proposed Masterplan for Infrastructure National Development (MIND) to help address the nationwide floods.

blocks.text: Published August 30, 2026 3:45pm
Senate Finance Committee Chair Senator JV Ejercito is pushing for the passage of the proposed Masterplan for Infrastructure National Development (MIND) to help address the nationwide floods.

In an interview on told Super Radyo dzBB on Sunday, Ejercito said MIND aims to support the achievement of the overall long-term development vision of the country as a prosperous middle-class society, and streamline private and public infrastructure investments.
It shall also ensure policy continuity and further define and clarify the role of various government agencies and instrumentalities in the development of critical infrastructure projects, he added.
Ejercito said MIND could not only provide better flood-mitigating facilities but also help prevent corruption, such as the current flood control anomalies.
“Identified na 'yung flood prone areas, major river basins, kung sakali mang magkakaroon ng flood control project, dapat within priority 'yung top 10 flood prone areas sa bansa,” the senator saud.
(The flood-prone areas and major river basins have already been identified, so any flood control projects should prioritize the country’s top 10 flood-prone areas.)

According to the Department of Budget and Management (DBM), the Marcos administration has set a P1.47 trillion budget for its “Build Better More” infrastructure initiative under the proposed P7.2-trillion National Expenditure Program (NEP) in 2027.
The bulk of the proposed infrastructure budget next year, or 42.2%, is allocated for the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) at P619.04 billion.
“We need to close the gaps. 'Yung mga puwang na naiwan, dapat saraduhan ng DPWH... 'Yung mga uncompleted flood control project, kumpletuhin na natin,” the senator said.
(We need to close the gaps. The DPWH should address the remaining gaps and complete unfinished flood control projects.)
During a recent congressional hearing, DPWH Secretary Vince Dizon said the agency has yet to create a national plan for flood control after experts advised a targeted approach.

"You are correct, Congressman Chel (Diokno), that's the strategy of the department over the course of the last couple of years, more than that even, to have masterplans per river, per major river basin. So, wala po talagang consolidated national plan (So, there really is no consolidated national plan)," Dizon said.
Where will the funds go?
Ejercito further told dzBB that the public must be informed where the country’s loans will be used, as the Marcos administration plans to borrow P3.304 trillion next year.

“Kailangan malinaw din sa atin, sa publiko kung saan mapupunta ang perang ito... Nakakalungkot na utang tayo nang utang para sa panggastos ng gobyerno, pero ang ating revenues, 'yung ating kinikita ay ganito lamang,” the senator said.
(It should also be clear to the public where these funds will go. It is unfortunate that we keep borrowing to finance government spending while our revenues remain at this level.)
Finance Secretary Frederick Go earlier said the “majority” of the planned P3.304 trillion borrowing next year “will be sourced domestically.”
Go said the administration is looking at a 72%-28% borrowing mix, in favor of domestic sources.

“Our 2027 financing strategy prioritizes lower risk domestic sources to secure cost-effective financing, maintain a prudent debt profile, and deepen our local bond market,” the Finance chief said. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: Video game in real life? LTO puts two sports cars on alarm, suspends drivers’ licenses after Skyway dash
articles.summary: A series of aggressive maneuvers reminiscent of a video game racing scene prompted the Land Transportation Office (LTO) to issue a show cause order against the drivers and registered owners of two…

blocks.text: At A Glance

items: The Land Transportation Office (LTO) placed two sports cars, including a Lamborghini Huracan Evo, under alarm after a video showed them making unsafe maneuvers along the Skyway.
The drivers were ordered to appear before the LTO's Intelligence and Investigation Division on Sept. 7 and explain alleged reckless driving and failure to use proper signals.
The drivers surrendered their licenses and faced a 90-day preventive suspension while the LTO investigated the incident.

blocks.text: (Courtesy of Land Transportation Office)

A series of aggressive maneuvers reminiscent of a video game racing scene prompted the Land Transportation Office (LTO) to issue a show cause order against the drivers and registered owners of two sports cars after a viral video showed the vehicles making unsafe moves along the Skyway.

LTO Chief Asst. Sec. Markus Lacanilao said the agency immediately placed the sports cars under alarm after receiving notice of a video posted on a Facebook page that showed the vehicles changing lanes, crossing the solid white line, and failing to use turn signals while traveling on the elevated tollway, “thereby endangering the safety of other road users.”
One of the sports cars was identified by the LTO as a Lamborghini Huracan Evo.

“The price of your car is not a measure of the law. Whether expensive or not, everyone must follow the same laws. There is no room for special treatment for anyone who violates traffic laws. They will face the LTO and undergo the appropriate proceedings in accordance with the law,” he said.

The drivers were directed to appear before the LTO Central Office’s Intelligence and Investigation Division in Quezon City on September 7, and submit sworn statements with supporting documents explaining why they should not be held liable for reckless driving and failure to give proper signals.
They were also ordered to explain why they should not be declared improper persons to operate a motor vehicle, which could lead to suspension or revocation of their licenses.
Pending investigation, the drivers were required to surrender their licenses, which were placed under a 90-day preventive suspension.

articles.title: Man dies after falling into open drainage canal in Angeles City
articles.summary: MABALACAT CITY, Pampanga — A man died after falling into a flooded, open drainage canal along the Fil-Am Friendship Highway in Barangay Cutcut, Angeles City, on Aug. 28. Closed-circuit television…

blocks.text: MABALACAT CITY, Pampanga — A man died after falling into a flooded, open drainage canal along the Fil-Am Friendship Highway in Barangay Cutcut, Angeles City, on Aug. 28.

Closed-circuit television footage circulating on social media showed the man, identified by the Angeles City Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (ACDRRMO) as Reiner Novero, walking along the highway sidewalk while carrying an umbrella at 2:04 p.m.
He fell into the open drainage canal and was swept away by the strong current.
Two men who witnessed the incident attempted to rescue him but were unable to due to the swift-moving floodwaters.

The ACDRRMO and city police immediately launched a search and rescue operation. After more than an hour, responders recovered Novero about 2 kilometers from where he fell, beneath a bridge in front of a subdivision in Barangay Sto. Domingo.
Novero was brought to the Rafael Lazatin Memorial Medical Center, where he was declared dead.

The incident prompted concern among social media users over the safety of open drainage systems during flooding and heavy rains, particularly the risks posed by uncovered canals along roads and pedestrian areas. /mcm

articles.title: Iran supreme leader calls for unity among Muslim countries
articles.summary: TEHRAN — Iran’s supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei on Sunday called on Muslim countries in the region to unite against the United States and Israel, in a written message issued six months on…

blocks.text: TEHRAN — Iran’s supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei on Sunday called on Muslim countries in the region to unite against the United States and Israel, in a written message issued six months on from the start of the Middle East war.

Khamenei, in power since shortly after his father Ali Khamenei was killed at the start of the war on February 28, has yet to be seen in public since his appointment, and authorities have not released any video or audio of him.

“The solution to the problems of the Islamic nations is unity of words, friendship, and cooperation on the path of goodness,” he said Sunday as Shia Muslims marked the birthday of the Prophet Mohammed.

“Anyone, in any position, who does anything that leads to division among Muslims and creates conflict in the Muslim community, knowingly or unknowingly, intentionally or unintentionally, has served the purpose of the enemies of Islam,” he added, according to his official website.
The supreme leader called on the rulers of regional countries to “recognise your real enemy, understand its plan, and confront it”, referring to the US and Israel.
During the war, Iran targeted US military bases across the Middle East including in Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar and Bahrain.
Relations with those nations have since soured.
Khamenei, who has the final say on major state policies, also called on Iranian officials and citizens to put aside differences and come together against Israel and the United States.
“Again, this servant’s advice to the Iranian people is to not allow any differences to arise among themselves in any way,” he said, echoing remarks made in another statement on Friday.
“I firmly declare that doing anything detrimental to social cohesion is prohibited,” he had said in Friday’s message.

He also called Friday for the gradual de-dollarization of the Iranian economy and for boosting economic production to support growth following months of a US naval blockade and years of crippling sanctions that have hit livelihoods. /dl

articles.title: Futsal Development Program launched in San Juan
articles.summary: The San Juan City government, together with the Philippine Sports Commission (PSC) and Philippine Football Federation (PFF), led the launch of the city’s Futsal Development Program on Saturday, Aug.…

blocks.text: The San Juan City government, together with the Philippine Sports Commission (PSC) and Philippine Football Federation (PFF), led the launch of the city’s Futsal Development Program on Saturday, Aug. 29, aiming to introduce and develop the sport among the youth.

San Juan City Mayor Francis Zamora, together with his son and Special Assistant to the Mayor Rocco Zamora, Philippine Sports Commission Chairman Patrick Gregorio (left), Philippine Football Federation President John Gutierrez (white shirt), and Vice Mayor Angelo Agcaoili, launch the San Juan City Futsal Development Program to provide young San Juaneños with opportunities to learn and develop their futsal skills. The PSC also turns over 120 futsal balls and 20 pairs of futsal goals to the city government. (Photo from San Juan LGU)

The event was held at the Barangay Tibagan Wooden Covered Basketball Court, with Mayor Francis Zamora, his son and Special Assistant to the Mayor Rocco Zamora, PSC Chairman Patrick Gregorio, and PFF President John Gutierrez in attendance.

Also present was Rafael Merino Rodriguez, Philippine National Futsal Team head coach and PFF technical director, who will support the rollout of the program and the Training of Trainers. He will share his expertise in grassroots futsal development and coach education as the city implements the program in partnership with the PSC and PFF.

Under the partnership, the local government said that the PSC will fund the program, while the PFF will provide technical expertise, train local coaches, and oversee the implementation of the program during its initial one-year run.
During the event, the PSC turned over 120 futsal balls and 20 pairs of futsal goals to the city government as part of an Equipment Endowment Ceremony.
“The PSC will also fund the Training of Trainers for San Juan City's local coaches, who will be trained by PFF coaches,” it said.

“Under the program, young San Juaneños will undergo futsal training within their respective barangays two to three times a week, making organized sports training more accessible to children in their own communities,” the city government explained.
It added that the initial training cycle will consist of 12 training sessions, after which participants will compete in their first futsal league tournament.
The first cycle will be followed by another 12-session training cycle and a succeeding league tournament, giving participants more opportunities to hone their skills through competitive play.
Following the program’s launch, the first futsal clinic was conducted, marking the beginning of its grassroots training activities for the youth in the city.

“Through this structured training-and-competition format, the program seeks to establish a sustainable grassroots futsal system in San Juan City, develop local coaching capabilities, identify promising young athletes, and encourage more children to participate regularly in sports,” the local government said.

The city government said the Futsal Development Program forms part of its continuing efforts to expand grassroots sports opportunities and provide young San Juaneños with structured avenues for physical fitness, discipline, teamwork, and athletic development while strengthening San Juan's long-term sports development program.
