articles.title: Pacific Islands Forum meeting in turmoil after several leaders pull out of Palau summit
articles.summary:
Solomon Islands prime minister cancels his appearance, along with leaders from Fiji, Vanuatu and Samoa

Several leaders have pulled out of a the Pacific Islands Forum leaders’ meeting in…
articles.byline: Krishani Dhanji and Australian Associated Press

blocks.text: Several leaders have pulled out of a the Pacific Islands Forum leaders’ meeting in Palau at the eleventh hour.
Solomon Islands prime minister, Matthew Wale, has cancelled his appearance after a no-confidence motion was lodged against him at home by the Solomon Islands home affairs minister, Manasseh Maelanga.

Maelanga accused Wale of “repeatedly making decisions of matters of national importance without proper consultation with, or the approval of, cabinet, thereby undermining the principles of collective cabinet responsibility, representative democracy and good governance”, according to the ABC.
Australia has been in negotiations with the Solomons on a security treaty, with the hope that further negotiations could have taken place on the sidelines of the summit.
Fiji’s prime minister, Sitiveni Rabuka, and his Vanuatu counterpart, Jotham Napat, will also not be attending, with the Samoan leader, La’auli Leuatea Schmidt, another notable absence.
The Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has confirmed he will still be attending.
Oliver Nobetau, the Lowy Institute’s Pacific Islands program director, said the pulling out by key leaders “dulls the flame” of the meeting.
“This has been shaping up to be quite a significant PIF … it’s really unfortunate that this is the case,” he told Guardian Australia.
“With the pulling out of this many key prime ministers within the region, it dilutes the potential of what could come out of this leaders’ meeting.”

Nobetau said there were high expectations that this leaders’ meeting could progress pilot projects around Pacific climate resilience, and was important ahead of the COP31 climate summit, where a pre-leaders summit will be held in Tuvalu in October.
He added the leaders not showing up could be read as those nations prioritising bilateral agreements with nations including Australia above region-wide commitments.

“PIF has to demonstrate its usefulness as well. While it is a useful forum for a lot of our Pacific members, maybe the bigger countries feel there are more pressing issues or they can achieve more benefits for their countries by engaging bilaterally or directly with other partners.”
Speaking at Queensland Labor conference on Sunday in Brisbane, Albanese said Australia had a duty to help Pacific nations thrive.
Albanese said allowing Pacific nations to succeed would also benefit Australia.
“The big challenges facing the Pacific require solutions designed and delivered for the Pacific, by the Pacific,” he told the
“Australia has a key role to play, as a partner and leader.

“In a time of strategic competition in our region, our engagement in the Pacific Islands Forum and our contributions to the infrastructure, regional security and climate action of the region matter more than ever before.”
after newsletter promotion
The visit follows the prime minister signing a security deal with Fiji, elevating the bilateral relationship to a formal alliance as Australia seeks to curb Chinese influence in the region.
Pacific leaders are set to discuss security and climate concerns during the summit.
Albanese said Australia would also seek to reiterate support for Pacific workers coming to the country.
Debate has recently raged over how the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility Scheme cohort would factor into immigration cuts flagged by various parties.

Representatives of the resurgent One Nation have been pressed to clarify that PALM workers, many of whom provide much-needed labour in regional areas, would not be included in a significant reduction to net overseas migration.
Albanese said the migration discussion had been fuelling division and the Pacific worker scheme would continue because of its critical economic benefit.
“People from the Pacific make an enormous contribution to Australia’s prosperity through their vital work in regional industries like agriculture and meat processing,” he said.
“So many of our farmers and food producers rely on them.
“We know also the wages they remit home help boost the economies of their families and communities, contributing to the prosperity and stability of the whole region.”

articles.title: SOCOTECO II-IGNITE Power deal backing remains firm
articles.summary: The support for the proposed partnership between South Cotabato II Electric Cooperative (SOCOTECO II) and IGNITE Power remained strong as the cooperative heads into a crucial September plebiscite.…

blocks.text: The support for the proposed partnership between South Cotabato II Electric Cooperative (SOCOTECO II) and IGNITE Power remained strong as the cooperative heads into a crucial September plebiscite.
This, even as an opposition prayer rally drew only about 2,000 people on Saturday, Aug. 29 — fewer than the 3,000 to 7,000 participants organizers had earlier projected.

The “Kahayag sa Tanan” prayer and candle-lighting activity was held at Plaza Heneral Santos, with church, academic, youth and civic groups calling for greater transparency and accountability over the proposed Conditional Joint Venture Agreement (CJVA).

The rally was supported by Akbayan Youth activists, Gamay Katilingban na Kristohanon (GKK), and the Notre Dame of Dadiangas University, who joined calls for greater scrutiny of the proposed agreement.

General Santos City Police Director Col. Ariel Acala said the gathering was peaceful and attended by about 2,000 participants, mostly from General Santos City, Sarangani and South Cotabato. Organizers had earlier projected attendance of between 3,000 and 7,000.
The gathering came as SOCOTECO II continues its district-wide information, education and communication campaign explaining the proposed partnership to member-consumer-owners (MCOs).
Thousands have attended the sessions since early August, with several MCOs voicing support for the proposal due to recurring outages, aging facilities and concerns over the cooperative’s finances.

Some MCOs wondered whether opposition to the proposed project was also opposition to the city and province’s development. They said they were perplexed as to why the Church and Bro. Manuel de Leon, President of Notre Dame of Dadiangas University, appeared to be against efforts seen as promoting progress in General Santos and the wider province.

The proposed partnership calls for IGNITE Power to fund a five-year modernization program covering rehabilitation of aging facilities, equipment upgrades and measures to improve power reliability. It also targets reducing system losses charged to consumers to 5.5 percent.

SOCOTECO II has reported accumulated financial losses of about P2.1 billion as of December 2025. Its system losses have climbed to nearly 14 percent, resulting in losses estimated at more than P40 million monthly.
IGNITE Power has said investments would be made first before seeking regulatory approval for cost recovery.

The final decision, however, rests with SOCOTECO II’s qualified MCOs. Around 200,000 members are expected to participate in the plebiscite scheduled over four weekends — Sept. 5-6, 12-13, 19-20 and 26-27.
The proposed CJVA must secure the required majority vote before the partnership can proceed.

articles.title: Boy goes missing amid rushing floodwaters in Olongapo City
articles.summary: OLONGAPO CITY — A three-year-old boy went missing after rushing floodwaters swept through his family’s home near a river in Villa Meranda, Old Cabalan Forestry, Olongapo City, authorities said…

blocks.text: OLONGAPO CITY — A three-year-old boy went missing after rushing floodwaters swept through his family’s home near a river in Villa Meranda, Old Cabalan Forestry, Olongapo City, authorities said Sunday, Aug. 30.

In a phone interview, Jeffrey Lapid, head of the Olongapo City Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (CDRRMO), said the boy was being held by one of his parents when a wall above their house suddenly collapsed, sending a strong surge of water toward the home.
The impact caused the parent to lose grip of the child, who Lapid said was carried away by the floodwaters.
The family’s house was damaged and partially inundated.
Rescue teams launched a search from the area where the boy was last seen and followed the waterway downstream toward the sea.
The search was still underway as of Sunday, with responders checking portions of the river and downstream areas where the strong current may have carried the child.
The incident occurred as persistent heavy rains caused flooding in several parts of Olongapo.
As of 11 a.m. Sunday, Lapid said 730 families, or 2,540 individuals, had been affected by flooding in 13 of the city’s 17 barangays. /mcm

articles.title: Ilocos Sur town imposes liquor ban, curfew amid severe weather
articles.summary: SAN ILDEFONSO, Ilocos Sur—The municipal government of Magsingal in this province imposed a temporary liquor ban and curfew amid severe weather brought by the southwest monsoon. Acting Municipal Mayor…

blocks.text: SAN ILDEFONSO, Ilocos Sur—The municipal government of Magsingal in this province imposed a temporary liquor ban and curfew amid severe weather brought by the southwest monsoon.
Acting Municipal Mayor Alrico Favis signed Executive Order No. 55, Series of 2026, on Sunday, Aug. 30, ordering the immediate implementation of the restrictions.

Under the order, the sale, distribution, purchase, serving, and consumption of alcoholic beverages are prohibited throughout the municipality for the duration of the habagat until the restrictions are officially lifted.
A curfew will also be enforced in all public places from 7 p.m. to 4 a.m.

The order exempts government workers on duty, medical doctors and veterinarians who need to report for work, public utility company personnel conducting construction, maintenance or emergency activities, and people responding to medical, emergency or disaster-related situations.
It noted that Magsingal police, barangay officials and barangay chairpersons were directed to patrol public areas, monitor coastal communities and enforce the temporary restrictions.
The municipal government said the measures were being implemented as a precautionary response to the severe weather and heightened risks brought by the continuing rains.

The executive order cited Republic Act No. 10121, or the Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act of 2010, and Republic Act No. 7160, or the Local Government Code of 1991, as legal bases for the emergency measures. /mcm

articles.title: Nepal’s high-tech disaster response meets low-tech reality
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — The floods in the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers have exposed a striking gap in the country’s emergency response. The government agencies are increasingly using digital portals,…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — The floods in the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers have exposed a striking gap in the country’s emergency response. The government agencies are increasingly using digital portals, drones, GIS, satellite images and artificial intelligence to collect and share information, while rescuers on the ground still lack enough specialized equipment to reach people trapped under mud and debris.

State agencies, including the Prime Minister’s Office, Nepali Army, Nepal Police and the national disaster management authority (NDRRMA), have launched extensive information drives across social media platforms, emergency SMS broadcasts, mobile ringtone alerts, and specialised applications.

Concurrently, independent tech groups and civic initiatives have rolled out digital mapping tools, tracing scripts, and open-source data repositories to track missing individuals and compile disaster statistics.

Yet, as the death toll rises and survivors remain isolated, technical analysts, emergency responders, and affected citizens point out a stark contrast. While the country’s digital communication strategy appears polished, its physical search, rescue, and early warning infrastructure remains woefully underdeveloped.

On Saturday, a video circulated widely on social media showing a Nepali Army search team navigating the tunnel of the Trishuli Hydroelectric Project to locate trapped workers. The soldiers relied entirely on the small beams of their smartphone flashlights.

The video sparked immediate public outcry. “Without proper equipment, in the faint light of a mobile phone?” commented social media user Irsad Ansari. Many others echoed his disbelief, asking how complex subterranean rescue operations could succeed without specialized industrial lighting, heavy demolition tools, and advanced tunneling equipment.

Though the government has attempted to project a modern, ‘smart’ response through digital maps and online dashboards, critics argue that these efforts fail to translate into tangible assistance on the ground. Public frustration has mounted into a familiar refrain across affected communities: The government is active on social media, but absent in society; it lives in the cloud, but fails on the ground.

On paper, several tech-driven coordination systems have been activated. The Ministry of Home Affairs and NDRRMA, in collaboration with the Department of Roads, recently launched the ‘Setu Rapid’ portal. The platform aims to integrate field rescuers, regional command posts, and heavy equipment operators onto a single live map.

Similarly, the Prime Minister’s Office established an integrated emergency assistance portal to process rescue requests, log missing persons reports, and track relief supply distributions. Emergency communications are also being funneled through the National Emergency Operation Centre, the Flood Forecasting Division, and NDRRMA’s dedicated hotline (1234).

To streamline relief donations, the government has set up integrated QR code payments through platforms like Nepal Clearing House Limited (NCHL), ConnectIPS, eSewa, and major commercial banking applications. Authorities have urged the public to donate solely through official channels, warning against unverified QR codes circulating online.

Minister for Education, Science, Technology and Innovation Mahabir Pun defended the state’s technological strategy, assuring that the government is utilizing available digital tools to the fullest extent for search, rescue, and rebuilding.

“We are currently working alongside a dedicated team of young IT professionals and artificial intelligence specialists to collect and process critical damage data,” Pun said. “Our nation has never properly established an integrated early warning system. That neglect in the past is precisely why we are facing such immense destruction today. Moving forward, prioritizing early warning systems across all vulnerable river basins will be our absolute top duty.”

Security forces maintain that advanced rescue teams have been deployed to the affected zones. Netra Bahadur Karki, spokesperson for the Armed Police Force, stated that specialized personnel including live detection equipment operators, drone squads, rope rescue teams, swift-water divers, and collapsed-structure search teams are actively working in the field.
Nepali Army spokesperson Rajaram Basnet added that heavy physical breaching tools, such as demolition hammers, rotary hammers, and helicopter rescue baskets, are being utilized where feasible.

To assess the damage across devastated swathes of Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading districts, civil tech groups have stepped in to assist state agencies. Bikas Krochme Gurung, an engineer and president of the Robotics Association of Nepal, explained that his organization’s Drone Rapid Response Team is deploying aerial photography, thermal imaging, and LiDAR sensors to map devastated areas.

“Where landslides have completely washed away highways and bridges, drones have proven crucial for measuring the distance between severed riverbanks, assessing erosion depth, and analyzing mudflow density,” said Gurung. “We are sending geo-referenced data directly to the NDRRMA and the Ministry of Home Affairs to help prioritise immediate rescue missions. Currently, between 80 and 100 trained drone pilots are on standby across the country.”

According to Gurung, the Drone Federation of India and Indian security forces have offered to supply additional drone units. However, because low-altitude drone operations can interfere with air traffic, aerial drone missions are being strictly managed alongside emergency military helicopters, which are currently dedicated exclusively to airlifting trapped survivors rather than dropping relief supplies.

Despite these efforts, social media influencers and public commentators argue that the disaster has laid bare Nepal’s structural vulnerabilities. Popular social media influencer Victor Paudel noted that the country’s physical response mechanism relies heavily on manual labour.

blocks.caption: Specialised teams drill a rock in Trishuli on Saturday in search of a hydropower project tunnel to rescue people trapped inside, in Rasuwa. RSS

blocks.text: “This disaster has exposed our severe lack of modern emergency response technology,” Paudel said. “If we had deployed the advanced rescue systems used in countries like South Korea, India, or China, the search operations would be far further along. Those nations possess extensive technical expertise in rescuing workers trapped in underground coal mines, hydroelectric tunnels, and highway caverns.”

Paudel pointed out that while security personnel on the ground deserve praise for working tirelessly, seeing soldiers clearing tons of thick mud and retrieving bodies with their bare hands proves that Nepal lacks a resilient disaster management system.

The stark operational contrast is visible across the border. In neighboring China, advanced heavy-lift drones capable of carrying humans have been deployed during flood rescues. In Nepal, however, hydro-project workers remained trapped inside dark water tunnels for four consecutive days due to a total lack of subterranean breaching equipment.

“We still suffer from a critical lack of high-level technology and unified data,” Gurung said. “We do not possess specialised machinery to break into tunnels, nor do we have redundant emergency communication systems. Nationwide, we have only four or five drones capable of lifting payloads between 5 and 20 kilograms. In times like this, the vital importance of satellite internet and heavy rescue hardware becomes painfully obvious.”

Technical analysts also stress that the failure of early warning systems directly caused the heavy loss of life. Neither the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology nor NDRRMA managed to deliver timely, precise warnings to at-risk communities before floodwaters hit.

Analysts often point to the Koshi Barrage as a functional contrast, where continuous water-level telemetry stretching from the upper Koshi basin down to Barahakshetra allows authorities to issue timely warnings. Yet, such monitoring networks remain missing across the torrential rivers of central Nepal.

Rajib Subba, an IT expert and current Election Commissioner, warned that the proliferation of uncoordinated digital forms and competing web portals across various government ministries could backfire, leading to data duplication and operational confusion.

“Government teams are working hard with the limited tools they have, but systemic preparation should have happened long before,” Subba said. “Collecting data on missing persons must be handled strictly through a centralised, single-window system. When different agencies release separate forms and helpline numbers, coordination breaks down and vital information gets scattered.”
Subba, who previously worked on early warning studies for the volatile Tsho Rolpa glacial lake, questioned the sustainability of past investments.

“Why haven’t we installed 24-hour automated monitoring and warning systems along our most dangerous rivers?” he asked. “Despite massive funding from international donor agencies in the name of early warning systems, there is almost no lasting, practical impact on the ground.”

Unregulated settlement expansion and poorly engineered road construction along riverbanks have exacerbated the destruction. While mountain communities historically built homes on high, stable ridges, modern infrastructure has drawn settlements directly down to river margins.

“It is long past time we re-evaluated our entire approach to national development,” Subba said. “In this era of severe climate crisis, if we fail to deploy the right technology in the right places, we will never stop these recurring cycles of multi-billion-rupee destruction.”
Model example of AI use

Amid government shortcomings, private initiatives have attempted to fill the gap. Niraj Bhushal, an assistant IT officer at the Ministry of Finance, independently built the ‘Rasuwa-Bhote Koshi Flood Rescue Portal’. Hosted on GitHub and powered by Grok AI, the open-source platform has become a model for leveraging AI in emergency situations.

Bhushal’s portal automatically collects data every five minutes from official digital feeds published by the NDRRMA, Nepal Police, Nepali Army, and the Rasuwa District Administration Office. The AI model processes missing persons requests submitted via Google Forms, cross-referencing them against lists of rescued survivors to eliminate duplicates.
Furthermore, the system processes satellite imagery provided by the European Union’s UCOS, using AI to map structural damage such as collapsed bridges, buried houses, and blocked road segments.

“I built this portal independently, but I am now collaborating with young volunteers from the civic group Speak Up Nepal,” said Bhushal. “A non-resident Nepali in Australia, Shristi Mainali, provided $210 to power the system, while community chief at SpaceX AI, provided an additional $100 to ensure the servers stay online.”

Before any data is published on the portal, Grok AI assists in fact-checking and verifying the details. “The portal automatically compares missing persons reports with records of recovered individuals,” Bhushal explained. “For official PDF reports released by the Nepali Army and local authorities, I manually convert the data into CSV files before running them through the system.”

To protect citizens from fraudulent links, Bhushal linked his platform directly to official government portals. Clicking the ‘Rescue’ button redirects users to the Prime Minister’s emergency portal, while the ‘Donate’ button routes directly to the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund.

“I work full-time at the Ministry of Finance during the day and devote my nights until 1-2am to updating this portal,” said Bhushal. “I created this so that panicked families wouldn’t have to search frantically across scattered websites during a crisis. AI has proven immensely effective in bringing clarity to this chaotic situation.” /dl

articles.title: Barbers hails prosecutor Divinagracia's 'pro bono passion' in VP Duterte trial
articles.summary: If anybody among the private prosecutors in Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial has exemplified what "pro bono passion" is all about, it's lawyer Mae Divinagracia. This, as House…

blocks.text: If anybody among the private prosecutors in Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial has exemplified what "pro bono passion" is all about, it's lawyer Mae Divinagracia.
This, as House impeachment adviser Robert Ace Barbers recognized Divinagracia's efforts as well as the rest of the prosecution in the high-stakes trial, which will soon enter its third month.
Barbers singled out Divinagracia for her courtroom work, describing her handling of evidence and witness examination as an example of the legal talent assembled by the prosecution.

“And we appreciate the fact that itong magagaling na mga abogado na ito kagaya ni Atty. Divinagracia, magaling sa presentation ng ebidensya at sa kanyang pagdi-direct examination sa witness,” the former three-term Surigao del Norte told a news forum over the weekend.
(And we appreciate the fact that these excellent lawyers, such as Atty. Divinagracia, are skilled at presenting evidence and conducting direct examinations of witnesses.)
Divinagracia grabbed headlines during the impeachment hearing last Aug. 25 when she used "strong language" during her direct examination of OVP Assistant Secretary Lemuel Ortonio.
This caused her to get called out by Duterte’s defense lawyers, and in the end presiding officer Senator Francis "Chiz" Escudero asked her to tone down her choice of words.
“But you know, ito sila 'yung ating mga private prosecutors, sila po ay volunteers, pro bono po ito sila. Kaya nga ang kanilang slogan ‘Para sa Bayan,’” he explained.
(But you know, these private prosecutors are volunteers, they are pro bono. That’s why their slogan is ‘Para sa Bayan [This is for the country].')

The House formally assembled its 15-strong private prosecution team in June to supplement the 11 House prosecutors assigned across the four articles of impeachment. It brought together experienced litigators, former government lawyers and legal practitioners to assist in trial preparation and courtroom presentation.
Barbers said the lawyers offered their services voluntarily as part of what they regarded as a public-service undertaking rather than a paid engagement.
Private prosecutors have since participated in direct examinations of witnesses and the presentation of evidence against respondent Duterte.
Barbers disclosed that interest from lawyers willing to volunteer was so high that the prosecution had to limit the size of its private legal contingent.
“Pero kami as far as the private prosecutors are concerned, ni-limit pa nga po 'yun dahil nga marami pong gustong mag-volunteer at hindi naman pupwedeng napakarami,” he noted.
(But as far as the private prosecutors are concerned, we even had to limit it because so many wanted to volunteer, and it wouldn’t be possible to have too many.)

articles.title: A lone Black woman’s defiance of Swedish neo-Nazis, 10 years on
articles.summary:
Protester Tess Asplund on the photo that made headlines, and why she sees it as a sign of the change in Sweden today

The striking photograph showed a lone Black woman, her fist raised,…

blocks.text: The striking photograph showed a lone Black woman, her fist raised, standing in the path of hundreds of uniformed neo-Nazis on parade in 2016, and it made headlines across the globe.

At the time, it was held up as a symbol of the resistance to the far right. But 10 years on, as Sweden gears up for elections in which the far right is expected to emerge as the second most-voted-for party, the woman in the photo sees it as a sign of the bewildering change that has gripped the Scandinavian country.
“Ten years ago, people would say, ‘Oh we dislike the far right, the Sweden Democrats, we despise Nazis,’” said Tess Asplund, 52. “And now, they’ve become normalised. It’s like, what happened?”

Her comments hint at the recent reshaping of Swedish politics, where the far right – once a pariah – has steadily marched into the halls of power. “I’m sad, afraid and ashamed of Swedish citizens,” said Asplund in an interview at a cafe in central Stockholm. “It’s pure racism.”
Ahead of a general election on 13 September, polls suggest that the centre-left opposition has a lead over the ruling rightwing coalition, meaning a change of government could be on the cards.

But the Sweden Democrats, a party with neo-Nazi roots, is expected to garner the second-most votes in the country. In the 2022 elections, it also came second, paving the way for it to play a supporting role in a minority-run coalition.

blocks.caption: Supporters of Sweden Democrats party leader Jimmie Åkesson listen to him at an election campaign event in Huddinge on 18 August. Photograph: Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The party has long been dogged by accusations of harbouring violent racists and swastika-wearing Nazi sympathisers. It has used its leverage in government to consistently target migrants, including asylum seekers, as well as Muslims, ushering in ultra-restrictive migration policies and a discourse that routinely disparages the millions of people from around the world who have made Sweden their home and seek to contribute to it.

Earlier this year, the Swedish prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, mused that if his four-party coalition won the upcoming election, the far right could enter government, in what was seen as a watershed moment for Swedish politics.

It was a sharp contrast to the Sweden that Aspland had stood up for on 1 May 2016. She and scores of others had travelled to the central Swedish city of Borlänge to rally against a planned march by the Nordic Resistance Movement, one of the country’s largest neo-Nazi groups.
As she faced off against them, her act of defiance was caught on camera by photographer David Lagerlöf of Expo, the anti-racism foundation in Stockholm.

It soon went viral, with Swedish media likening it to another iconic image of resistance: a 1985 photo in which photographer Hans Runesson captured a woman taking aim at a skinhead with her handbag in the south-western city of Växjö.

blocks.caption: A woman takes aim at a skinhead with her handbag in the south-western city of Växjö in 1985. Photograph: Hans Runesson

blocks.text: Media requests poured in from around the world. In Sweden, people began stopping Asplund on the streets, thanking her for her gesture, though she also grappled with a stream of online harassment and death threats on her home telephone line.

For Asplund, who has spent much of her life campaigning against racism, it was a sobering frontline encounter with the far-right spectrum of Sweden, which ranges from the extremist Nordic Resistance Movement, which in 2024 was designated as a terror group by the US, to the Sweden Democrats, who have long worked to make over their image.

A 2023 study noted that the presence of the two groups, both of which have shared roots in their militant opposition to immigration, probably works to bolster their causes by keeping issues of immigration and integration on Sweden’s political agenda.

Or, in the words of Mohammad Aluaudt Allah, a Syrian refugee who was kicked unconscious on a street in central Stockholm last year, the politicians who blame immigrants for all of the country’s issues have “created a sense of impunity for violent Nazi groups”.
after newsletter promotion
“They may feel that they are being given permission to exercise their hatred and attack us,” he told newspaper Dagens Nyheter.

The view was echoed by Asplund. “The Nordic Resistance Movement, they’re kind of small now, we don’t hear so much about them any more,” she said. “They don’t have to be big because Sweden Democrats are big, so they’ve got people doing their work in the government. The Nazis are in the shadows.”
The resulting rhetoric had then been amplified by some in media, she said, pointing to those who had uncritically swallowed the far right’s blaming of all social and economic ills on migration.

What had emerged was a hardened Sweden, one where, for example, dozens of young people who had lived their whole lives in Sweden had been deported to their parents’ countries of birth after they failed to meet the increased earnings thresholds for migrants. “Thirty years ago, we would be on the street fighting against this. Now it’s like, ‘That’s sad for him or her.’ It’s a shift that really scares me,” she said.

“If Olof Palme were alive today, he would turn over in his grave,” she added, citing the assassinated former leader of Sweden’s Social Democratic party, who is credited with many of the progressive policies long associated with Sweden, from the robust social welfare system to a pro-refugee discourse that welcomed those escaping dictatorships and war.
She noted, however, that her disappointment and shame did not extend to everyone in Sweden. “We are many, many people here fighting for human rights and against racism,” she said.

blocks.caption: Police intervene against Tess Apslund during the neo-Nazi parade in 2016. Photograph: TT News Agency/Alamy

blocks.text: But in some ways, the photo – hailed in 2016 for capturing one of the conflicts of our time – seemed to pit Palme’s Sweden against the march of the far right.
In the years since, Asplund despaired that it may have been the far right who had emerged victorious.

“I’m afraid and heartbroken because when I speak to people they’re like, ‘Oh for God’s sake, forget that. It was 20 years ago that there were Nazis and skinheads, now it’s gone,’” she said. “They’ve normalised it. It’s not my safe Sweden any more, it’s not the Sweden that I’m used to.”

articles.title: Nepal floods: Indian, Chinese, Korean teams support rescue effort
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — The Nepali government, which was initially reluctant to accept various kinds of support offered by friendly nations, has started allowing them to carry out search and rescue…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — The Nepali government, which was initially reluctant to accept various kinds of support offered by friendly nations, has started allowing them to carry out search and rescue operations for people trapped inside hydropower tunnels in the Trishuli basin.
On Saturday, three different teams from India, China and South Korea reached disaster-hit areas and hydropower projects in the search and rescue of stranded individuals.
An Indian team from the National Disaster Response Force that arrived in Kathmandu on Friday flew to Chilime and Langtang in coordination with the Nepali Army and the Armed Police Force.

A technical team from India carried out on-site reconnaissance of hydropower tunnels in the area affected by the flash flood, the Indian Embassy in Kathmandu stated. It would help facilitate early search and rescue of stranded individuals.
The 11-member Indian team was flown to the two designated areas but the Nepal government on Saturday turned down another Indian request to send a bigger search and rescue team.
Indian experts conducted a recce of tunnels in Chilime and Langtang power plants area with the Nepali Army, Indian Ambassador Naveen Srivastava wrote on X.

Kathmandu has been selective in accepting external assistance and decided to seek the support of foreign experts on tunnel rescue, DNA and forensic examination. As Nepal is looking for large-size freezers to manage bodies, the government is in close consultation with immediate neighbours and the international community, said Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal.

Writing on Facebook on Saturday, Prime Minister Balendra Shah said that the government has received 2,000 airtight bags each from India and China for managing bodies of victims. The government has requested 30 Bailey bridges with China, he stated.

As many foreign nationals are also missing, a dedicated Emergency Control Room has been established at the foreign ministry, Khanal told a news conference on Saturday. “Our diplomatic missions are also constantly sharing and updating verified information, and facilitating communication with families and extending any necessary assistance, identification and repatriation procedures.”
Hinting at why the government earlier did not accept foreign teams, the minister said Nepal’s security agencies and other response teams are currently handling the situation effectively.

“As operations continue, we have requested specific and specialised assistance from our friendly neighbours in areas where their support can further strengthen our search-and-rescue efforts such as opening the tunnels where people have been trapped,” Khanal said. Also useful would be technologies that help us locate people alive in the affected areas, quick forensic and DNA analysis and mortuaries.

On the question of why the government was reluctant to allow the foreign teams for search and rescue operations, Minister Khanal said Nepali security agencies are well familiar with the geography and terrain.
“Since the disaster struck in difficult terrain and narrow passes this time, the foreign teams may face difficulties flying over the affected areas.”
Only helicopters can fly in the narrow gorge, possibly only by Nepali pilots, he stressed. “Since the terrain is risky, we are sensitive to the safety of personnel deployed.”
An eleven-member specialised technical reconnaissance team for tunnel rescue from India has been mobilised and a tunnel rescue team from China has also arrived, he said.

The government has also allowed some South Korean experts to visit and inspect the disaster-hit areas. A team was moved on Saturday itself, said an official. Another team is seeking permission to deploy.
Soon after the disaster, South Korea had offered to conduct aerial surveys using drones to locate victims and rescue survivors but the Nepal government declined.
According to the Chinese Embassy, at the request of the Nepali government, China’s Ministry of Emergency Management urgently dispatched five tunnel experts to Nepal on Saturday.
The experts flew by helicopter from Kerung near the Chinese border to the disaster-hit areas in Nepal. They immediately joined the tunnel rescue operation at a hydropower station, the embassy stated.
In response to the needs of the rescue operation, another four Chinese tunnel experts will be urgently dispatched to Nepal soon, said the embassy.

On the modality of sharing of information between Nepal and China prior to a potential natural disaster, Minister Khanal said that the Tribhuvan University and the Chinese Academy of Science and Technology were working on it.
“After the disaster, we have had excellent coordination, communication and cooperation with China on sharing data and information,” said Khanal.

Prior to Wednesday’s floods, even the Chinese had no proper information about the looming disaster, Khanal said. There are no arrangements between the neighbours for the sharing of prior information. “We are in the process of having it,” said Khanal.
A six-member Chinese team landed in the Trishuli area by a Chinese helicopter. It will begin the rescue operation in close coordination with a Nepali Army team, according to statements.

Although the conditions inside the Trishuli 3 B tunnel in Rasuwa remain extremely challenging, the government of Nepal,the Nepali Army and Chinese expert team are making every possible effort, the PM’s Office stated.
Nepal and China have maintained close communication on transboundary disaster management, the Chinese Embassy in Kathmandu said in a public notice on Saturday.

In May this year, a delegation from the Ministry of Water Resources of China and the Department of Water Resources of Xizang Autonomous Region visited Nepal and made substantial progress with the Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation and the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority of Nepal in promoting the establishment of a transboundary disaster information-sharing mechanism, the embassy said.

In August, a team from the Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment of the Chinese Academy of Sciences visited Nepal for scientific research exchanges and shared China’s practical experience in glacial lake monitoring, said the embassy. On August 26, the day the flood disaster struck, the China Meteorological Administration held an urgent virtual meeting with the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology of Nepal to assess the disaster situation and share data simultaneously. /dl

In a Facebook post, the MMDA said the amount of rainfall was monitored by the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration from 9 a.m. on Aug. 29, Saturday, to 8 a.m. on Aug. 30, Sunday.

The MMDA noted that it would continue to conduct flood mitigation measures in flooded areas in Metro Manila, such as using mobile pumps, declogging, and dredging operations in drainages and waterways, and clearing debris and garbage from drainage inlets.
The incessant rains brought by the habagat caused severe and widespread flooding in many areas of Metro Manila and parts of Luzon.
Metro Manila was placed under the red rainfall warning at 12:10 p.m. on Sunday, and serious flooding is still expected in flood-prone areas. /atm

articles.title: DPWH halts alleged illegal reclamation projects in Taguig
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) Secretary Vince Dizon said the agency has issued cease-and-desist orders against alleged illegal reclamation projects linked to…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) Secretary Vince Dizon said the agency has issued cease-and-desist orders against alleged illegal reclamation projects linked to Laguna de Bay in Taguig City.
He said the orders were issued on Aug. 20 upon the directive of the Office of the President through the Philippine Reclamation Authority (PRA), and the orders were effective immediately.
“Let’s just discuss it if there is any problem there; then let’s determine the way forward,” Dizon told reporters in an interview.
He also said a meeting had been scheduled with stakeholders, including the Taguig City government, PRA, and the Laguna Lake Development Authority.
Senator Panfilo Lacson earlier said that during his meeting with Dizon, the secretary guaranteed that the orders would be issued once the agency received the PRA’s request.
Lacson previously said that reclamation activities may threaten the Laguna Lake ecosystem, where garbage that was supposed to end up in the Rizal provincial sanitary landfill ends up there.

Last Saturday, Lacson also disclosed that four parcels of allegedly illegally reclaimed land in Taguig City were flagged with “fraudulently” issued titles and will be turned over to the Office of the Ombudsman for investigation. articles.title: Flood damage to Nepal’s hydropower sector could run into billions
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — Nepal’s electricity authority says the devastating Bhotekoshi floods may have caused losses running into hundreds of billions of rupees across more than a dozen hydropower projects…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — Nepal’s electricity authority says the devastating Bhotekoshi floods may have caused losses running into hundreds of billions of rupees across more than a dozen hydropower projects and electricity transmission infrastructure, far exceeding initial estimates by private sector developers.
The scale of the destruction has also raised urgent questions over how damaged projects will be rebuilt and who will bear the cost.
Rajan Dhakal, spokesperson for the Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA), said on Friday that the authority’s preliminary assessment pointed to losses worth hundreds of billions of rupees.

“For now, our priority is rescue operations, the search for missing people and restoring electricity supply,” Dhakal said. “There has been unimaginable loss of life and property. The Rasuwagadhi Hydropower Project has been completely washed away, while the Chilime project has been buried. Our preliminary estimate is that the damage runs into hundreds of billions of rupees.”

His estimate is substantially higher than that of the Independent Power Producers’ Association, Nepal (IPPAN), whose senior officials have put average losses in the sector at around Rs25 billion to Rs30 billion.
Uttam Bhlon Lama, senior vice-president of IPPAN, said older hydropower projects with ground-level powerhouses suffered extensive or complete damage.

“Newer projects with underground powerhouses and desanders have suffered comparatively less damage,” Lama said. “Overall, we estimate losses at around 25 to 30 percent of the total project cost, although a complete assessment is still pending.”
At least 13 hydropower projects, both operational and under construction, have been damaged in Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts.

Affected operational projects include the 20MW Langtang Khola project, which was in the testing phase, the 5MW Mailung Khola, 14.8MW Mailung Khola, a 25MW solar project operated by the NEA and its subsidiaries, the 14MW Devighat, 24MW Trishuli, 60MW Upper Trishuli A, 22MW Chilime and the 111MW Rasuwagadhi Hydropower Project.

Projects under construction that have been affected include the 37MW Upper Trishuli 3B, jointly owned by the NEA and Nepal Telecom, the privately developed 120MW Rasuwagadhi Bhotekoshi, the 6.42MW Upper Mailung A, the 216MW Upper Trishuli 1 and the 15.6MW Middle Trishuli Ganga project.
Insurance could play a crucial role in determining how quickly the projects are rebuilt.
While private hydropower projects are generally insured, government-owned infrastructure may not have comprehensive insurance coverage, according to industry experts.
Raju Raman Paudel, former executive director of the Nepal Insurance Authority, said insured projects should be able to claim compensation after losses are assessed.
“Once the damage is evaluated, insurance companies will make the payments,” he said. “But there are concerns that not all NEA projects are insured. That could create difficulties.”
Despite growing climate risks, many government-owned structures in Nepal remain uninsured, he said.

Sushil Dev Subedi, executive director of the Nepal Insurance Authority, said a detailed assessment of physical damage had yet to begin because rescue and relief operations remained the immediate priority.
“Once restoration work begins, insurance companies will start assessing the risks and losses, after which claims can be processed,” he said.

Some of the affected projects have investments from Nepali banks and multinational companies, he added, but all are insured through Nepali insurance companies. Licensed surveyors will assess the damage on behalf of insurers.

“It is rare for hydropower projects to be uninsured,” Subedi said. “All projects under construction are generally insured, but we cannot yet say with certainty whether every operational project has coverage. Everyone is still focused on rescue operations.”
He said insurance companies had the capacity to settle legitimate claims.
Mohan Kumar Dangi, president of IPPAN, said all private-sector hydropower projects had insurance coverage and developers expected to use insurance payouts to finance reconstruction.
“Some structures have been buried, and others may have been washed away,” he said. “The assessment will take some time.”

Projects with limited damage could be rebuilt relatively quickly, while severely damaged projects would take longer to restore, he said. IPPAN would also coordinate with the government on reconstruction.
Dangi said the damage was unlikely to create an immediate electricity shortage in Nepal because domestic generation currently exceeds national demand.
Flood shock hits stock market
The disaster has also rattled Nepal’s stock market, with hydropower and non-life insurance companies among the hardest hit.

Of the 13 sectoral indices traded on Wednesday, the hydropower index fell 2.84 percent and the non-life insurance index dropped 3.90 percent, reflecting investor concerns over the scale of losses and potential insurance liabilities.
On Thursday, while the benchmark Nepse index slipped by just 1.04 points, the hydropower sub-index fell by 19.48 points and the non-life insurance index dropped by 201.81 points.
Many of the companies whose share prices fell most sharply were hydropower projects located in Rasuwa and Nuwakot, the districts worst affected by the flooding.

Non-life insurers are particularly exposed because they provide coverage for damaged hydropower infrastructure. Investors fear that large insurance payouts could affect the companies’ profitability, brokers said.

The non-life insurance index fell by 404.05 points on Wednesday and another 201.81 points on Thursday. The hydropower index dropped 104.33 points on Wednesday and 19.78 points the following day, while the life insurance index fell by 175.13 points and 28.10 points respectively.

By contrast, the manufacturing and processing index rose by 41.44 points on Wednesday and 178.18 points on Thursday, as investors anticipated increased demand for construction materials during the reconstruction phase.

On Wednesday, shares in Rasuwagadhi Hydropower fell 15 percent, followed by Mailung Khola Hydropower at 14.99 percent, Trishuli Jal Vidyut at 12.95 percent, Upper Mailung Khola at 11.56 percent, Sanjen Jalvidyut at 11.18 percent and Chilime Hydropower at 10.12 percent.
Meanwhile, shares in Sarbottam Paints Industries rose 15 percent, Upper Hewakhola gained 10.43 percent and Kalinchok Hydropower increased 3.21 percent.
Broker Narendra Sijapati said the contrasting movements were a predictable response to the disaster.

“It is natural for the shares of hydropower companies operating in devastated areas to fall,” he said. “Non-life insurers also face major payouts. But reconstruction will eventually begin, and that will increase investment and demand.”

On Thursday, Upper Hewakhola fell 9.45 percent, Trishuli Jalvidyut 9.23 percent, Emerging Nepal 8.38 percent, Rasuwagadhi Hydropower 8.38 percent, Upper Mailung Khola 8 percent, Mailung Khola Jalvidyut 7.75 percent and Chilime Hydropower 5.15 percent.

Construction-related companies moved in the opposite direction. Sarbottam Paints rose 15 percent, followed by Ghorahi Cement at 8.19 percent, Sonapur Minerals and Oil at 5.05 percent, Bhagawati Hydropower at 4.72 percent, Palpa Cement at 4.53 percent and Shivam Cement at 4.17 percent.
Sijapati said the decline in hydropower shares would not necessarily extend across the entire sector, as companies outside the disaster zone remained largely unaffected.
He added, however, that broader investor confidence remained fragile, partly because of government policies and uncertainty surrounding the economic impact of the disaster.
He recalled similar market behaviour after Nepal’s devastating earthquake, when shares of cement companies rose on expectations of increased reconstruction activity.

The life insurance sector could also face pressure because travel insurance is mandatory for pilgrims undertaking the Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimage and the disaster has resulted in significant loss of life, he said. /dl

articles.summary: QUEZON, Bukidnon — The municipality of Quezon, Bukidnon, is in mourning following the passing of former Mayor Gregorio Lloren Gue. He passed away on Aug. 27 in Davao City. Gue died of heart disease,…

blocks.text: QUEZON, Bukidnon — The municipality of Quezon, Bukidnon, is in mourning following the passing of former Mayor Gregorio Lloren Gue.
He passed away on Aug. 27 in Davao City.

Gue died of heart disease, leaving an 18-year legacy of development that transformed Quezon through projects like a new municipal hall, securing 37 hectares of land for local government use, and earning the tribal title “Datu Makapukaw” in 2011 for supporting the Manobo community.
Datu Makapukaw means a “leader who awakens or inspires.”

His remains will arrive in Quezon on Monday, Aug. 31, at 2 a.m., with wakes scheduled in Quezon from Aug. 31 to Sept. 2 and in Cagayan de Oro City from Sept. 3 to 5, followed by his interment on Sept. 6. /mcm

articles.title: [Finterest] Meet the young Filipina teaching AI to read crumpled payslips for loans
articles.summary: Built to help lenders make sense of messy financial records, Carmel Limcaoco and Rhea Malhotra's Kita has processed over $130 million in loan volume and raised $4.5 million in seed funding

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – A loan application in the Philippines doesn’t always come with crisp bank statements and complete payslips.

It may instead be a blurry rural bank form, a handwritten record folded one too many times, or screenshots of GCash transactions from someone outside the formal banking system. But somewhere in that jumble could be evidence that the borrower can repay.
Young Filipino founder Carmel Limcaoco wants AI to do the digging.

Limcaoco and her co-founder — longtime best friend and Stanford classmate Rhea Malhotra — founded Kita, an artificial intelligence platform that helps banks, fintech companies, microfinance institutions, and other lenders process loan applications.

Kita is not a lender. Working behind the scenes, its “AI credit officer” requests documents based on a borrower’s circumstances, spots missing information, and follows up through Viber, WhatsApp, or SMS.
“Lenders in the Philippines face two problems at once. They are badly backlogged, and they lack sufficient data to decide with confidence. We address both,” Limcaoco told Rappler in an interview.

Kita said its technology can read more than 50 types of documents, from PDFs and e-wallet screenshots to handwritten notes and photos of crumpled paper. Using vision-language models, it can understand Tagalog, Taglish, and Cebuano, alongside Spanish, Bahasa, and other languages.
“We read documents the way a person does, from what is on the page, so a rural bank’s handwritten passbook or a format nobody has encoded works on first submission,” Limcaoco said.
Kita extracts the figures, flags inconsistencies, applies the lender’s credit rules, and drafts a credit memo for human review. Each figure is linked back to its source document.
In its first five months, Kita said it processed more than $130 million in loan volume, over 60% of it from the Philippines.

One client is TRBank, a rural bank whose four years of lending history sat in thousands of paper folders. Kita said it converted the archive into searchable data in under three days, with accuracy verified at above 97%.
Kita began with a friendship, a shared one-bedroom apartment in Boston, and eventually, a trip to Manila.

Limcaoco and Malhotra met in 2020, when the pandemic threw them into unusually close quarters. They later studied computer science at Stanford and began searching for something they could build together. In Manila, they found it in an unlikely place: loan paperwork.

Raised in Manila, Limcaoco received United Nations recognition at 16 for her work with One Million Lights Philippines. She later studied at Stanford, worked on audio and music products at Apple, and helped launch Kaya Founders’ fellowship for aspiring product managers.
Malhotra entered research at 13, contributed to Pfizer’s COVID-19 vaccine effort at 17, and studied computer vision and robotics at Stanford. She deferred a Princeton doctorate in AI to build Kita.

blocks.caption: START-UP. Founders Rhea Malhotra (left) and Carmel Limcaoco (right). Photo by Kita

blocks.text: That pedigree has attracted some heavyweight believers. Kita raised $4.5 million in a seed round led by BoxGroup, with Lisa Gokongwei-Cheng joining as an angel investor alongside Kaya Founders, the venture capital firm she co-founded and whose funds her family helped anchor. Other backers include Apex Star Capital, the family office of Xiaomi co-founder Lin Bin.

Kita also passed through Y Combinator, the start-up kingmaker that backed Reddit, Airbnb, and Stripe at their earliest stages. The company says Limcaoco is the first Filipina founder admitted to YC in over five years.

But competition is already brewing, sometimes under the same investor’s roof. Kaya Founders also backs Moneta, an AI platform that helps banks analyze corporate borrowers’ documents and produce lender-ready credit assessments. Not exactly the same but pretty close to Kita’s turf.
Limcaoco isn’t too bothered.
“We would expect any fund serious about fintech infrastructure to look at more than one company in a category this size,” she said.

She argues that Kita stands apart by reading unfamiliar formats without advance configuration, tracing every output to its source, and choosing “the hardest path first” by working with traditional banks and large microlenders carrying decades of legacy records.

Kita will remain close to San Francisco’s AI talent pool while hiring in the Philippines, where it says it is investing most deliberately. Its new funding will expand its engineering team and strengthen its underwriting and fraud-detection tools as it pursues customers across Southeast Asia, Latin America, the US, and Africa.
“A rural bank in the Philippines and a microlender in Mexico are not the same institution, but the sequence they move through is similar enough that lessons carry,” Limcaoco said.

Even with those global ambitions, the founders draw a line around what the technology should do. Yes, AI can read the rumpled notes, find the missing figures, and write a digestible credit memo. Tedious work, but largely routine.
What AI should not have is the final word on a decision that could shape someone’s financial future.
“Decisions that deeply affect people’s livelihoods should always involve human oversight,” Malhotra said. – Rappler.com
Finterest is Rappler’s series that demystifies the world of money and gives practical advice on managing your personal finances.

articles.title: Nepal issues fresh flood warning as 3,000 still missing
articles.summary: Rescuers are trying to reach dozens of hydropower workers trapped in flooded tunnels, but have been hampered by further rainfall.

image.caption: Several countries and the European Union have pledged millions in aidImage: Lhasa fire/Xinhua/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The combined death toll from the devastating floods in Nepal and Tibet rose to 750 on Sunday, with more than 3,000 people still missing, authorities said.
A fresh flood alert was issued after river levels rose again, while Tibetan authorities warned of a new barrier lake forming behind landslide debris.
Several scientists believe a glacier collapse in the Himalayas may have triggered Wednesday's disaster, sending huge volumes of water down a river valley.
Nepal flood survivors still searching for some 3,000 missing
What's the latest on the floods?
Nepal's disaster authority put the number killed on its side of the border at 734, while Chinese state media confirmed 16 dead in Tibet, an autonomous region of China.
Chinese authorities said the dead included over a hundred Nepalis and people from more than a dozen countries.
The Nepalese disaster agency issued a warning for fresh floods on Sunday and told residents around the Bhotekoshi River to remain on high alert as water levels rose.
Flood warning notices were sent to residents' phones, advising them to move to higher ground.
On the Tibet side, Chinese state media said monitoring drones on Saturday night had picked up a new lake forming from a barrier created by a landslide near the Gyirong border port.
Rescue teams near the Gyirong border port were moved because of the risk of the barrier bursting.

blocks.caption: Nepal's disaster agency has issued a warning for fresh floodsImage: Rajesh Kumar Singh/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Hydropower workers still trapped in tunnels
Meanwhile, Nepalese rescuers are trying to reach more than 100 hydropower workers believed trapped and still alive in tunnels swamped by flood debris.
Rescue teams are focusing on several hydropower projects on the Trishuli River, where more than 900 workers went missing during the floods.
At one of the sites on Saturday night, army teams used drills to break into the upper part of a mud-swamped tunnel to pump oxygen and deliver a camera inside.

Nepal's prime minister's office said that teams faced "continuous rainfall and difficult conditions" but had worked nonstop overnight, "making tireless efforts to search for and rescue those who may be trapped."

blocks.caption: Several thousand people remain missing, four days after the floods hitImage: Niranjan Shrestha/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Rescue effort bolstered by neighbors
Specialized teams from India and China have joined the rescue effort, along with Nepal's mountain rescue squad, which helps climbers on the world's highest peaks, including Everest.
Nepalese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lok Bahadur Chhetri said the country needed assistance in such areas as tunnel rescue, DNA testing and identifying the victims.

The US State Department wrote on X that it would provide $3.6 million (€3.1 million) in "life-saving humanitarian assistance" to Nepal, including up to three months of emergency food aid for up to 10,000 flood-affected households.
The ⁠Red Cross estimates that more than 90,000 people are likely to have been affected by the disaster.

articles.title: Filipino students win 1 silver, 3 bronze medals in international AI olympiad
articles.summary: Four Filipino high school students won one silver and three bronze medals in the Philippines’ debut at the International Olympiad in Artificial Intelligence (IOAI) held in Astana, Kazakhstan from…

blocks.text: AI OLYMPIAD MEDALISTS—The Philippines’ first delegation to the 2026 International Olympiad in Artificial Intelligence (IOAI) displays the national flag after all four students won medals. Shown from left are bronze medalist Jhareign S. Solidum of University of Mindanao Ilang High School; silver medalist Theo Lorenzo T. Bustamante of Philippine Science High School–CALABARZON Region Campus; team leader Martin Gomez; and bronze medalists Juan Mateo J. Desuasido of Brent International School Manila and Ellison Matthew S. Ang of Philippine Science High School–Main Campus. (PHOTO: IOAI Philippines)

Four Filipino high school students won one silver and three bronze medals in the Philippines’ debut at the International Olympiad in Artificial Intelligence (IOAI) held in Astana, Kazakhstan from Aug. 2 to 8.
The week-long competition drew 466 high school students from 108 countries and territories.
Now in its third year, the IOAI tests students in machine learning, computer vision, natural language processing, and multimodal processing.
Theo Lorenzo T. Bustamante of Philippine Science High School–CALABARZON Region Campus won the silver medal.

Ellison Matthew S. Ang of Philippine Science High School–Main Campus, Juan Mateo J. Desuasido of Brent International School Manila, and Jhareign S. Solidum of University of Mindanao Ilang High School each won a bronze medal.
Their results gave the four-member Philippine delegation a 100-percent medal rate.
Bustamante ranked 80th overall, placing him among the top 17 percent of competitors.
The Philippines was also among only 11 of the 18 countries that debuted in the IOAI in 2026 to win at least one silver medal.
Overall, the competition awarded 37 gold, 73 silver, and 110 bronze medals.
“A 100% medal rate on our global debut proves that Philippine talent can immediately compete at the highest level of international AI,” IOAI PH Executive Director and Team Leader Martin Gomez said.
The students qualified through a merit-based national screening process, with participation offered free of charge.

They were selected, trained, and managed by International Olympiad in Artificial Intelligence Philippines (IOAI PH), which is hosted by the Ateneo Business Insights Laboratory for Development (BUILD) under the John Gokongwei School of Management of Ateneo de Manila University.

Over a 10-month period, Ateneo BUILD provided the Philippine team with cloud testing infrastructure and proctoring environments. It also conducted intensive, expert-led boot camps covering machine learning theory, computer vision, natural language processing, audio processing, and VRAM constraint optimization.

“Outranking competitors from traditional global STEM powerhouses in our very first year establishes a baseline for what our students can accomplish with structured training, corporate backing, and national support,” Gomez said.

“This victory is a shared triumph made possible by the tireless dedication of our coaches, the academic foundation of our schools, the sacrifices of our families, and the whole-of-nation backing of our community,” he added.
The IOAI Board and Committee provided full financial assistance covering the delegation’s travel, lodging, meals, and registration.
Government support came through the Office of the President, Office of the Executive Secretary, Department of Education, and Department of Science and Technology–Science Education Institute.

Held under the patronage of the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO), the IOAI was hosted by the Kazakhstan Competitive Programming Federation with support from Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development and Ministry of Education.
Singapore will host the fourth IOAI in 2027.

articles.title: Dizon relieves Las Piñas–Muntinlupa District Eng’g Office maintenance chief over ‘unsatisfactory performance’
articles.summary: Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) Secretary Vivencio “Vince” Dizon has relieved the maintenance chief of the Las Piñas–Muntinlupa District Engineering Office over repeated reports of…

blocks.text: (DPWH PHOTO)

Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) Secretary Vivencio “Vince” Dizon has relieved the maintenance chief of the Las Piñas–Muntinlupa District Engineering Office over repeated reports of unsatisfactory performance and delayed response to calamities.
In a memorandum dated Aug. 29, Dizon ordered the immediate relief of Engr. Loreto C. Balena Jr. from his duties as maintenance chief.

“In view of repeated reports concerning your unsatisfactory performance, lack of urgency, and delayed response to calamities, you are hereby relieved of your duties as Maintenance Chief of the Las Piñas–Muntinlupa District Engineering Office, effective immediately,” it stated.
As such, the DPWH chief directed Balena to complete and sign all pending documents and deliverables to ensure the uninterrupted delivery of public services.

“To ensure the uninterrupted delivery of public service, you are directed to conduct an inventory, accomplish, complete, and sign all pending documents and deliverables, and formally turn over all official records, papers, and properties in your custody to the appropriate office,” the memorandum read.
Dizon said the order superseded previous issuances to the contrary and directed Balena to strictly comply with it.
A copy of the memorandum was furnished to Engr. Ryan N. Dela Cruz, officer-in-charge of the Office of the District Engineer.

articles.title: PCG: Last missing Aeta passenger in Lake Mapanuepe tragedy in Zambales found dead
articles.summary: The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) confirmed Sunday, August 30, that the body of the final passenger who went missing after a boat sank in Mapanuepe Lake in San Marcelino, Zambales, has been recovered.…

blocks.text: At A Glance

items: The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) recovered the body of a 26-year-old Aeta woman, the final missing passenger from the Mapanuepe Lake boat tragedy, at around 11:20 a.m. Sunday, Aug. 30.
The Aug. 27 incident killed nine of the 13 Aeta passengers, including three adults and six minors. Four others survived.
The group had traveled to Barangay Buhawen for food, medicine and vaccinations before strong winds and waves struck their boat while they were returning to Sitio Lumibao.

blocks.text: Search and rescue personnel from the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) recover the lifeless body of the last missing passenger from a capsized motorboat in Mapanuepe Lake, San Marcelino, Zambales, on August 30, 2026. The tragedy has now claimed nine lives, including three adults and six minors, making it one of the deadliest incidents in the area in recent years. (Photo: Philippine Coast Guard)
The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) confirmed Sunday, August 30, that the body of the final passenger who went missing after a boat sank in Mapanuepe Lake in San Marcelino, Zambales, has been recovered.

PCG spokesperson Commodore Noemie Cayabyab said the search and rescue (SAR) team found the body of the 26-year-old female passenger off the coast of Sitio Naban in Barangay Buhawen, where the boat sank, at around 11:20 a.m.
“The cadaver was found at 11:20 a.m. today, 1,100 meters from the location of the subject motorbanca,” Cayabyab said.
The tragedy has now claimed nine lives, including three adults and six minors, making it one of the deadliest incidents in the area in recent years.
To recall, a motorboat carrying 13 members of the Aeta community from Sitio Lumibao capsized and sank in Mapanuepe Lake on Aug. 27.
The group had traveled to Barangay Buhawen to obtain food, medicine and vaccinations. They were on their way home when strong winds and waves struck the boat.
Six people were initially confirmed dead on Aug. 28, while four others were rescued. Two children were found dead on Aug. 29, with their bodies later identified by their fathers.
Mapanuepe Lake was formed after the 1991 Mount Pinatubo eruption, which blocked river channels and created a deep body of water in San Marcelino.
