articles.title: Las Piñas maintenance chief axed over 'slow' calamity response
articles.summary: Slow response to calamities has cost a DPWH district maintenance chief his post.

blocks.text: A Las Piñas Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office 6x6 truck is deployed to assist stranded individuals through floodwaters at Zapote Junction amid heavy rain.
Las Piñas LGU / Released

MANILA, Philippines — Public Works Secretary Vince Dizon relieved the maintenance chief of the DPWH Las Piñas-Muntinlupa District Engineering Office over repeated reports of slow response to calamities and lack of urgency as Metro Manila continues to bear the brunt of continuous rainfall and flooding.
In a memorandum dated August 29, Dizon ordered the immediate relief of engineer Loreto Balena Jr. as maintenance chief.

"In view of repeated reports concerning your unsatisfactory performance, lack of urgency, and delayed response to calamities, you are hereby relieved of your duties as Maintenance Chief of the Las Piñas-Muntinlupa District Engineering Office, effective immediately," Dizon said in the memo.
Balena was directed to complete an inventory, sign and finish pending documents and deliverables, and turn over official records, papers and government properties in his custody.
The Department of Public Works and Highways said the action followed President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.'s directive to remove officials who neglect their duties and tighten discipline within the agency.

articles.title: DepEd: Over 9,800 classrooms damaged by ‘habagat,’ enhanced by cyclones
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Over 9,800 classrooms sustained damage due to the combined effects of the southwest monsoon or “habagat,” enhanced by tropical cyclones Luis, Maymay, Neneng, and Obet, according…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Over 9,800 classrooms sustained damage due to the combined effects of the southwest monsoon or “habagat,” enhanced by tropical cyclones Luis, Maymay, Neneng, and Obet, according to the Department of Education’s (DepEd) latest situation report.
As of 8 a.m. on Sunday, the assessment covered 5,731 classrooms with minor damage, 2,055 with major damage, and 2,083 totally damaged.
This brings a total of 9,869 damaged classrooms.
Central Luzon recorded the highest number of affected schools at 3,732, followed by Region I with 2,746 and the Cordillera Administrative Region with 1,266.
DepEd estimated that P280 million is needed for minor repairs, P1 billion for major repairs, and P5.2 billion for the reconstruction of affected schools.
DepEd also said that 59 schools experienced flooding, including 47 in Central Luzon.
Meanwhile, 348 schools with 1,309 classrooms are being used as evacuation centers, accommodating 11,320 families.

DepEd’s Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Service (DRRMS) said it was closely coordinating with field offices to monitor emerging impacts and facilitate the clearing and repair of damaged schools.
The DRRMS also “validates class suspension data through the ‘Walang Pasok’ Monitor.”

Amid growing concerns over prolonged class suspensions, DepEd earlier proposed giving school heads the authority to determine whether it is safe to resume face-to-face classes during inclement weather.
DepEd submitted a draft executive order to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. after three weeks of monsoon rains triggered widespread flooding and landslides. /das

articles.title: Palace backs Marcos over singing at wife’s birthday amid floods
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Malacañang on Sunday defended President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. over a viral video showing him singing during a post-birthday celebration for First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos at…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Malacañang on Sunday defended President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. over a viral video showing him singing during a post-birthday celebration for First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos at their home in Makati City, while several parts of Luzon were flooded by heavy rains.

Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said Marcos has been closely monitoring the situation and directed government agencies to urgently respond to communities affected by the continuous downpour, despite spending time with his family.
“The president is the president wherever he may be. Spending a few hours with his family does not mean that he has stopped performing his duties or that government operations have ceased,” she added.

In the video, Marcos was seen serenading his wife with Basil Valdez’s “You” and The Beatles’ “And I Love Her” during her birthday celebration at their home on Aug. 26, not Aug. 29, as the administration’s critics were implying.
The first lady turned 67 on Aug. 21.
Based on the weather bureau’s forecast for the evening of Aug. 26, the southwest monsoon was expected to bring gloomy skies with scattered rains over Luzon and Western Visayas.
A yellow rainfall warning was raised over Zambales, with 50 to 100 millimeters of rain forecast.
The video was originally posted by former Vigan City Mayor Jose “Bonito” Singson Jr. on his Facebook account on Aug. 28, two days after the celebration.
It had been reposted by critics of the administration, including supporters of Vice President Sara Duterte and her family, since Saturday.
They said it was offensive and ill-timed for Marcos to be singing while many parts of Luzon were reeling from heavy flooding brought by month-long rains.
Floods and landslides triggered by monsoon rains and enhanced by four weather disturbances so far this month have left more than 30 people dead, mostly in Luzon.
Nine Aetas in Zambales and Pampanga and two workers at Subic Bay Freeport were among the latest fatalities confirmed on Saturday.

“Luzon is drowning. Families are trapped. Children are being rescued from floodwaters. People are literally fighting to survive. And somewhere above all that chaos, our president is singing like everything is perfectly fine,” posted Mary Ann, a Duterte supporter with almost 200,000 followers on Facebook.
She called Marcos “unbothered, untouched and detached [from reality].”
“While ordinary Filipinos are wading through floodwater just to save their families, our highest leader seems more concerned with keeping the mood light,” she said.
“Terrifying picture of leadership,” she added. /mcm

articles.title: Learning from cooperatives: Key lessons for media viability
articles.summary: How do we build trust and support among our audiences and sustain it? How can we diversify revenue streams without compromising editorial independence? How can democratic decision-making be…

blocks.text: How do we build trust and support among our audiences and sustain it? How can we diversify revenue streams without compromising editorial independence? How can democratic decision-making be maintained as a media organization grows and needs to move faster?

At the 14th edition of Festival Gabo, the most important gathering of journalists in Latin America, DW Akademie created spaces for reflection and discussion on the viability of journalism today. Journalists, founders of independent and community media outlets and media practitioners from across the region, including Colombia, Brazil, Venezuela, Bolivia and Argentina, explored independent journalism approaches. Particular attention was given to media cooperatives.

blocks.caption: Participants exchange ideas during one of the workshop sessions. Image: Benedikt Borchers/DW Akademie

blocks.text: “What characterizes cooperative media is their boldness,” said Ernesto Lamas, researcher and community radio pioneer from Argentina. “They aren’t afraid of new technologies or AI, while always remaining aware of the risks. They create media with their own rules, defining their own topics and aesthetics and find deep satisfaction in that editorial freedom.”

Lamas also gave a preview on an upcoming DW Akademie study, scheduled for publication at the end of 2026. Lamas conducted a series of interviews with representatives of media organizations organized according to cooperative principles — media organizations that operate on a non-profit basis and are oriented toward the public good. They seek to guarantee decent working conditions and employee participation in decision-making, while dedicating significant efforts to building active connections with their communities.
From TV to loans to funerals

William Galindo is director of Viboral TV, a local television channel located in a rural community in Colombia. The channel is part of a cooperative that offers various services to its members, including affordable credit, funeral services and internet access.

blocks.caption: From left to right, Ernesto Lamas, University of Buenos Aires, Gemma Terés Arilla, taz Panter Foundation, William Alberto Galindo Muñoz, Cooperativa Viboral Telecomunicaciones, Luis Rómboli, Cooperativa La Diaria, and Michelle Nogales Cardozo, Muy Waso, reflect on how to build sustainable media.…

blocks.text: According to Gallindo, being a cooperative means operating under strict state oversight and therefore requires highly organized administrative and financial management. The reward for these efforts is strong institutional recognition, which can translate into support from other entities, including financing.

The cooperative provides stability for the television channel and, according to Gallindo, the community media outlet is also a major asset for the cooperative because it reflects community life: local festivals, football matches and also local politics. Journalists are not afraid to criticize politicians because they do not depend on government funding. Instead, the channel is sustained through member subscriptions.
For , community is at the center of their work.
“92% of our revenue comes from subscriptions. We have a very close relationship with our community, with constant two-way communication,” Rómboli explained.

blocks.caption: Luis Rómboli, president of the La Diaria cooperative in Uruguay. Image: Benedikt Borchers/DW Akademie

blocks.text: Every day, the La Diaria newspaper sends a newsletter to 250,000 people. The newspaper transitioned to a cooperative in 2006 and during this process, received support from the German taz Panter Foundation. The foundation is part of the German newspaper taz – die tageszeitung, a longstanding example of cooperative journalism that emerged from the left-wing social movements of the 1970s in Germany.
“You don’t just have readers — you have a committed community,” said Gemma Terés Arilla, director of the taz Panter Foundation.

Agencia Mosquetero brought that relationship to a co-creational level. It is a communications and content agency affiliated with the alternative Colombian media collective El Cuarto Mosquetero, founded as a sustainable model to provide journalistic and creative services to organizations, unions and companies.

“Our greatest achievement is co-creating content with communities,” said Alejandra Mayorga, editor at El Cuarto Mosquetero. “Media viability requires diversifying revenue streams according to each media outlet’s reality, with editorial independence and transparency as fundamental principles.”
Tremendous challenges in a volatile environment

In some countries, bureaucratic barriers make it more difficult to establish a cooperative. Bolivia is one such example and one of the reasons why Muy Waso, a feminist community media platform, chose to establish a foundation instead. Nevertheless, their model is based on collective decision-making, as co-founder Michelle Nogales Cardozo stressed.

blocks.caption: Michelle Nogales Cardozo, Co-founder of Bolivia’s Muy Waso Image: Benedikt Borchers/DW Akademie

blocks.text: In a world of increasingly rapid change, media organizations must redefine their strategies in order to survive and fulfill their role in society. Cooperative models offer an alternative for those seeking to build media organizations with a social purpose.
1. Sustainability is about more than money
Participants viewed sustainability as not only an economic challenge, but also a social and political one.
2. Communities can be a crucial source of support
Strengthening relationships with audiences helps build trust and long-term support.
3. Revenue diversification and independence can go hand in hand
Cooperative models aim to balance financial viability with editorial autonomy.
4. There is no single cooperative model
Some media organizations embrace cooperative principles without necessarily adopting a cooperative legal structure.
5. Legal contexts matter
National regulations can either facilitate or complicate the creation of cooperatives.
6. Democratic governance requires effort
Maintaining participatory decision-making becomes more challenging as organizations grow.
7. Cooperatives can provide stability
The experience of Viboral TV shows how cooperative backing can strengthen the sustainability of community media.
8. Community support reinforces editorial independence
Membership and subscriber-based models can reduce reliance on other funding sources.
9. Audience engagement is a strategic asset
Experiences such as La Diaria demonstrate that involving communities can be a key factor in success.
10. Cooperative journalism deserves attention
Although it is not the only solution for the media sector, it offers valuable lessons for organizations committed to serving the public good. /dl

articles.title: P569-M flood-control structures in Zambales damaged amid heavy rains
articles.summary: SAN ANTONIO, Zambales — Flood-control structures in Zambales bore the brunt of the recent heavy rains, with damage to dikes, revetments and slope protection facilities now estimated at P569.27…

blocks.text: SAN ANTONIO, Zambales — Flood-control structures in Zambales bore the brunt of the recent heavy rains, with damage to dikes, revetments and slope protection facilities now estimated at P569.27 million, based on government data.

According to the latest combined assessment by the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) 1st and 2nd district, an estimated P1.28 billion is needed for the recovery, rehabilitation and reconstruction of the damaged infrastructure.
The DPWH 1st District recorded the larger share of the damage at P472.42 million, with the cost of recovery and reconstruction estimated at P1.17 billion.
An initial assessment showed that several flood-control structures were totally damaged, including multiple sections of the Bucao River Dike 7 in Barangay San Juan, Botolan.
The damaged sections involve a combined stretch of more than 3 kilometers of slope protection, based on the lengths listed in the DPWH assessment.
Other totally damaged slope protection structures were reported along the Tapuac River in Masinloc; Tanguay River and Kiling River in Cabangan; Bancal River in Botolan; and Dalayap Creek in Cabangan.
The DPWH 2nd District, meanwhile, recorded P96.85 million in damage, with P114 million estimated for recovery and reconstruction.

Among the structures listed as damaged were the Tamayok River revetment in Barangay Mangan-Vaca, Subic; three sections of the Matain River revetment in Barangay San Isidro, Subic; and the Sto. Tomas River revetment in Barangay Sta. Fe, San Marcelino.
The Sto. Tomas River structure was reported totally damaged, with both the dike and concrete revetment collapsing.
294 houses damaged
The latest provincial report also showed that 294 houses had been either damaged or destroyed as of Aug. 29. Of the total, 264 were damaged while 30 were destroyed.
Subic recorded the highest number of damaged houses at 165, followed by San Marcelino with 37, San Antonio with 33, and Palauig with 29.
Sta. Cruz reported 21 damaged houses, while Cabangan recorded 14.

Zambales continues to reel from widespread flooding that affected communities across the province. More than 14,000 fled their flooded homes and are now staying in evacuation centers or other safer areas.
The provincial board earlier approved the declaration of a state of calamity in Zambales amid the extent of damage caused by the recent weather disturbances. /mcm

articles.title: Nepali Army rescues 2,697 people from flood-hit Rasuwa
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — The Nepali Army has rescued 2,697 people affected by flooding in Rasuwa district as of 7am on Sunday, using helicopters and ground teams. A total of 2,497 people, including 216…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — The Nepali Army has rescued 2,697 people affected by flooding in Rasuwa district as of 7am on Sunday, using helicopters and ground teams.

A total of 2,497 people, including 216 foreign nationals, were evacuated by air from Timure, Syabrubesi, Dhunche and Mailung. The foreign nationals rescued include 121 Indians, 72 Chinese, 15 South Koreans, four Germans, two Americans, two Italians and one Omani. Ground teams rescued another 200 people, said the Nepali Army.
More than 8,300 Nepali Army personnel have been deployed across affected districts and are working in coordination with other agencies.

Meanwhile, efforts to locate the entrance to the 3A tunnel of the Trishuli Hydropower Project were temporarily halted after heavy rainfall from around 2am caused water levels to rise and flooded excavation areas. /dl

articles.title: 3-year-old boy stabbed dead allegedy by father in Ilocos Sur
articles.summary: SAN ILDEFONSO, Ilocos Sur, Philippines — A 3-year-old boy died after he was allegedly stabbed by his father inside their home in Barangay Lacong, Tagudin, Ilocos Sur, on Friday, Aug. 28, police said.…

blocks.text: SAN ILDEFONSO, Ilocos Sur, Philippines — A 3-year-old boy died after he was allegedly stabbed by his father inside their home in Barangay Lacong, Tagudin, Ilocos Sur, on Friday, Aug. 28, police said.
The suspect, the victim’s 29-year-old father, is also a resident of the town.
Initial reports said the victim’s grandmother and aunt heard the father berating the child at around 1 a.m. that day.
At about 11 a.m. the same day, the grandmother noticed that her grandson had not yet come out of their room.
She opened the room and found the child wrapped in a blanket. When she uncovered him, she saw that he had sustained a stab wound to the chest.
The child was immediately rushed to a hospital but was declared dead on arrival.
The suspect reportedly fled their home after the incident, and initial reports indicated the alleged weapon was not found at the crime scene.
Authorities were continuing efforts to locate and arrest the suspect. —Kenneth P. Tabin (Contributor)

blocks.text: The Pasay City Health Office has raised Code White effective Aug. 29, placing all health personnel on heightened alert as Habagat rains persist and pose risks to residents.
Pasay City Health Office raises Code White, placing health personnel on standby amid continuing Habagat rains. (Photo from Pasay PIO)
Mayor Emi Calixto-Rubiano has directed city health personnel to remain vigilant and ready to respond to any medical or public health emergency.
The alert will remain in effect until further notice.
Health center staff, along with the city’s water, sanitation and hygiene, and nutrition teams, were ordered to remain on call as authorities prepare for possible emergencies due to the ongoing rains.
The health office is also coordinating with other government agencies to ensure a quick and unified response should weather-related health emergencies arise.
Residents were urged to stay alert and follow government advisories as the Habagat continues to affect the city.

articles.title: Renee was at Gyirong Port minutes before flood struck, now her family want to travel from Australia to help search
articles.summary: Missing woman’s partner and daughters fundraise to join search in one of the hardest-hit areas of Nepal

blocks.text: Clair Spry says her sister would hate the attention. She would want it focused on the Nepali people, who have been displaced or are in need of aid. She would want it to be on the impact of the climate crisis, especially on the world’s most economically vulnerable populations.

“Her focus right now would not be on her; it would be on the families,” Spry said. “So many people, the Nepalese people, that have been horribly displaced and traumatised. She would want the attention on them and how we are going to help them.

“And global warming. This is something the poorest people of the world are affected by. It’s not the New Yorkers, it’s the people who are in these parts of the world. For Renee, that would be heartbreaking.”

blocks.caption: Renee, an Australian, was travelling in Nepal and is now missing.  Photograph: GoFundMe

blocks.text: Like many of the missing Australians, Renee arrived at Gyirong Port just 10 minutes before the flood struck. The area was one of the hardest hit – images from Chinese rescue teams show the area completely flattened. Huge buildings, power lines, everything – just wiped away.
Renee is a disability support worker who lives on the Sunshine Coast. She has been with her partner, Shaun, an emergency nurse, since they were 15, and they share two daughters in their 20s.
Clair has set up a GoFundMe to get the three of them over to Nepal – Shaun wants to travel to the port to try to find any signs of her. And their daughters, Lily and Ruby, don’t want him to go alone.
“Their first reaction is, we have to go. The practicalities, and what can actually be done in the first few days, it hasn’t been possible [to enter the area], but they still want to go,” she said.
“And if they are able to find her, to bring her home.”
Renee’s family understand how dire the situation is, and how unlikely it is that she, or anyone in that same area, survived. But until they know for certain, they would hold hope, she said.

“Everyone’s very realistic. We know how bad this was and where she was. But until they find her, everyone’s got this little slither of hope that maybe she’s stuck somewhere and can’t get out, or she’s injured.
“I’ve been looking through pictures trying to identify someone or see her. But we understand the reality of this situation.”
Like most Australians, Renee had come to Nepal on a pilgrimage. Spry said her sister was a “deeply spiritual” person who loved to help people.
“She had two degrees, and she chose to do something that was … a completely selfless vocation. Her priority was always other people,” she said.
“Every person she touched, they knew her love and kindness. She would be so uncomfortable with all this.”
The family of Michael Keats, an Australian who had been near the Tibet-Nepal border when flash flooding began, confirmed his death in posts to social media on Sunday.
Keats’s wife, Emily Boyd, said on Instagram he had been on a pilgrimage to Mt Kailash that had been a “dream for many years”.
“Mike went on a pilgrimage to Mt Kailash seeking enlightenment,” Boyd said.
“There’s a bittersweetness knowing that there was nothing more that Mike wanted then to know God, and to merge with the divine.

”He was a mystic, a medicine man, a teacher, leader, partner, father, brother, son, uncle and dearly beloved friend. He showed up for so many people in so many ways. A heart of pure gold. We love you forever and always.”

articles.title: Marcos keeping track of Pinoys amid widespread flooding, Palace says
articles.summary: Malacañang said President Marcos is closely monitoring the situation of Filipinos affected by the intense flooding in various areas in the country. "Laging tutok ang Pangulo sa sitwasyon. Minomonitor…

blocks.text: Malacañang said President Marcos is closely monitoring the situation of Filipinos affected by the intense flooding in various areas in the country.

"Laging tutok ang Pangulo sa sitwasyon. Minomonitor ang kalagayan ng mga kababayan natin at ng mga bayan na apektado (The President is always closely monitoring the situation. He is keeping track of the condition of our fellow Filipinos and the towns affected)," Palace Press Officer and Communications Undersecretary Claire Castro said in a statement on Sunday, Aug. 30.
According to Castro, Marcos has directed and reminded government agencies to respond quickly to the needs of the victims affected by the heavy rainfall.

The Palace official's statement came amid criticisms against the President after a video of him singing during First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos' birthday celebration on Aug. 26 surfaced on social media.
It drew attention online as parts of Luzon grapple with widespread flooding due to continued heavy rains.
Castro stressed that spending some time for his family does not mean Marcos is neglecting his duties.

"Ang Pangulo ay Pangulo saan man siya naroroon. Ang paglalaan ng ilang oras para sa kanyang pamilya ay hindi nangangahulugang tumitigil ang kanyang tungkulin o ang operasyon ng pamahalaan (The President is the President wherever he may be. Setting aside some time for his family does not mean that he is neglecting his duties or that the government’s operations have come to a halt)," Castro said.
She assured the public that he continues to monitor the situation.

"Sa gitna ng matinding pag-ulan, patuloy ang kanyang pagbabantay at pag-uutos sa mga ahensya upang matiyak ang kaligtasan at agarang pagtulong sa ating mga kababayan (Amid the heavy rains, he continues to monitor the situation and direct government agencies to ensure the safety of our fellow Filipinos and provide immediate assistance to those in need)," Castro said.
Parts of the National Capital Region (NCR), Central Luzon, and other nearby regions experience severe flooding caused by relentless downpours due to the enhanced southwest monsoon or habagat.
The Office of Civil Defense (OCD) said 2.3 million families or 8.1 million individuals were affected by the enhanced southwest monsoon, with 646 areas flooded across seven regions.

articles.title: Erwin Tulfo pushes for amendments to Oil Deregulation law to include oil pricing transparency
articles.summary: Senator Erwin Tulfo said on Sunday, August 30 that he is resolute in amending the outdated Oil Deregulation Law to mandate pricing transparency among Philippine oil companies. The Senate Committee on…

blocks.text: Senator Erwin Tulfo said on Sunday, August 30 that he is resolute in amending the outdated Oil Deregulation Law to mandate pricing transparency among Philippine oil companies.

Sen. Erwin Tulfo reiterates his call for the removal of the system loss charge, pointing out how electric cooperatives became complacent in upgrading their facilities because the Electric Power Industry Reform Act (EPIRA) enables them to pass on the system loss charge to consumers. (Senate PRIB photo)

The Senate Committee on Energy chairman said transparency in oil pricing has been a longstanding concern, especially from the transport sector, as crude prices have indiscriminately increased through time, while price rollbacks remain minimal.
“The oil companies will just say ‘tomorrow, we will increase the prices by 5 pesos per liter,’ then we will have no choice but to pay,” Tulfo said.

“What we will do is we will strengthen the powers of the Department of Energy (DOE) over these companies. No more arbitrary price shocks—they will have to explain why they increase their prices in a certain way,” he stressed.
The senator also noted how the Oil Deregulation Law has been a burden to Filipinos, likening its effects to those of the Electric Power Industry Reform Act (EPIRA).
“Because of these outdated laws, system losses are being charged to the consumer,” he lamented.
“Electric companies are well-aware that they need to upgrade their systems, but they just let them deteriorate because they can easily charge those loss fees to the public,” Tulfo remarked.

While critics argue these reforms could only diminish the prices by just a few pesos, Tulfo said these are still savings considered significant by ordinary Filipino families already suffering from inflation.
“What matters is the principle. You cannot just sit idly and let the ordinary Filipinos pay for services that they did not benefit from, or pay fuel without understanding how it was priced,” he said.

articles.title: 8.1M individuals affected by ‘habagat’ as massive flooding strikes entire country – OCD
articles.summary: Severe weather systems due to the enhanced southwest monsoon (habagat) continued to batter the country, displacing 8.1 million individuals composed of 2.3 million families, as relentless downpours…

blocks.text: Severe weather systems due to the enhanced southwest monsoon (habagat) continued to batter the country, displacing 8.1 million individuals composed of 2.3 million families, as relentless downpours triggered widespread inundation and critical infrastructure failures across multiple regions.
A report from the Office of Civil Defense (OCD) on Sunday, Aug. 30, showed 646 areas were submerged in floodwaters across seven regions.
Most affected by flooding was Central Luzon (Region 3) as 402 areas in Bataan, Bulacan, Nueva Ecija, Pampanga, Tarlac, and Zambales were inundated.
In Mimaropa (Region 4B), there were 151 areas that were flooded in Occidental Mindoro, Oriental Mindoro, and Romblon.
A total of 53 areas in the National Capital Region (NCR) were also swamped by floodwaters, specifically in Malabon City, Quezon City, Valenzuela City, and Caloocan City.
There were 26 areas that were also flooded in Western Visayas (Region 6), with all those affected located in Iloilo.
In Ilocos (Region 1), seven areas were flooded, affecting Pangasinan, Dagupan, La Union, and Ilocos Sur.
Six areas were flooded in Cavite, Laguna, Rizal, and Batangas – all in Calabarzon (Region 4A).
And in Zamboanga Peninsula (Region 9), one area was flooded in Zamboanga del Sur.
Meanwhile, the death toll remained at 32, including 19 injured individuals and three missing.
The continuing rainfall has also forced 43,500 individuals or 13,500 families into 523 evacuation centers. Some 3,200 houses were damaged, including 2,800 partially damaged and 355 totally destroyed.
The OCD placed infrastructure damage at P6.16 billion and agricultural losses at P2.32 billion. Assistance extended to affected communities reached P1.69 billion.
La Mesa Dam, Marikina River overflow

OCD Deputy Administrator for Administration Assistant Secretary Bernardo Rafaelito Alejandro IV said that authorities were closely watching La Mesa Dam as it overflowed due to continued rains, raising concerns over further flooding in Metro Manila.
“We continue to monitor La Mesa Dam. Many low-lying communities in Metro Manila will be affected,” Alejandro said.

He said nearly three million residents in Quezon City alone could be affected, particularly in Fairview, Quirino Highway and San Bartolome. Flooding could also reach Caloocan, Valenzuela, Malabon and Navotas.
The Marikina River was also being monitored for a possible forced evacuation, while early warnings were being issued to communities at risk.
Rescue and evacuation efforts

As flooding affected many parts of the country, the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) deployed disaster response units to Tarlac, Pampanga, and Bataan to support local government units in relief distribution and rescue missions.
In Tarlac, the Philippine Air Force (PAF) continued its search and rescue operations after a vehicle plunged into Agana Bridge on August 29. One passenger was rescued, while four remain missing.
PAF units also assisted in evacuation operations in Paniqui, Tarlac.

Meanwhile, the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) carried out multiple humanitarian assistance and disaster response (HADR) operations as it evacuated 190 residents in Abucay, Bataan; assisted 27 individuals in Balayan, Batangas; and rescued 30 people in Olongapo City, Zambales.
Various coast guard units also conducted forced evacuations in Metro Manila, Cavite, Zambales, Bataan, and Pampanga; and evacuated families in Santa Cruz, Zambales and Agno, Pangasinan.
Meanwhile, 48 passengers were stranded while 30 vessels took shelter in various ports around the country due to the bad weather.
Enough resources
Despite weeks of monsoon rains, Alejandro said the government still had sufficient food and non-food supplies.
“We have enough resources available, both food and non-food. The DSWD still has many food items,” he said.

“The challenge now is how to replenish what we have prepositioned because they have already been used. We are planning to do augmentation. Perhaps we will wait for the rains to ease, but we are making sure helicopters and trucks are ready to move once the weather improves so we can replenish immediately,” Alejandro added.
