The death toll in Nepal and Tibet from last week’s catastrophic floods hit 750 on Sunday, August 30, with 3,044 missing, authorities said, while rescuers moved to higher ground as rain swelled river levels.

Rescue operations have been suspended several times since Friday, August 28, because of bad weather and concerns that a lake formed across the Nepal-China border by a mudslide from Wednesday’s glacier collapse could trigger fresh flooding after it began overflowing into rivers in Nepal.
The Red Cross estimates that more than 90,000 people are likely to have been affected by the disaster, which China has linked to the effects of climate change.

China’s Foreign Minister Wang Yi told his Nepalese counterpart in a Saturday telephone call that the mudslide was their “most severe cross-border disaster” in recent years and that rescue operations were of unprecedented difficulty and complexity, Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported.
Nepal’s rescue effort is now focused on hundreds of people believed to be trapped in tunnels at hydropower plants after a torrent of ice, rock, mud and debris crashed down Himalayan rivers.

Deaths in Nepal have risen to 734, with 2,498 missing and 7,514 rescued, the nation’s disaster authority said. In China, 16 people had died in Gyirong County as of Saturday evening and 546 were missing, officials in Tibet told a press conference.

Among the 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries missing on the Tibetan side were 104 from Nepal, 49 from neighboring India, as well as 33 Latvians, 18 Americans and 15 Britons, they said in China’s first breakdown by nationality.

Beijing and Kathmandu are working together to identify missing citizens and foreign nationals, as well as strengthening cooperation in disaster prevention and mitigation, and climate-change response, CCTV said.
Water levels in the Trishuli River rose on Sunday after fresh rain, prompting residents and rescue workers to seek higher ground, Nepalese police told Reuters.

Nepal says it does not need foreign help for general rescue, but Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lok Bahadur Chhetri said the country needed assistance in such areas as tunnel rescue, DNA testing, refrigerated storage for bodies and forensic identification of decomposed remains.
Indian and Chinese experts are on the ground helping efforts to open tunnels, Chhetri said.

The lake that had formed upstream and threatened rescue operations had largely drained by Saturday evening, CCTV said. But drones detected a landslide late on Saturday 2.8 km (1.7 miles) downstream of the lake, forming a new dam and a fresh pool of water, CCTV said.
The authorities relocated rescue personnel near the Gyirong border crossing to safety, the broadcaster said.
The flood was “caused by glacier instability under the long-term effects of global warming”, CCTV reported, saying it was a “new and prominent feature of cryosphere disasters” on the Tibetan plateau.

The mudslide from the Nepalese side took six to seven minutes to reach the Gyirong border crossing, CCTV said, citing the findings of Chinese scientists. Dramatic surveillance footage shared worldwide showed torrents of water and debris engulfing buildings while people tried to flee.

China has mobilized over 2,100 rescue workers and allocated at least 220 million yuan ($32.7 million) to support relief efforts. It is also providing emergency cash aid, disaster relief supplies, satellite and hydrological data and tunnel rescue experts to Nepal, CCTV said.

China used heavy-lift drones as helicopters began airdropping equipment and supplies to frontline rescuers near the border crossing. Soldiers have used life-detection equipment, drones and a navigation system to continue searching for those still missing. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Humanitarian crisis worsening in refuge for civilians fleeing Sudan’s civil war
articles.summary:
Conditions are deteriorating in city of El Obeid and camps on its outskirts, with more people arriving every day

Humanitarian conditions in the Sudanese city of El Obeid and two camps on its…

blocks.text: Humanitarian conditions in the Sudanese city of El Obeid and two camps on its outskirts are dire and deteriorating, according to people on the ground, as civilians displaced by fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces and Rapid Support Forces (RSF) militia continue to pour in from the surrounding countryside.

The UN says more than 15,000 families have arrived since mid-July, joining more than 200,000 people who arrived in the first half of the year, according to government figures cited by Save the Children.

“The situation is very harsh and is deteriorating as El Obeid is receiving IDPs [internally displaced people] on a daily basis … The city is shockingly overcrowded,” said Maryam, a humanitarian volunteer whose name has been changed for her safety.
The new arrivals came on foot, carrying almost nothing, she said. “They also suffer from a shortage of food and they definitely arrive traumatised.”
The city, the capital of North Kordofan province, was home to around half a million people before the war broke out more than three years ago.

blocks.caption: Tens of thousands of people are living in tented camps around El Obeid.  Photograph: AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: While many of the new arrivals have been absorbed into the city, tens of thousands are living in two main tented camps. According to analysis of satellite data by the Yale Humanitarian Research Lab, 800 new tents appeared in one of the camps between 4 and 25 August.

“During my visit, I saw 450 arrivals coming from the surrounding villages just that morning,” said Paul Byars, the Sudan country director for the Danish Refugee Council, who was in El Obeid last week. “The authorities’ estimates are correct, that 85% of them are women and children. Most of the men are staying behind because this is the only time for farming.”
Civil war erupted in Sudan’s capital, Khartoum, about 250 miles (400km) north-east of El Obeid, on 15 April 2023, when a power struggle between the armed forces and RSF descended into open conflict.
Since then, about 11.3 million people have been displaced, more than a fifth of the population. Some parts of the country, including El Obeid and surrounding areas, are at risk of famine.

Estimates of the number of people killed in the war range from tens to hundreds of thousands. More than 10,000 people are thought to have been massacred by the RSF in El Fasher over two days when they seized the city in Sudan’s western Darfur region in October 2025 after an 18-month siege.

blocks.caption: The damaged interior of a lawyers' syndicate in El Obeid, reportedly targeted by the RSF in July. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: A surge in RSF drone strikes on El Obeid and nearby areas in June led the UN to warn that the city could face a repeat of what happened in El Fasher.

The number of strikes has since fallen. The armed forces also recaptured a key road leading north to Khartoum in late July, which at least partly lifted the threat of besiegement. However, drones are still killing and injuring civilians, while violence rages in the surrounding districts, pushing people to the city.

Recently, volunteers in El Obeid had noticed more “double-tap” drone strikes, where a second drone follows the first, hitting rescuers at the scene, Maryam said. “It is hard, so hard, living with this, hearing the sound of a drone hitting somewhere,” she said. “It’s very disturbing.”

Sudan’s civil war has become dominated by drones, accounting for half of all violent incidents, up from 4% at the start of the war, said Nohad Eltayeb, who monitors Sudan for Acled, a conflict tracking group.
Both sides used drones, but the RSF’s usage had become more volatile since the US war with Iran began to interrupt supply lines in February, she said. “They rely on fewer, very targeted strikes.”

So far this year, there have been 322 incidents of violence affecting civilians in the wider Kordofan region, compared with 388 for the whole of 2025, according to Acled data. While the RSF was responsible for half of those, the SAF has also killed and injured civilians. On 10 August, armed forces and an allied militia killed five civilians and injured 10 about 60 miles north-east of El Obeid, according to Emergency Lawyers, a non-governmental group.

With the threats to delivery trucks, food prices have rocketed. In north Kordofan in July, according to World Food Programme data, a litre of groundnut oil cost 17,000 Sudanese pounds (£21), up from 13,000 in June and 7,700 a year ago. The prices of wheat flour and goat and sheep meat have also more than doubled in the last year.

blocks.caption: Conditions in the camps around El Obeid are said to be poor.  Photograph: AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Meanwhile, El Obeid’s power and water infrastructure still has not fully recovered from RSF drone strikes in June.

“The main problem is the big [water] source that is in the north of the city has been severely damaged and it has not been repaired,” said Esperanza Santos, an emergency coordinator in Sudan for Médecins Sans Frontières. “The water pipes in the city have [also] been impacted. So mostly, both in the city – for example, in the hospital – and also in the IDP camps, they are relying on water trucking and it’s not enough.”

Conditions in the camps were poor too, Santos said. “In terms of sanitation, it’s very, very bad. It’s not enough. The ratio of latrines per person is impossible – there are more than 100 people for a latrine. So basically there is open defecation.”

Maryam said she and her fellow local volunteers remained committed, despite the difficulties. “The situation is deteriorating, but we are trying to stay together, to stay strong in the face of the drone attacks and the influx of IDPs … We are living with this and we hope things will become better.”

articles.title: ‘Tiny bit of rain and the sewage comes’: Brighton swimmers vent fury at sea pollution
articles.summary: Checking for sewage spills has become as normal as checking the weather forecast, say swimmers on East Sussex beaches

blocks.text: “I’m furious,” says Jo Armstrong, 75, sitting on Brighton beach with her daughter and granddaughter.

Armstrong lives in Lewes, a town 8 miles from Brighton, and usually goes swimming in nearby Seaford in East Sussex every day. But over the past week the water there has been too polluted to swim. “Brighton beach was the only place that stayed clean,” she says.

In the week Friends of the Earth ranked the UK’s water companies for their environmental damage, and news of further sewage leaks emerged, the Guardian headed to Brighton beach to talk to swimmers. According to public data, a sewage alert was issued twice at the beach in August, and 158 alerts recorded overall in 2025.

blocks.caption: Jo Armstrong usually likes to swim in the sea in East Sussex every day. Photograph: Martin Godwin/The Guardian

blocks.text: “There’s a tiny bit of rain and then the sewage comes, I just don’t understand it. It’s extraordinary that we can’t have clean beaches,” says Armstrong.

This summer England has endured record-breaking heatwaves during which scores of people have spent time on beaches and rivers. In Brighton, the state of the country’s water is an issue on many people’s minds.

Hildi Mitchell, 55, runs a programme called Pool to Pier, where she teaches pool swimmers to swim safely in open waters. Increasingly, she is finding that pollution is stopping people from taking the leap to the sea.
“There are swimmers who have swum with us in the pool all year round but won’t come out in the sea in the summer because they’re worried about becoming ill,” she says.

blocks.caption: Hildi Mitchell teaches pool swimmers to swim safely in the sea in Brighton. Photograph: Martin Godwin/The Guardian

blocks.text: When it comes to the safety of the water, checking for sewage spills has become as important as checking the weather and tidal patterns. “I would love to be able to swim anywhere, rather than thinking about trying to avoid pollution,” Mitchell says.

Through Pool to Pier, Mitchell offers free workshops to children from families on low incomes. “These families already have limited things they can do in the summer to keep their children active, healthy and entertained. Swimming should be something that’s free and available to local families, but it’s not and that’s really sad.”

Greg Veros, 59, has lived in Brighton for 22 years and swum all his life, but after falling ill due to what he believes was sewage pollution a few years ago, he now spends more time at Brighton’s outdoor swimming pool than he does in the sea.

“I’m an enthusiastic swimmer, I can’t get enough of it,” Veros says. He used to have to skip his daily swim if there was a rainstorm or a sewage scare, but now the pool has given him an alternative. “It’s the best thing to have happened to Brighton,” he says.

blocks.caption: Greg Veros has switched to swimming in Brighton’s outdoor pool after he fell ill, he believes, from swimming in the sea. Photograph: Martin Godwin/The Guardian

blocks.text: But for Mitchell, there is nothing that can replace swimming in the sea.

“It’s about freedom. You’re not constrained by the black line on the pool. Nobody’s in your lane, you’re not worried about getting in anyone’s way. It’s a place where you can just swim in the way you want to swim,” Mitchell says.

Anna Field, 54, moved to Brighton so she could swim regularly, but, like Mitchell, she says checking for sewage spills is as important as checking the weather. There have been several times when she has come down to the beach and could smell the sewage, although this has been less common this summer amid the dry weather. When pollution stops her from swimming, it’s a bit like not being able to walk in the park because it’s raining, “except with this, you feel people [are] to blame”.

blocks.caption: Anna Field and her husband, Jim, take the plunge in Brighton. Field checks for sewage spills before she goes for a swim. Photograph: Martin Godwin/The Guardian

blocks.text: She is more angry than sad. “I absolutely love being in the ocean. It’s got its own personality, you look out of the window in the morning and it’s a different colour from yesterday or on some days it will tell you, no, you’re not coming in today,” Field says.
“Swimming is such a nice thing for people to be able to do and it’s public, anyone can go in – it would be a real shame if that was less accessible.”

articles.title: DPWH Las Piñas-Muntinlupa’s maintenance chief sacked
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The maintenance chief of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) Las Piñas – Muntinlupa District Engineering Office has been relieved from duty following…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The maintenance chief of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) Las Piñas – Muntinlupa District Engineering Office has been relieved from duty following reports of delayed response to calamities, among others.
In a memorandum dated August 29, Public Works Secretary Vince Dizon ordered the removal of engineer Loreto Balena Jr. from his duties, effective immediately.

“In view of repeated reports concerning your unsatisfactory performance, lack of urgency, and delayed response to calamities, you are hereby relieved of your duties as Maintenance Chief of the Las Piñas–Muntinlupa District Engineering Office, effective immediately,” the memorandum read.
Dizon directed Balena to conduct an inventory, accomplish, complete and sign all pending documents and deliverables, and turn over his papers and official records to the office.

Metro Manila has been placed under a red rainfall warning, according to an advisory issued by the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration at 12:10 p.m. Sunday. /das

articles.title: Africa’s aging autocrats fight to stay in power
articles.summary: Power can be seductive, and many who possess it want to hold on for as long as possible. The leaders of China and Russia, for example, cleared the way for additional terms years ago, and in the…

blocks.text: Power can be seductive, and many who possess it want to hold on for as long as possible. The leaders of China and Russia, for example, cleared the way for additional terms years ago, and in the United States, the president occasionally speaks of another run for office, even though the US Constitution does not allow it.
From the perspective of Paul Biya, however, Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump are still relatively new to office.
Cameroon’s president has been head of state since 1982. In 2025, Biya began his eighth term — which is officially due to end on November 6, 2032, just a few months before his 100th birthday.
The 93-year-old has given no official indication that he intends to step down, and the position of vice president remains vacant.
Paul Biya in Cameroon: A loyal leadership circle with one weak spot
During his 44 years in office, Biya has built a stable network of loyal allies that keeps the machinery of government running despite his lengthy absences.

The 93-year-old has now spent two and a half months in Geneva, Switzerland, continuing to issue decrees and make personnel decisions from abroad. In mid-June, his spokesperson denied rumors Biya was receiving treatment in a hospital and stated that the president was in good health.
“There is continuity, but that also means there is little momentum for reform within the government,” Beverly Ochieng, senior analyst at consultancy Global Risk, told DW.

And while Biya’s power apparatus has helped cushion the impact of the president’s long absence, that does not necessarily mean the most influential figures on the ground are united. After all, a post-Biya era is now in sight, and several of his allies are rumored to have ambitions of succeeding him.

“When everyone is lining up to potentially succeed Biya, it also means that the elites may begin challenging one another,” Ochieng said. Such rivalry, she warned, could lead to major disruptions, including the possibility of a military coup.
Analyst Levi Mboushou recently voiced similar concerns on DW’s AfricaLink podcast.

“Everyone feels the fear and uncertainty, but no one dares to look directly at it because we all have to deal with this repressive regime. You see something, but you say nothing. That is the situation in Cameroon at the moment,” he said.
Yoweri Museveni in Uganda: Signs of a dynasty?
Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni is only slightly younger, both in age and years in office.

The 81-year-old has been president since 1986 and, like Biya, recently embarked on another term. His succession also remains unresolved, although his son, Muhoozi Kainerugaba, has recently attracted considerable attention as head of the military.
According to Ochieng, the dynamics in Uganda are complex, not least because military elites and the ruling National Resistance Movement (NRM) have their own internal power structures.

blocks.caption: Is Muhoozi Kainerugaba (center, seen here in 2019) being groomed to eventually succeed his father? Image: Joseph Kiggundu/Photoshot/picture alliance

blocks.text: “Muhoozi has become the most visible figure primarily because he has a strong personality and enjoys the discreet backing of his father. His rise is not the result of support from either the NRM or the military leadership,” she said.
Kainerugaba is increasingly emerging as a political figure, including on issues beyond military affairs.

In early July, he ordered the closure of several media outlets. At the time, a source from an international foundation who requested anonymity told DW: “We are witnessing a transfer of power to the president’s son.”
A similar development has been unfolding for years in Equatorial Guinea, where Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo, who has ruled since 1979, appears to be gradually transferring power to his son.
Known by the nickname “Teodorin,” he has served as first vice president since 2016 and now also controls the military.

In June, Teodorin announced the resignation of the entire government on behalf of his father. Observers interpreted the move as a sign that he is gradually becoming the public face of state authority.
Whether Museveni will actually arrange his succession during his lifetime remains uncertain.
Ochieng believes that, in the event of a sudden power vacuum, Uganda could either hold constitutionally mandated elections or follow a scenario similar to that seen in Chad in 2021.
Then-President Idriss Deby was killed in clashes with rebels. The constitution was suspended, allowing his son, Mahamat Idriss Deby Itno, to take power.
Emmerson Mnangagwa in Zimbabwe: Party before people
Zimbabwe also amended its constitution this year, making it far less likely that President Emmerson Mnangagwa could be voted out of office.

In June, both chambers of parliament approved changes extending the terms of parliament and the president from five to seven years. Even more fundamentally, the president will no longer be elected directly by the people but by parliament, where the ruling ZANU-PF party enjoys comfortable majorities.

In July, the 83-year-old Mnangagwa signed the amended constitution into law. However, the opposition and some constitutional experts argue that a referendum should still be held. The government, by contrast, considers the constitutional amendment process complete.
“We are not surprised,” Chiedza Mlingwa, deputy spokesperson for the Constitution Defenders Forum, said at the time on DW’s AfricaLink podcast.

“The only thing one could be surprised by is the audacity, nothing else. We have observed this pattern since independence in 1980: ZANU-PF works to stay in power. The party does not believe in relinquishing power.”
Ochieng noted that countries such as Togo and Cote d’Ivoire have also implemented constitutional changes aimed at preserving power in recent years.

Meanwhile, in Senegal, a constitutional amendment is being discussed amid tensions between former allies at the top of the state, President Bassirou Diomaye Faye and Speaker of Parliament Ousmane Sonko, both of whom are significantly younger than the continent’s other long-ruling leaders.

“Even when legal safeguards exist, if they are not designed in a way that guarantees citizen participation, public debate, civil society engagement, or oversight by other institutions, then it becomes possible for unilateral decisions to be made at the highest levels of government,” said Ochieng.
The weakening of institutions to allow individuals to remain in power, she added, is not an African problem but a global one. /dl

articles.title: Del Pilar rites in Bulacan scaled down due to heavy rains
articles.summary: BULAKAN, Bulacan — Officials scaled down Sunday’s commemoration of the 176th birth anniversary of Filipino hero and journalist Marcelo H. del Pilar due to continuous heavy rains brought by the…

blocks.text: BULAKAN, Bulacan — Officials scaled down Sunday’s commemoration of the 176th birth anniversary of Filipino hero and journalist Marcelo H. del Pilar due to continuous heavy rains brought by the enhanced southwest monsoon, or habagat.
The 8 a.m. program at the Marcelo H. del Pilar Shrine in Sitio Cupang, Barangay San Nicolas, was canceled and replaced with a simple wreath-laying ceremony at the hero’s monument.

“Due to the weather disturbance, the originally planned commemorative program will not push through. Instead, a simple flower wreath offering will be prepared at the Marcelo H. del Pilar Monument … as a gesture of remembrance and respect for our great Bulakenyo hero,” the municipal government said in an advisory.
Guests may still visit the shrine to pay tribute to Del Pilar. Commission on Elections Chair George Erwin Garcia was scheduled to serve as guest of honor and speaker.

The annual Aug. 30 commemoration dates back to 1984, when local officials, residents and journalists organized a grand civic parade to welcome Del Pilar’s remains to his hometown after they were repatriated from Spain.

Del Pilar, born on Aug. 30, 1850, in Bulakan, was a lawyer, writer and editor who became known as the Father of Philippine Journalism. He spent his final years in Spain editing and publishing La Solidaridad, using funds sent by his family to sustain the reformist newspaper.
He died of tuberculosis in Barcelona on July 4, 1896, and his remains were brought back to the Philippines in 1920 before being buried in his hometown.
Del Pilar’s birth date was declared National Press Freedom Day under Republic Act No. 11699, which was signed into law in 2022.
The annual civic parade was suspended during the COVID-19 pandemic and has not been revived despite the lifting of pandemic restrictions.
Del Pilar’s writings and advocacy for reforms, equality and freedom during Spanish colonial rule helped shape the reform movement that preceded the Philippine Revolution.
In last year’s commemoration, then Foreign Affairs Secretary Theresa Lazaro described Del Pilar as a champion of human rights and urged Filipinos to defend their rights and dignity. /das

articles.title: Pacific leaders to meet in Palau amid China, Taiwan tension
articles.summary: KOROR — Pacific island leaders will tackle transnational drug crime as they meet in Palau from Monday for a summit where tensions between Taiwan and China risk overshadowing regional priorities…

blocks.text: KOROR — Pacific island leaders will tackle transnational drug crime as they meet in Palau from Monday for a summit where tensions between Taiwan and China risk overshadowing regional priorities like climate change.
Palau, this year’s host of the 18-member Pacific Islands Forum, is among three members holding diplomatic ties with Taiwan and not China, a large creditor to many island states.
China, Taiwan and the United States are among the aid partners invited to the forum, although not the leaders’ meeting. Beijing has protested Taiwan’s invitation.
On Sunday, Taiwan’s foreign minister Lin Chia-lung cut the ribbon with Palau President Surangel Whipps at a ceremony handing over a fleet of electric buses donated by Taipei.
China retaliated against Lin’s arrival in Palau by declaring the tourism-dependent island an “unsafe” place for travellers, Whipps later told reporters.
Chinese tourists are the largest group of visitors to Palau, data shows.
The US Embassy issued a statement accusing China of attempting to “weaponize tourism to coerce Palau”.
“The Pacific is our home, not a theatre for geopolitical competition,” Whipps said in an interview on Sunday.

Tensions between the Pacific’s partners should not detract from island priorities of action on renewable energy, drug crime, food security and climate change, which had real impact on lives, he urged.
Island populations are struggling with rising fuel and food costs caused by the Middle East war.
Transnational policing
Around 110 police drawn from various Pacific islands will provide security at the forum, the first large-scale demonstration of Pacific-wide cooperation on policing.
Australia, the biggest forum member and aid donor, has led efforts for the Pacific to provide its own security, arguing there is no need for China to have police in Kiribati and the Solomons.
Whipps said the Pacific leaders would seek to build on policing ties to tackle drug crime.
Fiji, a major transport hub for the Pacific, is experiencing the world’s fastest HIV outbreak, driven by what health authorities say is risky injecting of methamphetamine.

Police seizures of cocaine and methamphetamine in Fiji, the discovery of abandoned “narco subs” in the Solomon Islands and drug packages washing to shore in remote islands have reinforced fears of drug cartels forming a Pacific Ocean trafficking highway.
A regional maritime response to rising drug crime will be discussed by the leaders, with Australia and Fiji expected to be major contributors if it is approved, Australian officials told AFP.
Whipps gave the example of a Chinese drug gang that had operated in Palau before moving to Fiji.

“Clearly the same people are roaming around the whole Pacific and is evidence of why we need to collaborate and share information. They are destroying our youth and destabilising our nations,” he said.
Tensions over China

Australian National University Pacific expert Graeme Smith told AFP “climate change is at the top of the Pacific priority list, but the challenge of transnational crime is growing with the outbreak of HIV in Fiji”.

Fourteen island leaders are expected in Palau, after pro-Beijing Kiribati said its leader could not attend and the Solomon Islands prime minister Matthew Wale left unexpectedly on Sunday, returning home to deal with a political crisis — a no confidence motion lodged against his leadership.
Solomon Islands had been China’s closest partner in the Pacific until Wale was recently elected, vowing to review a secret security pact and repairing ties with the US and Australia.

US deputy secretary of state Christopher Landau and US Coast Guard Commandant Admiral Kevin Lunday will arrive in Palau on Monday to strengthen ties with Pacific countries before travelling to Solomon Islands and Kiribati.
The East-West Center’s Henry Puna, previously the forum’s secretary general, told AFP that climate change should be the most important issue for Pacific leaders.
But the impact of China’s ballistic missile test into the region last month was still being felt.
The forum has been unable to issue a joint statement of condemnation after Kiribati and Nauru held out and leaders will continue to discuss it in Palau, Whipps said. /dl

articles.title: [Two Pronged] Why do some happy family memories become painful later in life?
articles.summary: ‘I loved spending time with my father then….But now it feels different and I don’t know why.’

blocks.text: Rappler’s People section runs an advice column by couple Jeremy Baer and clinical psychologist Dr. Margarita Holmes.

Jeremy has a master’s degree in law from Oxford University. A banker of 37 years who worked in three continents, he has been training with Dr. Holmes for the last 10 years as co-lecturer and, occasionally, as co-therapist, especially with clients whose financial concerns intrude into their daily lives.
Together, they have written two books: Love Triangles: Understanding the Macho-Mistress Mentality and Imported Love: Filipino-Foreign Liaisons.
Dear Dr. Holmes and Mr. Baer,

Everyone is excited about Alex Eala nowadays. I don’t blame them. I, too, would pay hundreds just to see her play in person. Like watching basketball, Filipinos love spectator sports, especially boxing.
I wonder why I hate boxing matches.
My father used to bring me to such matches because he loved boxing. This was when I was 6-9 years old.
Then, my parents were constantly fighting about my father’s infidelity. It sounded like he did it except when he went to these boxing matches.

I loved spending time with my father then. He was always so busy, or upset because of their (my parents’) fighting. He was different during our “boxing dates.” He was in a better mood and would even joke those nights we went out together.
I remember those nights being so special to me. It was a chance to be alone with him. But now it feels different and I don’t know why.
I would appreciate anything helpful you could tell me…even if it is just theories. It feels like this sudden hatred for boxing is now affecting my mental health. Thank you.
Jan
Dear Jan,
It may be helpful to look at what boxing represented to you when you were a child and what it represents now that you are an adult.

As a child, the sport offered you two main attractions: the opportunity to have what is now labeled as “quality time” with your father, a precious resource that children cherish in the moment and a memory that warms the heart long after the actual occasions have passed.

These were ideal times when you had your father all to yourself and the two of you were temporarily freed from the constant tug of war between your parents (over your father’s infidelity) that seems to have been a permanent feature of your childhood. Boxing was an oasis of calm in a world of turmoil.

With maturity, however, came the realization that these supposedly innocent outings were not actually as innocent as you had thought. You began to understand the broader context within which these boxing events should be viewed. Once you fully connected the dots, you saw how your father had in fact used you as a pawn in his endless struggles with your mother and how he used boxing as yet another excuse to be out of the house without your mother.

Boxing therefore became associated in your mind with escaping from the harsh realities of a difficult home life and also highlighted the stark contrast between the two faces of your father: the philanderer who made your mother’s life a misery and your childhood a battleground, on the one hand, and the relaxed joker on boxing nights on the other. Your role in the latter was innocent but your father’s use of you as a foil in his marital woes was deliberate, definitely not in your best interests and a low point in his parenting.

Your current sudden hatred for boxing is of concern. It is not clear why this has surfaced now but as it is affecting your mental health, it should be added to the other issues already discussed and raised with your therapist who will hopefully be able to delve further into the history behind this new development and help you deal with it.
Wishing you the best of luck,
JAF Baer
Dear Jan:

Thank you very much for your letter and I thank Mr. Baer for answering this letter first, so that now I can jump off from his analysis and move on to mine. To be sure, his analysis is a realistic and possibly accurate rendering of what your boxing dates with your father represented.

My analysis is another interpretation and, admittedly, while realistic, can also be inaccurate. One of the first things we learn as students of the human psyche is that two contradictory qualities can exist in the same person even when discussing the same event!

Take your father’s boxing dates with you. Yes, he may have “used you as a pawn” as Mr. Baer suggests, because this was the only time he was able to leave home without a major fight. So of course he was in an even better mood and was even able to joke with the whole family, HE knew he would be able to escape your mother’s ire and was looking forward to a peaceful time…even if it lasted only as long as the boxing matches did.

But that does not diminish his time with you, Jan. After all, he chose you, and not your other siblings and/or your mother to be with him. He chose you, and not anybody else, to share this little bit of paradise with you.

Yes, it would probably mean a lot more to you if you felt his only motive for being with you was because he wanted to. But life is not that simple, and neither you nor he can isolate this joy of being together from all the rancor going on at home. It is even possible that being with him in the stadiums where the matches took place added to the joy of your time together precisely because it was so far away and so different from what you both had at home.

True, he may not have been the strong and stalwart father protecting you from your mom. It is more likely that you both looked forward to these dates more like siblings, laughing about having escaped from the ogre at home. But so what, right? We cannot be all things to all people at all times.
Sometimes he was the protector, and sometimes he was the companion who joked because like you, he too needed escape from home.

Perhaps you are disappointed because he is, after all, your dad. Perhaps you hoped he would always be the strong one, buffering you from all the bad things in the world. But, again, life doesn’t work that way and many would consider you lucky, because he didn’t walk away from you even when I am sure there were many times he was sorely tempted to.
The English poet, Philip Larkin has a poem that starts:
“They fuck you up, your mum and dad. They may not mean to, but they do. ”
Transgressive, that, but also true and actually also pretty horrible if that were all there was to it. But Mr. Larkin adds, in the second and third stanza, a reason for this:
“But they were fucked up in their turn… …(because) Man hands on misery to man ”
So you see, dearest Jan, your father did not fool you on purpose…(perhaps) he even did the best he could do under the circumstances he was in.
Philip Larkin has another poem, The Arundel Tomb, where the final words are:
“What will survive of us is love”
I hope, unless it is patently and completely false, that what will survive among the memories of times with your Dad is also love.
All the best,
MG Holmes
Life got complicated? Write to our Two Pronged duo at twopronged@rappler.com.

articles.title: Student blinded in one eye after being bullied in Baguio
articles.summary: BAGUIO CITY – Parents are calling for justice for their 13-year-old son who went blind in one eye after he was punched by a 12-year-old student on August 20 in Barangay Quezon Hill Proper, Baguio…

blocks.text: BAGUIO CITY – Parents are calling for justice for their 13-year-old son who went blind in one eye after he was punched by a 12-year-old student on August 20 in Barangay Quezon Hill Proper, Baguio City.

The incident occurred at around 2:10 p.m. on August 20, according to an appeal sent by a family friend to Bombo Radyo Baguio and a police report sent to the office of City Director Ruel Tagel of the Baguio City Police Office.
The incident was allegedly not given enough attention because it did not go viral, unlike the previous bullying incident in Pinsao Proper.
The victim’s family is calling for justice, saying they were helpless because the response of the authorities was unacceptable to them.

The family said it felt like authorities were paying more attention to the welfare of the boy who punched them than the victim, especially since he will have to live with the effects of losing his eyesight in one eye for the rest of his life.

Medical records from the Baguio General Hospital and Medical Center showed that the victim was admitted on August 20 after being "suddenly punched in the face", with the impact focused on the left periorbital area.

The hospital's clinical abstract stated that he complained of pain in his left eye and loss of vision. Doctors diagnosed him with a ruptured left globe and left periorbital contusion. He was discharged on August 23.
According to Tagel, the reported incident is being thoroughly investigated, and authorities have begun handling the case under the juvenile justice system.

He said the 12-year-old was immediately sent to the City Social Welfare and Development Office for assessment, intervention, and proper disposition under Republic Act 9344, or the Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act.

articles.title: Apalit police lead rescue of residents trapped by rising floodwaters
articles.summary: APALIT, Pampanga — Police personnel in Apalit, Pampanga, led a rescue operation to assist residents trapped inside the Camella community as floodwaters continued to rise amid persistent rains on…

blocks.text: (Liezle Basa Inigo) RESCUE OPERATION IN APALIT — Police personnel of the Apalit Municipal Police Station assist residents trapped by rising floodwaters at Camella amid continued heavy rains in Apalit, Pampanga. (Photo courtesy of PNP Apalit)

APALIT, Pampanga — Police personnel in Apalit, Pampanga, led a rescue operation to assist residents trapped inside the Camella community as floodwaters continued to rise amid persistent rains on Sunday, August 20.

Apalit Municipal Police Station (MPS) chief Lt. Col. Jesus O. Manalo Jr. reported that police personnel immediately proceeded to the affected area to assess the situation and locate residents needing urgent assistance.
Despite heavy rains and hazardous conditions, rescuers pressed on with the operation to reach and evacuate residents to safer areas.
The Apalit MPS continued to monitor flood-affected communities and coordinate with local disaster response authorities as water levels remained a concern.
Residents in flood-prone areas were urged to stay and immediately follow evacuation orders and other safety advisories issued by authorities.
Related Tags

articles.title: Japan to dispatch SDF helicopters to wildfire-hit Indonesia
articles.summary: TOKYO (Jiji Press) -- Japan will deploy three CH-47 transport helicopters of its Ground Self-Defense Force to Indonesia as part of an international emergency relief operation in response to the…

blocks.text: Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi speaks to reporters at the country's parliamentary building in Tokyo on Friday, Aug. 28.

TOKYO (Jiji Press) -- Japan will deploy three CH-47 transport helicopters of its Ground Self-Defense Force to Indonesia as part of an international emergency relief operation in response to the ongoing forest fires in the Southeast Asian country, Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi has said.
The helicopters will be used for firefighting activities. This will be the first time for the SDF to conduct firefighting operations overseas.

According to the Defense Ministry, around 600 personnel will participate in the relief mission. The Maritime SDF transport vessel Kunisaki, carrying the three helicopters, is expected to depart for Indonesia soon.
Koizumi told reporters on Friday, "We will do everything possible to help prevent further expansion of the damage."
Following a request for assistance from the Indonesian government, the Japanese government discussed possible support measures.
On Friday, Koizumi ordered the commander of the SDF's Joint Operations Command to carry out the mission.
Related Tags

articles.title: Baguio City mayor warns residents against landslides caused by habagat
articles.summary: BAGUIO CITY – Baguio City Mayor Benjamin Magalong alerted residents to be prepared, be careful, and evacuate landslide-prone areas in connection with the ongoing rains caused by the Habagat. In…

blocks.text: BAGUIO CITY – Baguio City Mayor Benjamin Magalong alerted residents to be prepared, be careful, and evacuate landslide-prone areas in connection with the ongoing rains caused by the Habagat.

In PAGASA's August 30, 2026 Weather Advisory No.30, the province of Benguet, including Baguio City, will experience Orange Rainfall from 100-200 mm, while some parts of the Cordillera will experience 5-100 mm rainfall.

Magalong also alerted responders of the City Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (CDRRMC) to continue to attend incidents involving soil erosion, landslides, and fallen or leaning trees as persistent monsoon rains continue to affect the city.

The prolonged rainfall has resulted in various incidents in different areas, prompting response teams to conduct assessments, clearing, mitigation, and other necessary interventions to ensure public safety.
Among the recent incidents attended to by responders as of 12 noon Sunday, August 30, 2026, were:
*Purok 3, Happy Hallow – A landslide and fallen boulder damaged a wall, window, and water line in the area.
*Springhills, Loakan Apugan – Responders assisted in the installation of a tarpaulin over an area affected by soil erosion to help prevent further deterioration.

*Purok Greenhills, Slaughter Compound – Soil erosion behind a single-storey house was first observed on August 9. No further movement was noted until the early morning of August 26, when rocks began falling and damaged the rear portion of the house. As of the latest assessment, the erosion continues to slowly encroach into the house.
*Tiptop, Pacdal – A damaged drainage structure affecting nearby residences was attended to by responders for assessment and appropriate intervention.
*Loakan Road, Loakan Proper – Responders addressed leaning trees along the road and undertook the cutting of an unstable eucalyptus tree to prevent possible hazards to motorists and pedestrians.
The CDRRMC, led by Mayor Magalong, continues to closely monitor weather-related incidents and deploy response teams as needed.
He reminded residents to remain vigilant as the rains continue, particularly those living near slopes, waterways, and other hazard-prone areas.
Residents are urged to follow official advisories and immediately report dangerous conditions to the authorities by calling the emergency hotline 911 or the Baguio In My Pocket application.

articles.title: Nepal warns of more possible floods as communities grapple with devastation
articles.summary: DHADING, Nepal (AP) — Authorities in Nepal are warning of possible fresh flooding on Sunday and urged residents in flood-affected districts to remain on high alert after water levels rose in the…

blocks.text: A drone view shows rescue workers inspect the area and damaged structures following recent flash flooding along the Trishuli River in the Devighat area of Nuwakot district, Nepal, Saturday, Aug. 29, 2026. (AP Photo/Rajesh Kumar Singh)

DHADING, Nepal (AP) — Authorities in Nepal are warning of possible fresh flooding on Sunday and urged residents in flood-affected districts to remain on high alert after water levels rose in the Bhotekoshi River.

Flood warning notices were sent to people's phones throughout Sunday morning, as rescue crews worked to clear a major highway connecting Kathmandu to one of the areas worst-hit by Wednesday's catastrophic floods.

In the town of Galchhi, a group of residents sought higher ground on a nearby bridge and watched as the river roared by. People pointed to enormous rocks that had been washed downriver during the earlier floods, as others standing on a suspension bridge over the water were warned off with whistles.

Along the river entire homes, vehicles and farm tractors could be seen jutting from the thick grey-brown sediment that has enveloped entire villages in the worst-hit flood areas. Rice terraces along riverside had experienced landslides, dropping parts of their field into the river.

The combined toll in Nepal and Tibet rose to 750 dead and over 3,000 people missing after the latest updates on Sunday. Nepal’s disaster agency said the death toll had climbed to 734 with 2,498 people missing, while Chinese authorities reported 16 deaths and 546 missing, including over a hundred Nepalis and people from over a dozen countries.

The latest warnings came after Chinese authorities informed their Nepalese counterparts of increased water flow upstream, Dharam Raj Uprety, chief executive of Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, told the Associated Press.
But residents of the flood-hit villages said they were struggling to make sense of near-constant alarms they've received since the initial floods.

“Sometimes they say a flood is coming, then we have to run again to higher ground, even at night. There is also rain,” said local resident Govind Shreshta. “It’s really difficult for me. I have a 72-year-old father and 70-year-old mom. I must carry them and I am exhausted. It’s going on like this for those who are still alive.”
Large concrete and smaller suspension bridges were destroyed, leaving communities on the other side of the river less easy access.

“Those that are there are now stuck there. Those who are here are stuck here. It’s going to be very difficult,” said Sattan Singh Tamang, 47, who was working near a bridge when Wednesday’s the floods came.
Homes and businesses left intact after the flooding were still without electricity on Sunday, as twisted power line poles and wires lay tangled in the mud.

Prithivi Highway is crucial supply route for food, fuel and other goods entering Kathmandu from other parts of the country. While most of the highway is operational, other parts still face repair challenges.

articles.title: Ontario premier answers Trump’s ‘Lake America’ with giant ‘Lake Ontario’ sign
articles.summary: TORONTO (AP) — Ontario Premier Doug Ford answered President Donald Trump’s “Lake America” decree Saturday with a billboard-sized message on the Canadian shoreline — “Lake Ontario. Now and Always” —…

blocks.text: Ontario Premier Doug Ford, right, and Niagara West Member of Provincial Parliament Sam Oosterhoff unveil a sign for Lake Ontario at the Fifty Point Conservation Area in Grimsby, Ontario, Canada, on Saturday, Aug. 29, 2026. (Keito Newman/The Canadian Press via AP)

TORONTO (AP) — Ontario Premier Doug Ford answered President Donald Trump’s “Lake America” decree Saturday with a billboard-sized message on the Canadian shoreline — “Lake Ontario. Now and Always” — as Canadian leaders met the move with ridicule rather than outrage.

Wearing a Team Canada soccer jersey, Ford unveiled the sign near Grimsby, Ontario, and posed for photographs. The 24-by-12-foot (7.3-by-3.6 meter) sign stands on 6-foot (1.8-meter) legs, putting its top about 18 feet (5.5 meters) above the ground — roughly two stories high. The message is repeated in French, one

The display followed Trump’s executive order directing U.S. federal agencies to call Lake Ontario “Lake America.” After months of tariffs, threats to make Canada the 51st U.S. state and personal attacks on its leaders, the reaction in Canada has mixed defiance with mockery.
Ford said Trump was trying to rename the lake because Ontario and Canada were “standing up for ourselves” and argued the name would outlast the president.
“Long after President Trump is gone, it will still be called Lake Ontario,” Ford said in a video posted on social media.
Canadians mock Trump
Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew compared Trump to an aging rock band trying to revive an old hit

“You know when a rock band is really over the hill and you see them like in a casino playing some song from like 50 years ago. I think that’s the part of Donald Trump’s presidency we’re at now, Like he thought they had a real hit, a real golden oldie, with the Gulf of Mexico,” Kinew said, referring to Trump's executive order renaming the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America. “And he’s trying to bring back that, and he’s trying to play the hits for his base. But I think everybody here thinks it’s a little sad and it’s not his best work.”
The mockery was not limited to politicians. Canadian historian Robert Bothwell was even more scathing.
“The greatest country on earth takes this moron seriously?” Bothwell said.
But Bothwell said the dispute was more serious than the jokes, arguing Trump’s broader aim was “to subordinate Canada and at best make it a colony, at worst absorb it into the United States.”
Nelson Wiseman, professor emeritus at the University of Toronto, said Trump “would like Canada to act like a vassal state, but it refuses to do so. That irritates him.”
Canada and the US trade barbs over collapsed talks

The dispute comes as relations between the longtime allies worsen over trade. Negotiations collapsed last week, both governments accused the other of making late demands, and Canada announced retaliatory tariffs set to take effect next month.

Trump’s order also came amid an escalating war of words with Ford. In an interview with The Associated Press earlier this week, Ford said Ronald Reagan would be “throwing up” over Trump’s tariff policies and “disgusted with President Trump.”

Trump fired back by dismissing Ford’s comments as “bluster,” calling him Prime Minister Mark Carney’s “flunky” and mocking him as the “less charismatic, intelligent, and overall unimpressive brother” of the late Toronto Mayor Rob Ford.
Trump continued promoting the new name Saturday, reposting a meme showing Canada geese with Trump-like blond hair firing rifles as they “protected” Lake America.

Trump has repeatedly used maps to make political points. A “Gulf of America” map was displayed for a time beside the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office, and Trump has posted images depicting Canada as part of the United States or as the 51st state.
Ontario name has Indigenous origins

The name Lake Ontario comes from the Huron Indigenous people’s word “oniatarí:io,” which means “lake of shining waters.” The Canadian province of Ontario, founded in 1867, took its name from the lake.

Wendat Nation Grand Chief Pierre Picard, whose people historically lived from the St. Lawrence Valley to the Great Lakes and whose language gave Lake Ontario its name, called Trump’s move an attempt to erase Indigenous history.
“I want to tell him that it is unacceptable for us, as a nation, to have a president who can eradicate our history, our culture and our identity,” Picard said.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney rejected the move, noting the lake’s Indigenous roots and that the name predates both Canadian Confederation and the U.S. Declaration of Independence. Trump cannot require Canada to adopt the new name.

articles.title: Toddler stabbed to death by own father in Ilocos Sur
articles.summary: TAGUDIN, Ilocos Sur — A three-year-old child was allegedly stabbed to death by his own 29-year-old father in Barangay Lacong here on Friday, August 28, police said in a belated report. Police said…

blocks.text: TAGUDIN, Ilocos Sur — A three-year-old child was allegedly stabbed to death by his own 29-year-old father in Barangay Lacong here on Friday, August 28, police said in a belated report.
Police said the suspect, also a resident of this town, fled after the incident and is now the subject of a manhunt.
Initial investigation disclosed that, before the incident, the victim’s grandmother and aunt reportedly heard the victim and the suspect talking to each other at around 1 a.m. on August 28.
At around 11 a.m., the grandmother became suspicious after noticing that her grandchild had not come out of the room.
She opened the door and found the child covered with a blanket. When she removed it, she saw blood on the victim’s chest.
The child was immediately rushed to a hospital but was declared dead on arrival.
The suspect had already fled the house when authorities arrived. Investigators said no bladed weapon believed to have been used in the killing was recovered from the crime scene.
Police are conducting follow-up operations to locate and arrest the suspect.
