articles.title: Simple math: Adiong says VP Duterte allegedly spent P473,000 an hour in confidential funds
articles.summary: House prosecution panel "layman" spokesperson Lanao del Sur 1st district Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong used simple math to illustrate the scale of Vice President Sara Duterte's alleged misuse of the Office…

blocks.text: House prosecution panel "layman" spokesperson Lanao del Sur 1st district Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong used simple math to illustrate the scale of Vice President Sara Duterte's alleged misuse of the Office of the Vice President's (OVP) confidential funds.
Adiong was referring to the P125 million in confidential funds that were spent by the OVP in just 11 days in December 2022.

"Nung natapos na nilang gastusin in 11 days, by the way, kung i-quantify natin yung 11 days, P473,000 every hour ang nagagastos, para ma-consume, in 11 days, ang P125 million, ganun kabilis at kalaki yung paggasto ng P125 million in 11 days," Adiong said in an online interview.

(But when they finished spending it in 11 days, by the way, if we quantify those 11 days, they were spending P473,000 every hour to consume the P125 million in 11 days. That is how fast and how large the spending of P125 million was in 11 days.)
"Not mentioning the fact na in 11 days na yan, merong mga holidays diyan,” he noted.
(Not mentioning the fact that there were holidays during those 11 days.)

The OVP received the P125-million cash advance in December 2022 and reported utilizing the entire amount from Dec. 21 to Dec. 31, a period that state auditor Roderick Wamil earlier flagged during his testimony because the allocation was intended for the fourth quarter.

The prosecution has also questioned an OVP explanation referring to obligations that had already been incurred before the money was released, arguing that this sits uneasily with the treatment of confidential funds as cash advances governed by specific rules on utilization.

“Ang confidential funds nga is, ano 'yan cash advance 'yan. Why would you reimburse something that have already been implemented from the confidential funds, which is actually is intended for specific purpose, guided by a specific criteria on how you handle that, bawal 'yun,” Adiong said.

(Confidential funds are cash advances. Why would you reimburse something that had already been implemented using confidential funds, which are actually intended for a specific purpose and guided by specific criteria on how they should be handled? That is prohibited.)
Beyond the speed of the spending, prosecutors have questioned whether the geographic reach reflected in the records could realistically have been accomplished within the same compressed period.
“Meron pang pag-distribute nung confidential funds in 11 days, 134 areas all over the country in one day, so paano mo mate-testify 'yun?” asked the assistant majority leader from Mindanao.
(There was also the distribution of the confidential funds in 11 days, covering 134 areas all over the country in one day, so how can you testify to that?)

The 11-day expenditure has become one of the central factual issues under article I of the articles of impeachment as the prosecution traces how the first P125-million confidential-fund tranche was requested, withdrawn, distributed and eventually liquidated.

Adiong says the prosecution is placing particular weight on contemporaneous official records because they provide fixed reference points against which subsequent explanations from OVP officials can be measured.

“Whatever testimony that they would give to the court, whatever narrative that they would provide to the court, still we go back to the documents, the official documents, at hindi nagsisinungaling yung official documents, at hindi nagsisinungaling yung figures na nagre-reflect doon sa official documents, as compared to Colonel Lachica, wala siyang pinirmahan,” Adiong said.

(Whatever testimony that they would give to the court, whatever narrative they provide to the court, we still go back to the official documents. Official documents do not lie, and neither do the figures reflected in those official documents, unlike Colonel Lachica, who did not sign anything.)
Can VP Sara be trusted with public funds?

The prosecution’s concerns also extend to the rules governing who may handle and account for confidential funds, with Adiong arguing that an alleged breach of basic safeguards could have implications beyond accounting procedures.

“Can we trust the Vice President with the resources of the government, knowing that the policy, a very basic policy, hindi pa niya masunod given the fact na she is a lawyer and she has been using confidential funds for over three years now?" Adiong said of the impeachment trial respondent.

(Can we trust the Vice President with the resources of the government, knowing that she cannot even follow a very basic policy, given that she is a lawyer and has been using confidential funds for over three years now?)

Joint Circular (JC) No. 2015-01 requires the head of an agency to oversee the use of confidential funds, maintain effective internal controls, approve cash advances and liquidation reports, and ensure compliance with the rules. The designated special disbursing officer (SDO), meanwhile, is responsible for actually disbursing and accounting for the funds.
Adiong argued that Duterte’s previous experience with confidential funds as Davao City mayor makes the alleged departure from those rules at the OVP particularly relevant in assessing accountability.

“Pero the mere fact na maski 'yung simpleng joint circular na alam mo namang may joint circular, kasi naging mayor ka, at saka gumagamit ka na ng confidential funds before ka pa naging Bise Presidente, tapos viniolate mo ito very simple lang na policy, hindi mo finallow, tapos nag-utos ka pa ng tao para i-disregard ito at i-violate ito,” Adiong said.

(But the mere fact that you did not follow even this simple joint circular, which you knew existed because you had been a mayor and had already been using confidential funds before becoming Vice President, and then you violated this very simple policy and even instructed someone to disregard and violate it.)

Former OVP SDO Gina Acosta testified that Duterte instructed her to turn over the confidential-fund cash to Lachica despite Acosta being the designated bonded officer accountable for the funds--an arrangement prosecutors contend violated the governing circular.

For Adiong, that alleged departure from a basic safeguard raises a leadership question extending beyond the mechanics of accounting because the impeachment charge asks whether or not Duterte betrayed the public trust attached to her office.

Adiong said the prosecution therefore intends to have the senator-judges assess the confidential-fund transactions against the standard of responsibility expected from an official entrusted with public money and constitutional power.

“So that alone proves na meron talagang culpable violation of the Constitution, because ang sinabi naman sa Constitution, public office is a public trust. So how can you be trusted with the mandate you have given by the people, kung yung simpleng polisiya ng paggamit ng confidential funds ay binaliwala mo?” he noted.

(So that alone proves that there really was a culpable violation of the Constitution, because the Constitution says public office is a public trust. So how can you be trusted with the mandate given to you by the people if you disregarded the simple policy governing the use of confidential funds?)

articles.title: PVL Invitational fires off on Monday
articles.summary: Six teams bannered by defending champion PLDT open their respective title campaigns when the PVL Invitational Conference fires off at the Smart Araneta Coliseum on Monday, Aug. 31. The High Speed…

blocks.text: Six teams bannered by defending champion PLDT open their respective title campaigns when the PVL Invitational Conference fires off at the Smart Araneta Coliseum on Monday, Aug. 31.

The High Speed Hitters raise the curtain when they take on Thai guest team EST Cola at 1:30 p.m., while fancied Creamline and Nxled square off at 4 p.m. Vietnamese squad Ho Chi Minh and Farm Fresh clash in the 6:30 p.m. nightcap.
There will be little time for the six participating teams to rest, with the tournament set to run for six playdates in eight days, making every game crucial.

PLDT coach Rald Ricafort has plenty of weapons at his disposal in setting the tone for their title-retention campaign, with Savi Davison, Kim Dy and Alleiah Malaluan at the forefront of their assault.
Majoy Baron and Mika Reyes are also there to provide support for the squad, which seeks to regain its championship ways after finishing third in the last All-Filipino Conference.
EST Cola, however, is no pushover with the team parading Thailand’s Under-20 national team that placed fourth in its first appearance in 2024.

Hitters Papatchaya Phontham and Nannaphat Moonjakham, middle blocker Waruni Kanram, and liberos Jiratcha Naoprachum and Nichakorn Wansuk anchore the team, boasting of familiarity after having played together in last year’s VTV International Cup.

Meanwhile, Creamline is expected to showcase its veteran crew reinforced by Jaja Santiago, where she joins forces with Alyssa Valdez, Jema Galanza and Pangs Panaga in their bid to regain the crown they last won in 2024. They are set to challenge the equally talented Nxled frontline composed of Brooke Van Sickle, Myla Pablo and MJ Phillips.
The Farm Fresh-Ho Chi Minh tussle is equally enticing, with the Vietnamese expecting to pull off a surprise against the Foxies, which has skipper Ces Molina teaming up with Ara Galang.

articles.title: Barasoain Church flooded as Bulacan remains waterlogged
articles.summary: Barasoain Church remains surrounded by floodwater as rains continue.

blocks.text: Floodwaters cover the grounds outside Barasoain Church in Malolos, Bulacan, on Aug. 30, 2026, following persistent southwest monsoon rains.
Barasoain Church - Our Lady of Mount Carmel Parish

MANILA, Philippines — Floodwaters inundated the historic Barasoain Church in Malolos on Sunday, August 30 as persistent southwest monsoon rains continued to soak Bulacan, with PAGASA warning that more rain could worsen flooding in already saturated areas.
Photos shared Sunday morning by Barasoain Church Our Lady of Mount Carmel Parish showed floodwaters surrounding parts of the church grounds and reaching portions of the interior.
Despite the flooding, the parish said Masses would still be held at 10 a.m. and 5 p.m.
Barasoain Church is among the country's most historic religious sites. It hosted the Malolos Congress and the inauguration of the First Philippine Republic in 1899.
Floodwaters surround Barasoain Church and its grounds in Malolos, Bulacan, on Aug. 30, 2026, as southwest monsoon rains continue to affect the province.
Barasoain Church
Floodwaters reach the interior of Barasoain Church in Malolos, Bulacan, on Aug. 30, 2026, amid persistent southwest monsoon rains.
More rain for Bulacan
In an 11 a.m. advisory, state weather bureau PAGASA said Bulacan may receive 50 to 100 millimeters of rain from Sunday through noon Monday, Aug. 31, due to the southwest monsoon, or habagat.
Another 50 to 100 mm may fall from Monday noon through Tuesday noon.
The weather bureau warned that rainfall could be higher in mountainous and elevated areas and that impacts may be worsened by significant rain that has already fallen.
Another flood advisory for Central Luzon identified rivers and tributaries in Bulacan as likely to be affected by moderate to heavy rain.
Residents in low-lying areas and near waterways were advised to take precautions and follow instructions from local disaster officials.
The southwest monsoon is forecast to continue bringing heavy rain to parts of Luzon through the middle of the week. — with John Marwin Elao

articles.title: Heavy rains cause landslide in Taguig
articles.summary: Heavy rains caused a landslide and collapse of a wall of a house in Barangay Pembo, Taguig, on Aug. 29. The Pembo Fire & Rescue Brigade reported that the landslide occurred on Dahlia Street in the…

blocks.text: The area in Barangay Pembo, Taguig, where the landslide occurred on Aug. 29 (Photo from Barangay Pembo Disaster Risk Reduction Management Council/Pembo Fire & Rescue on Facebook)
Heavy rains caused a landslide and collapse of a wall of a house in Barangay Pembo, Taguig, on Aug. 29.
The Pembo Fire & Rescue Brigade reported that the landslide occurred on Dahlia Street in the barangay.
The team received a radio report of the incident at about 2:16 p.m. and went to the area. A family of 11 members was evacuated because of the incident.

The Taguig City Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office and City Social Welfare and Development Office arrived and conducted a preliminary hazard and welfare assessment. The affected area was cordoned off.
They were followed by the City Search and Rescue, which conducted a structural and safety evaluation.
The owner of the adjacent property where a construction was being conducted agreed to assist the affected family.
Meanwhile, the Taguig City government cleared fallen trees in different barangays, including Central Signal and Western Bicutan.
At 11:05 a.m. on Aug. 30, Metro Manila was under red rainfall warning.

blocks.text: TARLAC CITY — Four people were missing and another was rescued after a sport utility vehicle (SUV) plunged into a river when the Agana Bridge in Tarlac City collapsed Saturday night, Aug. 29, authorities said.
Nathaniel Dion, 20, was rescued shortly after the incident as authorities launched a search for the four other passengers.
The missing passengers were identified as Shanen Tuhao, 26; Paul Harvey Collado, 30, the SUV owner; James Harvey Taborlupa, 35; and Shiel Mae Taborlupa.

The Agana Bridge had been serving as an alternative route after the middle portion of the Aquino Bridge in Tarlac City collapsed shortly before midnight Friday, Aug. 28, amid heavy rains brought by the southwest monsoon.
Authorities continued search and rescue operations for the missing passengers as heavy rains persisted in the province. /das

articles.title: Zambales evacuees top 14,000 amid heavy rains, flooding
articles.summary: SAN ANTONIO, Zambales — More than 14,000 residents in this province have fled their homes due to widespread flooding brought by persistent heavy rains, according to the Provincial Disaster Risk…

blocks.text: SAN ANTONIO, Zambales — More than 14,000 residents in this province have fled their homes due to widespread flooding brought by persistent heavy rains, according to the Provincial Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (PDRRMO) on Sunday, Aug. 30.

A total of 710 families or 14,052 individuals have been evacuated, with 552 families or 10,242 individuals staying in various evacuation centers across the province. The rest have sought shelter elsewhere.

Out of 13 towns in the municipality, Botolan had the highest number of evacuees staying in evacuation centers, with 1,310 families or 3,491 individuals, followed by neighboring Cabangan with 695 families or 1,938 individuals.

Some residents were preemptively advised to move to evacuation centers as the province experienced non-stop heavy rains, while others were forced to leave their homes as floodwaters rose in their communities.

In its 5 a.m. advisory on Sunday, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (Pagasa) maintained its heavy rainfall outlook for Zambales, with 100 to 200 millimeters of rain expected through Tuesday, Sept. 1.
Pagasa was also monitoring a low-pressure area (LPA) inside the Philippine area of responsibility (PAR), which had a “high” chance of developing into a tropical depression on Sunday.
Meanwhile, Tropical Depression “Saudel” (formerly “Obet”) was being monitored outside the PAR. /das

articles.title: Over P200,000 marijuana plants discovered in Ilocos Sur
articles.summary: SAN ILDEFONSO, Ilocos Sur — Police discovered four marijuana plantations containing an estimated 4,000 seedlings and 660 mature plants during an operation in a disputed area in Sugpon, Ilocos Sur,…

blocks.text: SAN ILDEFONSO, Ilocos Sur — Police discovered four marijuana plantations containing an estimated 4,000 seedlings and 660 mature plants during an operation in a disputed area in Sugpon, Ilocos Sur, authorities said.

Personnel of the 2nd Ilocos Sur Provincial Mobile Force Company, in coordination with other police units, conducted the operation on Saturday (Aug. 29) at the disputed boundary of Mt. Teba in Barangay Licungan, Sugpon.
The operation was led by Maj. Ryan Afos, officer-in-charge of the 2nd Ilocos Sur Provincial Mobile Force Company.
Police said the confiscated marijuana plants had an estimated total standard drug price of P292,000.

The operation was conducted under Oplan Deicesais 2026, with personnel from the Ilocos Sur Provincial Drug Enforcement Unit, Ilocos Sur Provincial Intelligence and Detection Management Unit-KIMAT, Sugpon Municipal Police Station, 1st Ilocos Sur Provincial Mobile Force Company and the Police Intelligence Team of the Ilocos Sur Regional Intelligence Unit 1.
The marijuana plants were uprooted, inventoried and documented before being destroyed by burning at the site.
Police secured samples for laboratory examination. No cultivator was arrested during the operation. — Kenneth P. Tabin/Contributor /das

articles.title: India’s citizen-led school audits test limits of activism
articles.summary: The Indian activist movement dubbing itself the “Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)” shot to national prominence in May by leading weeks-long protests over a scandal involving highly competitive…

blocks.text: The Indian activist movement dubbing itself the “Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)” shot to national prominence in May by leading weeks-long protests over a scandal involving highly competitive entrance exams.
The student-led campaign put the government under intense political pressure and ended with the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan in July.
Now, the CJP is taking aim at India’s government schools, organizing volunteer visits to classrooms, documenting conditions and demanding accountability for problems.

Launched on August 15, Independence Day in India, the campaign asks parents, students and volunteers to inspect schools and record basic facilities including toilets, drinking water, electricity, classroom furniture and school buildings. The CJP has said the findings will be used to pressure authorities to make improvements.
The initial target is to audit 100 rural government schools over two months. It has also proposed giving recognition to village leaders who improve their schools.

Unlike the first campaign, which was based on street protests, the school audits require a more sustained form of local activism. Volunteers are expected to work consistently at the local level, document conditions and follow up with officials, parents and communities.

blocks.caption: Students celebrated in New Delhi after the resignation of India’s education minister in July Image: Raj K Raj/Hindustan Times/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: The organization is dealing with different layers of the Indian administration. Responsibility for government schools is divided between state governments, local administrations and elected village bodies. The CJP is therefore set to tackle different rules and political interests across the country.
India has over a million government schools, according to Education Ministry data. They make up nearly 70% of all schools in the country but serve less than half of its 247 million schoolchildren.
CJP: ‘We are not afraid’
That scale has given CJP a vast field for its campaign. But it has also brought a new set of challenges.
The authorities are raising questions regarding rules and locations for the CJP scrutiny, as well as safeguards when children are present.
The response is already varying from state to state. Some authorities have ordered their own inspections, while others have restricted access or taken police action against CJP volunteers.
Authorities in Maharashtra and Rajasthan states have objected to school visits carried out without permission.
In one case, a complaint by school authorities resulted in police action against CJP members after they entered the premises to conduct an audit.

In Rajasthan, restrictions have been imposed on outsiders entering government schools, as well as on filming, interviews and other forms of documentation. CJP volunteers in Rajasthan have also said they were attacked while inspecting a school.
“We are not afraid. We are seeking accountability from the government,” said CJP spokesperson Ashutosh Ranka.
Officials say schools are not open spaces

In the state of Uttar Pradesh, Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath has ordered officials to conduct on-the-spot checks of school facilities and directed police to register cases over what he called misleading videos about schools and colleges.
The CJP has said such measures undermine public scrutiny. Authorities have said schools are not open spaces for unauthorized inspections, particularly when children are present.
Vinita Gursahani Singh, managing trustee of We, The People campaign, which works on citizen empowerment, said the limits are set by law.

“Under the Right to Information Act, any citizen can inspect schools but you need to submit an application. And that makes sense as there has to be consideration for students and teaching,” Singh told DW.
“All public scrutiny is legitimate. It is our job to scrutinize. But the scrutiny has to follow process. It has to be even-handed. What applies to one citizen must apply to all,” she said.
Can activists serve as inspectors?
The CJP maintains government schools are publicly funded institutions and citizens have a legitimate right to ask how they are functioning.
Its volunteers use standardized audit forms to record conditions and send their findings to the CJP, which has said it will use the material to press local administrations to respond.

But critics question whether citizen activists can assume the role of inspectors. There are concerns about whether volunteers have the expertise to assess safety or infrastructure problems and how allegations posted on social media are verified.
Mohandas Pai, an education advocate, supports CJP’s focus on government schools but disagrees with its methods.
“I like young people taking interest in school education. It’s a broken system, and we need reforms,” Pai told DW.
But he objected to large groups entering schools and questioning headmasters and children.
“You can’t just barge into a school just because you think you are entitled to do it,” Pai said, stressing that “children have to have a safe, secure environment.”
Pai said the CJP should instead send small teams with permission, collect systematic data, publish regular reports and use the evidence to pressure governments.
CJP spokesperson Saurav Das rejected the argument that the campaign should rely on conventional channels, saying such approaches have failed to bring meaningful change.
Responding to Pai on X, he challenged him to join the next school visit and show the volunteers how it should be done.
Questions of student privacy
The audit campaign has also raised questions about privacy, consent and disruption of teaching when volunteers enter schools, film inside classrooms or question students.
However, Kavita Srivastava, president of the People’s Union for Civil Liberties (PUCL) Rajasthan, opposes restrictions on outsiders entering schools and taking photos and videos in her state.

“Activists were visiting government schools to document their condition and demand accountability. Protecting children’s privacy should not be used to prevent legitimate public scrutiny of government schools,” Srivastava told DW.
A new role for the CJP
Activist Amrita Johri said the CJP’s first campaign tapped into a longstanding accountability gap in India’s examination system, which cost millions of young people time and money.
“The demand for accountability had popular resonance because there was no real response from the government,” Johri told DW.
She backed the school audit campaign, saying public scrutiny should be welcomed.

“Public audits are an integral part of citizens’ right to information and should be welcomed as an opportunity to fix accountability,” she said. Johri added that the CJP needs to train volunteers, document problems and follow up with authorities to make the campaign effective. /dl

articles.title: 1,415 remain in Parañaque evacuation centers as habagat continues
articles.summary: A total of 1,415 residents remained in evacuation centers in Parañaque City Sunday morning as persistent rains brought by the southwest monsoon, or habagat, continued to threaten flood-prone…

blocks.text: Evacuees take shelter at a designated evacuation center in Parañaque City on Sunday as persistent rains brought by the southwest monsoon, or habagat, continue to affect the city (Photo from Parañaque PIO)

A total of 1,415 residents remained in evacuation centers in Parañaque City Sunday morning as persistent rains brought by the southwest monsoon, or habagat, continued to threaten flood-prone communities.

The City Social Welfare and Development Department said the figure was recorded at 7 a.m. Sunday, August 30, lower than the 1,906 evacuees recorded Saturday night, August 29, as heavy rains prompted residents in vulnerable areas to seek safer shelter.
Mayor Edwin Olivarez ordered city officials and barangay authorities to keep evacuation centers operational and remain on alert for possible flooding and additional rainfall.
The city government said 14 evacuation centers had been opened to accommodate residents affected by the weather disturbance, with seven facilities actively housing evacuees as of the latest count.

Evacuation centers were opened in several barangays, including BF Homes, San Antonio, San Dionisio, and San Isidro, as local authorities continued to monitor conditions in low-lying and flood-prone areas.
Olivarez also urged residents to remain vigilant and follow instructions from barangay officials and disaster response teams, particularly those living in areas vulnerable to rising floodwaters.

articles.title: Philippines, UK open talks on visiting forces pact
articles.summary: If concluded, the UK would follow France as the Philippines’ second European visiting forces partner.

blocks.text: The Philippines and the United Kingdom (UK) commenced the first round of formal negotiations for the proposed Status of Visiting Forces Agreement (SOVFA) Aug. 27, 2026.
Department of National Defense
MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines and the United Kingdom opened formal negotiations for a defense pact that would let British and Filipino troops train and operate on each other's soil.
The talks which started Thursday, August 27 mark Manila's latest push to widen its web of military partnerships as it faces more frequent confrontations with Chinese vessels in the South China Sea.

A Status of Visiting Forces Agreement (VFA) sets the terms for foreign troops entering the country for joint exercises, training and humanitarian missions, covering matters such as jurisdiction and entry procedures.
The meeting marked the first formal negotiating round for the proposed Philippines-UK pact.
Salvador Melchon Mison Jr., defense undersecretary for acquisition and resource management, led the Philippine panel.
Amy Senior, head of Indo-Pacific at the UK's Ministry of Defence, headed the British delegation.

"We appreciate UK's unqualified support as a like-minded partner in upholding the rules-based international order and preserving freedoms ensured by the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS)," Mison said, in a statement shared by the Department of National Defense.
Second European partner
If concluded, the pact would make the UK the Philippines' second SOVFA partner in Europe, after France, which signed its own agreement with Manila in March.
The Philippines already has VFAs or similar defense pacts with the United States, Australia, Japan, New Zealand and Canada.

Britain first proposed the pact in September 2025, when Minister of State for Defence Lord Vernon Coaker visited Manila and handed Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. a letter from UK Defence Secretary John Healey.
The push for more defense partners comes as China Coast Guard patrols around Scarborough Shoal have surged this year.
Philippine and Chinese forces clashed three times in a single week in July around the waters of the Scarborough and Ayungin shoals.
China has continued to reject a 2016 international arbitration ruling that struck down its expansive claims over nearly the entire South China Sea.

articles.title: Dear You, and the stories of love and migration the Filipino-Chinese pass down
articles.summary: Dear You tells a migration story different from that of many Filipino-Chinese families, but in its letters and lives rebuilt across the sea, you might find the same threads of how this diaspora came…

blocks.text: I went into Dear You expecting a tear-jerker. I came out thinking about my Gua-kong, the small boat that carried him out of China, and the life he built on this side of the sea. How wonderful, then, that a Teochew story could closely echo across so many Filipino-Chinese families.

But before I get ahead of myself, a bit about the movie first. Made on a modest budget, Dear You has become a surprise hit in China, remarkable because the whole film is spoken not in Mandarin but in Teochew, the regional language of the Chaoshan area in Guangdong and of a sprawling diaspora across Southeast Asia.

It was, in fact, a real tear-jerker, full of secret letters, long-lost relatives, families split across oceans, and love expressed in just about every possible way except through the word itself. The story centers around Chinese migrants in Thailand and the qiaopi, letters sent home together with remittances, making it particularly resonant across Southeast Asia, where generations of Teochew families settled.

But Dear You has been warmly received in the Philippines too, especially among Filipino-Chinese viewers, most of whom trace their roots not to Teochew-speaking communities, but to Hokkien-speaking southern Fujian.
I think part of the reason is simple. I had never heard anything on the big screen that sounded this close to what we spoke at home.

Technically, I still haven’t. The movie is in Teochew, not Hokkien, or Lannang-ue, literally “our people’s language.” They’re different languages and not interchangeable, but every so often Dear You produces a line that makes a Hokkien speaker’s ears perk up.
At one point, a character being teased for never having ridden a plane before is reassured: “Bue-gi bhoi ziah nang.” (Airplanes don’t eat people.)
In Hokkien, we would say something closer to: “Hui-ki bhoi chia lang.”
It’s not quite the same, but close enough.
In the cinema, I could hear Filipino-Chinese families excitedly echoing Hokkien-sounding tidbits. It was the little thrill of catching a word even before the subtitles told you what it meant.
There’s just something so intimate about hearing a language that sounds like the one your grandparents used at the dinner table.

Mandarin was the Chinese of school. Hokkien was the Chinese of home, shops, restaurants, family spats, and phone calls with uncles and aunties. For many younger Filipino-Chinese, it’s also a language we speak badly – or so our a-ma and ang-kong would like us to believe. E hiao tia, bue hiao kong, they would tease. (You can understand Hokkien, but you can’t speak it.)
But I think the representation goes deeper than language. There definitely is something familiar about the film’s characters themselves, the brusque way they speak and move through the world.

After all, we Filipino-Chinese are a practical bunch. Commerce runs through so much of the community’s history, from the massive conglomerates that dominate Philippine business to the mom-and-pop restaurants in Binondo that’ve been running for three generations. Business is such a natural part of everyday life that a conversation with even your closest relatives might go something like this:
“Seng-di ho bo?” (How’s business?)
“Ho ah. Seng-di chin ho.” (Good. Business is very good.)
There. Everybody’s caught up. Now we can sit beside each other in silence for the next two hours.

That practicality carries over into almost everything else, even love. Filipino-Chinese families are not particularly effusive people. We don’t fawn over one another or fill conversations with words dripping in honey. Love lives beneath the sentence. It’s in the subtext, the gesture, the thing somebody does for you with an easily missed yet unmistakable tenderness.
Concern is “Chia lo bue?” (Have you eaten yet?) Care is a bowl of oranges, peeled and placed by your bedside, or a wad of crumpled cash pressed into your hand when you protest that you don’t need it.

That’s also part of what makes Dear You feel so close to our hearts. Its characters can carry an entire lake of love while remaining almost maddeningly indirect about them. Feelings are tucked into letters, sacrifices, obligations, a bicycle sent home, a hurried wave of the hand to a boat setting sail.
Still, Dear You isn’t exactly the Filipino-Chinese story.

At its heart, the film is about a different kind of migration where a husband leaves China for opportunites elsewhere while wives, children, or other relatives stay behind. They send money home. They send letters home. Crucially, China is still home.

That’s not the case for most Filipino-Chinese families. For us third, fourth, even fifth-generation Chinoys, we see China as something ancestral. Sure, there are family associations, Chinese schools with trips to Xiamen, distant relatives whose exact relationship requires a family tree. If you’re a billionaire shoe tycoon, you might even build a mall, school, and road in your hometown.
But we don’t land in China as balikbayan. Our home is here.

That’s why Dear You works so well. A good film is particular yet universal at the same time. Watching it made me think less about coming back to China than about how my own family arrived in the Philippines in the first place.
It made me think about my Gua-kong.
My grandfather had his own boat story.

As he told it, he was a young man in Shanghai during the Chinese Civil War, when his family feared he would be pulled into Chiang Kai-shek’s Kuomintang army. He was their only son. They refused to let him fight and possibly die in a war they wanted no part of.
So they scrunched up what money they had and sent him away.

I grew up hearing the dramatic retelling: how he was smuggled out of China aboard a small motorboat, crammed together with other passengers, leaving with little more than the suitcase he could carry – not unlike Iron Fish, I imagine.
But in my grandfather’s case, there would be no great return, not even the ambition of it.

A relative helped him find work at Philippine Bank of Communications (PBCOM) then an important fixture in the Filipino-Chinese business world of Binondo. It wasn’t easy. Gua-kong spoke Mandarin, a bit of English, and not a word of Filipino. Perhaps most damningly for someone entering Manila’s Chinese community, he didn’t even speak Hokkien, having come from Shanghai and not Fujian. (I would eventually pick up the language from my father’s side of the family.)
But he proved capable enough that the bank shipped him off to St. John’s University in New York for his master’s degree. He came back with an accent – and enough business savvy to work his way up.

By 1980s, my grandfather had risen to become an executive vice president of PBCOM and was a director of PBCOM Finance, the bank’s financing affiliate, sitting on the board alongside heavyweight bankers like Luy Kim Guan and Maurice Nubla. Luy would later serve as chairman of PBCOM itself and belonged to the family that became the bank’s single biggest shareholder bloc. Maurice Nubla, meanwhile, was an original incorporator of PBCOM Finance alongside Ralph Nubla, who led the group that took majority control of PBCOM in 1974. Gua-kong counted the Nublas among his closest friends, attending dinners and parties togehter.
Quite the rise for a young man far away from home.
Then there was Gua-ma.
Their romance is worth telling. Because as accomplished as my grandfather would eventually become, when he first started courting my grandmother, he wasn’t exactly the best of suitors.

Gua-ma was an only daughter from the Cham family behind Cham Samco & Sons, one of old Manila’s prominent hardware stores and construction material importers. Gua-kong, meanwhile, was still building his name, and apparently decided that what he needed to improve his chances was a car.
Problem: he didn’t own one. Worse, he didn’t know how to drive.
So he borrowed a friend’s car. His cousin would drive him almost all the way to my grandmother’s house, stop around the corner, and let Gua-kong take the wheel for the final stretch.
He faced stiff competition for sure, but apparently the strategy worked. He got the girl.
Years later, he would tell another story involving perhaps the Philippines’ most famous businessman and certainly one of its richest.

According to Gua-kong, Henry Sy Sr. remembered him from his years at PBCOM, when the bank regularly helped finance SM as it grew and my grandfather was among the senior officers giving the final go-ahead on loans.

Years later, with the mall business already taking shape, the Sy family patriarch came back with a new idea from his son: bring Ace Hardware to the Philippines. Would he perhaps want to join the venture? He was a seasoned banker, after all, and one who had married into a hardware family.

This was in the 1990s, back when hardware stores were still mostly small, family-run places where you knew the owner and tawad was simply part of the transaction. An air-conditioned hardware store in a mall? Who would go out of their way to pay higher prices and not even be able to bargain? My grandfather passed.
Every time I walk into an Ace Hardware inside an SM mall, I have to remind myself that even successful businessmen are allowed at least one spectacularly bad call.

But Gua-kong kept building things. After retiring from PBCOM, he hardly slowed down. He set up a garments export factory, owned a branch of Panciteria Lido – a Chinese restaurant that may ring a bell with older members of the Filipino-Chinese community – and put up both a high-rise condominium and a smaller apartment building.
Here is where Gua-kong‘s story diverges from the many true stories that inspired Dear You. They spent their lives with China in their heart, through letters, remittances, visits.

My grandfather crossed the same sea, but set his feet firmly on Philippine shores. He built his life – his family – here. By the time it got to us grandchildren, China no longer felt like somewhere to return to. We were left with the language, the food, the traditions we choose to still keep alive, and most of all, the stories.

Maybe that’s what our generation inherited instead of the qiaopi: the stories of how we got here. Looking back so many years after that young man first stepped on that boat, I hold them close until it’s my turn to pass them on to the next. – Rappler.com
In memory of Edward Ting, the author’s late grandfather.

articles.title: 1,141 Manileños remain in evacuation centers amid habagat
articles.summary: A total of 367 families or 1,141 individuals are currently staying in active evacuation centers across Manila as the city continues to monitor communities affected by the Southwest Monsoon or…

blocks.text: A total of 367 families or 1,141 individuals are currently staying in active evacuation centers across Manila as the city continues to monitor communities affected by the Southwest Monsoon or Habagat, the Manila Department of Social Welfare (MDSW) reported Sunday, August 30.

Evacuees line up for registration at an evacuation center in Manila as heavy rains brought by the southwest monsoon, or habagat, continue to affect the city on Sunday, Aug. 30, 2026. (Photos courtesy of Manila PIO)
The latest evacuation center status, as of 8 a.m. on Aug. 30, showed that evacuees are being housed in facilities across the city, including areas in Districts 3, 5, and 6, as well as Baseco.
The largest number of evacuees was recorded in District 6, where 171 families or 562 individuals were staying at various evacuation centers.
This included 157 families or 518 individuals from Barangays 602 and 601 who were staying at Don Bosco School.

blocks.caption: MDSW personnel distribute grocery packs to evacuees at an evacuation center in Manila amid heavy rains brought by the southwest monsoon or habagat on Sunday, Aug. 30, 2026. (Photo courtesy of Manila PIO)

blocks.text: MDSW personnel distribute grocery packs to evacuees at an evacuation center in Manila amid heavy rains brought by the southwest monsoon or habagat on Sunday, Aug. 30, 2026. (Photo courtesy of Manila PIO)
Meanwhile, 150 families or 450 individuals from Blocks 1 Gasangan and 1 Aplaya were staying at the Baseco Evacuation Center.

Other active evacuation centers included the Barangay 326 Hall, with eight families or 23 individuals; Barangay 333 Hall, with three families or nine individuals; DWO V (Sagat, Bahay Kalinga), with 35 families or 97 individuals; Barangay 598, with seven families or 28 individuals; Barangay 607 Covered Court, with three families or seven individuals; Barangay 893 Barangay Hall, with four families or eight individuals; and Barangay 894 Multipurpose Hall, with one individual.
The MDSW said it has been assisting evacuees with hot meals, dinner, sleeping mats, and breakfast.
The city government continues to monitor the situation in affected communities and evacuation centers amid the effects of the Habagat.

articles.title: Manila continues aid for over 1,000 evacuees as rains persist
articles.summary: The Manila city government continued providing food and other assistance to over 1,000 evacuees staying in evacuation centers on Sunday, August 30, as heavy rains brought by the southwest monsoon or…

blocks.text: MDSW personnel distribute hot meals to evacuees at an evacuation center in Manila amid heavy rains brought by the southwest monsoon or habagat on Sunday, Aug. 30, 2026. (Photo courtesy of MDSW)

The Manila city government continued providing food and other assistance to over 1,000 evacuees staying in evacuation centers on Sunday, August 30, as heavy rains brought by the southwest monsoon or habagat persisted in the capital.
The Manila Department of Social Welfare (MDSW)distributed hot meals to evacuees to ensure their food needs were met while they temporarily remained in evacuation centers.
MDSW personnel also continued monitoring the condition of families who evacuated from flood-affected areas and assessing their immediate needs.
MDSW DirectorJay Dela Fuente visited evacuees at an evacuation center in Barangay 598, Damka Street, Sta. Mesa, Manila, to check on their condition and the assistance being provided.
The continued response came as Metro Manila remained under an Orange Rainfall Warning on Sunday due to the southwest monsoon.
The Manila city government also activated Code White, placing emergency and medical response teams on heightened readiness amid the inclement weather.
The city's localized heavy rainfall advisory was issued at 10:45 a.m. Sunday warned that Manila could experience heavy to intense rainfall that may last for two to three hours.
Residents were urged to remain alert for possible flash floods, avoid flooded and low-lying areas, and evacuate when necessary.
The MDSW said it would continue attending to the needs of evacuees and providing immediate assistance while they remain in temporary shelters.
Residents were also advised to monitor weather updates from the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA).

articles.title: Search opens for Gesmundo's successor as chief justice
articles.summary: Alexander Gesmundo is set to retire from the high court in November.

blocks.text: A hall at the Supreme Court building in Manila in an undated image.
SC PIO
MANILA, Philippines — The Judicial and Bar Council has opened applications for the next chief justice of the Supreme Court ahead of Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo's retirement on November 6.
The JBC said applications will be accepted until 4:30 p.m. on October 13.
Associate Justice Amy Lazaro-Javier is also set to retire on November 16, opening another vacancy in the high court.
Gesmundo was appointed the country's 27th chief justice by former President Rodrigo Duterte on April 5, 2021, succeeding Diosdado Peralta.
He joined the Supreme Court as an associate justice in 2017 after serving on the Sandiganbayan since 2005, where he later chaired its 7th Division.

Gesmundo previously served as assistant solicitor general and as commissioner of the Presidential Commission on Good Government on secondment from 1998 to 2001. He joined the Office of the Solicitor General after passing the Bar Examinations in 1985.

articles.title: Highest heavy rain warning issued in central Japan’s Fukui
articles.summary: Japan’s weather agency issued Sunday a special heavy rain warning for some areas in Fukui Prefecture, central Japan, and around 244,000 people have been urged to take emergency safety measures…

blocks.text: Japan’s weather agency issued Sunday a special heavy rain warning for some areas in Fukui Prefecture, central Japan, and around 244,000 people have been urged to take emergency safety measures amid reports of mudslides and vehicles stranded on flooded roads.

The Level 5 warning, the highest for heavy rain, was issued for the cities of Fukui, Ono and Katsuyama, indicating that a disaster has likely occurred or is imminent. The Japan Meteorological Agency later lowered it to Level 4, but it still means residents should evacuate from affected areas.
Houses and roads were inundated and rivers swelled due to heavy rain. Around 111,000 people in five municipalities have been urged to evacuate.
The Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism may take the emergency step of discharging water from a dam in Sakai to secure more room as water levels are rising.
In the 24 hours to Sunday morning, Katsuyama, Sakai and Fukui received a record rainfall of over 300 millimeters.
“It’s dangerous if water levels continue to rise. I hope the rain will let up,” a man in his 30s said in Katsuyama.
Earlier, the weather agency had warned that it might issue a special heavy rain warning for more areas.
Heavy rain is forecast for western to eastern Japan on Sunday as atmospheric conditions are unstable.
The Hokuriku region, including Fukui, may receive up to 120 mm of rain while 80 mm is forecast for the Chugoku region in the 24 hours through 6 a.m. on Monday, according to the agency. /dl

articles.title: Vietnamese coffee farmers ride China’s durian wave
articles.summary: DAK LAK, Vietnam — Vietnam’s Central Highlands produces around one sixth of the world’s coffee, but farmers are switching their traditional crop for durian to cash in on surging…

blocks.text: DAK LAK, Vietnam — Vietnam’s Central Highlands produces around one sixth of the world’s coffee, but farmers are switching their traditional crop for durian to cash in on surging Chinese demand for the pungent “king of fruits”.
“You can live okay with coffee, but it’s durian that makes you rich,” said Pham Xuan Lan, as he showed AFP journalists around his farm.
Blessed with a tropical climate and rich basalt soil, the lush Central Highlands produces vast quantities of robusta beans, and Vietnam trails only Brazil in coffee output.
But the area dedicated to durian has soared more than fivefold to 200,000 hectares (494,000 acres) nationwide over the past decade, according to the agriculture ministry.
Vietnam only officially entered the Chinese durian market after a 2022 trade protocol but last year became the country’s biggest supplier by volume, ending Thailand’s near two-decade dominance.
Lan was an early adopter, diversifying his crop two decades ago and now boasting 400 durian trees in Ea Knuec commune, part of Dak Lak province.
They produce 60 tonnes of the sweet yet smelly fruit, which is driven in frozen containers thousands of kilometres north into China.
The 56-year-old expects to make $76,000 this year — against $10,000 had he stayed with just coffee.
“With durian, I bought a car, houses for my children and built a villa for my family,” he said, his affluence evident around him.
Other local farmers have followed suit, focusing on the premium Ri6, Musang King and Dona varieties.

During the August-October harvest, Dak Lak’s roads are packed with trucks loaded with the spiky fruit, and at a durian festival this month, 525 vehicles formed what the Guinness World Records declared the largest ever parade of fruit-carrying vehicles.
Billions of views
The boom is driven by demand from China, fuelled by a combination of expanding supply and growing popularity on social media, particularly among young people.
On Douyin, China’s equivalent of TikTok, videos of users cracking open fruit with their bare hands have been watched billions of times.
“This tastes really sweet. It’s almost like it’s been coated in sugar,” said Douyin influencer Liulianzi in a clip liked more than 17,000 times.
Once a luxury food, increased competition between Thailand and Vietnam and improved transport links have helped cut prices and make the fruit more affordable.
At a durian tasting event in Beijing last month, Ada Song told AFP that she had spent almost 1,000 yuan ($150) on the fruit in recent weeks.
“I have tried nearly 20 different varieties,” Song said.
Durian “tastes just as sweet as cake, without the greasiness and heaviness”.
China imported almost $7.5 billion worth of fresh durian last year, a near 12-fold rise from 2015.
Now Beijing is seeking to boost its homegrown produce, with more than 3,000 hectares of plantations on the southern island province of Hainan, which has a similar climate to northern Vietnam.
But “our Hainan durians will always be just a supplement to Southeast Asian durians”, acknowledged Feng Xuejie, a durian expert at the Hainan Academy of Agricultural Sciences.
“It’s not even a competition.”
Improving quality
Vietnam’s durian exports are expected to reach $4 billion this year, up from $180 million in 2021 — 90 percent of them going to its northern neighbour.
But in the Central Highlands there are concerns about the reliance on China, as well as the risks of oversupply as more farmers join the rush.
Many anxiously eyed a recent price crash in Malaysia, blamed on an unusually bumper harvest.
Many farmers there have also switched to durian, focusing on premium varieties and fresh fruit, although the country has only a small slice of the Chinese market.
Vietnam’s government warned in early August of the “risks of oversupply and loss of quality control as the planted area is increasing rapidly”.
Farmers warn durian is not a one-way bet, requiring a strict mix of humidity, water and fertilisers.
Lan likened growing it to “raising a child — I can give you all the tricks but I cannot guarantee you similar success”.
He still grows coffee as his land is leased from a coffee company, allowing him to hedge his bets.
For some, the durian dream has already turned sour.
Hung, a farmer who gave only one name, switched entirely from coffee to durian five years ago, but switched back two years ago, admitting it was too hard to produce the quality required.
“I could not do it. I failed,” the 42-year-old said. “So I would never go back to durian again.” /dl

articles.title: LPA develops into Tropical Depression Pilandok
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – The low-pressure area inside the Philippine area of responsibility (PAR) developed into Tropical Depression Pilandok on Sunday morning, state meteorologists said. As of 10 a.m.,…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – The low-pressure area inside the Philippine area of responsibility (PAR) developed into Tropical Depression Pilandok on Sunday morning, state meteorologists said.

As of 10 a.m., Pilandok was last spotted 1,225 kilometers east of extreme northern Luzon, moving west northwestward at 15 kilometers per hour, according to the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (Pagasa).
Pilandok has maximum sustained winds of 45 kph, and gusts of up to 55 kph, Pagasa added.
But the state weather bureau noted that the cyclone is “less likely to make landfall over the country and will remain far from the Philippine landmass.”
It also noted that Pilandok is expected to be a “short-lived” tropical cyclone and is likely to weaken over the Philippine Sea by Tuesday, Sept. 1.
From today, Pilandok is forecast to move west-northwestward until Monday, Aug. 31.
Then its movement will shift northwestward to north northwestward until it dissipates, Pagasa said. /das

articles.title: 10 days’ worth of rain falls on Manila in one day — DRRM office
articles.summary: Rainfall that lashed Manila on Saturday, Aug. 29, was equivalent to around 10 days’ worth of rain, triggering flooding in several parts of the city and sending more than 1,000 residents to evacuation…

blocks.text: Rainfall that lashed Manila on Saturday, Aug. 29, was equivalent to around 10 days’ worth of rain, triggering flooding in several parts of the city and sending more than 1,000 residents to evacuation centers, the Manila City Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Department (MCDRRMD) said.

Christian John Evangelista, MCDRRMD resident meteorologist and chief of research and planning, said the city recorded its highest daily rainfall at Dr. Alejandro Albert Elementary School in Sampaloc, reaching147.4 millimeters (mm).
“Katumbas po ng sampung araw na ulan ang bumuhos sa Maynila kahapon (The rainfall that poured over Manila yesterday was equivalent to 10 days’ worth of rain),” Evangelista said.

“Ang pinakamataas na narecord natin ay sa Dr. Albert ES na umaabot sa 147.4mm at ang pinakamataas na hourly rate ay bandang 4 p.m., 23.6mm (The highest rainfall we recorded was at Dr. Albert Elementary School, reaching 147.4 mm, while the highest hourly rate was recorded at around 4 p.m., at 23.6 mm).”
Rainfall intensified at several points throughout the day, with the city experiencing two episodes of heavy to intense rain around 1 p.m. and 4 p.m.

“Makikita po na tayo nakaranas ng dalawang episodes ng heavy to intense rainfall sa siyudad bandang 1 p.m. at 4 p.m. (We experienced two episodes of heavy to intense rainfall in the city, around 1 p.m. and 4 p.m.),” Evangelista said.

The rain intensified again around 1 p.m., when all four MCDRRMD monitoring stations reached the “Intense” category. After briefly easing, rainfall peaked again at around 4 p.m., with hourly readings ranging from 23.6 mm to 27.2 mm.
Other monitoring stations also recorded significant rainfall, withCayetano Arellano High School at 143 mm, BASECO Evacuation Center at 135.8 mm, and Manila City Hall at 129.6 mm.
The heavy downpour left several major roads flooded throughout the afternoon.
MCDRRMD reported gutter-deep flooding along most of Taft Avenue and portions of España Boulevard.

The Pedro Gil portion of Roxas Boulevard and the Magsaysay-V. Mapa area in Sta. Mesa recorded around eight inches of flooding, while Kalaw Avenue going toward Taft reached 10 inches, the deepest recorded in the city.

“Sapat po ang dami ng ulan na ito upang makapagtala ng mga pagbaha lalo na po sa ating low-lying areas (The amount of rainfall was enough to cause flooding, particularly in our low-lying areas),” Evangelista said.
The afternoon rainfall also coincided with a sharp increase in evacuees.
Data from the Manila Department of Social Welfare (MDSW) showed that the number of families and individuals staying in evacuation centers more than doubled between 2 p.m. and 4 p.m. on Saturday.
As of 8 a.m. Sunday, Aug. 30, a total of 367 families or 1,141 individuals were staying in evacuation centers across Manila.
The biggest increases were recorded in Districts V and VI and BASECO.
Don Bosco School in District VI sheltered 157 families, or 518 individuals, while the BASECO Evacuation Center sheltered 150 families, or 450 individuals.
Manila City Social Welfare Officer Jay Dela Fuente said the MDSW provided evacuees with hot meals, dinner, sleeping mats, and breakfast.
Meanwhile, the Market Administration Office (MAO) distributed doxycycline to vendors at the Central Market as part of the city’s efforts to help prevent leptospirosis amid the threat of flooding.
Vendors were also reminded to take precautions and follow health protocols to protect themselves from illnesses associated with flood exposure.
The MCDRRMD said the rainfall data showed how quickly heavy rain can translate into flooding, particularly in Manila’s low-lying areas.

articles.title: Iceland EU referendum on a knife edge as counting continues
articles.summary: A vote on whether to resume membership talks with the European Union is too close to call.

blocks.text: Iceland's closely fought referendum on whether to resume membership talks with the European Union is going down to wire, with the result too close to call.

Based on the first 153,197 votes counted of the 270,000 voters eligible, 50.1% rejected the government's proposal, while 49.9% said yes, public broadcaster RUV said, with just 435 votes splitting them.

Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir's centre-left government promised to hold a referendum by 2027, but brought it forward because of international tensions, including US President Donald Trump's threats against Greenland.
However, debate in this island nation of almost 400,000 people centred more on its fishing industry rather than security concerns.
Already part of the EU's single market and Schengen border-free zone, EU membership would bring Iceland into the customs union and eventually the euro.
Iceland began its application to join the EU in 2009 in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis and the collapse of Iceland's banking system.
Its application was already well advanced when a eurosceptic government came to power in 2013 and put talks on hold. Fishing rights was the biggest obstacle then - as it remains today.

Fish and marine industries account for almost 40% of Iceland's exports and many No voters feared they would cede some control of their lucrative fishing grounds under the EU's common fisheries policy.
The referendum campaign has fuelled debate about Iceland's place in the world, Frostadottir said after casting her ballot in the capital on Saturday.
"This is a great day, we've been waiting for this for years to be able to have a vote," Frostadottir said, adding that her government would continue its work regardless of the outcome.
The question on the ballot was: "Should Iceland resume accession negotiations with the European Union?"
A Yes vote would not be a final decision on joining the EU, but a move towards an accession agreement, which would then have to be approved by a second referendum.
Equally, the No vote would not rule out the chance of Iceland resuming talks in the future.
While economic issues dominated the referendum campaigns, security concerns also featured.
Iceland is a founder member of Nato but it has no military and relies on its allies for defence.
The country has backed Ukraine during Russia's full-scale invasion and officials have been alarmed by Russia's increased maritime manoeuvres near the island.
Trump's expressed interest in taking over Greenland has also raised concerns.

articles.title: Binangonan e-library receives book donations
articles.summary: The Binangonan Municipal e-Library and Museum received a donation of grade school and junior high school textbooks from a private school in the municipality, expanding access to learning materials…

blocks.text: The Binangonan Municipal e-Library and Museum received a donation of grade school and junior high school textbooks from a private school in the municipality, expanding access to learning materials for local students and residents.

The donation drive, spearheaded by both the Calumpang and Batingan campuses of the Child Jesus of Prague School (CJPS), aims to expand learning materials available to the public and foster an enriched academic environment for the youth across the municipality.
Representatives from the Binangonan Municipal e-Library and Museum expressed their profound gratitude to the school administration, faculty, and students for their generosity.

Mr. Joshua Mabanglo of Binangonan e-library and museum (right) receives the donation of books from representatives of Child Jesus of Prague School (red uniform) (photo from Binangonan Municipal 3-library and museum)

Vice Mayor Russel Ynares, whose initiative led to the establishment of the municipal library and museum, said that the turnover of books represents more than a charity drive; it serves as a cornerstone for building long-term institutional partnerships between the local government and the private educational institution.

"This CJPS and municipal government initiative is just the beginning of a stronger collaboration between our local educational institutions and the municipal government. By working together, we can continuously elevate the quality of education and provide better learning opportunities for all Binangonan students," Ynares said.

The newly donated textbooks will be integrated into the library’s growing collection, ensuring that public school students, researchers, and young learners have ready access to high-quality reference materials for the current school year.

Officials from both CJPS and the local government led by the full support of Mayor Rhea Ynares, are optimistic that this collaborative framework will inspire other private and public organizations to invest in community-based learning initiatives, driving sustainable educational development across the province.

The municipal library, in turn, is donating books and other learning materials to public schools in the municipality as part of its community literacy and e-learning programs for the people of the municipality.

articles.title: Kai’s knowledge, instincts ‘like a point guard’
articles.summary: Gilas Pilipinas head coach Tim Cone has nothing but praises for Kai Sotto in his first game back since fully recovering from an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury that sidelined him from…

blocks.text: Gilas Pilipinas head coach Tim Cone has nothing but praises for Kai Sotto in his first game back since fully recovering from an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury that sidelined him from national team duty for almost two years.

The veteran mentor pointed out that more than Sotto’s length, the 7-foot-3 center has the basketball instinct and knowledge comparable to point guards, making the rest of his teammates better while he’s on the floor.

“The thing about Kai, yes, he’s 7-foot-3 but his knowledge of the game, instinct for the game is like a point guard. He is like RJ Abarrientos or Juan Gomez de Liano,” said Cone after Gilas’ 82-81 win over Jordan.

“He’s really that smart and that intelligent, that makes people around him better. Everybody’s better when he’s on the floor whether through passing, scoring or rolling, the attention he grabs, he just makes everybody better,” he added.
And Cone certainly has the numbers to support that.
Without Sotto, Gilas has not beaten teams inside the top 60 of the world rankings through the FIBA Asia Cup qualifiers and main tournament and the World Cup Asian qualifiers.
When Sotto’s playing, Gilas is defeating teams way above its ranking in the likes of Latvia and New Zealand. And this time, against a potent Jordan team.
Of course, Sotto’s length also made a ton of differences — evident in the final play when he swatted away what could have been Jordan’s game-winning attempt.

“What was really big tonight was his defense patrolling against Al Dwairi who was a really top class center and also patrolling the paint especially in the second half not allowing Harris and Ybrahim to get to the rim on us,” Cone pointed out
“And Olajuwon at the end. Remember, Olajuwon earlier was getting to the rim with impunity but the last play he get to the rim but of course Kai rejected him,” he added.

articles.title: PH marks 75th anniversary of Mutual Defense Treaty with US
articles.summary: The Department of National Defense (DND) and the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) on Sunday, Aug. 30, marked the 75th anniversary of the Mutual Defense Treaty (MDT), an agreement which provides…

blocks.text: The Department of National Defense (DND) and the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) on Sunday, Aug. 30, marked the 75th anniversary of the Mutual Defense Treaty (MDT), an agreement which provides the legal and strategic framework for defense cooperation with the United States, giving both countries a basis for working together when faced with a common security threat.
DND spokesperson Asst. Sec. Arsenio Andolong said the MDT remains a key part of Manila and Washington’s commitment to peace, stability, and the defense of a free and open Indo-Pacific.

“As we commemorate the 75th anniversary of the Philippines-United States Mutual Defense Treaty, we honor an alliance that has endured through generations and has evolved to meet the demands of an increasingly complex security environment,” he said in a statement.

The treaty was signed in Washington, D.C., on Aug. 30, 1951, recognizing that an attack in the Pacific on either country would endanger the peace of both, and obliges them to act together to meet the common danger.
Over the past seven decades, the DND said the defense pact has served as a framework for sustained defense and security cooperation between Manila and Washington.

The partnership has expanded from the original defense arrangement to exercises, maritime security cooperation, humanitarian assistance and disaster response, capability development, and greater interoperability between Filipino and American forces.

“For seven decades, the MDT has provided a framework for sustained cooperation between the two countries, strengthening interoperability, enhancing defense capabilities, and contributing to peace, stability, and security in the Indo-Pacific region,” AFP public affairs office chief Col. Xerxes Trinidad said.

The DND said the cooperation was significant because the Philippines faces security challenges in a region where maritime disputes and other threats require stronger defense capabilities and closer coordination with allies and partners.
The DND also cited the growing scope and sophistication of bilateral and multilateral exercises and engagements as evidence of the alliance's continuing development.
“The strength of our alliance is evident in the success, sophistication, and growing scope of our bilateral and multilateral exercises, engagements, and people-to-people exchanges,” Andolong noted.
He said such efforts have enhanced interoperability and strengthened deterrence while demonstrating the two countries’ resolve to support regional security and stability.

“As we look to the future, we remain committed to building a more sustainable, agile, and productive partnership anchored on mutual respect, shared interests, and adherence to international law,” Andolong concluded.

articles.title: LPA develops into Tropical Depression Pilandok
articles.summary: PAGASA says Pilandok is expected to be a short-lived tropical cyclone

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – The low pressure area inside the Philippine Area of Responsibility has developed into a tropical depression at 8 am Sunday, August 30.

Tropical Depression Pilandok was located at 1,225 kilometers east of extreme Northern Luzon, according to the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA). It is moving west northwestward at 15 kilometers per hour, with maximum sustained winds of 45 km/h and gustiness of up to 55 km/h.

Pilandok is expected to continue moving in the same direction until Monday, August 31, before turning northwestward to north northwestward. PAGASA said the tropical depression is “less likely” to make landfall and will remain far from the Philippine landmass.

“Pilandok is expected to be a short-lived tropical cyclone and is forecast to remain a tropical depression throughout the forecast period before weakening into a remnant low over the Philippine Sea south of the southern islands of Japan on Tuesday (September 1),” PAGASA said in its 11 am bulletin Saturday.

Meanwhile, Tropical Depression Saudel (formerly referred to as Obet), which is being monitored outside PAR, has weakened into a low pressure area. It still has a “medium” chance of redeveloping into a tropical depression.

articles.title: Nepal floods: A disabled couple offer strangers the little they have
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — On a hillside in Dabile of Bidur Municipality-10 stands a lone house with a corrugated zinc-sheet roof. There are no other houses nearby. From the house, the only view below is of a…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — On a hillside in Dabile of Bidur Municipality-10 stands a lone house with a corrugated zinc-sheet roof. There are no other houses nearby. From the house, the only view below is of a settlement devastated by Wednesday’s flooding of the Bhotekoshi River. Concrete houses lie submerged, while those on the opposite bank stand intact but eerily deserted.
Yet since the flood, the small house has rarely been without guests.

On August 16, the day the flood struck, 31 students and teachers who escaped the disaster spent the night there. The house became a safe haven for those who fled the nearby Uttargaya Public Secondary School.

Since then, it has become a refuge for people arriving in search of relatives missing in the flood. Between 15 and 20 people come here every day. At the edge of a forest, the house has become a place where people exhausted from walking in the sun can find drinking water, a meal and a place to sleep. More than 200 people have taken shelter here since the flood.
With no other houses around, it has become a sanctuary for families searching for relatives swept away by the flood and landslides, as well as for those who fled to save their lives.

The homeowners, Prem Bahadur Tamang and his wife, Maiya, are both disabled. Prem Bahadur has a spinal injury and can barely move around the house with the help of a walking stick. Maiya has difficulty moving her left leg. Despite their own physical limitations, the couple continue to take in anyone who comes to their doorstep. They do not let their guests go hungry.

blocks.caption: With no other houses around, it has become a sanctuary for families searching for relatives swept away by the flood and landslides Angad Dhakal/TKP

blocks.text: Government support for food and shelter has yet to adequately reach the area. In its absence, the Tamang couple have been helping those in distress with whatever little they have.
Asked how they make a living, Maiya says her husband receives a monthly old-age allowance of Rs3,000 and she receives Rs2,000. Their children also send them money occasionally.
“That is how we survive,” she says.
The grain they grow on their hillside farmland does not last the year. The couple also complain that they cannot protect their crops from monkeys.
On the day of the flood, Prem Bahadur was sitting outside his house when the Bhotekoshi began roaring. He approached the river with the help of his walking stick and was alarmed by what he saw.
“Look, the flood is destroying everything,” he recalls telling Maiya as he called her to see the river.

“People were swept away and houses were buried right before our eyes. We were in no condition to go and rescue anyone. We kept watching the Bhotekoshi, thinking the flood would not reach this high. But within seconds, Betrawati Bazaar had turned into a riverbed. The road used by vehicles was swept away. The school was submerged and school buses were buried.”
Prem Bahadur, who has lived in the area for four generations, says he had never witnessed such a disaster.
“It did not even look like a flood. It looked as if a volcano had erupted,” he says.
The couple say they feel they must do whatever they can to help people affected by the disaster.
Maiya says their stock of rice and lentils is running low. Despite her physical limitations, she cooks for the people who come to their home. Some guests cook for themselves.

“What else can we do? When things are normal, everyone can cook and eat on their own. Who would come looking for our house? It is at times like this that we have to help. We do whatever we can,” she says.

Her brother-in-law, Juhanlal Tamang, is also taking shelter there with his family after losing their home. Five members of his family are staying at the house. Juhanlal’s grandson was swept away by the Bhotekoshi and remains missing.

Haribahadur Rai, whose family members are also missing, is sheltering there as well. His house at Angitar was swept away. His wife, granddaughter, mother-in-law and father-in-law are among those missing.
The couple have taken in several families in similar circumstances.

“Although the house is small, we are all living and sleeping inside and outside, sharing our joys and sorrows,” Maiya says. “We are not in a position to go out and bring food and water. If supplies could come from somewhere, at least we would not have to send away people who come here for shelter on an empty stomach.”
She says they have enough rice and lentils for only a few more days.

The couple have two sons and two daughters, but none lives with them. Their eldest son, Bishal, is in India for work. Their younger son, Buddha, used to drive an auto-rickshaw along the Trishuli-Betrawati route, earning a living for himself while also helping his parents.
The Bhotekoshi flood not only swept away Buddha’s auto-rickshaw but also destroyed the route on which he worked.
“What are we going to do now?” Buddha asks, his face downcast. “My parents are disabled and our family is struggling. I would do any labouring job if I could find one.”
No government agency has yet been able to reach the area. Bodies floating in the river have begun to decompose, while the bodies of people trapped inside houses have yet to be recovered.
Amid the devastation, the Tamang couple’s house is the only one still standing intact. /dl

articles.title: Cone amazed by Quiambao’s rapid improvement
articles.summary: Gilas Pilipinas head coach Tim Cone raved at the quick development of young forward Kevin Quiambao, who is now emerging as one of the team’s reliable players in the 2027 FIBA World Cup Asian…

blocks.text: Gilas Pilipinas head coach Tim Cone raved at the quick development of young forward Kevin Quiambao, who is now emerging as one of the team’s reliable players in the 2027 FIBA World Cup Asian Qualifiers.
Quiambao, who has been playing superb for Gilas through the last two windows, stepped up big in the Nationals’ much-needed 82-81 win over Jordan at the Mall of Asia Arena on Friday, Aug. 28.
The 6-foot-6 forward nailed a booming triple with 11.7 seconds left to break a 79-all deadlock and put Gilas ahead for good.
He finished with 14 points and five rebounds after getting extended minutes on the floor due to the absence of Justin Brownlee and later on the injury to Carl Tamayo.

“He came in as the young guys of the team when we put this together two and a half years ago. We said at that point that at some point, he's going to be the guy that takes over the program. Him and Carl,” said Cone.
The veteran coach, however, admitted that he did not expect Quiambao to take such a big role at this point of his career but he nonetheless welcomes the fast growth of his prized forward.

“They were the two young guns that were gonna come up and be our main guys at some point. I was expecting that to happen when they're 26, 27, 28 but it’s happening now when they are 23, 24 years old,” he added.
Quiambao had a breakout performance in the July window when he fired 23 points in the tough 106-102 double-overtime defeat at the hands of New Zealand. His performance took off from there.
“They got a tremendous future in front of them. I really enjoy coaching KQ. He's such a good kid too. Carl also. It’s really fun to coach those guys,” said Cone.

Despite heavy rains, the group decided to continue with the concert held at MUFG Stadium in Tokyo.
But the stage became wet and slippery, causing some of them to fall while performing.
Fans posted videos and photos of the stage accidents online, expressing concern for the group.
Among members who fell were Lee Know, Changbin and Felix.
Bang Chan also fell and actually suffered a cut on his arm.
The second day of the Japan concert is scheduled Aug. 30.
Meanwhile, JYP Entertainment, Stray Kids’ agency, announced that Lee Know donated 100 million won (about $72,600) to the victims of the massive flood in Nepal.
Lee Know made the donation through World Vision on Aug. 28.

"I hope my heartfelt gesture can be a small source of strength for those going through difficult times. I sincerely hope that the victims and everyone working hard on relief efforts on the ground will return to their peaceful daily lives as soon as possible,” he said.

blocks.text: Weljon Mindoro suffered a knockout defeat against Mexican veteran Carlos Ocampo in their 10-round non-title catchweight bout at the Galen Center in Los Angeles on Sunday, Aug. 30 (PH time).
The Filipino pug just couldn’t sustain the impressive start to the bout and suffered a ninth round technical knockout defeat.
The veteran Ocampo unloaded a slick right counter which landed to the jaw of Mindoro, who immediately went down after the hit.
The 29-year-old Filipino managed to get back up and beat the count but his corner waved the flag, formally ending the fight at the 1:29 mark of the penultimate round.
Undefeated prior to the contest, Mindoro was actually dictating the tempo in the early round, even opening a cut above Ocampo’s right eye with a big right hand in the third

Ocampo, who has been in several title fights against Tim Tszyu and Sebastian Fundora, rallied back into the contest and began landing big hits during the middle rounds before finally drilling the decisive right hand in the ninth round.
The World Boxing Council Federación Centroamericana de Boxeo middleweight crown was supposed to be at stake in the bout but Ocampo came in overweight at 165-pounds.
Mindoro dropped to a 17-1-1 record with 16 knockouts while Ocampo improved to a 39-4 slate.
