blocks.text: KATHMANDU – Devastating floods near the border with China this week have killed at least 675 people in Nepal, the Himalayan nation’s disaster authority said on Saturday.
Chinese state media earlier confirmed seven dead in Tibet following Wednesday’s disaster, taking the total killed to 682.
The number of missing in Nepal remained constant at 2,426, after a sharp hike in numbers on Saturday morning.

That missing list includes 517 foreigners, as well as 933 workers on hydropower projects on the river where the torrent smashed down, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority.
The number of missing also includes 45 Nepali Army soldiers, 40 police officers, and 19 immigration and customs officers.
In India, authorities said they had recovered seven bodies from rivers flowing from Nepal, believed to be flood victims. However, they are not included in the toll.

articles.title: Zimbabwe crash involving church minibus kills 27
articles.summary: Dozens of people were killed when a minibus carrying churchgoers collided head-on with a truck in central Zimbabwe. The crash near the town of Chivhu is the latest deadly road accident in the African…

image.caption: The accident occurred on Friday about 87 miles south of the capital Harare [FILE: April 20, 2020]Image: Zinyange Auntony/AFP

blocks.text: At least 27 people were killed in a minibus crash in central Zimbabwe after the vehicle carrying churchgoers collided head-on with a truck, police said Saturday. Seven people were injured.

Police spokesperson Paul Nyathi said members of a popular Indigenous African Christian denomination, known for wearing white robes, were traveling to a conference on Friday when their minibus collided with a truck on a major highway near the town of Chivhu, about 140 kilometers (87 miles) south of the capital, Harare.
The foreign-registered haulage truck was overtaking another vehicle when it collided with the minibus. Both vehicles were carrying an "unspecified" number of passengers, Nyathi said in a statement.
Footage shared on social media by public broadcaster ZBC showed the mangled minibus charred to a shell.
Zimbabwe faces road safety crisis

Authorities say 94% of road accidents occur due to human error. Many Zimbabweans rely on privately operated minibus taxis, known locally as kombis, for everyday transportation. The vehicles are often criticized for carrying more passengers than allowed.
Zimbabwe’s roads are also riddled with potholes after years of underfunding and neglect, while driving standards can be poor.

In April, at least 18 people were killed when a minibus burst into flames on a highway in southern Zimbabwe. Earlier that month, a woman and her five children were killed when their vehicle collided with a haulage truck on another highway linking Zimbabwe and South Africa.

blocks.caption: Rescue personnel work at the site of a bus accident on a major highway near Harare [FILE: January 18, 2015]Image: Xinhua/imago images

blocks.text: Road crashes kill about 300,000 people across Africa each year, accounting for roughly a quarter of the global road death toll, according to the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa. The continent has the world’s highest road fatality rate, the commission says.
This is despite Africa’s 1.5 billion people accounting for only about 3% of the world’s vehicle fleet.

articles.title: Right-wing commentator Milo Yiannopoulos deported from US to UK
articles.summary: The self-styled provocateur had been detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

blocks.text: British right-wing political commentator Milo Yiannopoulos has been deported from the United States after being detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
Yiannopoulos, 41, a former editor of Breitbart News and onetime political aide to rapper Kanye West, was deported on Friday, according to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).
Yiannopoulos, "an illegal alien from the United Kingdom" had been sent "back to his home country", a DHS spokesperson said in a statement given to the BBC.
The self-styled provocateur has called himself the "most fabulous supervillain on the internet" and advocated for stricter US immigration controls. His critics call him a purveyor of hate speech.
Yiannopoulos, who grew up in Kent in the south of England, was arrested on 27 August after arriving at Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport.
He flew into the US in May 2019 and "chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation's laws", the DHS said.
He has previously cheered on ICE raids, last year calling for "total legal immunity for ICE agents when they're on duty".
He wrote on social media in 2025: "We have got to deport millions and millions of people. Without that, nothing else matters."
Yiannopoulos also advocated "on the spot deportation for anyone who can't prove they are in the US legally" on social media.
Yiannopoulos was an early supporter of Donald Trump during the 2016 election, headlining an event that year called Gays for Trump during the Republican National Convention.

The commentator has since become a critic of the US president, but still voices support for his agenda. He wrote on X in March this year that Trump had "lost his way, bought off by foreign interests".

Yiannopoulos has courted controversy with his comments on transgender people, Muslims, Black Lives Matter, feminists and gay people, even though he himself identified as gay. He now calls himself an "ex-gay".

In 2020, he assisted West in the rapper's unsuccessful bid to become president. He also worked for Marjorie Taylor Greene, a former Republican congresswoman who fell out with Trump and became a fierce critic before resigning from office.

Laura Loomer, a far-right commentator and Trump ally who has feuded with Yiannopoulos, took credit for his arrest by ICE, claiming on X on Friday night that his flight back to the UK had already departed.
"This subversive foreign agent is already out of the United States and DHS tells me he's NEVER allowed to come back to the United States ever again," she wrote.

In 2017, he was disinvited from speaking at CPAC, a US conservative conference that also hosted Trump, after footage emerged of Yiannopoulos appearing to condone paedophilia. He also later apologised and resigned from Breitbart.
He denied the allegations and said he had been speaking about his own experiences as a child.

Yiannopoulos was once regularly linked with the alt-right, a disparate group that is outspoken against political correctness and feminism, and which includes neo-Nazis and white supremacists among its ranks.
He has said he does not consider himself part of the alt-right, although he has called it "energising and exciting".

articles.title: 'We didn’t want them:' Hamilton rallies against Dominion Society, as group holds event in Burlington, Ont.
articles.summary: More than 100 people gathered outside of Hamilton city hall around midday Saturday to denounce the fact that a self-proclaimed nationalist group that wants to deport millions of people from Canada…
articles.byline: Paul Forsyth, Eva Salinas, Lauren Kuivenhoven

image.caption: The parking lot at The Atrium in Burlington was full on Saturday. People with Dominion Society lanyards were seen in the parking lot. (Jaskaran Singh/CBC)

blocks.text: More than 100 people gathered outside of Hamilton city hall Saturday to denounce the fact that a self-proclaimed nationalist group that wants to deport millions of people from Canada planned to host a day-long conference in the city the same day.
The Hope Not Hate rally said it was a gathering to “stand up against racism and bigotry,” in light of the Dominion Society’s organizing.
In the end, the anti-immigration group, which had previously announced its DomCon event would take place in Hamilton on Saturday, held it down the highway in Burlington, Ont.

CBC Hamilton observed several men in suits wearing Dominion Society lanyards in the parking lot of The Atrium Banquet and Conference Centre. One of them, Max Genest, identified himself as a member of the group. The parking lot was nearly full. Around 30 masked protesters were also on site, as were several members of the Halton Regional Police Service.
Protesters outside the Atrium centre said they were not part of an organized group but declined to speak on the record, citing fear of being targeted by Dominion Society supporters.
They told CBC they were protesting what they called "fascist and racist" beliefs.
The venue said it had no knowledge of the group when it accepted its reservation.

"Atrium was not aware of the Dominion Society of Canada's background upon booking and is not aware of any client's social political views, nor is it a contractual requirement for any … client to disclose that information," Alexandre R. Figueiredo, who identified himself as owner and CEO of Atrium, said in an email to CBC News.
"Atrium respects the rights of all citizens, including the right to protest."
The Canadian Anti-Hate Network first reported the venue to CBC News earlier on Saturday.
"Hamilton beat Dominion Society," Evan Balgord, executive director of the Canadian Anti-Hate Network, told CBC Hamilton in response to the conference being held in Burlington.
Efforts from groups in Hamilton to spread awareness about the Dominion Society and have bookings cancelled were ultimately successful, Balgord said.

"The day's not over yet but I’m relieved that this time, they did not successfully host their racist and anti-immigrant event in Hamilton," Lyndon George, executive director of the Hamilton Anti-Racism Resource Centre (HARRC), told CBC Saturday. "Full credit goes to a coordinated effort to keep hate out of Hamilton."

Dominion Society did not confirm the location to CBC directly. "Despite the best efforts of angry anti-Canadians activists and their sympathizers in the Hamilton police, they were not able to cancel DOMCON26," group founder Daniel Tyrie wrote in an email Saturday.

When CBC shared its observations with the City of Burlington, the city said in an email it was previously not aware of the conference taking place there but that the "event is not taking place at a city-owned or city-operated facility.

"Burlington is proud to be a diverse and inclusive community. We reject hatred, discrimination and intolerance in all forms. Hate has no place in Burlington, and we remain committed to creating a city where everyone feels welcome, valued, respected and safe," the email statement said.
At least 2 Hamilton venues cancelled booking

In the lead up to Saturday, groups like HARRC, followed by Hamilton Mayor Andrea Horwarth, some Niagara municipalities and Hamilton police said venues should be aware of who is making a booking before accepting it.
On Saturday, people gathered at Hamilton city hall said the group was not welcome.

“It’s very important to us to make sure that we stand up, that we speak out, that we contact politicians, and we don’t just sit in discomfort when we hear about a rise in white supremacy,” said Karen Goodfellow, who came to Hamilton from Toronto to show support.

"As working class people we decided we needed to get together in this city and say we’re all in this together," Hamilton labour organizer Ritch Whyman told CBC Hamilton. "We didn’t want them... to bring their racist politics into our city.”
Hamilton is a "welcoming" place, added Vivyan Salih, who works at the Immigrants Working Centre.

The Dominion Society did not reveal the venue in the lead up to the event. Then came word from Hamilton police that two different venues in Hamilton had pulled the plug on hosting the conference, one just days before.
Police joined call-out to venues before event
Police had joined the call for venues to “consider the impact” of hosting the event in the days leading up to it.
"The messaging associated with DomCon is divisive and exclusionary and can negatively impact the sense of safety and belonging within our community," police said in a news release Thursday.
Dominion Society in turn accused the police of an “abuse of power.”

items: What is Dominion Society of Canada and why are people of different political backgrounds worried?

blocks.text: Dominion Society said it was planning to have Canadian and international speakers at DomCon, such as far-right Austrian extremist Martin Sellner. But Sellner, who is permanently banned in the UK, posted on social media that the Canadian government blocked him from travelling here by not replying to his visa application in time.
Richard Robertson, B’nai Brith Canada’s director of research and advocacy, commended the blocking of Sellner.
“Extremists such as Sellner have no business coming to Canada to attack our multicultural society and incite hate and intolerance,” he said.
Protesters rally at Hamilton City Hall against anti-immigration group

A livestream of the conference on Saturday showed co-founder Ken Jones giving opening remarks, followed by a speaker singing the national anthem in front of a Canadian Red Ensign flag held up by two men.
Later, attendees were heard chanting "remigration now". following a pre-recorded video address by Sellner.
Balgord, of the Canadian Anti-Hate Network, previously said Dominion Society likely has thousands of members — mostly young white men and boys.
On its website, Dominion Society describes itself as "promoting Canadian nationalism and immigration reform."
However, "when they're talking just to their supporters, they're talking about how they need to deport people from Canada who are not the right kind of white and European," Balgord told CBC Hamilton.

Dominion Society's website outlines a plan for "remigration," or the mass deportation of five to nine million people, including temporary foreign workers, permanent residents and people born in Canada to non-Canadian citizens.
It also promotes the great replacement conspiracy theory, which suggests white people are being replaced by racialized people.
'We are equally free to condemn them'
On Aug. 4, several Hamilton groups, including HARRC and Hamilton Centre for Civic Inclusion, signed an open letter urging businesses and institutions not to rent space to Dominion Society.

They called on elected officials to denounce the group, and asked leaders to commit that their policies and statements "will not contribute to the scapegoating of immigrants and racialized communities that is on the rise in Hamilton."
Horwath wrote letters to local businesses, asking them to be wary of an anti-immigration group advertising a conference.

"While people are free to express their views, our community must also be clear about the values we stand for and are proud of: inclusion, respect and ensuring that everyone feels they belong in Hamilton," she said.

items: Hamilton police join call for venues to 'consider the impact' of hosting anti-immigration group Saturday

blocks.text: Hamilton Centre MP Aslam Rana issued a statement on Aug. 18 condemning the planned conference, saying it and Dominion Society "represent a racist and extremist ideology masquerading as a nationalist movement."
He said Hamilton has already seen a significant increase in hate crimes. "Organizations and events like these only work to divide Canadians and seek to pit neighbour against neighbour," he said.
Fear that DomCon could be move neighbouring Niagara Region also spilled over into that region this week.

Saleh Waziruddin, with the Niagara Region Anti-Racism Association, wrote to municipal chief administrative officers across Niagara warning that Dominion Society could be planning to move its "hate" conference there.

The Township of West Lincoln, nestled against the border with Hamilton, made it clear it wasn't interested in having DomCon in the township and urged private facilities to not allow "hate-based" events.

"We are working hard to unite our community and build a strong sense of safety, civic pride and belonging," the township statement said on Thursday. "We strongly condemn hate-motivated groups who would dismantle our efforts, spread hatred or breed division within our community."
St. Catharines Mayor Mat Siscoe told CBC News he hoped no facility in his city would "lower itself" to rent to Dominion or other groups like it.
"They are free to express their views, and we are equally free to condemn them and make clear that those views are not welcome here," he said. "That, too, is freedom of speech.”

articles.title: Daughter traces mother and aunt’s last known location in Nepal through TikTok video
articles.summary:
Tulshi Patel says mother Hemangini Jitendra Patel and aunt Hema Sunil Amin were last seen at Friendship Bridge on Nepal-China border

•

blocks.text: The daughter of a woman missing in Nepal has told how she traced her mother’s location through a TikTok video posted hours before the devastating flash flood hit.
The catastrophic flash floods that hit Nepal and Tibet on Wednesday, thundering down valleys and sweeping away entire villages, have killed at least 675 people, while more than 3,000 remain missing.
Among the missing are 33 British nationals, including a 13-year-old, NHS workers and a priest. A team from the UK will arrive in the Nepali capital, Kathmandu, on Saturday.

Tulshi Patel’s mother, Hemangini Jitendra Patel, and her aunt, Hema Sunil Amin, set off on a pilgrimage in which they had planned to travel into Tibet, but the pair have not been contactable since the flash floods hit.
In an interview with LBC’s Matt Frei, Patel said the two women had been talking about the trip since the start of the year and the journey had been “on their bucket list”.

She said she had last spoken to her mother and aunt on Monday, had received a photo of them on Tuesday, and their last known location had come from a GPS signal from the tour group at a place called Friendship Bridge at the Nepal-China border.

Patel, a pharmacist from Milton Keynes, said: “We did our own deep-dive research and we found a TikTok video that verified and showed my mum and auntie and three other people from the tour at the border waiting to cross, I guess, that the local Nepali tour guide had made.”
Of the video, Patel said: “It was Wednesday morning, just before 6am, Nepal time.
“They were supposed to have crossed the border on Tuesday, but I guess due to weather conditions, or whichever it was, they got delayed and unfortunately crossed over on Wednesday.”
The flood is believed to have occurred after a magnitude 5.2 seismic event near the border between Nepal and China on Wednesday at 8.37am local time, according to the US Geological Survey.
Patel said her mother and aunt had been in good health and had prepared well for the trip. “They’d gone on walks regularly, they were looking forward to it. This is all they wanted,” she said.
“Their positive viewpoints, health, mental health was great and they were very strong and positive about everything.

“This was something that they were both looking forward to. They’d been talking about this from the beginning of the year. It was something that was on their bucket list that they really wanted to do.”

Patel said she had messaged the two women “in the hopes that maybe we’ll see a tick to say they’ve seen it or read it” and had attempted to contact the tour guide. “We’ve messaged the tour guide in case he has a signal because he’ll have a local Sim as well.

“Every day we’re calling via WhatsApp … We’ve not given up, but, from our end, all we can do is research, but we just need kind of eyes and ears there from our side to basically get them out. Get all of them out and safe.”
Patel said the family had considered travelling to Nepal to join search efforts but had decided against this as they did not know how close they could get to the region in order to help.

blocks.caption: Leena Bector. Photograph: Facebook

blocks.text: Some of those missing were visiting Kailash Mansarovar, a high-altitude site in ‌Tibet revered by Hindus and Buddhists. Neetu Goyal Tiwari, 51, was on her “dream” trip to complete a pilgrimage when the flash floods hit.

The family have been desperately phoning contacts in Nepal in an attempt to find her, though they increasingly believe her to still be in China. As many of the family members are based in India, it is difficult for them to obtain visas to search for her. Her brother, Naresh Goyal, said Neetu’s husband and daughter remained in the UK for now.

“We’re not sure what the next second holds and what we should do from our end, because we’re trying to reach everyone we can,” he said. “She was a very fun-loving woman [and] really had a great heart. I really hope she comes back soon.”
Other families of those missing have travelled to the affected region from the UK. Leena Bector, 53, from Slough, was among 27 travellers who are unaccounted for.
Her husband, Bhupesh Bector, told the Times he was booking the next flight to Kathmandu after the Home Office had failed to confirm whether Leena was on its missing persons list.
He said: “Even if they find her today or tomorrow, I need to be there. She must be in trauma.”

articles.title: Old soup factory takes on new high-tech life as quantum computing firm gets $195M federal boost
articles.summary: In the echoey void of a gutted Campbell's Soup factory in Toronto’s west end, Canada's minister of artificial intelligence and digital innovation announced the federal government’s biggest bet to…

image.caption: A former Campbell's Soup plant in Toronto, shown here in 2018, will become a site for advanced manufacturing for Xanadu Quantum Technologies' quantum computers. (CBC)

blocks.text: Business

In the echoey void of a gutted Campbell's Soup factory in Toronto’s west end, Canada's minister of artificial intelligence and digital innovation announced the federal government’s biggest bet to date on homegrown technology that could revolutionize artificial intelligence, medical science and a host of other key sectors of the economy.
Former Campbell's Soup facility to become manufacturing site for Xanadu Quantum Technologies

In the echoey void of a gutted Campbell Soup factory in Toronto's west end, Canada's minister of artificial intelligence and digital innovation announced the federal government's biggest bet to date on homegrown technology that could revolutionize artificial intelligence, medical science and a host of other key sectors of the economy.

Against the backdrop of the Canada-U.S. trade war, and U.S. President Donald Trump's frequent threats to Canada's sovereignty, Evan Solomon leaned heavily into patriotism as he announced $195 million in repayable federal funding for Toronto-based Xanadu Quantum Technologies.
"This is absolutely a great day for Canada, for Xanadu, and I think for science around the world," he said on Friday. "It shows what Canadians do best: We build."
Solomon said Canada is going to take "big swings" in that endeavour.
"We are going to not just make a bet on solving the biggest problems in the world, and being the best in the world.... We're going to do it big, fearlessly."

Founded in 2016, Xanadu builds software and quantum computers powered by light instead of electricity. Unlike traditional computers that generate heat as electricity moves through metal wires, Xanadu's chips guide particles of light without electrical friction.
While other quantum computers require aggressive, power-hungry cooling to work, Xanadu's units largely operate at room temperature.
Last June, the company unveiled a breakthrough chip capable of generating error-resistant photonic qubits, the basic unit of information for quantum computers.
"The countries that will have built what's called a fault-tolerant quantum computer would have the capacity to break cybersecurity," Solomon said.

"This is why China, the United States, Europe, everyone's racing. And the best companies are right here in Canada, and the IP is in Canada. So, from a sovereign national security point of view, this technology is absolutely critical."
'Like riding a rocket'

Xanadu held the announcement inside a former Campbell's Soup factory in Toronto, where the company plans to set up advanced manufacturing for its fault-tolerant utility-scale photonic quantum computers. The 158,000-square-foot facility is expected to cost $893 million and employ 275 workers.
"If digital computing is like galloping on a horse, quantum computing is like riding a rocket," Solomon said. "It's that much quicker."

In 2023, the federal government launched its $360-million National Quantum Strategy. Friday's $195-million repayable financing pledge to Xanadu represents its largest single financial commitment to manufacturing quantum technology.

Friday's announcement ranks among the government's top single-company investments in Canada's tech sector. One of the largest was in 2024, when the government provided a $2.14-billion loan to Ottawa-based satellite operator Telesat.

In March, Xanadu announced negotiations with the federal government and the province of Ontario for as much as $390 million in combined financial support to establish advanced semiconductor and photonic manufacturing capabilities in Canada.
Xanadu CEO Christian Weedbrook said on Friday that up to $195 million in funding is "still being discussed" with Ontario's government, describing the talks as "final negotiations and discussions."

The company said Friday's announcement represents Ottawa's full share. Unlike a traditional loan, there's no fixed date for repayment. The money will come from Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada's Strategic Response Fund, which provided $40 million to Xanadu in 2023.
'Obligations to keep the jobs here'
Weedbrook, who is originally from Australia, says the money will bolster his company's presence in Canada.
"A building that once fed Canadians will now help the technology of the next generation," he said. "Where we are today will allow us to do most of this work here in Canada, in Toronto."
In May, the U.S. government agreed to invest about $2 billion US in nine quantum companies.

Xanadu is growing its footprint south of the border. In 2025, it secured partnerships with the U.S. Department of War and the U.S. Air Force Research Laboratory. The company also works with big-name U.S. firms like Lockheed Martin and chipmaker AMD.

items: University of Calgary to house quantum defence hub to develop tech for armed forces
Xanadu CEO on Canada's quantum future

blocks.text: "I think there's obligations to keep the jobs here for some time," said Amy Karam, a business consultant and fellow at the Canadian Global Affairs Institute.

"By having the government have a seat at the table in terms of business decision-making, I think that is one way that we as a country can really be more involved, or more part of encouraging companies to stay. Just funding and doing research and creating talent, it's not enough anymore."

In March, Xanadu dual-listed its shares on the Toronto Stock Exchange and the tech-heavy Nasdaq. The latter raises the company's profile among U.S. investors, as its stock trades next to household names like Apple, Microsoft and Nvidia.
"It's a big challenge to get companies to stay here," said Karam.
"If you look at the Global Innovation Index, we are slipping drastically," she said.
"We need to do some serious catch-up. We need to take our global technology leadership back, and I have the confidence that this government knows this, sees this and is executing accordingly."

Matthew da Mota is a senior policy researcher at the Canadian SHIELD Institute. The Toronto-based think-tank was launched by BlackBerry co-founder Jim Balsillie to modernize public policy on tech and national security and safeguard Canadian intellectual property.
From developing new pharmaceutical drugs to cybersecurity, da Mota said Xanadu's work could actually be dangerous in the wrong hands.

"It allows for really, really fast processing, really, really fast computation and doing multiple things at once in a way that we weren't able to do with traditional computing. It allows for the potential to break existing encryption," he said.
"That's very dangerous for Canada, and for allies, but it's also something that can be an extremely powerful tool for cyber security long-term."
Why Google's Willow chip could be a quantum computing game changer
Speaking to reporters, Solomon downplayed the potential risk of the government making a concentrated bet on a single company pioneering an emerging technology.
"Unless we are at the frontier with Canadian companies on quantum computing, we will be vulnerable in the future," he said.
"It is vital for this country from a security point of view, from a science point of view, from an economic point of view, to make sure that the best companies in the world are here in Canada."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jeff Lagerquist is a senior writer with CBC News based in Toronto. Originally from Erin, Ont., he studied journalism at Toronto Metropolitan University. Jeff previously worked as a senior reporter for Yahoo Finance Canada. He was also a reporter and digital producer for CTV National News, BNN Bloomberg and The Financial Post. He was also a Columbia University energy journalism fellow for 2025.

articles.title: Russian-American heads Trump's planned Caucasus trade route
articles.summary: A Russian-born businessman heads the investment fund financing the so-called "Trump Route," a planned corridor through Armenia linking Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan. Who is Konstantin Sokolov, and what…

image.caption: The proposed 'Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity' would follow the path of a former Soviet railway, near the border with IranImage: Anthony Pizzoferrato/Middle East Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: Until recently, few people in the South Caucasus had heard of Konstantin Sokolov. Now the 52-year-old Russian-American businessman is at the center of new investment fund backed by US President Donald Trump.

In mid-July, Sokolov — who emigrated from Russia to the US at age 21 and later founded the investment firm IJS Investments in Chicago — was appointed to head a new investment fund of the US State Department.

The TRIPP+ EnterpriseFund, registered in the US as the Trans-Caspian Enterprise Fund and launched with more than $200 million (about €172.5 million) in capital, is expected to invest in countries across the South Caucasus and Central Asia and help finance the large-scale TRIPP infrastructure project, also known as the "Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity."

The "Trump Route" is a transit corridor that aims to connect Azerbaijan with its autonomous exclave of Nakhchivan through Armenian territory. The ambitious infrastructure project is part of a peace deal that Armenia and Azerbaijan signed in August 2025 with US mediation. In early June 2026, Washington and Yerevan signed a framework cooperation agreement for the project.
Experts have said construction of the "Trump Route" fits Washington's strategy of creating a trade corridor between Europe and the region that bypasses existing routes through Russia and Iran.
Sokolov buys up Russian assets in Armenia
Long before he was appointed to head TRIPP+, Sokolov had already established a foothold in Armenia.

In 2024, he acquired Viva Armenia, the country's largest telecommunications provider. Despite its subsequent partial nationalization, Sokolov continued to expand his holdings. Recently, his companies also bought up the Armenian subsidiary of Russian telecom giant Rostelecom.

blocks.caption: In August 2025, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev (left) and Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan (right) signed a joint declaration 'peace road map' after talks with TrumpImage: Azerbaijan Presidency/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: An even more significant deal, however, was carried out largely out of the public eye: the purchase of the Teghut copper-molybdenum mine. The mine, which holds an estimated 450 million metric tons of ore and has Armenia's second-largest reserves, had been taken over by Russia's state-owned VTB Bank after the company accumulated massive debts. VTB is now under Western sanctions. According to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty's Armenian service, the deal was carried out through a third-party company.
"Sokolov wanted to avoid a direct deal with the Russian bank," said Mkrtich Karapetyan, a Radio Liberty journalist who has been investigating the flow of foreign capital into Armenia.
Sokolov: Trump supporter, MAGA backer
While Armenia's government and its supporters have welcomed the influx of Western capital into the country's infrastructure projects, the opposition has highlighted serious risks.

Mesrop Manukyan, a lawmaker from the opposition Armenia Alliance, is among Sokolov's most vocal critics in parliament. He said it's alarming that a US investor has been able to acquire major stakes in the finance, mining and telecommunications sectors in just a few years.

Manukyan's faction, which advocates close ties between Armenia and Russia, opposes the TRIPP+ project. It views the "Trump Route" as a disguised "extraterritorial corridor" and the "greatest threat" to Armenia's security.
Armenia looks to EU after decades of relying on Russia

Despite his extensive investments, Sokolov remains largely unknown to the Armenian public. There are no official photos of him, and he generally avoids interviews with the local press during business trips.

His most recent visit to the capital, Yerevan, was in early August, when he met with Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan and Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan. He was accompanied by Aryeh Lightstone, senior adviser to US special envoy Steve Witkoff.

In Western media, however, Sokolov is known not only for his business ventures in the US and Switzerland but also for his political involvement. Sokolov is a major donor to the US Republican Party and a Trump supporter. According to The Associated Press, he donated about $11 million to Trump's MAGA movement over the course of a year.
'Compromise' between Moscow and Washington?
Benyamin Poghosyan of the Armenian think tank APRI sees two main reasons for Sokolov's appointment to head the fund.
The first is political. Appointing an American with Russian roots could be "a subtle gesture by Washington aimed at easing Moscow's fierce criticism of the project," he told DW.

The second, however, is pragmatic. "Perhaps Russia has nothing to do with it at all. Sokolov may simply have been chosen because he has a deep understanding of the business environment in the former Soviet Union — and because he knows Armenia and how its government works," said Poghosyan.

blocks.caption: Armenia and Azerbaijan were locked in a conflict over the Nagorno-Karabakh region for decadesImage: Tofik Babayev/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: At the same time, the sheer scale of the investment and the financier's Russian roots are fueling speculation in Armenia. Social media users in the country are debating whether Sokolov, who was born in St. Petersburg, could be a secret "compromise figure" between Moscow and Washington. Supporters of the theory point to the ease with which US companies have acquired formerly Russian assets subject to Western sanctions.

Other observers have refuted the idea, noting that Sokolov has publicly and sharply criticized the Russian government and its war against Ukraine. The funds provided by the US State Department, running through 2036, are seen as flagging Washington's long-term strategic intentions in the region. During his visit to Yerevan, Aryeh Lightstone told Armenian news outlet CivilNet that the more than $200 million in initial funding could be viewed as a starting point for future investments.

Aram Sargsyan, head of the Republican Party of Armenia and an ally of Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, also rejects the idea that Sokolov is a "compromise figure" for Moscow. He emphasized the practical value of Sokolov's background, seeing it as an opportunity rather than a cause for concern.
"Sokolov has significant business contacts, understands the Russian mentality perfectly, speaks the language and knows how to work with relevant Russian institutions," he said.
This article was originally written in Russian.

articles.title: Saxony-Anhalt election: Why the AfD is so strong
articles.summary: The AfD is polling above 40% ahead of Saxony-Anhalt's election on September 6. What is driving support for the far right in this predominantly rural eastern German state?

image.caption: Though the AfD has been classified as a 'confirmed right-wing extremist' organization, this has done little to dent its popularityImage: Klaus-Dietmar Gabbert/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Saxony-Anhalt, one of Germany's 16 federal states, boasts a rich cultural and historical heritage.

Many of the world-famous architects associated with the Bauhaus in Dessau lived and worked here. The towns of Eisleben and, above all, Wittenberg preserve the memory of the great reformer Martin Luther. It was in Wittenberg that he famously nailed his 95 theses to the door of the Castle Church, setting the Reformation in motion.

Saxony-Anhalt is also home to the Chemical Triangle around Leuna and Bitterfeld in the eastern part of the state, which still accounts for around 10,000 jobs. To the west lies the Harz mountain range, while the Elbe River, one of Europe's major waterways, flows through the state from southeast to north.

The southern part of Saxony-Anhalt is being forced to reinvent itself as it undergoes structural change following the decision to phase out lignite coal. Unemployment remains slightly above the national average.
How one region in eastern Germany is getting a second chance
Home to around 2.1 million people, it is one of Germany's more sparsely populated states. Only two cities, the state capital Magdeburg and Halle, have more than 200,000 inhabitants.

Nevertheless, in September, international attention is likely to turn to this small eastern German state. For the first time in postwar German history, a candidate from a party that Germany's domestic intelligence agency has classified as "confirmed right-wing extremist" in parts could become the head of a state government. The Alternative for Germany (AfD), whose lead candidate is Ulrich Siegmund, holds a clear lead in all opinion polls.
AfD far ahead in latest polls

Just before the election, the AfD is polling at more than 40% in Saxony-Anhalt. The conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which has been the dominant governing party in the state since German reunification in 1990, trails far behind, with support ranging between 23% and 26%.

The state office for the protection of the constitution has classified the AfD as a "confirmed right-wing extremist" organization, but this has done little to dent its popularity among voters. The Left Party is polling at 13%, while support for the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) stands at between 6% and 7%. It remains uncertain whether the Greens and the pro-business Free Democratic Party (FDP) will succeed in returning to the state parliament.

CDU politician Reiner Haseloff served as state premier of Saxony-Anhalt for 15 years before stepping down in January 2026. In an interview with Der Spiegel, Haseloff said he had often felt, while sitting in the state parliament in Magdeburg, "as though I were in the final phase of the Weimar Republic's Reichstag, or later in Berlin's Sportpalast."

The Weimar Republic, Germany's first democracy, came to an end in 1933 when the Nazis seized power. It was in Berlin's Sportpalast that Nazi propaganda minister Joseph Goebbels, a close confidant of Adolf Hitler, delivered his notorious 1943 "total war" speech.

Haseloff's successor, Sven Schulze, also of the CDU, must now take on the AfD in the upcoming election. If he fails, the CDU's long dominance of state politics could come to an end. Most recently, the conservatives governed in coalition with the Social Democrats and the FDP.
Saxony-Anhalt's unusual political history

From 1994 to 2002, Saxony-Anhalt was also at the center of national political attention. In July 1994, the Social Democrat Reinhard Höppner formed a minority government with the ecologist Greens that relied on the support of the left-wing Party of Democratic Socialism (PDS), successor to East Germany's ruling Socialist Unity Party.

Just five years after the fall of the Berlin Wall and German reunification, cooperation with the heirs to East Germany's former ruling party was widely seen across the country, especially by conservatives, as crossing a political red line.
What if Germany's far-right AfD party wins in Saxony-Anhalt?

Support for extremist parties has long been stronger in Saxony-Anhalt than in many other parts of Germany. In 1998, the far-right German People's Union (DVU), classified as right-wing extremist, won 12.9% of the vote and entered the state parliament. However, internal divisions within the party were so deep that it chose not to contest the 2002 state election.
What's driving AfD support in Saxony-Anhalt?

Experts attribute the AfD's strong showing in the polls largely to the widespread dissatisfaction many people in the state feel with developments in Germany. Many jobs disappeared in the years following reunification, particularly in the lignite mining and chemical industries.

Saxony-Anhalt also faces pronounced demographic challenges. With an average age of 48.3 years, it had Germany's oldest population in 2024. The state also has a pronounced gender imbalance among younger age groups, with approximately 120,240 men aged 18 to 29 compared with around 103,177 women. At the end of 2025, foreign nationals accounted for about 9% of the population, compared with roughly 15% nationwide. Many young people left the state and never returned.

Many people oppose further immigration, even though the state's foreign population remains comparatively small. Nevertheless, its size has increased markedly over the past decade. According to the state's Statistical Office, the number of people without German citizenship has more than doubled since 2015.
What would AfD rule mean for Saxony-Anhalt?

According to many observers, the success of the far-right DVU some 25 years ago demonstrates that right-wing extremist parties have long had a loyal core electorate in Saxony-Anhalt. Today, that electorate largely backs the AfD, regardless of its election manifesto or policy program.
Threat from the far right: Never quite German enough?

Political scientist Benjamin Höhne of the Chemnitz University of Technology told public broadcaster Deutschlandfunk that he believes the AfD would seek to reshape the constitutional order if it were to take power in Saxony-Anhalt. Liberal democratic and rule-of-law principles, he argued, would be systematically eroded.
"I think the AfD is currently watching the United States very closely," he said. In his view, President Donald Trump's administration in the US is pursuing a similar course.

Höhne believes, however, that such radical agendas would be difficult to implement in a single federal state. "You cannot simply pull a lever in one state and expect everything to fall into line with a far-right script," he said.
One thing seems certain: on September 6, all eyes will be on this small state in the center of Germany.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Trump hails 'historic' deal for US to control 65bn barrels of Venezuela's oil
articles.summary: Venezuelan interim president says the unusual agreement will help revive her country's economy.

blocks.text: The US has struck a deal with Venezuela to control more than 65 billion barrels of its proven oil reserves, Donald Trump announced.
The US president wrote that the agreement would more than double American oil reserves and "substantially lower Gas Prices for all Americans".
Venezuela's interim President Delcy Rodríguez hailed the deal as one that would help her nation's economic revival.
But some analysts have reacted with scepticism, including questioning whether the deal would address long-running obstacles that have deterred investment in Venezuela's oil industry.
Trump has recently been under domestic pressure to tame petrol prices, which have spiked due to the Iran war.
He vowed to tap into Venezuela's reserves, the world's largest, after the US captured its then-President Nicolás Maduro in January, ostensibly to stand trial on drug charges in New York.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio called the oil deal "a huge win for both the American and Venezuelan people". Few details were released.
"For the Venezuelan people, this deal will bring nearly $100bn (£74bn) in private investment, support thousands of high-paying jobs and drive the reconstruction of Venezuela's economy," he said.
Trump said Rubio and Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth had reached the agreement with Venezuela's leadership "through a partnership with private business".
He did not elaborate on the partnership or describe possible commitments and terms for the US in the deal, but he claimed the agreement was reached "at no cost to the American Taxpayer".
Under the deal the US government will retain 55% control of a joint venture with an "experienced private operator in Venezuela", a US official told the BBC's US partner CBS News.

The Wall Street Journal reported on Friday that US energy firms Chevron and Halliburton were nearing deals to invest billions in overhauling the infrastructure in Venezuela's oil fields, many of which have not been developed.
David Goldwyn, president of energy consultancy Goldwyn Global Strategies, said there was "no precedent" for the US government entering into a lease to operate Venezuelan oil fields.
It's not clear if such a move would violate Venezuela's constitution or its hydrocarbons law, he told the Reuters news agency.
"It is hard to see how this kind of arrangement would accelerate investment at any material scale," he added, citing Venezuela's political uncertainty, weak power grid, and limited export capacity.
Venezuela's interim president said in a statement that the agreement would have "a significant impact on our nation's revival".

The deal calls for the development of 17 strategic oil fields with a proven potential of 65 billion barrels, as well as "an investment of more than $100bn and more than $209bn in taxes" for Venezuela, Rodríguez said.

"These investments will contribute not only to the recovery and modernisation of our industry, but also to our country's economic growth, the energy security of our hemisphere and greater balance in international markets," she said.
Oil, gas and mineral lawyer Alexander Kuiper told the BBC the deal could be "very significant" but expressed some caution.

"This is definitely a headline to help with oil prices," he said, but added: "What we don't know, is whether or not those reserves turn into actual investment, and how long that investment takes to produce results."

Asked how it would affect oil prices in practice, Kuiper said: "There isn't a switch that you can flip - contracts and agreements have to be put in place... this could take a long time, but it's an important first step."
Delcy Rodríguez - Maduro's former vice-president, who the US backed following his capture - gave the venture a 100-year concession to operate in the oil fields, the unnamed US official told CBS.
Trump gave few specifics of the highly unusual agreement, which apparently grants the US direct governance over a foreign country's sovereign national resources.
The deal would also appear to be wider in scope than the US-led Coalition Provisional Authority's control over Iraq's oil revenues after Saddam Hussein was ousted in an American-led invasion in 2003.

But it is unclear whether the Venezuela agreement could face legal and constitutional challenges in the South American nation. The official text of the agreement between Washington and Caracas has not been published.
Venezuela has the largest proven oil reserves in the world - an estimated 303 billion barrels.
However, production has plummeted since its peak in the late 1990s, in part due to a tightening of controls over its state-run oil firm and US sanctions targeting its main economic lifeline.
Hours after US special forces captured Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, in a raid on the Venezuelan capital, Trump said the US would indefinitely control the sale of the country's oil.

He has also claimed the rights to Venezuela's oil after saying that the country had in the past "unilaterally seized and sold American oil, American assets and American platforms, costing us billions and billions of dollars".

His framing of the deal as part of efforts to drive down domestic petrol prices comes as the global price of oil has jumped up significantly as supply via the Strait of Hormuz in the Persian Gulf has effectively been stymied - spurring discontent ahead of the US midterm elections in November.

However, Venezuela's oil reserves are made up of so-called "heavy, sour" oil, which is harder to refine and used for making diesel and asphalt, while the US typically produces "light, sweet" oil useful for making petrol.
Trump has asked US oil firms to invest at least $100bn (£75bn) to restore the country's oil industry.

articles.title: Artemis II astronauts receive nation's highest space honor for their successful moonshot
articles.summary:
Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen received the Congressional Space Medal of Honor

The Artemis II…

blocks.text: The Artemis II astronauts who flew around the moon in April received the US’s highest space honor on Friday.
Donald Trump presented the Congressional Space Medal of Honor to the three Americans and one Canadian whose lunar flyby for the US space agency Nasa set a new distance record for humanity.

Nasa’s administrator, Jared Isaacman, and other dignitaries took part in the packed ceremony at Houston’s Johnson Space Center, home to mission control. The president used the occasion to announce the creation of a US space academy for the nation’s space force as well as Nasa and the commercial space community.
“Space is the hot thing,” Trump told the crowd, adding that the academy’s location has yet to be determined.

Cmdr Reid Wiseman, pilot Victor Glover, and mission specialists Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen, a Canadian, became the first astronauts to travel to the moon in more than half a century, coming within 4,067 miles (6,545km) while test-driving Nasa’s new Orion capsule. They were the first to launch onboard Nasa’s new moon rocket, a 30-story behemoth that had soared only once before from Florida’s Kennedy Space Center.

While they didn’t stop at the moon, the four set the stage for next year’s Artemis III docking rehearsal in orbit around Earth. Artemis IV’s moon landing by two astronauts, near the lunar south pole, could follow as soon as 2028.
Trump said Americans will land back on the moon before his second presidency ends. Mars is next – “very shortly”, he said.
The president called the newest recipients “four intrepid space heroes”. He pointed out that they did not do it alone, thanking all who contributed to the Artemis II mission.
“There are no finer humans we could have sent as our ambassadors to the stars,” Isaacman added.

Wiseman and his crew are in good company, with only 30 astronauts receiving the prestigious honor before them. Many of the recipients were honored posthumously following their spaceflight-related deaths.

Apollo 11 commander Neil Armstrong – whose phrase “that’s one step for man, one giant leap for mankind” gripped the world when he became the first person to walk on the moon on 20 July 1969 – was the first to receive the Congressional Space Medal of Honor.

President Jimmy Carter awarded six of these medals in 1978, which also went to Alan Shepard, the first American in space; John Glenn, the first American in orbit; and Apollo 8 commander Frank Borman, whose 1968 mission marked humanity’s first lunar voyage.

The most recent recipients were Doug Hurley and Bob Behnken, the first astronauts to launch aboard a SpaceX rocket. Coming nine years after the space shuttle program’s close, their 2020 test flight to the International Space Station restored the US’s ability to launch crews from home soil. Joe Biden awarded them the medals in 2023, during the third year of his presidency.
Dozens of astronauts participated in the ceremony, including Apollo 17 moonwalker Harrison Schmitt, who is now 91 – and the four men assigned to Nasa’s upcoming Artemis III mission.
Schmitt noted that his mission – Apollo’s last moonshot – was the most productive lunar exploration yet.
“Soon to be surpassed by Artemis,” he said of active astronauts standing behind him.

Nasa plans a sustainable moon base staffed by astronauts and robots near the lunar south pole, where permanently shadowed craters are thought to hold tons of frozen water that could be turned into rocket fuel and drinking water. China is eyeing the same region.
“The second space race has begun,” Nasa’s deputy administrator, Matthew Anderson, said.

As the two-hour ceremony came to a close, the Artemis II astronauts presented Trump with his own blue flight jacket complete with space patches, which they had promised him while visiting him in the Oval Office after their mission.

The president then hustled over to mission control to call the three US astronauts onboard the International Space Station. He informed them of the new US space academy, then briefly handed the phone to two of their spouses for a quick hello.

articles.title: Ombudsman questions bail for convicted officials
articles.summary: Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla has questioned the courts’ decision to grant bail to individuals while their convictions are under appeal, saying convicted government officials should start…

blocks.text: Building of the Office of the Ombudsman.
Ombudsman office via FB

MANILA, Philippines — Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla has questioned the courts’ decision to grant bail to individuals while their convictions are under appeal, saying convicted government officials should start serving their sentences immediately.
Remulla criticized how the Sandiganbayan has convicted and imposed sentences on erring government officials but only a few were imprisoned.

“Once convicted by the Sandiganbayan or a lower court for graft, you go to jail. But the courts are being too kind. Instead, they grant bail,” Remulla said during his radio show Executive Session on dzRH.
He also criticized the low amount of bail usually set by the court, proposing that it should be equivalent to “the cost of damage” committed by the convicted official.
Remulla said his office will look at the list of officials who have been convicted by the Sandiganbayan to check whether they are in prison or not.
The ombudsman also pointed out how some cases take a long time to be resolved, with some spanning for 15 years, particularly in resolving appeals.
He said there should be stricter requirements and a deadline for resolving appeals so that the convicted individual is not set free indefinitely.
“The problem is once a motion for reconsideration is filed, a bail is granted with no deadline. Will they sit on that forever?” Remulla pointed out.
He urged the Supreme Court to police the judiciary and called on the public to keep watch on the duties of both the ombudsman and the judiciary.
“I urge members of the judiciary to do their jobs,” he said.

articles.title: Beyond the beaches: The story Panglao tells through Hudyaka Festival 2026
articles.summary: PANGLAO, BOHOL, Philippines — The streets of this tourist town came alive on Friday, Aug. 28, as 10 barangays showcased their culture, traditions and faith through the Hudyaka sa Panglao Festival…

blocks.text: PANGLAO, BOHOL, Philippines — The streets of this tourist town came alive on Friday, Aug. 28, as 10 barangays showcased their culture, traditions and faith through the Hudyaka sa Panglao Festival 2026.

Known as a major tourism destination in Bohol, Panglao is famous for its white-sand beaches, clear waters and dive sites. But during the annual festival, residents showed that the town’s attractions go beyond its natural wonders.
The festival’s main events—the street dancing and ritual showdown—featured performances inspired by the history, livelihood, food and communities of Panglao.
The contingents highlighted stories from their respective barangays, including fishing, tuba gathering, local products and tourist destinations.

Barangay Poblacion paid tribute to pan pati, a popular local bread, through its performance. The presentation honored the people who started making the bread and the generations that kept the tradition alive.

Barangay Danao, meanwhile, presented a story of perseverance through a working student who finished his studies, found a job and eventually fulfilled his dream of providing a home for his father, with faith in St. Augustine playing an important role in his journey.
The performances drew residents, tourists and expatriates who lined the streets to watch the colorful costumes, elaborate props and synchronized dances accompanied by drums and native gongs.
Danao won the street dancing competition, followed by Bil-isan in second place and Poblacion in third.

Poblacion won the ritual showdown, with Bil-isan placing second and Danao third. Poblacion also received Best in Choreography and Best in Costumes. Tangnan won Best in Andas (processional carriage), while Danao received Best in Musicality.

blocks.caption: Performers bring energy, color, and rhythm to the Hudyaka sa Panglao 2026 Street Dancing Competition on Friday, August 28, in Panglao town, Bohol.

blocks.text: For 17-year-old Poblacion performer Gwenn Balbiran, the weeks of nightly rehearsals were worth the effort.
“We offer our dance to Saint Augustine, and for our love of Panglao,” she said.
Kyla Tiempo, 20, another Poblacion dancer, said their performance was an expression of their faith.
“This is our devotion to God and our patron Saint Augustine,” she said.
Rooted in faith
Hudyaka sa Panglao, which means merrymaking in Cebuano, was first held in 1987 as part of the town’s annual fiesta in honor of St. Augustine of Hippo. It is the oldest festival in the province.
According to co-founder Rosario Estoquia, the festival has continued to grow each year, becoming bigger and more colorful while maintaining its connection to the community.
The celebration was held online in 2020 and 2021 because of the COVID-19 pandemic. It returned to the streets in 2022.
Panglao’s contingent has also competed in the Sinulog Festival in Cebu, where it won a competition.
Mayor Edgardo Arcay said Hudyaka helps strengthen unity among residents while promoting Panglao as a tourist destination.
“This festival is about celebrating who we are as Panglaonons—our culture, our heritage, our devotion, and our gratitude to our patron Saint Augustine,” Arcay said.
He said the festival also reminds residents to protect Panglao’s natural and cultural treasures for future generations.
Panglao has experienced rapid growth as a tourism destination. Once a fourth-class municipality, it became a first-class municipality in 2022, largely due to the expansion of tourism.

blocks.caption: Saint Augustine of Hippo, patron saint of Panglao, Bohol

blocks.text: The Bohol-Panglao International Airport has helped make the town a major gateway to the province.
Panglao recorded around a million tourists in 2024 and more than 500,000 visitors during the first half of 2026, according to the local government.
The growth, however, has brought environmental challenges, including coral vandalism and the impact of mass tourism on the island’s natural resources.
Apart from its beaches, Panglao also has important cultural heritage sites.

The Panglao Parish Church of Saint Augustine, completed in 1924 under Bishop Juan Gorordo, is one of the town’s major landmarks. The church features Corinthian columns, ceiling paintings and machuca tile flooring.
The church was declared an Important Cultural Property in 2011 and sustained minimal damage during the 2013 Bohol earthquake.
Five cultural property markers were installed at the church complex by the National Museum of the Philippines in 2023.

Panglao’s tourism attractions also include Balicasag Island, known for its coral walls and marine life; Virgin Island, popular among snorkelers; and South Farm in Barangay Bolod, which features organic farming and tourism activities.
Through Hudyaka, Panglao continues to promote not only its beaches and tourism industry but also the faith, traditions, and stories that form part of its identity. /cb

articles.summary: Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi is in Uzbekistan for a two-day state visit, after which he will go to Kyrgyzstan for the SCO Summit. Meanwhile, hundreds of Indians are still missing in Nepal. DW…

image.caption: Indian Prime Minister Modi thanked Uzbekistan's President Shavkat Mirziyoyev for his warm welcomeImage: Uzbekistan's Presidential Press Office/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: August 29, 2026
Modi lands in Uzbekistan en route to Russia-Asia summit

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi posted pictures of himself and Uzbekistan's President Shavkat Mirziyoyev to social media on Saturday, thanking his political counterpart for the warm welcome and writing on X: "Landed in Tashkent to a warm welcome by President Shavkat Mirziyoyev. Grateful to him for the special gesture."
Modi went on to emphasize, "This is my fourth visit to Uzbekistan, reflecting the depth and growing momentum of our bilateral relations."
Modi is scheduled to attend dinner with Mirziyoyev on Saturday.
The two will hold bilateral meetings on Sunday before departing for the Kyrgyz Republic and the 26th Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Summit.
Modi is scheduled to hold bilateral talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin during the Kyrgyz summit.

articles.title: MILF candidate to seek SC relief after Comelec cancels candidacy
articles.summary: COTABATO CITY, BARMM, Philippines — The camp of Anwar Alamada, a candidate for district representative of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) in Maguindanao del Sur’s fifth parliamentary…

blocks.text: COTABATO CITY, BARMM, Philippines — The camp of Anwar Alamada, a candidate for district representative of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) in Maguindanao del Sur’s fifth parliamentary district, disqualified by the Commission on Elections (Comelec), is bringing his case to the Supreme Court.

Lawyer Badrodin Mangindra, Alamada’s lawyer, said they followed the process, filing an appeal before the Comelec en banc after its Second Division cancelled his candidacy in the Sept. 14 Bangsamoro parliamentary elections.
But the Comelec en banc affirmed the second division’s cancellation.
Alamada is an official candidate of the MILF’s United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP) and served in the erstwhile rebel group’s ceasefire panel mediating warring families and field commanders.
In a resolution promulgated on Thursday, Aug. 27, the Comelec en banc said Alamada failed to prove that he is a resident of Barangay Kudal, Pagalungan, Maguindanao del Sur.
Rafsanjani Ali, a candidate for the same seat under the rival Bangsamoro Federalist Party (BFP), challenged Alamada’s candidacy, claiming he misrepresented his residency.
Ali said in his complaint that Alamada falsely declared that he is a resident of Barangay Kudal for the past 49 years.
On July 7, Alamada filed a motion to overturn the ruling, but the division denied Alamada’s attempt to introduce new evidence in his motion.
Despite the ruling disqualifying him in next month’s balloting, Alamada continued his campaign sortie along with the UBJP candidates in Buluan, Maguindanao del Sur on Friday, Aug. 28.
With Alamada’s candidacy cancelled, the lone seat in Maguindanao Sur’s 5th parliamentary district will be contested by Ali and Nasser Guialal Dalgan of Bangsamoro Party (BAPA).

Maguindanao del Sur 5th parliamentary district is composed of the towns of Datu Montawal, Gen. Salipada K. Pendatun, Pagalungan, Rajah Buayan, Sultan sa Barongis and Paglat, with 114,737 registered voters.

The poll body also cancelled the registration and accreditation of Moro Ako Party as a Regional Parliamentary Political Party (RPPP) after finding out it made untruthful representations about having established chapters throughout the region, which were required for accreditation.
A certain Aladin Abdul filed the petition to cancel Moro Ako Party’s registration with the poll body.
In a statement, a member of Moro Ako Party shared with local media that it would bring the matter to the Supreme Court and that it continues its campaign activities. /cb
