articles.title: Europe’s monarchs, world leaders mourn Norway’s King Harald
articles.summary: OSLO, Norway — European monarchs and world leaders paid tribute Friday to Norway’s King Harald after the royal palace announced his death at age 89. Harald was the continent’s oldest…

blocks.text: OSLO, Norway — European monarchs and world leaders paid tribute Friday to Norway’s King Harald after the royal palace announced his death at age 89.
Harald was the continent’s oldest reigning monarch. His son, Haakon, automatically succeeded him to the throne.
Here are some of the main tributes:
Britain’s King Charles
Britain’s King Charles III hailed his “dear cousin,” who he said had served “with unwavering dedication, guiding Norway through times of great change with warmth and humility.”

“As Norway mourns the loss of so towering a figure, my whole family join in remembering a much-loved kinsman and friend whose kindness, compassion and deep sense of duty echoed from across the sea and across the decades,” the king said in a statement personally signed Charles R.
Danish and Swedish monarchs
The kings of Denmark and Sweden called Harald an “extraordinary” leader and good friend who unified his country.
“Both as head of state and a successful athlete, he was an outstanding representative of his country. He gave ‘All for Norway,'” Sweden’s King Carl XVI Gustaf said, referring to Harald’s royal motto.
Denmark’s King Frederik X said the late monarch was “an extraordinary man” who “joined duty and responsibility with presence and compassion.”
Dutch royal family

The Dutch royal family recalled “unforgettable” journeys with King Harald around Oslo and the rest of Norway. “We cherish the memory of our special friendship with him in our hearts. King Harald served his country with love, pride, and conviction,” the family said in a statement.
Belgian royals
Harald’s “humour, humanity and sincerity made him a truly special man,” Belgium’s King Philippe and Queen Mathilde said.

“Generations of Norwegians grew up with him. For decades, he was a familiar and reassuring presence, a beacon of stability for his country. He fulfilled his role with unwavering dedication, loyalty and dignity,” they said in a statement.
Spain’s royal family
Spain’s royal family hailed King Harald as an “example of responsibility, dignity, simplicity, and tireless dedication to the service” of his country.
“With respect and admiration for him, as well as deep sadness, we offer our condolences” on the king’s death, they wrote on social media.
Jordan’s royal family
Jordan’s Royal Hashemite Court said it mourned the passing of King Harald, “may his soul rest in peace.”
The court “expresses the deepest sympathies of His Majesty and the Jordanian people, as they stand with Norway and its people at this difficult time.”
King Abdullah ordered his court to observe three days of mourning, a statement from the court added.
UN chief
A spokesman for UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said he was “deeply saddened” by the king’s death.
“He will be remembered for his engagement for children’s welfare and environmental issues, his support for diversity and calls for generosity,” the statement added.
NATO, EU chiefs
Harald “showed himself to be a dedicated leader,” Mark Rutte, head of the NATO alliance that includes Norway, posted.
“His own military roots made him a champion of the Norwegian military and a long-time friend of NATO,” he wrote online.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said that Harald “served his country with warmth, humility and an unwavering sense of duty.”
French president

Harald “worked tirelessly throughout his reign to strengthen the ties uniting Norway and France,” French President Emmanuel Macron wrote on X, recalling a “warm welcome” on his visit to Oslo in June 2025.
Ukraine’s president
“His Majesty embodied dignity, wisdom, and an unwavering commitment to his country,” said Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in a statement.
“Ukraine will always remember his steadfast support and solidarity with the Ukrainian people during the darkest days of Russia’s aggression.”
Canada’s PM
“Canada mourns with you,” said a statement from Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, offering the condolences of his government.
“I had the privilege of meeting his Majesty last March in Oslo, and he spoke of the ties between our nations with great warmth and affection.”
Italy’s PM

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, in a post on X, called Harald “a monarch who served his nation with equanimity, authority and a deep sense of institutional duty, helping to strengthen the ties between Norway and Italy throughout his long reign.”
Israeli president
Israeli President Isaac Herzog hailed the “loyalty and devotion” of Harald, who early in his reign supported the landmark Oslo Accords between Israel and the Palestinians.
Swiss president
Swiss President Guy Parmelin wrote on X that Harald “will be remembered for his steadfast leadership and devoted service to his country.” /das

articles.title: South Korea leans toward military conscription for women
articles.summary: Facing a population decline, fewer potential service members and calls for social equality to be extended to national military service, Korea is inching closer to breaking the taboo on women on the…

image.caption: South Korea's armed forces are experiencing significant personnel shortagesImage: Xinhua/IMAGO

blocks.text: Nearly 60% of South Koreans are now in favor of young women serving mandatory military service alongside their male counterparts, according to a recent survey, representing a significant shift in the long-held taboo against women being obliged to defend the nation.
Thousands of women already serve in the South Korean armed forces on a voluntary basis, but the debate over mandatory service has always been delicate.

Now, for a series of reasons that include a falling birth rate and shrinking number of recruits as well as an insistence that social equality means that women should also serve, the issue has re-emerged ahead of a reform of the national defense plan scheduled to be released this autumn.
Yet, there are still those who insist women should be kept away from the front lines and, instead, that South Korea should invest more in drones and other advanced technologies.
"South Korea's male-centered conscription system has long been closely connected to traditional gender roles," said Hyobin Lee, a professor at Sogang University in Seoul.

"Men were generally expected to protect the country and the family and to fight in wartime, while women were expected to take primary responsibility for childbirth, childcare and the household," she told DW.
A second factor is the intensifying debate about gender equality, a debate in large part driven by young men, she said.
Warfare moves beyond the physical
"South Korean men generally perform their military service in their early 20s, which interrupts their education, employment or early career development," Lee said.
"At the same time, gender equality has become an increasingly important social value, and women's opportunities in education and employment have expanded."

"As a result, some younger men ask a very simple question: If society expects equality in rights and opportunities, why does one of the country's most significant civic obligations — military service — still fall only on men?"
South Korea proposes talks to officially end war with North

Another contributing factor is the change in the nature of the military itself, with a shift away from physically demanding combat roles that were perceived as being more suited to men and the emergence of a national defense more heavily reliant on technology.
This includes unmanned systems, cyber capabilities, information and communications technology and others that do not require physical strength.
What does the study show?

According to the study, carried out by the Reform Institute, the policy research arm of the conservative-leaning Reform Party, and published on August 20, almost 60% of the respondents were in favor of changing the law to require women to undergo national service. Just 34% were opposed to the idea.
Nearly 65% of men were in favor — a figure that rose to 71.7% among men in their 20s and 30s — with 54.5% of women across all age groups similarly supportive.

At present, all able-bodied men are required to complete a minimum of 18 months and up to 21 months of service and can be called back into service in the event of a national emergency, such as war breaking out on the tense Korean Peninsula.
The latest figures highlight, however, personnel shortages that have affected South Korea's armed forces.

According to the Defense Ministry, around 332,000 men were eligible to perform mandatory military service in 2019. That number fell to 257,000 men in 2022 and is forecast to shrink to just 120,000 men in 2043.

While Hyobin Lee is strongly in favor of equality throughout South Korean society, she fears that obliging women to serve the same military terms as men may turn out to be a negative because so many other elements in society still lag.
Women's traditional responsibilities remain unchanged
"Women in South Korea still bear a much greater share of the responsibilities associated with pregnancy, childbirth and childcare," she underlined.

"Having a child can still lead to career interruption or withdrawal from the labor market, and women's responsibilities for caregiving have not declined to the same extent that their participation in education and employment has increased," Lee added.
Korean 'comfort women' memorial angers Japan
"If women were also required to complete military service, the cumulative burden across their life course could become even greater," she pointed out.
"In a country that is already experiencing an extremely low birth rate, it is also possible that this additional compulsory obligation could further delay or discourage marriage and childbirth."
Lee comes from a family with a strong military background, with a grandfather an admiral in the navy and her father serving in the same branch of the military.
But she would have had reservations in completing mandatory service herself.
"If someone chooses a military career, that is completely different from compulsory service," she said.

"Eighteen months in your 20s is a very significant period in a person's life. It is a time when people are studying, beginning their careers, and making important personal choices. Having to put all of that on hold because the state requires it is a substantial burden," she said.
"Personally, I would have found it extremely difficult to give up 18 months of my younger years in that way."

Song Young-Chae, a Seoul-based academic and human rights activist, completed two years in the infantry as a younger man, when periods of service were longer. He is opposed to mandatory service for women.
"The defense of the nation is traditionally the responsibility of men, and I do not believe that there is such an urgent need to conscript women into front-line service," he told DW.
Need to invest in modern technology

"I served along the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) with North Korea, and it was a hard posting," he added. "I believe that we should be investing far more in drones, robots and other advanced military technologies to protect our borders."
How China's rise is shaping Trump's strategy in Asia

The South Korean government set up a task force in 2025 to revise the nation's basic defense plan, with troop modernization and an overhaul of the conscription system — introduced in the 1950s — high on the agenda.

In an interview with the Yonhap News Agency on August 9, Military Manpower Commissioner Hong So-young admitted that the nation faces a "demographic cliff" and that reforms are urgently required. Those include potentially reducing the number of people exempt from service and requiring foreign-born people who have taken South Korean nationality to also serve.
Hong made no comment about mandatory service for Korean women, but said the system needs a "fundamental" overhaul.

articles.title: This extremely successful author polarizes German readers
articles.summary: She's young and she says what she thinks: Caroline Wahl is topping Germany's bestseller lists with her novels. But she has also faced a public backlash.

image.caption: Author Caroline Wahl, shown here at the 2026 German Film Awards, has topped Germany's bestseller listsImage: Sebastian Christoph Gollnow/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Caroline Wahl, 31, has published three novels to date. All three shot to the top of Germany's fiction bestseller lists.

Now, her fourth book is set to be released on August 28: "1999 Meter über dem Meer" (1999 Meters Above Sea) tells the story of a young woman who takes on a false identity to mingle among the high society in St. Moritz, Switzerland.
It is one of the most anticipated new books of the summer in Germany.
So what is the secret to Caroline Wahl's success?
Debut with a bang
Wahl's breakthrough came with her first novel, in 2023: "22 Bahnen" (22 Lengths) sold more than a million copies in German-language editions.
The story of the young student Tilda, who has to navigate everyday life alongside her alcoholic mother and her little sister, was praised by critics for its straightforward, modern writing style.
What's more, the novel managed to fascinate readers across generations, including references to contemporary pop culture as well as to classic literature.

"The many references make the novels both diverse and ambiguous," said Matthias Schaffrick, a research associate at the Collaborative Research Center "Transformations of the Popular" at the University of Siegen, who recently organized a two-day symposium on Wahl's works.

"What stands out most is how she experiments with different narrative styles and questions them, instead of simply telling a story," Shaffrick told DW. "This opens up a literary space with multiple possibilities, enabling different interpretations and certainly contributing to the appeal of her novels for many readers."
Polarizing ambition

The book's success led to media interest in the young author, and quickly showed that Wahl does not care much for conventions. She speaks her mind freely and doesn't mind facing backlash. "I enjoy being polarizing," she told the Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper in late August. "I like that there's no gray area, people either hate me, and then they really hate me [...]. Or they like me."

In the podcast "Hotel Matze," she said she wanted to become one of Germany's most famous authors. Her words quickly created a stir, but Wahl didn't mind. "I'm really not up for false modesty. It's not wrong to state your goals ambitiously," she said on the arts and culture TV show "Twist" on the Arte channel. "For young women in particular, it's more extreme than for men — people get irritated when a young woman says, 'I want to be the best.' I want to change that with my attitude."
A passion for fast cars

Part of that is openly speaking about enjoying her newfound wealth. In an interview with SZ-Magazin, Wahl said: "It's not only the writing that is enjoyable, but also being successful. Financial success is also important." She loves fast cars, drives a convertible and bought a camper van she likes to park somewhere with a view of the sea to work.

On social media, Wahl has faced a lot of criticism. She has been accused of making money off the literary depiction of poverty in "22 Bahnen," despite never having lived an impoverished life herself. It's an age-old discussion about whether authors are only allowed to write about things they have experienced themselves. Wahl replied to this criticism on the Deutschlandfunk radio station, explaining that above all, writing to her means "exploring spaces that I don't know and feeling empathy for people who live a different life than mine."

blocks.caption: Wahl is no fan of false modestyImage: Felix Hörhager/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: But even without the debate on her credibility, a young woman who speaks openly about material success still seems to be unsettling for many people in Germany — men and women alike — as the many negative reactions show. To Wahl herself, the debate is misogynist.

On Instagram, she wrote a caption for a photo of her light blue BMW: "I find it weird and don't quite get why it's cool for rappers or other men to show off their AMGs, etc., but when a woman author wants to buy a sports car (and can afford to do so!!!), people advise her not to do it and more importantly, not to show it in public."
Author and influencer

"What happens when something becomes very popular?" asked literary scholar Schaffrick. "The popularity starts being scrutinized, which you can observe in Caroline Wahl's case. And we can see what it means to be a popular author. It's not only her novels that play a role, but also the persona she creates for herself as an author."

By being active on Instagram, where she has even tested energy drinks, Wahl also taps into the role of an influencer, said Schaffrick. "It makes her even more popular and offers new topics for conversation. At the same time, the public debate shifts the focus away from her literature, which is what's actually interesting about the Caroline Wahl phenomenon."

Wahl herself has admitted that the intensity of the backlash and criticism has hurt her. In an interview with the SWR TV channel, she explained that social criticism is not necessarily her intention. "I'm not trying to change anything with my stories. Above all, I want to tell stories."
'22 Lengths' on school curricula

When it comes to bestsellers, opinions always differ among German literary critics: Is this entertaining literature, or serious literature with high artistic aspirations? The arts and feature sections of numerous newspapers have come to different conclusions on whether Wahl's novels can be classified as part of the latter. In an interview with Spiegel, Wahl said she finds "drawing a line between entertaining and serious simply annoying."

So far, Wahl's novels have not been nominated for the German Book Prize, Germany's highest literature award. In 2024, the writer voiced her disappointment in typical fashion on Instagram: "I'm sad and angry that I have not been included on the longlist, even if I somehow knew this would happen. Too successful, says my agent."
Back then, her debut novel could have been included on the list — a book that was quickly added to school curricula and has now been made into a film.

Likewise, Wahl's novel "Die Assistentin" ("The Assistant") has not been included on this year's longlist. A literature critic from Frankfurter Rundschau had this to say about the decision: "Why is good literature always supposed to hurt before it can be deemed 'valuable'? [...] The fact that an author like Wahl has been ignored, simply because her captivating writing fascinates millions of readers, makes me really angry."
Presumably, Wahl's fans will ensure that her new novel becomes another bestseller — even without the German Book Prize.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Serbia keeps EU, Russia in play ahead of key election
articles.summary: As Serbia heads toward an uncertain election, President Aleksandar Vucic is balancing ties with Russia and EU ambitions. But growing geopolitical tensions and pressure at home are narrowing his room…

image.caption: Aleksandar Vucic is trying to balance Serbia's ties with the EU and RussiaImage: Djordje Kojadinovic/REUTERS

blocks.text: Smoke from the wildfires still hangs over parts of Serbia, but as the flames slowly recede another debate is taking shape in their wake — one that has less to do with firefighting and more with politics.

In early August, wildfires swept across Serbia, burning through more than 3,500 hectares (8,600 acres) in the Deliblato Sands Special Nature Reserve. Firefighters, soldiers and helicopters battled the flames for days.

blocks.caption: Serbia turned to Russia for help in fighting wildfires in the Deliblato Sands Special Nature ReserveImage: Marko Dimic/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Then a Russian Ilyushin Il-76 firefighting aircraft arrived in the southern city of Nis. Serbia had turned to Moscow for help, making Russia the first foreign country it asked to provide a firefighting aircraft. Pro-government media greeted its arrival with celebratory coverage, dubbing the aircraft the "Russian beast."

"Considering that there are no firefighting aircraft of this capacity available within the European Union, the arriving Russian aircraft will significantly strengthen our capacities to fight the fires," said Luka Causic, head of the Serbian Interior Ministry's Department for Emergency Situations.
A pragmatic choice between EU, Russia — or a political signal?
The episode, however, was already being viewed through a geopolitical lens, as Serbia had sought Russian assistance before activating the EU's emergency mechanism.

When it did call on the EU, the response was swift. Brussels mobilized four helicopters from its strategic rescEU reserve, based in Czechia, Romania and Slovakia, along with ground firefighting teams from Germany and Romania.

blocks.caption: Emergency services, including German firefighters, were on hand to help Serbia battle wildfiresImage: Feuerwehr Bonn/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: President Aleksandar Vucic rejected the idea that turning to Russia first was a foreign-policy decision or a sign of Serbia's political alignment with Moscow.

"As far as equipment and resources are concerned, we are a European giant. The helicopters we received from Europe to fight the fires are less capable than ours and have a lower carrying capacity than our own," Vucic said during a visit to the Deliblato Sands.
Zelenskyy in Belgrade
The wildfire episode came less than two weeks after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy made his first official visit to Serbia.

The two presidents reaffirmed their support for each other's territorial integrity, which is particularly significant for Belgrade because Ukraine does not recognize the independence of Kosovo . Kosovo declared independence from Serbia in 2008, which Belgrade still does not recognize.
But Vucic is also trying to keep the other side on board, said Vuk Vuksanovic, a political scientist and foreign policy lecturer at King's College London.

Vuksanovic argues that Vucic's engagement with Zelenskyy must therefore be portrayed in Moscow not as a fundamental shift in Serbia's relationship with Russia, but as a response to Western pressure and Serbia's own interests.
"Vucic is now trying to make sure that neither the West nor Russia becomes an open opponent during the election campaign," said Vuksanovic.

"Zelenskyy was primarily received so that the ruling coalition could present itself to Europeans as a great friend of Ukraine. In the same way, Vucic is trying to present himself to the Trump administration as a great friend of Israel, primarily to ensure that neither the European Union nor the United States becomes an opponent of the ruling party during the election campaign," he added.
Vucic's room to maneuver is shrinking
The problem is that the room to maintain these relationships may be shrinking.
The deeper the confrontation between Russia and the West becomes, the harder it is for Serbia to remain close to both without facing pressure to choose.

The European Union increasingly expects candidate countries to align their foreign and security policies with those of the bloc. Serbia's refusal to impose sanctions on Russia remains one of the most visible obstacles to closer alignment.

But Moscow, too, has reasons not to take Belgrade's loyalty for granted, Vuksanovic said. He argued that Russia does not fully trust Vucic, even as Moscow continues to support his narrative about "color revolutions" — a reference to anti-government protests, in this case the student-led protests in Serbia that gathered pace in early 2025. Vucic and Russia have both portrayed the protests as Western-backed attempts to destabilize the government.

For Vucic, however, the longer-term question of Serbia's ties with Russia can wait. The more immediate question is whether he will survive the election, tentatively scheduled for October, and remain in a position to preserve that delicate balance himself.
Serbia: A small village takes on the EU

articles.title: Ex-White House teleprompter operator ordered to pay $172,000 for Trump speech bets
articles.summary: The staffer was found to have used his prior knowledge of the president's speeches to place lucrative bets.

blocks.text: A former White House teleprompter operator has been ordered to pay more than $172,000 (£127,000) for using inside information to bet on Donald Trump's speeches.

Gabriel Perez was found to have made trades concerning what the US president would say during addresses between December 2025 and February 2026 on Kalshi - a prediction markets platform where users can bet on real-world events.
Its regulator, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), said Perez would have to surrender profits of $107,539.02 and pay a civil penalty of $65,000.
The White House has not yet commented. In July, then-press secretary Karoline Leavitt said Perez was on unpaid leave and would not return to his post.
Announcing the settlement on Friday, the CFTC said Perez had "misappropriated" his prior knowledge of Trump's speeches to place bets "in breach of his duty of trust and confidence".
It said his civil penalty had been reduced due to his "exemplary co-operation" with the investigation.
Perez has also been banned from trading for three years.
Kalshi's lead lawyer Bobby DeNault welcomed the decision, writing on X: "It doesn't matter who you are: violate our rules or federal law and you will face the consequences."

The company previously told the BBC that its analysts had noticed unusual betting on "mention markets" – contracts through which users predict whether a speaker will use common terms, such as specific countries, campaign slogans or words – in March.
It said it had used account data to find that the user had been a federal employee operating White House teleprompters, and reported the activity to the regulator.
"The words of political leaders like presidents and Fed chairs cause billions of dollars of movement in FX markets, oil futures [and] the stock market," it said in a statement in July.
The same month, the White House Management Office had sent a letter to aides telling them not to place bets on prediction markets, administration officials told the BBC's US media partner CBS News.

articles.title: Trump to mark 9/11 at Pentagon, not New York
articles.summary: WASHINGTON, United States — US President Donald Trump said Friday he would mark the 25th anniversary of the September 11, 2001, attacks at the Pentagon — but angrily denied skipping a memorial in New…

blocks.text: WASHINGTON, United States — US President Donald Trump said Friday he would mark the 25th anniversary of the September 11, 2001, attacks at the Pentagon — but angrily denied skipping a memorial in New York because of a row over a speech.

The New York Times reported that Trump originally intended to commemorate the day with remarks at the site of the Twin Towers but changed his plans because the memorial’s organizers do not allow speeches.
Asked by reporters why he was not going to New York for the anniversary, Trump replied: “Because I’m going to the Pentagon.”
When asked why he could not attend both locations, Trump repeated his answer.
The 9/11 attacks killed nearly 3,000 people.

Hijackers from the Islamist Al-Qaeda network crashed two airliners into the Twin Towers in New York and a third into the Pentagon near Washington, while a fourth plane crashed in a field in Pennsylvania after a revolt by the passengers.
The White House told AFP that Vice President JD Vance was “still traveling” to New York and said that “all three sites will be represented with administration officials in attendance.”

“On the 25th anniversary of this tragic day, the President will remember those who were killed at the hands of evil terrorists, honor their loved ones, and pay tribute to the brave first responders who put their lives on the line to rescue their fellow Americans,” White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said in a statement.
The Pentagon declined to comment.
Trump had earlier issued a lengthy social media post slamming The New York Times report, with a harsh, renewed attack on one of its journalists, Maggie Haberman, whom he called “Maggot Hagerman.”
“This is more Corrupt News, I’ve been to New York many times over the years, and no one ever speaks, it’s a ‘solemn ceremony!'” Trump said on his Truth Social network. /das

“I never even thought of what Maggot made up, and besides, I would love not to speak, because I’m speaking all the time, and this is a day to remember the victims, and their beautiful family members.”

articles.title: US judge throws out confessions of alleged 9/11 mastermind — report
articles.summary: WASHINGTON, United States — A US military judge ruled Friday that confessions made by alleged 9/11 attacks mastermind Khalid Sheikh Mohammed to FBI agents are inadmissible and cannot be used against…

blocks.text: WASHINGTON, United States — A US military judge ruled Friday that confessions made by alleged 9/11 attacks mastermind Khalid Sheikh Mohammed to FBI agents are inadmissible and cannot be used against him at trial, The New York Times reported.
The ruling comes just before the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks that killed nearly 3,000 people in New York, Washington and Pennsylvania.
This week, the trial date for Mohammed and three other alleged plotters was set for June 5, 2028, at the US naval base in Guantanamo Bay, Cuba.
Mohammed, also known as “KSM,” was considered one of Al-Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden’s top lieutenants before he was captured in March 2003 in Pakistan.

Prosecutors have already excluded statements that Mohammed made after his capture when he was held by the CIA in overseas prisons and subjected to brutal treatment, including waterboarding, before his transfer in 2006 to Guantanamo, the Times reported.
But the trial judge, Lt. Col. Michael Schrama, has concluded that Mohammed’s subsequent interrogations in 2007 at Guantanamo were also inadmissible.

“The prosecution has failed to prove by a preponderance of the evidence that Mr. Mohammed’s statements to the FBI were voluntarily given,” Schrama wrote in his ruling, which was not immediately released to the public. The Times said its unclassified contents were confirmed by several lawyers who had seen it.
A spokesman for the US military court did not immediately respond to an AFP request for comment.

Schrama cited an “unbroken continuation of the CIA’s psychological conditioning and severe coercion,” and also found that FBI agents intentionally failed to tell Mohammed that he had a right to remain silent and to consult a lawyer.
Prosecutors can appeal the ruling.

Mohammed’s trial has been repeatedly delayed, and a plea deal that would have seen the death penalty taken off the table was withdrawn last year following protests from the relatives of some victims of the 9/11 attacks.
Much of the legal jousting in the 9/11 defendants’ cases has focused on whether they could be tried fairly after having undergone torture at the hands of the CIA. /das

articles.title: Ecuador ex-president convicted of corruption
articles.summary: QUITO, Ecuador — An Ecuadoran court on Friday convicted ex-president Lenin Moreno of accepting bribes from a Chinese company that built the country’s biggest hydroelectric dam. The Attorney…

blocks.text: QUITO, Ecuador — An Ecuadoran court on Friday convicted ex-president Lenin Moreno of accepting bribes from a Chinese company that built the country’s biggest hydroelectric dam.

The Attorney General’s office said that Moreno, who governed from 2017 to 2021, was among four people convicted in the case involving the construction of the Coca Codo Sinclair dam by China’s Sinohydro.
Moreno was vice-president under socialist president Rafael Correa at the time of the alleged corruption, between 2007 and 2013.
He succeeded Correa, with the latter’s backing, but later fell out with his mentor by shifting to the right and aligning himself more closely with the United States.
The court in Quito has not yet sentenced him.
Moreno remains free pending his sentencing.
Prosecutors have asked for him to receive a six-and-a-half-year prison term.
The 73-year-old paraplegic, who served as the United Nations special envoy on disability issues, insisted Friday after the ruling that he had never received “a single cent” from Sinohydro.
He blamed the case on “the Correa regime,” saying his former-backer-turned-rival, who has also been convicted of corruption but is exiled in Belgium, “promised to take revenge on me.”
Prosecutors say Sinohydro paid bribes totaling $76 million, around four percent of the cost of the hydroelectric project.
Three other Ecuadoran nationals were convicted alongside Moreno, including two former managers of the power plant.
Around 20 people have been implicated in the case in total, including Moreno’s wife, his daughter, businesspeople, and a former Chinese ambassador to Quito. /das

articles.title: Rescuers recover mud-caked survivors as Nepal-China flood toll rises
articles.summary: KATHMANDU, Nepal (AP) — Rescuers pulled out survivors caked in dark brown mud and helicopters lifted stranded people to safety, as Nepal and China raced to respond to catastrophic flash floods that…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU, Nepal (AP) — Rescuers pulled out survivors caked in dark brown mud and helicopters lifted stranded people to safety, as Nepal and China raced to respond to catastrophic flash floods that killed nearly 600 people and left almost 2,500 missing.

The rescue efforts included a team that rappelled into a severely damaged checkpoint area on the Chinese side of the border between the two countries. Rescuers were on high alert for more flooding from a new lake that formed high up in the Himalayan mountains after the initial floods Wednesday. Experts warned that the lake, created after a glacier collapse that triggered the floods, was starting to overflow.

Nepal’s army was deployed to help rescue more than 100 people believed trapped inside a tunnel at a hydropower plant located in the country’s worst-hit district. Like elsewhere in the disaster zone, their work was complicated by thick layers of mud that covered the site.
The rappelling rescue team descended into the once-bustling border-crossing area from wooded mountain slopes, the state broadcaster China Central Television said.

“As far as I can see, it’s nothing but debris,” rescue official Zou Mingqi told state media. The area where travelers went through border control to enter or leave China has been flattened to a muddy area, according to satellite images.

The floods have killed 579 in Nepal, the country’s disaster-management authority said Friday. Nepali police later put the number of deaths at 553. There was little information on survivors on the Chinese side, where the death toll rose to seven Friday as state media showed evacuations of villages and leaders’ efforts to direct the relief response.

More than 3,700 people have been rescued in Nepal so far. Meanwhile, the number of people who were unaccounted for in the country nearly doubled to 1,924 as more local residents were added to the tally. China’s state media said 554 people were missing on the Chinese side. Hundreds of the missing are foreigners in the area to work, trek or make a pilgrimage to a sacred peak.

In other developments, Nepal on Friday reversed an earlier decision and said it would allow foreign teams and experts to help with rescue efforts, apparently under pressure from other countries, especially those whose citizens are unaccounted for, a leading English-language newspaper, The Kathmandu Post, reported.
Authorities warn of flooding from a new lake

Nepali police issued a fresh alert Friday after receiving information that a dam on the Tibet side had burst. Security personnel and rescue and relief workers were told to stay on high alert and move to a safe location if necessary.

It was unclear if the dam bursting was related to flooding concerns over the lake that formed after the initial flash floods. Chinese broadcaster CCTV said the newly formed lake, located more than 10 kilometers (6 miles) from Gyirong Port, the hard-hit border crossing with Nepal, sits at an elevation of 2,950 meters (9,680 feet).

Nepali and Chinese authorities earlier warned of more flooding from the lake, which was already overflowing. Rescue workers heading to the disaster zone were ordered to stop temporarily Friday due to concern the lake would release more water and debris, and people in potentially affected areas were urged to move to safer ground.

Monitoring data from the Chinese Ministry of Water Resources later showed that the lake had dwindled in size. The water level dropped by 10 meters (32 feet) from the high point on Thursday morning, the state broadcaster said.

Some 680 rescuers eventually reached the Gyirong area by foot and via rafts. Some were dropped down from drones flown to the area, CCTV footage showed. “Anyone, anyone?” rescuers yelled, according to footage by the broadcaster.
It was not immediately known how many people were at the border checkpoint building when the floods hit.
Thousands of people have been evacuated while others await rescue

In Nepal’s Rasuwa district, Nepali army rescuers struggled to help more than 100 people believed to be trapped by thick mud in a tunnel that’s part of the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project. The army said it had rescued 350 people from the tunnel so far.
Video from the scene showed rescuers helping a man covered in mud out of the tunnel by pulling and pushing.
“It is complicated to find the entry and exit points of the tunnel because everything has been covered by mud,” Army spokesperson Brig. Gen. Raja Ram Basnet said.
Nepal’s disaster-management authority said 3,253 people had been airlifted by helicopter from the disaster area.

The search-and-rescue efforts have been supported by an outpouring of financial support from neighboring countries, including small, poorer countries like Sri Lanka, said Kanni Wignaraja, the United Nations development agency’s regional director for Asia and the Pacific.
“Sri Lanka has its own huge fiscal problems, but it has just sent $1 million immediately to the Nepal government,” Wignaraja said.
Some felt the ground shake, then saw a ‘black storm’

Scientists who studied satellite images said bedrock underneath a glacier high in the Himalayan region had collapsed, taking part of the glacier with it. The rockfall was so extreme that it registered as magnitude 5.2. The rocks and melted water then swelled the rivers in the valleys below, causing a torrent of water that swept buildings, bridges and earth downstream in Tibet and Nepal.
Customs officer Karbir Gaire was among some of the survivors in Timure, the closest Nepalese village to the border with China, where some 1,500 people had lived.
Gaire reached his office around 8 a.m. Wednesday and was working on his computer when he first felt the ground shake.

“Right after the shake, I noticed a black storm coming towards us,” he recalled from Kathmandu, where he is back with family. “We all immediately started running out, and within a few seconds, we were climbing uphill on the opposite side of our office building. I think those 10 or so seconds saved some of us.”
Fifteen of Gaire’s colleagues are missing. “It was like a Hollywood movie scene. I don’t call it a flood. It was a tsunami.”
Families around the world hope for news of loved ones
Nepal’s tourism board has said that among the missing are more than 500 foreigners.
While the Nepal government shared a public list of people they rescued, there was little information about victims on the Chinese side of the border.

Chinese government officials stuck to their tight media controls. Information about major disasters is typically released with a delay and without personal stories of victims. State media has focused on stories of rescuers working to reach the disaster site or reporting on instructions from top leaders.
About 90 Americans were unaccounted for.
Some of the missing may have been on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet, a sacred site for Hindus, Buddhists and others.

Indian spiritual guru Jaggi Vasudev, also known as Sadhguru, said in a post on X that 77 people returning from Mount Kailash with groups organized by his Isha Foundation were at the immigration center in Gyirong when the flooding struck.

Vishnuram Ramaswamy, who works at a private company in the southern Indian city of Puducherry, said that he spoke to his mother and two sisters who were on that pilgrimage Wednesday morning. It was a highly anticipated trip, something his mother had always wanted to do, he said.
“This was the last we spoke to them,” he said. “They have been unreachable since.” /das

articles.title: 32 reported dead due to Habagat, cyclones; 8M people affected --OCD
articles.summary: The combined effects of the Southwest Monsoon (Habagat) and tropical cyclones Luis, Maymay, and Neneng have reportedly killed at least 32 people, with 8 million people being affected across the…

blocks.text: Published August 29, 2026 1:51pm

The combined effects of the Southwest Monsoon (Habagat) and tropical cyclones Luis, Maymay, and Neneng have reportedly killed at least 32 people, with 8 million people being affected across the country, according to the Office of Civil Defense (OCD) on Saturday.
In its latest situation report, the OCD said that the deaths were reported in the following areas:

items: Rizal - 4 due to rockslide, fallen tree, drowning
Batangas - 4 due to drowning, electrocution, landslide)
Rizal - 2 due to electrocution and drowning

blocks.text: Meanwhile, the OCD recorded 19 injuries. Three people are still missing - one each in Quezon City, Manila, and Batangas.
There are at least 8 million people affected by the inclement weather, which translates to 2.3 million families. At least 25,800 of them are still in evacuation centers.
The cost of damage to infrastructure has reached P6.11 billion, with agricultural damage recorded at P2.32 billion. Almost 3,000 houses were damaged, with 349 of them being totally destroyed.
The OCD said that 117 local government units have declared a state of calamity.
The government has released P1.65 billion in assistance.
The Southwest Monsoon has again gained strength following the presence of a low pressure area in the Philippine Area of Responsibility, with its rains causing widespread flooding. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: Family seeks help locating doctor missing in Nepal
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The family of Filipino doctor Juan Carlos Manalo has appealed for help locating him after losing contact following flash floods near the Nepal-Tibet border. Manalo’s sister,…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The family of Filipino doctor Juan Carlos Manalo has appealed for help locating him after losing contact following flash floods near the Nepal-Tibet border.
Manalo’s sister, Chiara Manalo, said on Friday that the family had not heard from him since Tuesday, a day before the disaster.
In a Facebook post, Chiara said the family’s last contact with Manalo was at 1:21 p.m. Philippine time on Tuesday or 11:06 a.m. Nepal time.
She said Manalo was traveling with the Isha Sadghuru group on a Kailashyatra tour. The group’s last known location was at the Immigration Office in Gyirong, according to the family.
“Please help us look for my brother,” Chiara said.
Awaiting confirmation

The family appealed to anyone with information about Manalo or members of the group to contact them. It also asked for help connecting with agencies that could coordinate with Nepali authorities and assist in search operations.
“Receiving and seeing the news about the catastrophe has been very difficult for us. We humbly ask to include him in your prayers, that he may return to us safely soon,” the family said.

The Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) said on Friday the Philippine Embassy in New Delhi and the Philippine Honorary Consulate General in Kathmandu were coordinating with local authorities and were ready to assist Filipinos affected by the disaster.
DFA spokesperson Analyn Ratonel said the agency was awaiting confirmation from Nepali authorities on a Filipino national who was reported missing.
Unaccounted traveler
Ratonel also said the DFA had forwarded to the concerned office information provided by Chiara about her brother.

The reported missing Filipino appeared in a preliminary record released by the Nepal Tourism Board, which listed one Filipino among travelers unaccounted for in the affected areas. The Philippine government has yet to independently confirm the report.
The disaster struck on Wednesday after a glacial collapse triggered a massive debris flow, sending water, mud, rocks and ice crashing on communities along the Nepal-Tibet border.
The DFA has not confirmed that Manalo is the Filipino listed in the preliminary Nepal Tourism Board record.
Chiara said receiving news of the disaster had been difficult for the family as she asked the public to pray for her brother’s safe return. INQ

articles.title: Forget Starbucks coffee - Gen Z like their drinks ice cold
articles.summary: Young consumers are choosing cold, customisable drinks and coffee chains are racing to catch up.

blocks.text: Elaine Ling splits her time between New York and California, but wherever she is and needs a coffee, she doesn't visit a Starbucks.
She only goes there for her cold drinks. Her "real coffee" comes from local cafes.
"I don't really like to go to Starbucks for coffee. I think their coffee is like too sweet," Ling, 21, told the BBC. "I'm more of a refresher girl when it comes to going to Starbucks."

Though founded as a coffee shop more than five decades ago, Starbucks says that three out of every four drinks it now sells are cold. Think iced fruity drinks, protein shakes and so-called dirty sodas - a concoction of foam, syrups and juices.
Ling's preferences are echoed by younger customers across the US.
Gen Z consumers - people born between 1997 and 2012 - are increasingly choosing cold drinks that they can customise themselves over traditional coffee.
Tristan Höver, global insight manager for hot drinks at Euromonitor International, says younger consumers increasingly see drinks as something they can tailor to a specific moment or need.
"Customisation gives them a sense of control," he told the BBC.
He says Gen Z is price-sensitive but willing to pay more if the drink feels special, larger, or functional.
With cold drinks, he says, size, layers and visual appeal help justify the higher price.
Jerry Sheldon, an analyst at IHL Group, sees these habits as part of a larger cultural shift.
"Cold drinks are a form of self-expression," he says. It is another way to signal identity, much like clothing or hair colour.

Kelly Goldsmith, a Professor of Marketing at Vanderbilt University, says consumers are "not paying for what's in the cup, but what's on the cup," comparing Starbucks to an affordable luxury handbag made by the likes of Louis Vuitton.
She says that image has helped Starbucks maintain a price premium for years.
Social media plays a role too.
Starbucks' Unicorn Frappuccino was much-hyped on TikTok and available for only three days in August.

The dense, brightly coloured blended drink with swirls of pink, blue and purple, topped with whipped cream and a crunchy topping lifted foot traffic at Starbucks by 44% during its brief emergence, according to Placer.ai, a data analytics firm.
Other chains are trying to tap into the trend.
Dunkin' Donuts is experimenting with protein-boosted drinks and customisable cold options, recently partnering with celebrities like Kylie Jenner to promote limited‑time drinks.
TikTok food‑and‑drink creator Natalie Ludwig, who has more than 500,000 followers, has sampled Dunkin's cold drinks.
She says the campaign with Jenner is one example of how the chain is trying to tap into a younger audience, adding that if the promotion succeeds "maybe that younger audience sticks".
Fast food chains like McDonald's, Chick-fil-A, and Taco Bell have launched fruit-based so-called refreshers and coffee-adjacent options and other non-caffeine cold drinks aimed at the same audience.
UK data suggests the trend isn't limited to the US.
Isabella Reeve, a consumer insight director at Worldpanel by Numerator, says shoppers under 25 buy more cold drinks than hot when they're out of the home.
Over 60% of their drink purchases are cold, compared with just 30% for shoppers 55 and older.
She says cold drinks aren't just a summer habit either. More than 70% of people buy them year-round, while over 80% do so in the summer months.
Tirtha Dhar, a marketing professor who studies consumer choice at the University of Guelph in Canada, says cold drinks have become a "sweet spot" for Starbucks' bottom line.
The "infinite personalisation" through foams, flavours, and protein are "almost pure profit" for the chain.

Cold drinks have also helped revive Starbucks after a stretch of weaker sales, with the category making up more than 70% of its US beverage sales - a shift that has become central to its turnaround strategy.

articles.title: Footage of Tibet floods isn't being shown in China - and we know little about victims there
articles.summary: Some of the most dramatic footage from the deadly flash flooding is hidden from public view in China.

blocks.text: The dramatic footage was almost impossible to miss. A torrent of water tearing through Gyirong Port, one of the main border crossings between Nepal and Tibet, sweeping away all in its path as hundreds of people fled for their lives.
The scenes, captured by CCTV cameras, quickly spread on social media and onto screens around the world.
Except here, in China.
Only a single still-frame shot has been broadcast so far by the country's state-run flagship news bulletin.

It has also been difficult to find the video on China's heavily censored internet. It is just as hard to even find posts describing the flash flooding that has claimed hundreds of lives, with just as many still unaccounted for since Wednesday.

Beijing has launched a massive rescue operation involving hundreds of emergency workers, which is continuing, and President Xi Jinping chaired an emergency meeting with officials to co-ordinate efforts.
But when you compare the country's internet content to what much of the world has been seeing online these past few days, China's firewall becomes more visible than ever.
Tibet, which Beijing annexed in the 1950s, had long resisted rule by the Chinese Communist Party.

China has quashed protests over the years, sometimes violently, and has been accused of grave rights violations in the Buddhist region. It has labelled the exiled spiritual leader, the Dalai Lama, a separatist.
That history means the very name Tibet draws China's censors. Beijing's sensitivities are especially apparent at times likes this.

On Thursday night, as global headlines led on the devastation in a Himalayan valley, China's state broadcaster opened its main bulletin with the launch of Xi's new book, a selection of his "most important and fundamental works".

Foreign journalists cannot travel to Tibet without government permission. We have just a few hours to get as much information as we can on huge stories like this before videos are scrubbed and voices stifled.
Instead, we have to rely on state media, which has so far focused on incredibly dramatic rescue efforts.

Specialist search teams scaling mountains and cliff faces, or crossing raging rivers to try to get to the worst-affected areas. We don't yet know what happened afterwards, or who they were able to save.
This is not to say that Beijing is unconcerned. Rather, they are very concerned.
China's Premier Li Qiang was quickly despatched to the region, where he was seen inspecting debris removal - a rare visit by the country's second-most important leader so soon after a major disaster.
The reason for what the world might see as a muted response is to preserve the one thing Xi covets for his country: stability.
The Communist Party will fear that such a disaster could fuel discontent, either with the response or the lack of foresight to prevent it.
It may also fear the impact of a tragedy like this and its potential to be a rallying factor, especially in a community where faith has long played a central role.

Although the region has not seen protests in a long time, Tibetan groups abroad have expressed concern over increasing Chinese control, such as new education laws that they say aim to weaken the role of monasteries and the Buddhist faith.
Just hours after the disaster struck, the Communist Party machine tried to rally its grassroots to stem any signs of discontent of its handling of the landslide.
A notice came from the local party office urging members to step up and help in disaster relief efforts in their area and provide emotional guidance or psychological support to affected residents.

The key line instructs them to "make every effort to maintain social order and ensure stability and public confidence in the disaster areas". Those who perform well would be rewarded - and those who do badly "would be held accountable".

It is a warning that will not be taken lightly. Tibetans in the region can be detained or arrested for speaking to journalists or posting anything online that is seen as contrary to the government narrative, according to rights activists.
That is making it difficult for Tibetans outside the region to find out what has happened to their relatives.

The International Campaign for Tibet, while praising the work of first responders in the area, said Beijing had been removing videos and other first-hand information from social media. It called on Chinese authorities to "disclose complete and verifiable information about the damage and casualties".

To try to understand what life is like for Tibetans, the BBC travelled to a town that sits on the edge of the Himalayan plateau last year - just outside what China calls the Tibetan Autonomous region.
There, we spoke to monks at the Kirti monastery in Aba, or Ngaba in Tibetan, which was once at the heart of its resistance to Beijing. "We Tibetans are denied basic human rights," one monk told us.

They said they lived under constant surveillance and claimed the Chinese government oppressed and persecuted Tibetans. The conversations were brief because we could not be seen speaking to anyone for long.
Beijing denies it is violating Tibetans' rights, and points to the heavy investments it has made in the region to boost tourism and integrate it with the rest of the country.
Nevertheless, people in China will not know very much about what is happening in Tibet right now.

articles.title: Search continues as number missing in Nepal-Tibet floods rises to 2,478 – as it happened
articles.summary: This live blog is now closed
articles.byline: Wendy Frew ; Lucy Campbell, Keely Aouga, Nadeem Badshah, Tom Ambrose, Mabel Banfield-Nwachi, Taz Ali and Adam Fulton

blocks.text: Death toll now stands at 579 in Nepal, seven in Tibet
Nepal’s official death toll from Wednesday’s flash flood now stands at 579 people, while China says seven people have died in Tibet, the state Xinhua news agency reported early Saturday.
Chinese authorities said also they had evacuated 555 stranded tourists and 499 Chinese residents from Tibet.
In India, authorities said they had recovered seven bodies from rivers flowing from Nepal, believed to be flood victims.
Scores of Hindu devotees from across the world are among those missing on the border, as many were on a pilgrimage to Tibet’s Mount Kailash.
Sivaranjani Muthunathan was travelling by bus with 56 others to the Chinese border when they became stuck in what they thought was a traffic jam.

“Then there was fog, smoke, something that seemed to suddenly engulf us,” Muthunathan, 46, told Agence France-Presse on Friday, showing a phone video she recorded of a torrent surging towards her. Around them, vehicles were swept away or buried under mud.

blocks.text: Closing summary
We’re wrapping up the Nepal-Tibet flash flood for the time being. Here are the latest developments:

items: Reuters reports the death toll from the catastrophic flash flood that hit the China-Nepal border on Wednesday has today risen to 626, according to Nepal police, while China’s Xinhua news agency earlier today reported seven people confirmed dead in Tibet.

At least 2,478 people are missing. Nepal’s disaster agency on Friday said 1,924 people were missing on its side of the border, while China’s Xinhua news agency reports the total number of missing in Tibet is now 554.
More than 3,700 people have been rescued in Nepal so far but at least 93,000 people are estimated to have been affected by the disaster, according to the Red Cross.

At least 777 foreigners are missing, with Nepal’s disaster agency on Friday reporting 517 foreigners unaccounted for – which could include tourists and foreign workers – and Chinese officials putting the number of foreigners missing at 260.

A Chinese rescue team reached the all-but-obliterated Gyirong border crossing complex for the first time yesterday, finding “nothing but ruins.” More than 550 ‌remain unaccounted for in Tibet’s Gyirong County after the massive flash flood.

Reversing an earlier decision, Nepal’s foreign minister has said the country needs specialised and technical help from other countries for a tunnel rescue and for identifying and storing bodies. It has also asked China and India for bailey bridges that can quickly be erected.

The number of Australians who were reported missing in the catastrophic Nepal flooding disaster has risen to 41, with one family celebrating after an unaccounted-for woman made contact with them yesterday.

blocks.text: A Chinese rescue team reached the all-but-obliterated Gyirong border crossing complex for the first time yesterday, finding “nothing but ruins.”
More than 550 ‌remain unaccounted for in Tibet’s Gyirong County after Wednesday’s massive flash flood, including 260 foreigners, according to Chinese state broadcaster CCTV.
A rappelling rescue team descended into the once-bustling border-crossing area from wooded mountain slopes, the state broadcaster China Central Television said.

“As far as I can see, it’s nothing but debris,” rescue official Zou Mingqi told state media. The area where travellers went through border control to enter or leave China has been flattened to a muddy area, according to satellite images.
You can read more on that story here.

blocks.caption: In this photo released by Xinhua news agency, rescuers from the People’s Armed Police Force search for victims at the mudslide-hit area near Gyirong Port in China’s Tibet autonomous region on Friday. Photograph: Liu Shuang/Xinhua/AP

blocks.text: Nepal asks for foreign help with tunnel rescue, identifying and storing bodies
We’re just learning that Nepal’s foreign minister has said the country needs foreign help for a tunnel rescue and for identifying and storing bodies.

The country needs foreign ⁠help ⁠in specialised and ​technical areas in ⁠which it does ⁠not ​have expertise but not in ⁠search and rescue, ​foreign minister ​Shisir Khanal told ​Reuters late on Friday.
“We have already made requests for such specialised services and technical assistance in areas ‌where we don’t have enough expertise and technical knowhow,” Khanal said.

The Nepalese army has undertaken a dangerous and difficult rescue operation of people trapped in a tunnel of a hydropower project in the flood-hit district of Rasuwa. Rescuers are seen crawling on thick mud towards the trapped people and carrying them out to safety.

Khanal said Nepal has also asked India and China for bailey bridges – portable, prefabricated truss bridges made of standardised panels that can be assembled quickly – to reopen early transport and communication in the disaster-hit area where about two dozen bridges have been destroyed.

blocks.caption: One of the many bridges swept away by the flash floods, this one in DeviGhat village, Nepal.  Photograph: Ritesh Shukla/Getty Images

blocks.text: The number of Australians who were reported missing in the catastrophic Nepal flooding disaster has risen to 41, with one family celebrating after an unaccounted-for woman made contact with them yesterday.
It means three additional Australians were confirmed missing overnight – up from 38 who remained unaccounted for on Friday evening.

Other countries are regularly updating tallies for citizens missing or accounted for. Ninety US citizens are missing, according to the state department while three have been rescued. Tourism board figures released by Nepal on Friday showed 98 people from India were missing, but 85 others were rescued.

The Australian government’s Department of Foreign Affairs has been urgently working with local authorities to contact Cara Severino, 25, who became the first Australian reported missing who has been confirmed safe.
Interim summary
If you are just joining us, here’s the latest information coming out Nepal and elsewhere about the Nepal-Tibet calamity. It is 6.18am in Nepal on Saturday.

items: At least 2,478 people are missing after the catastrophic flash flood hit the China-Nepal border on Wednesday. Nepal’s disaster agency on Friday said 1,924 people were missing on its side of the border, while China’s Xinhua news agency early today reported the total number of missing in Tibet is now 554, with seven people confirmed dead.
More than 3,700 people have been rescued in Nepal so far but at least 93,000 people are estimated to have been affected by the disaster, according to the Red Cross.

At least 777 foreigners are missing, with Nepal’s disaster agency on Friday reporting 517 foreigners unaccounted for – which could include tourists and foreign workers – and Chinese officials putting the number of foreigners missing at 260.

Nepal on Friday reversed an earlier decision and said it would allow foreign teams and experts to help with rescue efforts, apparently under pressure from other countries, especially those whose citizens are unaccounted for, a leading English-language newspaper, the Kathmandu Post, reported.

The number of Australians who were reported missing has risen to 41, according to the Australian government, while one family celebrated after an unaccounted-for woman made contact with them yesterday.
Three American citizens have been rescued but at least 90 Americans are unaccounted for, the US state department told USA Today. It said it was not aware of any US citizen deaths so far.

Nepal is continuing to monitor two lakes upstream of the flood zone where hundreds died ⁠on Wednesday, an official with Nepal’s disaster management authority said. Flood risks will remain until the two lakes have ⁠fully drained, the official added, as one of the two lakes began overflowing on Friday.

blocks.caption: A flash flood survivor is taken to a medical camp in the Nuwakot district of Nepal on Friday. Photograph: Rajesh Kumar Singh/AP

blocks.text: The day so far

items: Nepal’s disaster authority raised sharply the number of missing to 1,924 on Friday, two days after devastating floods that killed at least 579 in the country. The number of missing includes 517 foreigners, as well as 933 workers on hydropower projects on the rivers where a wall of water powered down on Wednesday morning, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority. The AP is reporting a higher figure, with almost 2,500 are missing and nearly 600 people killed.

Authorities in Nepal and China issued warnings about the risk of a second wave of flooding. Chinese authorities said an artificial lake had formed after a mudslide hit the Tibet-Nepal border, which risked “sending flood waters downstream”, according to state media. Nepal’s disaster authority said a lake that had formed by debris blocking a river at the site was also rising and ‌at risk of bursting. Amid the mounting fears over a second wave of flooding, families are rushing to Nepal to search for the 33 British nationals who are still missing.

Rescuers were forced to suspend their search for survivors, while residents who had returned to Rasuwa were told to evacuate their homes, with many seen fleeing up the hillsides to escape a possible surge in the river.

The Red Cross has said at least 93,000 people may have been affected by the disaster, triggering a huge rescue operation that is being hampered by fears of new flooding. The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), the world’s largest humanitarian network, said it feared the death toll would continue to rise as some of the hardest-hit areas remained inaccessible after roads and bridges were destroyed by the torrents.

The European Union has promised €2m ($2.3m) in aid for Nepal. European Commission chief Ursula von der Leyen wrote on X that the “immediate humanitarian aid” would help “deliver life-saving assistance to families and communities hit hardest.”

Nepal has said it does not yet need foreign assistance as the search and rescue operation – complicated by the destruction of bridges and roads across the mountainous region – continues. “The offer for help is natural,” Lok Bahadur Chhetri, a spokesperson for Nepal’s foreign ministry, said on Friday. “Our security agencies ‌are doing the search and rescue operation. For now we don’t require such help.”

Rescue teams have reported finding bodies hundreds of miles downstream from the disaster zone in the Chitwan district of Nepal, near the Tibetan border. Dozens of injured people were transported to Kathmandu for advanced medical care and more than 100 people were rescued by Nepali army personnel in helicopters.

blocks.text: The number of missing individuals in the deadly flash flood has risen past 2,400, according to a count by AFP.
Nepal’s disaster authority added 933 hydropower workers to a missing persons list already including trekkers and pilgrims to Tibet’s sacred Mount Kailash, AFP reported.
The news agency also reported that emergency teams have recovered 586 bodies so far – with some of the dead swept downstream as far away as India.
Our most recent reporting indicates that 1,924 individuals are missing and at least 579 were killed, as of Friday, two days after the devastating floods.
Chinese control of information hampers assessment of Tibet flood damage

blocks.caption: Amy Hawkins

blocks.text: Amy Hawkins

As the scale of the devastation caused by the flash floods in Nepal and Tibet unfolds, the picture is emerging far more quickly in Nepal than in China, where strict controls on the flow of information from one of its most sensitive regions are hampering the public’s understanding of events.

The floods devastated villages along the Himalayan border region that straddles Nepal and the Chinese region of Tibet. On Friday, the official death toll in Nepal rose to 538 people, while in China it was just five, despite the fact that the villages around the Gyirong border crossing are home to several thousand people.

“Everything about Tibet is seen through the national security prism. And therefore nobody is going to say anything or report anything that has not been cleared from the very top,” said Steve Tsang, the director of the China Institute at Soas University of London.
For anyone on the ground, “you can’t report a higher figure of deaths, even if you have seen more bodies yourself, until the official statement says that the figure has gone up”.

Tibet, brought under Chinese control in the 1950s, is the most sensitive and tightly controlled region in the country. Sporadic protests, including self-immolations, by Tibetans calling for more autonomy and religious freedom have been cracked down on by the authorities.

International journalists cannot visit Tibet apart from on tightly choreographed government tours. Many Tibetans are not allowed passports and have very limited contact with the outside world. Tibetans can be punished for speaking to journalists. Human rights groups have for years criticised Beijing’s policies on Tibetan language and culture, which activists say are under attack.
As the Chinese government’s tight controls on information limit international coverage of its relief efforts, it continues to stress that the disaster is a national priority.

China’s leader, Xi Jinping, chaired a meeting on Friday to direct rescue work, according to state media, in which he called on the authorities to “make every effort to search for missing people from China and abroad”.

He also dispatched his number two, premier Li Qiang, to visit the affected area. According to the state-run Xinhua news agency, Li “emphasised that General Secretary Xi Jinping is deeply concerned about the people in the disaster-stricken areas”.
'Now I have nothing left to live for,' survivors grieve relatives and homes swept away in Nepal flooding
Hannah Ellis-Petersen and Gaurav Pokharel in Bidur, Nepal.

Sangke Dolma Tamang, 61, had been cheerily cooking snacks in her village of Mailung in the Rasuwa district when the floods came without warning. The whole family ran uphill for safety, but as she grabbed for her husband, he slipped from her grip and was washed into the dark, fast-moving waters.

“Others tried to pull him to safety, but the flood swept him away,” she said, tears rolling down her weathered cheeks. There was, she said, nothing left of her village now. She had spent a night sheltering on higher ground, until an army helicopter arrived and brought to her safety at the barracks. Her son too was missing since the disaster, and she waited anxiously for any news.
“Now I have nothing left to live for,” said Tamang. “The whole house is gone. We couldn’t salvage anything.”

blocks.caption: Sangke Dolma Tamang (in red), 61, grieves her family and home in the aftermath of the deadly flooding in Nepal. Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The Guardian

blocks.text: As a melting glacier high up in the Himalayas between Tibet and Nepal splintered and crashed into the valley below, it set off a deadly cascade of water, mud and debris down the Bhote Koshi River. The Nepali village homes that lined the riverbank and clung to the mountainside stood little chance.

Two days after the disaster, at least 579 people have been confirmed dead and more than 1,900 are still missing, the numbers rising by the day. Many in Nepal fear that the true scale of the disaster has yet to emerge, as the worst-hit areas in districts such as Rusawa are only accessible by helicopter. The situation remains even more opaque in Tibet, which is under tight Chinese media control. Though it was at the centre of the disaster, Chinese authorities insist only five people there have died.

In the army barracks in the town of Bidur, where Nepal’s rescue efforts were being coordinated, helicopters carrying those rescued from flooded areas continued to arrive every few minutes, while others carrying vital supplies of food and clean water flew out and high up into the mountains.

blocks.caption: Flood victims evacuate to Nepal army camp - loop

blocks.text: On Friday morning, ground rescue efforts were halted over fears that the river levels were rising once again. But the Nepali army spokesperson, Brig Gen Raja Ram Basnet, said the helicopter rescues would continue for as long as people were missing. He accepted that the death toll was hard to calculate. “Right now, our focus is mostly on finding the living,” he said.

Among those recently brought to safety was 60-year-old Murali Maiya Tamang, who had been in Rusawa and was found hanging in a tree. As the flash floods came down the valley, she had watched as her house was washed clean away. She convulsed with tears as she waited desperately for news of her son, who was in their village when the floods struck and has been missing since.
“My husband had already died in Nepal’s 2015 earthquake,” she said. “Now this flood has taken away the only son I had left. I am all alone now. What is the point of living now?”
You can read the full piece, with photographs and video by Ahmer Khan, here:
Here are some images coming through on the news wires of residents salvaging their belongings after the deadly flash flooding in Nepal.

blocks.caption: Residents salvage their belongings from damaged houses after flash flooding in the Devighat area of Nuwakot district in Nepal today.  Photograph: Rajesh Kumar Singh/AP
A woman carries a bag and suitcase of her belongings after her house was heavily covered in mud.  Photograph: Manan Vatsyayana/AFP/Getty Images
Residents salvage belongings from their destroyed home.  Photograph: Ezra Acayan/Getty Images

blocks.text: Footage shows glacier collapse that led to deadly flooding in Nepal – video

This drone video shared with the Guardian shows the moment of glacier collapse that led to the devastating flash flooding in Nepal. The numbers of people missing, killed or injured are feared to continue to rise as rescue efforts are under way.
The UK has deployed a rapid response team of specially trained volunteers to Nepal to help with the disaster there.
The foreign secretary Ed Miliband said: “The scenes from Nepal are devastating, and our thoughts remain with everyone affected.

“The safety and welfare of British nationals is our top priority. That is why we are deploying a Rapid Deployment Team to Nepal to provide additional support on the ground for British nationals and their families at what is an incredibly difficult time.
“Our staff are working closely with the Nepali authorities, emergency responders and our embassy in Kathmandu to ensure those affected can access the assistance and information they need.
“We will continue to do everything we can to support British nationals impacted by this tragedy.”
British nationals in Nepal who require consular assistance should contact the British Embassy in Kathmandu or call the FCDO on +44 (0)20 7008 5000.
Death toll in China rises to seven
The death toll has risen to seven and 554 remain missing after the mudslide at a border port in China’s Xizang region, according to local reports.

articles.title: Somali piracy surges as the impact of the US-Iran war ripples outwards
articles.summary: Two ships were seized within four days last week raising to at least 13 the number attacked since January.

blocks.text: A surge in piracy near Somalia has increased threats to shipping already under pressure from maritime blockades and conflict due to the US war with Iran.

Two cargo vessels were seized in the Gulf of Aden within four days last week, rising to at least 13 the number of ships attacked since the start of the year and triggering unprecedented drone strikes against the pirates.
It is the biggest escalation in hijackings in more than a decade, renewing concern about security in this region vital to international trade.
"Piracy is always a crime of opportunity," says Omar Mahmood, a senior Somalia analyst for the International Crisis Group (ICG), "and right now the pirates see an opportunity."
That opportunity comes from the impact of the war on regional waterways further north.
Iran and the US continue to battle over control of the strategic Strait of Hormuz.

And Tehran's Houthi allies in Yemen have imposed a targeted blockade in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which controls access to the Red Sea. This is focused on a dispute with Saudi Arabia but heightens insecurity for international shipping.

"I guess the pirates believe that with those two external events in Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab, they believe that the international forces will be dedicated to those crises instead of looking for pirates," says Vice-Admiral Ignacio Villanueva Serrano, operation commander for the European Union's naval force that protects shipping off Somalia's coast.

Among the latest vessels hijacked by the pirates was a Cameroon-flagged ship, the MV Lutuf, which was attacked off the coast of Somalia's semi-autonomous Puntland region on 17 August. A few days later pirates boarded an oil products tanker, the Eritrean-flagged MT Sibu 1, in waters near Yemen, on the other side of the Gulf.
The capture of the Lutuf has triggered unexpected consequences.

Thirteen men allegedly belonging to a network that supplies the pirates on the ship have been killed in two drone strikes since 18 August. No one has said they are behind the attacks, but local officials blamed them on Turkey, saying the vessel was carrying Turkish weapons.

The Lutuf is now among six vessels being held for demands of millions of dollars in ransom, four of which are anchored near the fishing town of Bander Beyla known as a hotbed for piracy, the BBC has learned.

That is nowhere near the peak levels of hijackings 15 years ago that cost the global economy billions of dollars. In 2011 Somali pirates carried out more than 200 attacks and held hundreds of crew members hostage.
A co-ordinated international naval response together with private security on commercial ships successfully drove down the scourge and contained a flare-up in 2023 and 2024.
But experts stress that while the pirate networks were suppressed, they remained intact, given the failure to address the poor economic and security conditions in Somalia that feed them.
Currently the resurgence is fuelled locally by anger over foreign trawlers which overfish in Somali waters, damaging the fishing industry that sustains communities in Puntland.
And there are more targets available now with a potentially bigger payload.

The regional maritime insecurity has driven some ships closer to the Somali coast as they divert south to avoid the conflict further north. Given the high price of oil, hijacking a tanker is more lucrative.
"You have that combined effect of less naval patrolling but more commercial shipping in these waters," according to the analyst Mahmood, "and that signals an opportunity.
"And once you've had a successful attack, I think that spurs other units to do copycat type incidents as well."
He and other researchers suspect there may be collaboration between the Somali pirates and Yemenis after several vessels were seized near Yemen's coast.

But Mahmood says these would more likely be criminal elements than Iran's Houthi allies, especially as one of the ships seized last week, the MT Sibu 1, allegedly belonged to an Iranian "shadow fleet" used to transport petroleum products trying to dodge US sanctions.
"I don't see something specifically Iran-directed," he says.
Turkey, however, reportedly has a stake in the latest hijackings.

Puntland security sources and a Somali government official have told the BBC that the Lutuf was carrying weapons bound for a Turkish military training facility in the Somali capital, Mogadishu. Ankara has an agreement with Somalia to strengthen its maritime security, as part of a wider defence and economic partnership.

The security sources say six international warships are now in the seas close to the Lutuf - two from Turkey and one each from Spain, Denmark, the US and India, something the BBC has not been able to independently verify.
